By @thm-dimension-formula-subspace-dim, \dim(U^{0} + W^{0}) = n - 0 = n = \dim V^{*}, so U^{0} + W^{0} = V^{*} (@thm-dim-impl-eq), and the sum is direct because the intersection is \{0\}. (b) The restriction of ho to W^{0} is linear. Its kernel is W^{0} \cap \kerho = W^{0} \cap U^{0} = \{0\} by @thm-dual-of-subspace and (a), so it is injective. Its domain has dimension n - \dim W = \dim U = \dim U^{*}. An injective linear map between spaces of the same finite dimension is an isomorphism (@cor-rank-nullity-consequences (e)). (c) Write functionals on 
R^2 as ax + by. W_1^{0} consists of those with b = 0, so W_1^{0} = \Span(x). W_2^{0} consists of those with a + b = 0, so W_2^{0} = \Span(x - y). Restricting to U: x|_U and (x - y)|_U both take the value 1 at \e_1, so both equal \xi. The elements x and x - y are different, so the subspaces W_1^{0} 
e W_2^{0} of V^{*} are two different copies of U^{*}, one for each complement.

title: 4.6 Hyperplanes and Linear Systems Revisited
content:
Hyperplanes and Linear Systems Revisited Chapter 2 met subspaces of F^n in two disguises. A parametric description lists spanning vectors, as in \col(\A). An implicit description lists equations, as in 
ul(\A). We moved from equations to spanning vectors by elimination, but we never asked whether the reverse is always possible, or how many equations it takes. Duality answers both questions at once: the equations of a subspace U are the elements of U^{0}. This section turns that sentence into an algorithm, proves once more that row rank and nullity add up to n, and ends the chapter with a dictionary between a space and its dual. Row vectors are functionals Recall from @thm-functionals-on-fn how functionals on F^n look. For \a = (a_1, \dots, a_n) \in F^n, put \varphi_{\a} \colon F^n 	o F, \qquad \varphi_{\a}(\x) = \a	p\x = a_1x_1 + \dots + a_nx_n . By that theorem, every \varphi \in (F^n)^{*} is \varphi_{\a} for exactly one \a, namely a_j = \varphi(\e_j), and \a \mapsto \varphi_{\a} is an isomorphism F^n 	o (F^n)^{*}. The functional \varphi_{\a} is “multiply by the row vector \a	p”. So the identification is really between functionals and row vectors, and that is what makes a system of equations a dual object. Write the rows of \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) as \a_1	p, \dots, \a_m	p with \a_i \in F^n. The i-th entry of \A\x is \a_i	p\x = \varphi_{\a_i}(\x), so the homogeneous system \A\x = \0 says exactly that \varphi_{\a_1}(\x) = \dots = \varphi_{\a_m}(\x) = 0. Hence 
ul(\A) = \ker\varphi_{\a_1} \cap \dots \cap \ker\varphi_{\a_m} . Each non-zero row contributes a hyperplane (@thm-hyperplane-kernel-functional), and the null space is their intersection. An equation is a functional, and a system is a list of functionals. The identification uses the standard basis of F^n, and nothing else. Under it, the coordinate functionals \x \mapsto x_i, which form the dual basis of (\e_1, \dots, \e_n), correspond to \e_1, \dots, \e_n, that is, to the rows \e_1	p, \dots, \e_n	p. Every subspace is a solution set To describe U by equations, we need equations that hold on U, that is, functionals in U^{0}, and enough of them that they hold only on U. The first requirement is the definition of U^{0}. The second follows from the separation of points, applied in the quotient. [A subspace is cut out by its annihilator] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space and U a subspace. For \v \in V, \v \in U \quad \iff \quad \varphi(\v) = 0 	ext{ for every } \varphi \in U^{0} . If (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k) is a basis of U^{0}, then U = \ker\varphi_1 \cap \dots \cap \ker\varphi_k. (\Rightarrow) This is @def-annihilator. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \v 
otin U. Then \v + U is a non-zero vector of V/U by @lem-coset-equality (b), and V/U is finite-dimensional (@thm-dimension-quotient). By @thm-functionals-separate-points there is \psi \in (V/U)^{*} with \psi(\v + U) 
e 0. By @thm-dual-of-quotient, \varphi = \psi \circ \pi lies in U^{0}, and \varphi(\v) = \psi(\v + U) 
e 0. This proves the contrapositive. For the last statement, U \subseteq \ker\varphi_i for each i since \varphi_i \in U^{0}. Conversely, if \varphi_i(\v) = 0 for all i, then every \varphi = \sum_i c_i\varphi_i \in U^{0} has \varphi(\v) = 0, so \v \in U by (\Leftarrow). The lemma is @cor-annihilator-of-annihilator in disguise. That corollary says U^{00} = U under V \cong V^{**}; the lemma unpacks it into a statement about vectors. In F^n, with rows in place of functionals, it becomes the main theorem of this section. Every Subspace Is a Solution Set Let U be a subspace of F^n with \dim U = k. 1. There is a matrix \A \in M_{(n-k) 	imes n}(F) with U = 
ul(\A). One may take as rows of \A the vectors \a_1	p, \dots, \a_{n-k}	p for any \a_i \in F^n such that (\varphi_{\a_1}, \dots, \varphi_{\a_{n-k}}) is a basis of U^{0}. 2. If \B \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and 
ul(\B) = U, then m \ge n - k. So U is the solution set of a homogeneous system of exactly n - k = \codim U equations, and of no system with fewer. (When k = n, that is U = F^n, this is the empty system, with no equations.) (a) By @thm-dimension-annihilator, \dim U^{0} = n - k. Choose a basis of U^{0}; by the identification above it is (\varphi_{\a_1}, \dots, \varphi_{\a_{n-k}}) for some \a_i \in F^n. Let \A have rows \a_1	p, \dots, \a_{n-k}	p. Then 
ul(\A) = \ker\varphi_{\a_1} \cap \dots \cap \ker\varphi_{\a_{n-k}} = U, where the second equality is @lem-subspace-cut-out-by-annihilator. (b) By @thm-rank-nullity-matrix, ank \B = n - 
ullity \B = n - k. By @thm-row-rank-equals-column-rank, ank \B = \dim ow(\B). The row space is spanned by the m rows of \B, so m \ge \dimow(\B) by @thm-size-bounds (b). Hence m \ge n - k. The count is the one promised by codimension: dimension counts free parameters, codimension counts independent equations, and in F^n the two add up to n. [Equations for a plane in 
R^4] Let U = \Span(\u_1, \u_2) \subseteq 
R^4, where \u_1 = (1, 1, 0, 1) and \u_2 = (0, 1, 1, 1). Find a system of linear equations whose solution set is U. The two vectors are independent (compare first entries, then third), so \dim U = 2, and we expect 4 - 2 = 2 equations. For \a = (a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4), the functional \varphi_{\a} lies in U^{0} exactly when it vanishes at both spanning vectors (@thm-annihilator-properties (b)): a_1 + a_2 + a_4 = 0, \qquad a_2 + a_3 + a_4 = 0 . This is the system \M\a = \0 for the matrix \M whose rows are \u_1	p and \u_2	p. Subtracting the second row from the first gives the RREF \M =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \ \longrightarrow\  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, with free variables a_3, a_4. By @thm-basis-null-space, a basis of the solutions is (1, -1, 1, 0) (from a_3 = 1, a_4 = 0) and (0, -1, 0, 1) (from a_3 = 0, a_4 = 1). The corresponding functionals form a basis of U^{0}, and by @thm-subspace-is-solution-set, U = \{ \x \in 
R^4 : x_1 - x_2 + x_3 = 0, \ \ x_4 - x_2 = 0 \} . Check. Both equations hold at \u_1: 1 - 1 + 0 = 0 and 1 - 1 = 0; and at \u_2: 0 - 1 + 1 = 0 and 1 - 1 = 0. The coefficient matrix  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} has rank 2, so its null space has dimension 4 - 2 = 2, and it contains the independent vectors \u_1, \u_2; hence it equals U (@thm-dim-impl-eq). The implicit description says: U consists of the vectors with x_4 = x_2 and x_1 + x_3 = x_2. From spans to equations and back The example is an instance of a general procedure. Both directions of the conversion are “compute a null space”, applied to transposed data. Parametric to implicit. Input: vectors \v_1, \dots, \v_p \in F^n with U = \Span(\v_1, \dots, \v_p). 1. Form \M \in M_{p 	imes n}(F) whose i-th row is \v_i	p. 2. Row reduce \M and find a basis 
_1, \dots, 
_d of 
ul(\M) as in @thm-basis-null-space. 3. Output the matrix \A \in M_{d 	imes n}(F) whose j-th row is 
_j	p, that is, the equations 
_j	p\x = 0 for j = 1, \dots, d. Implicit to parametric. Input: \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). Output: a basis of 
ul(\A), found by row reduction as in @thm-basis-null-space. The second half was proved correct in Chapter 2. The first half is new. [Correctness of the Conversion] Let \v_1, \dots, \v_p \in F^n, U = \Span(\v_1, \dots, \v_p), and let \M and \A be as in the algorithm. Then 
ul(\A) = U, and \A has exactly d = n - \dim U rows, which are linearly independent. The only thing to see is what step 2 computes. The i-th entry of \M
 is \v_i	p
 = \varphi_{
}(\v_i). So 
 \in 
ul(\M) says that the functional \varphi_{
} vanishes at every \v_i, that is, \varphi_{
} \in U^{0}. Step 2 therefore computes a basis of U^{0}, and the theorem of the previous subsection does the rest. For 
 \in F^n, the i-th entry of \M
 is \v_i	p
 = 
	p\v_i = \varphi_{
}(\v_i), where the middle equality holds because both sides equal \sum_j (\v_i)_j n_j. Hence 
 \in 
ul(\M) \iff \varphi_{
}(\v_i) = 0 	ext{ for all } i \iff \varphi_{
} \in \{\v_1, \dots, \v_p\}^{0} = U^{0}, where the last equality is @thm-annihilator-properties (b). So the isomorphism 
 \mapsto \varphi_{
} maps 
ul(\M) onto U^{0}. An isomorphism carries a basis to a basis (@thm-isomorphism-preserves-bases), so (\varphi_{
_1}, \dots, \varphi_{
_d}) is a basis of U^{0}. In particular d = \dim U^{0} = n - \dim U by @thm-dimension-annihilator, and the 
_j, hence the rows 
_j	p, are independent. By @thm-subspace-is-solution-set (a), the matrix \A with rows 
_1	p, \dots, 
_d	p satisfies 
ul(\A) = U. The algorithm does not need the \v_i to be independent. Redundant spanning vectors only produce zero rows in the RREF of \M, and the count d = n - ank \M automatically uses \dim U = ank \M. Running both halves in turn is a useful self-check. Starting from \A in @exm-implicit-equations and computing 
ul(\A) must return a basis of U; starting from that basis and running the first half must return equations with the same solution set, though not necessarily the same equations. Equations for a subspace are far from unique, and more equations do not mean a smaller solution set. In @exm-implicit-equations, the system x_1 - x_2 + x_3 = 0, x_4 - x_2 = 0, x_1 + x_3 - x_4 = 0 has the same solution set U: the third equation is the sum of the first and the negative of the second, so it adds a functional already in U^{0}. Three equations in 
R^4 cut out a two-dimensional subspace here, not a one-dimensional one. Each new equation lowers the dimension by one only if its functional is not a combination of the previous ones. A theorem later in this section makes this precise. Affine solution sets An inhomogeneous equation \a	p\x = b with \a 
e \0 defines a set that is not a subspace when b 
e 0. It is a translate of the hyperplane H = \ker\varphi_{\a}: if \p is one solution, then by @thm-general-solution-structure the solutions are \p + H. We call a coset \p + H of a hyperplane H (@def-coset) an affine hyperplane. In 
R^3, the plane x + y + z = 1 is an affine hyperplane, parallel to the hyperplane x + y + z = 0. A system \A\x =   with rows \a_i	p and right-hand sides b_i asks for the vectors lying on all the sets \{ \x : \a_i	p\x = b_i \} at once. Each such set is an affine hyperplane if \a_i 
e \0; if \a_i = \0, it is all of F^n (when b_i = 0) or empty (when b_i 
e 0). So the solution set of a linear system is an intersection of affine hyperplanes, apart from these trivial rows. The duality theorems give the converse. [Cosets as intersections of affine hyperplanes] Let U be a subspace of F^n of dimension k < n, and let \p \in F^n. Let \A \in M_{(n-k) 	imes n}(F) be as in @thm-subspace-is-solution-set (a), with rows \a_1	p, \dots, \a_{n-k}	p. Then \p + U = \{ \x \in F^n : \A\x = \A\p \} =  igcap_{i=1}^{n-k} \{ \x : \a_i	p\x = \a_i	p\p \}, an intersection of n - k affine hyperplanes. By @thm-subspace-is-solution-set, 
ul(\A) = U. The vector \p is one solution of \A\x = \A\p, so by @thm-general-solution-structure its solution set is \p + 
ul(\A) = \p + U. The i-th equation reads \a_i	p\x = \a_i	p\p. Each \varphi_{\a_i} is non-zero, because it belongs to a basis of U^{0}; so \ker\varphi_{\a_i} is a hyperplane (@thm-hyperplane-kernel-functional), and \{ \x : \a_i	p\x = \a_i	p\p \} = \p + \ker\varphi_{\a_i} is an affine hyperplane, again by @thm-general-solution-structure applied to this one equation. Unlike hyperplanes, which all contain \0, affine hyperplanes can be disjoint: x_1 + x_2 = 0 and x_1 + x_2 = 1 are parallel lines in 
R^2. That is the geometric picture of an inconsistent system. The row space annihilates the null space In Chapter 2, @thm-rank-nullity-matrix said ank \A + 
ullity \A = n, and its proof counted pivot and free columns in the RREF. The duality of this chapter explains the same equation without elimination: the rows of \A are exactly the equations satisfied by the null space. [The Row Space Is the Annihilator of the Null Space] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F). Identifying a row vector \a	p \in M_{1 	imes n}(F) with the functional \varphi_{\a} \in (F^n)^{*}, \{ \varphi_{\a} : \a	p \in ow(\A) \} = 
ul(\A)^{0} . Consequently \dim ow(\A) + \dim 
ul(\A) = n. Let T = T_{\A} \colon F^n 	o F^m. Its kernel is 
ul(\A), and @thm-kernel-image-dual-map says \im T' = (\ker T)^{0}. So it is enough to see that \im T' is the row space. Pull back a functional \varphi_{\y} on F^m: the result is \x \mapsto \y	p \A\x, which is multiplication by the row \y	p \A, the combination of the rows of \A with coefficients y_1, \dots, y_m. The transpose of Chapter 0 appears exactly here: \y	p \A = (\A	p\y)	p. Let T = T_{\A} \colon F^n 	o F^m, T(\x) = \A\x, so that \ker T = 
ul(\A). Every functional on F^m is \varphi_{\y} for a unique \y \in F^m, as recalled at the start of this section. By @def-dual-map, associativity of matrix multiplication, and @thm-transpose-properties,  egin{aligned} T'(\varphi_{\y})(\x) &= \varphi_{\y}(\A\x) = \y	p(\A\x) = (\y	p \A)\x \ &= (\A	p\y)	p\x = \varphi_{\A	p\y}(\x) \qquad (\x \in F^n), \end{aligned} so T'(\varphi_{\y}) = \varphi_{\A	p\y}. The columns of \A	p are \a_1, \dots, \a_m, where \a_i	p are the rows of \A, so \A	p\y = y_1\a_1 + \dots + y_m\a_m by @thm-matrix-times-vector-columns. As \y runs over F^m, these are all the combinations of \a_1, \dots, \a_m, and since transposing respects combinations (@thm-transpose-properties), they are exactly the vectors \a with \a	p \in ow(\A) (@def-row-space). Hence \im T' = \{ \varphi_{\a} : \a	p \in ow(\A) \} . By @thm-kernel-image-dual-map, \im T' = (\ker T)^{0} = 
ul(\A)^{0}, which is the first claim. For the count, \a	p \mapsto \varphi_{\a} is an isomorphism M_{1 	imes n}(F) 	o (F^n)^{*} (transposition followed by \a \mapsto \varphi_{\a}), so \dim ow(\A) = \dim 
ul(\A)^{0} = n - \dim
ul(\A) by @thm-dimension-annihilator. The count is Rank–Nullity for matrices once more, now as a statement about annihilators: ank \A = \dimow(\A) counts independent equations and 
ullity \A counts free parameters. It also says that the given equations generate all the equations satisfied by 
ul(\A): any linear equation that holds on the solution set of \A\x = \0 is a combination of the rows of \A. [Same solutions, same row space] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F) and \B \in M_{p 	imes n}(F). Then 
ul(\A) = 
ul(\B) if and only if ow(\A) = ow(\B). (\Leftarrow) If ow(\A) = ow(\B), then 
ul(\A)^{0} = 
ul(\B)^{0} by @thm-row-space-annihilates-null-space, so 
ul(\A) = 
ul(\B) by @cor-subspaces-determined-by-annihilator. (\Rightarrow) If 
ul(\A) = 
ul(\B), then \{ \varphi_{\a} : \a	p \in ow(\A) \} = 
ul(\A)^{0} = \{ \varphi_{\a} : \a	p \in ow(\B) \} by @thm-row-space-annihilates-null-space. Since \a	p \mapsto \varphi_{\a} is injective, ow(\A) = ow(\B). Chapter 2 showed that row operations preserve the null space (@thm-row-ops-row-space). The corollary gives a converse in terms of row spaces: two systems in the same unknowns have the same solutions exactly when each equation of one is a combination of the equations of the other. Sums and intersections by duality Parametric and implicit descriptions are good at different things. A sum is easy parametrically: U + W is spanned by a spanning list of U followed by one of W (@prp-sum-of-spans). An intersection is easy implicitly: if U = 
ul(\A) and W = 
ul(\B), then \x \in U \cap W exactly when \x satisfies both systems, so U \cap W = 
ul  egin{pmatrix} \A \ \B \end{pmatrix}, the null space of the matrix with the rows of \A above the rows of \B. Duality explains why each is easy where it is. The rows of the stacked matrix span ow(\A) + ow(\B), which corresponds to U^{0} + W^{0} = (U \cap W)^{0} by @thm-row-space-annihilates-null-space and @thm-annihilator-properties (d); and (U + W)^{0} = U^{0} \cap W^{0} says that the equations of a sum are the equations common to both pieces. [An intersection computed from equations] In 
R^4, let U = \Span((1, 0, 1, 2), (0, 1, 1, 1)) and W = \Span((1, 1, 0, 1), (1, 3, 0, 1)), as in @exm-intersection-by-elimination. Find U \cap W by first finding equations for U and for W. Equations for U. A row (a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4) annihilates both spanning vectors when a_1 + a_3 + 2a_4 = 0 and a_2 + a_3 + a_4 = 0. This system is already in RREF, with free a_3, a_4; the basic solutions are (-1, -1, 1, 0) and (-2, -1, 0, 1). Changing signs, which does not change the kernels, U = \{ x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 0, \ \ 2x_1 + x_2 - x_4 = 0 \} . Equations for W. Here a_1 + a_2 + a_4 = 0 and a_1 + 3a_2 + a_4 = 0. Subtracting gives a_2 = 0, and then a_1 = -a_4, with a_3 free. The basic solutions are (0, 0, 1, 0) and (-1, 0, 0, 1), so W = \{ x_3 = 0, \ \ x_4 - x_1 = 0 \} . Intersection. Stack the four equations. From W: x_3 = 0 and x_4 = x_1. Then x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 0 gives x_2 = -x_1, and the last equation 2x_1 + x_2 - x_4 = 2x_1 - x_1 - x_1 = 0 holds automatically. So U \cap W = \{ (t, -t, 0, t) : t \in 
R \} = \Span((1, -1, 0, 1)), in agreement with Chapter 2. The redundancy of the fourth equation is not a coincidence. The four rows span U^{0} + W^{0} = (U \cap W)^{0}, which has dimension 4 - 1 = 3, so exactly one of the four equations must be a consequence of the others. Contrast with Chapter 2. There we put the four spanning vectors as columns of one matrix and read the intersection off a null vector, a relation \u_1 - \u_2 = 2\w_1 - \w_2. Here we computed two small null spaces (the equations) and then one more (the intersection). The equation method pays off when the subspaces are given by equations in the first place, or when several intersections with the same U are needed: the equations of U are computed once. Independent functionals The warning above said that k equations cut out codimension k only when they are independent. We now make that precise, in any dimension. Given \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k \in V^{*}, bundle them into one linear map \Phi \colon V 	o F^k, \qquad \Phi(\v) = (\varphi_1(\v), \dots, \varphi_k(\v)), which is linear because each entry is. Its kernel is \ker\varphi_1 \cap \dots \cap \ker\varphi_k, the common solution set of the k equations. Independent Functionals Let V be a vector space over F, of any dimension, and let \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k \in V^{*}. The following are equivalent: 1. (\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_k) is linearly independent in V^{*}; 2. \Phi \colon V 	o F^k is surjective; 3. \ker\varphi_1 \cap \dots \cap \ker\varphi_k has codimension exactly k. A dependence \sum c_i\varphi_i = 0 says that \sum c_iy_i = 0 for every \y = \Phi(\v) in the image: the image lies in the kernel of a non-zero functional on F^k. Conversely, if the image is a proper subspace of F^k, some non-zero functional on F^k kills it, and its coefficients give a dependence. The First Isomorphism Theorem turns “surjective” into “codimension k”. (a) \Rightarrow (b). Suppose \Phi is not surjective. Then \im\Phi is a proper subspace of F^k, so \dim\im\Phi < k and, by @thm-dimension-annihilator, (\im\Phi)^{0} 
e \{0\}. Take a non-zero functional in it; as at the start of this section it is \varphi_{\c}, \y \mapsto c_1y_1 + \dots + c_ky_k, for a non-zero \c \in F^k. For every \v \in V, \Phi(\v) \in \im\Phi, so (c_1\varphi_1 + \dots + c_k\varphi_k)(\v) = \varphi_{\c}(\Phi(\v)) = 0 . Thus c_1\varphi_1 + \dots + c_k\varphi_k = 0 with \c 
e \0, and the list is dependent. This proves the contrapositive. (b) \Rightarrow (a). Suppose \Phi is surjective and c_1\varphi_1 + \dots + c_k\varphi_k = 0. For each j, choose \v_j with \Phi(\v_j) = \e_j, that is, \varphi_i(\v_j) = \delta_{ij}. Evaluating the relation at \v_j gives c_j = 0. So the list is independent. (c) \Leftrightarrow (c). By @thm-first-isomorphism, V/\ker\Phi \cong \im\Phi, and \ker\Phi =  igcap_i \ker\varphi_i. So the codimension of  igcap_i\ker\varphi_i is \dim\im\Phi, which equals k exactly when \im\Phi = F^k (@thm-dim-impl-eq). For V = F^n and \varphi_i = \varphi_{\a_i}, the map \Phi is T_{\A}, where \A has rows \a_i	p. The theorem then says: the rows of \A are independent if and only if \A\x =   is solvable for every   \in F^k. Independent equations never contradict each other. In 
R^3, consider \varphi_1 = x + y, \varphi_2 = y + z, \varphi_3 = x - z. What is the codimension of \ker\varphi_1 \cap \ker\varphi_2 \cap \ker\varphi_3? Is the system x + y = 1, y + z = 1, x - z = 1 solvable? \varphi_3 = \varphi_1 - \varphi_2, so the list is dependent, while (\varphi_1, \varphi_2) is independent (look at the coefficients of x and z). The three kernels intersect in \ker\varphi_1 \cap \ker\varphi_2, of codimension 2 by @thm-independent-functionals-surjective, so the intersection is a line, not \{\0\}. The system is not solvable: any solution would give 1 = x - z = (x + y) - (y + z) = 1 - 1 = 0. This is (b) failing: (1, 1, 1) 
otin \im\Phi. Summary and transfer The chapter has built a dictionary. On the left is a finite-dimensional space V of dimension n, or a linear map T \colon V 	o W between finite-dimensional spaces; on the right is its mirror image in the dual. title: Polynomials
content: Polynomials Integers and polynomials share one arithmetic. Both can be divided with a remainder, and from that single tool everything else follows: greatest common divisors, Bézout identities, unique factorization into primes or irreducibles, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. This chapter develops that arithmetic for F[x] in full, because from Chapter 8 on the structure of an operator is read off from polynomials: which polynomials kill it, how they factor, and which of their factors are coprime. Along the way we keep two promises made in Chapter 0: we prove division with remainder, stated there only for orientation, and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, that every non-constant complex polynomial has a root. We also prove that polynomials factor uniquely into irreducibles, just as integers factor uniquely into primes. The chapter ends by plugging an operator into a polynomial, where the arithmetic of F[x] turns into a splitting of the space into pieces. What you need. From Chapter 0, induction and well-ordering (@thm-strong-induction, @thm-well-ordering), divisibility of integers and Bézout’s lemma (@def-divisibility-prime, @lem-bezout-integers), the fields \nF_p (@thm-zp-field-iff-prime), polynomials, degree and evaluation (@def-polynomial, @def-degree, @thm-degree-of-product, @thm-evaluation-respects-operations) and complex numbers (@thm-de-moivre). From Chapter 2, the factor theorem and root bound for linear factors (@lem-factor-theorem-linear, @lem-root-bound) and interpolation (@thm-interpolation-unique). From Chapter 3, polynomials of an operator (@def-polynomial-of-operator), quotient spaces and the First Isomorphism Theorem (@def-quotient-space, @thm-first-isomorphism). From Chapter 4, dual bases (@thm-dual-basis). Roadmap - Division with remainder. Long division always works over a field, with a unique quotient and remainder; the remainder and factor theorems in general. - Ideals and greatest common divisors. Every ideal of F[x] is generated by one polynomial; gcds, Bézout identities and the Euclidean algorithm. - Irreducible polynomials and unique factorization. The primes of F[x], and why factorization into them is unique. - Roots, multiplicity and derivatives. Repeated roots detected by the formal derivative, and Taylor expansion of a polynomial. - The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. A complete proof, and what it says about real polynomials. - Interpolation and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. The Lagrange formula, solving simultaneous congruences, and the quotient-space picture behind both. - Polynomials of an operator. Every operator on a finite-dimensional space satisfies a polynomial, and coprime factors split the space. Named moves - Divide and look at the remainder. Most statements about divisibility reduce to one division. - The smallest-degree element generates. In an ideal, a non-zero element of least degree divides every other element. - Evaluate at a root. Plugging a root of the divisor into f = qg + r kills qg and reads off information about the remainder. - Compare degrees. Uniqueness of quotients, factorizations and interpolants usually comes from a degree count. - Bézout gives projections. When \gcd(p, q) = 1, write 1 = ap + bq; evaluated at an operator, the two terms split the space.

title: 5.1 Division with Remainder
content:
Division with Remainder Integers can be divided with a remainder: 17 = 3 \cdot 5 + 2, and the remainder 2 is smaller than the divisor 5. Polynomials over a field can be divided in the same way, with “smaller” measured by degree. Chapter 0 stated this fact without proof, and Chapter 2 proved the special case of dividing by x - c. This section proves division with remainder in general, over any field, and draws the first consequences: the language of divisibility, the Remainder and Factor Theorems for every divisor x - c, a sharper root bound, and the fact that over an infinite field a polynomial is determined by its values. Throughout, F is a field unless we say otherwise, and it matters: the warning in the second subsection shows division failing when the coefficients only form 
Z. Long division by hand At school one divides x^4 + 2x^3 - x + 3 by x^2 + x - 1 with a layout that imitates long division of numbers. Let us do it in words, so that we can see what each step does. Write f = x^4 + 2x^3 - x + 3 and g = x^2 + x - 1, in 
Q[x]. 1. The leading term of f is x^4, and the leading term of g is x^2. The quotient x^4 / x^2 = x^2 is the first term of the answer. Subtract x^2 g = x^4 + x^3 - x^2: f - x^2 g = x^3 + x^2 - x + 3 . 2. The leading term is now x^3, and x^3 / x^2 = x. Subtract x g = x^3 + x^2 - x: f - x^2 g - x g = 3 . 3. What is left, 3, has degree 0, smaller than \deg g = 2. No multiple c\,x^k g with k \ge 0 can remove it without creating terms of degree at least 2. We stop. So f = (x^2 + x)\,g + 3: the quotient is x^2 + x and the remainder is 3. Expanding (x^2 + x)(x^2 + x - 1) = x^4 + 2x^3 - x confirms it. Two questions are hidden in this routine. Why does it always stop? Each step removes the current leading term, so the degree of what is left drops by at least one. Degrees are natural numbers, and a strictly decreasing sequence of natural numbers cannot go on forever. Why is the answer unique? Someone else might hope to find a different quotient and a different remainder of degree less than 2. We will see that they cannot, by comparing degrees. There is also a third, quieter question. In step 1 we divided the leading coefficient of the current polynomial by the leading coefficient of g. Here that coefficient was 1. In general it is some b 
eq 0, and we need b^{-1}. Over a field this always exists. That is exactly where the field enters. The Division Theorem The routine above works for every pair of polynomials with non-zero divisor. Here is the precise statement. [Polynomial Division with Remainder] Let F be a field, and let f, g \in F[x] with g 
eq 0. Then there exist unique polynomials q, r \in F[x] such that f = qg + r \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \deg r < \deg g . The polynomial q is the quotient and r is the remainder of f on division by g. Because \deg 0 = -\infty, the condition \deg r < \deg g allows r = 0, which is the case “g goes into f exactly”. Existence is the hand routine turned into an induction on \deg f. If \deg f < \deg g, there is nothing to do: q = 0, r = f. Otherwise subtract (a/b)\,x^{n-m} g, where a x^n and b x^m are the leading terms of f and g. This kills the leading term of f, so the induction hypothesis applies to what is left. Uniqueness is “take the difference”: if qg + r = q'g + r', then (q - q')g = r' - r. The right side has degree less than \deg g, while a non-zero multiple of g has degree at least \deg g. Let m = \deg g, which lies in 
N since g 
eq 0, and let b 
eq 0 be the leading coefficient of g. Existence. If f = 0, then q = 0 and r = 0 work. For non-zero f we prove, by strong induction on n \in 
N (@thm-strong-induction with n_0 = 0), the statement P(n): for every f \in F[x] with \deg f = n, there are q, r \in F[x] with f = qg + r and \deg r < m. Let n \in 
N, assume P(k) for all k < n, and let \deg f = n with leading coefficient a. Case 1: n < m. Take q = 0 and r = f. Then f = 0 \cdot g + f and \deg r = n < m. Case 2: n \ge m. Since F is a field and b 
eq 0, the inverse b^{-1} exists. Put f_1 = f - a b^{-1} x^{n - m} g . By @thm-degree-of-product, the polynomial a b^{-1} x^{n-m} g has degree (n - m) + m = n and leading coefficient a b^{-1} \cdot b = a. So the coefficient of x^n in f_1 is a - a = 0, and all coefficients of higher powers are 0 as well. Hence f_1 = 0 or \deg f_1 < n. If f_1 = 0, then f = a b^{-1} x^{n-m} g + 0, and we take q = a b^{-1} x^{n-m}, r = 0. Otherwise k = \deg f_1 < n, and the induction hypothesis P(k) gives q_1, r_1 with f_1 = q_1 g + r_1 and \deg r_1 < m. Then f = f_1 + a b^{-1} x^{n-m} g =  igl( a b^{-1} x^{n-m} + q_1  igr) g + r_1 , so q = a b^{-1} x^{n-m} + q_1 and r = r_1 work. This proves P(n), and by strong induction P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. Uniqueness. Suppose f = qg + r = q'g + r' with \deg r < m and \deg r' < m. Then (q - q')g = r' - r. By @thm-degree-of-sum, \deg(r' - r) \le \max(\deg r', \deg r) < m, since -r has the same degree as r. Suppose q 
eq q'. Then \deg(q - q') \ge 0, and @thm-degree-of-product gives \deg igl((q - q')g igr) = \deg(q - q') + m \ge m, a contradiction. Hence q = q'. Then r' - r = 0 \cdot g = 0, so r = r'. This proves the theorem. The field axioms did essential work in two places: the inverse b^{-1} in Case 2, and @thm-degree-of-product in the uniqueness step, which needs a product of non-zero coefficients to be non-zero. The proof is also an algorithm. Case 2, repeated, is the long division of the previous subsection, and the induction guarantees that it stops after at most \deg f - \deg g + 1 subtractions. The hypothesis “over a field” is not decoration. The leading coefficient of g must be invertible. Division with remainder fails over 
Z. Write 
Z[x] for the polynomials in 
Q[x] whose coefficients are all integers. Try to divide f = x^2 by g = 2x inside 
Z[x]: we want q, r \in 
Z[x] with x^2 = 2x \cdot q + r and \deg r < 1, so r is a constant. Comparing coefficients of x^2 gives 2 q_1 = 1, where q_1 is the coefficient of x in q. No integer q_1 satisfies this, so no such q, r exist. Over 
Q there is no problem: x^2 = 2x \cdot 	frac12 x + 0. The obstacle is precisely that 2 has no inverse in 
Z. Division by a divisor whose leading coefficient is invertible still works over 
Z, for example by a monic polynomial; see Exercise C1. Why must the inequality \deg r < \deg g be strict? Find two different pairs (q, r) with x^2 = q \cdot (x^2 + 1) + r and \deg r \le 2. Both x^2 = 1 \cdot (x^2 + 1) + (-1) and x^2 = 0 \cdot (x^2 + 1) + x^2 work, with remainders of degree 0 and 2. With \deg r \le \deg g allowed, uniqueness fails, because we may move one copy of g between qg and r. The strict inequality is exactly what rules this out: in the uniqueness proof, \deg(r' - r) < \deg g is the step that forces q = q'. Now a division in which the leading coefficient of the divisor is not 1, so fractions appear. [Long Division with a Non-Monic Divisor] In 
Q[x], divide f = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 + 4x - 1 by g = 2x^2 - x + 3 with remainder. We follow Case 2 of the proof, where b = 2 and b^{-1} = 	frac12. Step 1. The leading term of f is 2x^4, and 2x^4 / 2x^2 = x^2. Subtracting x^2 g = 2x^4 - x^3 + 3x^2 leaves f - x^2 g = -2x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 1 . Step 2. The leading term is -2x^3, and -2x^3 / 2x^2 = -x. Subtracting -x g = -2x^3 + x^2 - 3x leaves -3x^2 + 7x - 1 . Step 3. The leading term is -3x^2, and -3x^2 / 2x^2 = -	frac32. Subtracting -	frac32 g = -3x^2 + 	frac32 x - 	frac92 leaves  igl(7 - 	frac32 igr)x +  igl(-1 + 	frac92 igr) = 	frac{11}{2}x + 	frac72 . This has degree 1 < 2 = \deg g, so we stop. Hence 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 + 4x - 1 =  igl(x^2 - x - 	frac32 igr)(2x^2 - x + 3) + 	frac{11}{2}x + 	frac72 , with quotient q = x^2 - x - 	frac32 and remainder r = 	frac{11}{2}x + 	frac72. By the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division, any other correct method must produce the same q and r. Notice that the quotient has a non-integer coefficient although f and g have integer coefficients. This is the warning above in action: over 
Z this division would be impossible. Divisibility With integers, “3 divides 12” means that 12 is an integer multiple of 3 (@def-divisibility-prime), and it is the case “remainder zero” of integer division. Polynomials get the same word. The field is part of the meaning, so we put it in the definition. g divides f when f is a polynomial multiple of g, with the multiplier taken over the same field. [Divisibility, Associates] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. - We say g divides f over F, and write g \mid f, if there exists h \in F[x] with f = gh. Then g is a divisor (or factor) of f, and f is a multiple of g. We write g 
mid f if g does not divide f. - We say f and g are associates if f = cg for some non-zero constant c \in F. In words: g \mid f asks for a multiplier h in F[x], so the same pair can behave differently over different fields. Associates differ only by a non-zero scalar factor. Since c^{-1} exists, “associates” is symmetric: f = cg gives g = c^{-1} f. Examples, simplest first. - Degenerate cases. Every g divides 0, since 0 = g \cdot 0. On the other hand 0 \mid f only for f = 0, since 0 \cdot h = 0. Every non-zero constant c divides every f, since f = c \cdot (c^{-1} f). These cases matter: they say that non-zero constants are invisible to divisibility, just as \pm 1 are for integers. - In 
Q[x], x - 1 \mid x^2 - 1, since x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1). Also 2x - 2 \mid x^2 - 1, since x^2 - 1 = (2x - 2) \cdot 	frac12 (x + 1). The polynomials x - 1 and 2x - 2 are associates. - In 
F_2[x], x + 1 \mid x^2 + 1, since (x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1 = x^2 + 1 there. In 
Q[x], however, x + 1 
mid x^2 + 1, as the next paragraph shows. - In 
C[x], x - i \mid x^2 + 1 = (x - i)(x + i). For a non-example by minimal change, keep x^2 + 1 and x + 1 but move from 
F_2 to 
Q. Both are still polynomials, and division with remainder still applies. What fails is the clause “there exists h \in F[x]”. If x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)h with h \in 
Q[x], then evaluating at -1 (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) gives 2 = 0 \cdot h(-1) = 0, which is false in 
Q. Over 
F_2 the same computation reads 0 = 0, and there is no contradiction. Divisibility depends on where the multiplier may live. In 
Q[x], 2x + 2 \mid x + 1, because x + 1 = (2x + 2) \cdot 	frac12. If we insisted on integer coefficients, 2x + 2 would not divide x + 1: any integer multiple (2x + 2)h has all coefficients even. Over a field, a non-zero scalar factor never affects divisibility, so it is pointless to ask whether x - 1 or 3x - 3 is “the” factor of x^2 - 1. Why this definition? Because it makes “divides” the case of remainder zero, which is the link to division we need. The basic rules follow quickly. [Rules for Divisibility] Let F be a field and f, g, h \in F[x]. 1. If f \mid g and g \mid h, then f \mid h. 2. If h \mid f and h \mid g, then h \mid af + bg for all a, b \in F[x]. 3. If g \mid f and f 
eq 0, then \deg g \le \deg f. 4. f \mid g and g \mid f if and only if f and g are associates or both are 0. In particular, if f \mid g, g \mid f, and f, g are both monic, then f = g. 5. If g 
eq 0, then g \mid f if and only if the remainder of f on division by g is 0. (a) Write g = fu and h = gv with u, v \in F[x]. Then h = f(uv) by @thm-polynomial-ring-laws, so f \mid h. (b) Write f = hu and g = hv. Then af + bg = h(au + bv) by @thm-polynomial-ring-laws, so h \mid af + bg. (c) Write f = gu. Since f 
eq 0, both g and u are non-zero, so \deg u \ge 0. By @thm-degree-of-product, \deg f = \deg g + \deg u \ge \deg g. (d) (\Leftarrow) If f = cg with c 
eq 0, then g \mid f and g = c^{-1} f gives f \mid g. If f = g = 0, both divide each other. (\Rightarrow) Suppose g = fu and f = gv. If f = 0, then g = 0 \cdot u = 0, so both are 0. If f 
eq 0, then f = f(uv), so f(1 - uv) = 0, and @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors gives uv = 1. By @thm-degree-of-product, \deg u + \deg v = \deg 1 = 0 with both degrees in 
N, so u and v are non-zero constants. Hence f = vg with v 
eq 0, and f, g are associates. If both are monic, comparing leading coefficients in f = vg gives 1 = v \cdot 1, so f = g. (e) If the remainder is 0, then f = qg, so g \mid f. Conversely, if f = hg, then f = hg + 0 with \deg 0 = -\infty < \deg g. This is a division with remainder, so by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division, the remainder of f on division by g is 0. This proves the proposition. Part (d) is the polynomial form of a move we will use again and again: to show two monic polynomials are equal, show that each divides the other. It also gives each non-zero polynomial a canonical representative. If f 
eq 0 has leading coefficient a, then a^{-1} f is monic and an associate of f, and it is the only monic associate: two monic associates divide each other, so they are equal by (d). For example, the monic associate of 3x^2 - 6 in 
Q[x] is x^2 - 2. The greatest common divisor in the next section will be defined as a monic polynomial for exactly this reason. The Remainder and Factor Theorems Division by a polynomial of degree 1 leaves a remainder of degree less than 1, that is, a constant. Which constant? Chapter 2 already answered this. The Factor Theorem for a Linear Divisor (@lem-factor-theorem-linear) showed, by an induction that was long division in disguise, that p = (x - c)q + p(c) for some q. We now read that lemma through @thm-polynomial-division. What is new is that q and the constant are unique, so p(c) is the remainder in the sense of division. [Remainder Theorem and Factor Theorem] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] and c \in F. 1. The remainder of f on division by x - c is the constant f(c). 2. c is a root of f if and only if x - c \mid f. (a) By @lem-factor-theorem-linear, f = (x - c)q + f(c) for some q \in F[x]. The constant f(c) has degree 0 or -\infty, which is less than \deg(x - c) = 1. So this is a division with remainder, and by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division, f(c) is the remainder. (b) By @prp-divisibility-properties (e), x - c \mid f if and only if the remainder is 0, which by (a) means f(c) = 0. This proves the theorem. In other words, the Factor Theorem of Chapter 2 is really a statement about division. Division alone would also give it: dividing f by x - c leaves a constant remainder r, and evaluating f = (x - c)q + r at c gives r = f(c). Since Chapter 2 already proved the lemma, we cite it rather than prove it again, and we will use the name “Remainder Theorem” for both parts. [Remainders Without Dividing] (a) Find the remainder of f = x^5 - 3x^3 + 2x + 7 on division by x - 2 in 
Q[x]. (b) Show that x + 1 
mid x^2 + 1 in 
Q[x], but x + 1 \mid x^2 + 1 in 
F_2[x]. (c) Find the remainder of x^5 on division by x^2 - x in 
Q[x], again without long division. (a) By @thm-remainder-theorem (a), the remainder is f(2) = 32 - 24 + 4 + 7 = 19. No long division is needed. (b) Here x + 1 = x - (-1). In 
Q, (-1)^2 + 1 = 2 
eq 0, so -1 is not a root and x + 1 
mid x^2 + 1 by part (b) of the theorem; the remainder is 2. In 
F_2, -1 = 1 and 1^2 + 1 = 0, so x + 1 \mid x^2 + 1. Indeed x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)^2 in 
F_2[x]. The same polynomial symbols, over two fields, give different answers. (c) The divisor has degree 2, so by @thm-polynomial-division, x^5 = q\,(x^2 - x) + r with \deg r \le 1, say r = ax + b. The divisor x^2 - x = x(x - 1) vanishes at 0 and at 1, so evaluating both sides there (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) kills the term q\,(x^2 - x): at 0, 0 = b; at 1, 1 = a + b. Hence a = 1, b = 0, and the remainder is x. As a check, x^5 - x = x(x^4 - 1) = (x^2 - x)(x^3 + x^2 + x + 1). The move is: evaluate at the roots of the divisor, one equation per root. The Factor Theorem peels off one root at a time. Doing it for several distinct roots at once strengthens the Root bound of Chapter 2 (@lem-root-bound), which said that a non-zero polynomial of degree at most n has at most n distinct roots. The stronger version says why there are so few: every root contributes its own linear factor. [Distinct Roots Give a Product of Linear Factors] Let F be a field, f \in F[x], and let c_1, \dots, c_k \in F be distinct roots of f, with k \ge 1. Then (x - c_1)(x - c_2) \cdots (x - c_k) \mid f . Consequently, if f 
eq 0, then k \le \deg f: a non-zero polynomial of degree n has at most n distinct roots in F. Peel off x - c_1 by the Factor Theorem. What remains, h, must still vanish at c_2, because f(c_2) = (c_2 - c_1)h(c_2) and c_2 - c_1 
eq 0. So peel off x - c_2 from h, and so on. Distinctness is what makes the factors c_k - c_i non-zero. We use induction on k. For k = 1, this is @thm-remainder-theorem (b). Let k \ge 2, and assume the statement for k - 1 distinct roots. By the induction hypothesis, f = (x - c_1) \cdots (x - c_{k-1})\,h for some h \in F[x]. Evaluating at c_k with @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, 0 = f(c_k) = (c_k - c_1) \cdots (c_k - c_{k-1})\, h(c_k) . Since the c_i are distinct, each c_k - c_i with i < k is non-zero, and a product of non-zero elements of a field is non-zero (@thm-field-basic-properties). Hence h(c_k) = 0, and @thm-remainder-theorem (b) gives h = (x - c_k) h_1 with h_1 \in F[x]. Therefore f = (x - c_1) \cdots (x - c_k)\, h_1, which completes the induction. For the count, suppose f 
eq 0 and write f = (x - c_1) \cdots (x - c_k)\, h_1 as above. Then h_1 
eq 0, and by @thm-degree-of-product, \deg f = k + \deg h_1 \ge k. This proves the corollary. The count is @lem-root-bound again, now as a consequence of a divisibility statement. The divisibility statement is the more useful one. For instance, it tells us at once that a polynomial vanishing at 1, 2 and 3 is a multiple of (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3). Polynomials and polynomial functions Chapter 0 warned that a polynomial is not the function it defines: over 
F_2, the non-zero polynomial x^2 + x has the zero function (@exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2). It also promised that over an infinite field the distinction disappears. Chapter 2 kept that promise in a paragraph right after @lem-root-bound. We record the fact here as a theorem, in a slightly sharper form that counts how many values are needed. [Values Determine a Polynomial] Let F be a field and p, q \in F[x]. 1. Let n \in 
N with \deg p \le n and \deg q \le n. If p(c) = q(c) for at least n + 1 distinct elements c \in F, then p = q. 2. If F is infinite and p(c) = q(c) for every c \in F, then p = q. (a) Let h = p - q. By @thm-degree-of-sum, \deg h \le n. By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, h(c) = p(c) - q(c) = 0 for each of the given n + 1 distinct elements, so h has at least n + 1 distinct roots. By @lem-root-bound, a non-zero polynomial of degree at most n has at most n distinct roots, so h cannot be non-zero. Hence h = 0 and p = q. (b) Let n = \max(\deg p, \deg q, 0) \in 
N. Since F is infinite, it contains n + 1 distinct elements, and p and q agree at each of them. Part (a) gives p = q. This proves the theorem. So over 
Q, 
R and 
C, we may compare polynomials by comparing their functions, and we may read off coefficients from values. Part (a) holds over every field, including finite ones: a quadratic over 
F_5 is determined by its values at any three distinct points. Part (b) is false over every finite field. Over 
F_p, the polynomial x^p - x is non-zero but vanishes at every element (@exr-polynomials-c2). So x^p and x define the same function 
F_p 	o 
F_p although they are different polynomials. There is no contradiction with (a): the degrees are at most p, and (a) would need agreement at p + 1 distinct points, but 
F_p has only p elements. Over 
F_3, do the polynomials x^3 + 2x and 0 define the same function? Does this contradict @thm-polynomial-function-determines-polynomial? Yes. The values of x^3 + 2x at 0, 1, 2 are 0, 1 + 2 = 3 = 0, and 8 + 4 = 12 = 0. So the function is zero, although the polynomial is not. There is no contradiction: 
F_3 is finite, so part (b) does not apply, and part (a) with n = 3 would need 4 distinct points. In fact x^3 + 2x = x^3 - x, the polynomial of the warning with p = 3. Division with remainder is the one tool this chapter keeps using. In the next section it shows that every set of polynomials closed under the right operations consists of the multiples of a single polynomial, and that gives greatest common divisors. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the theorem on division with remainder in F[x], including every hypothesis. 2. Determine whether the following statement is true: “for every field F and all f, g \in F[x], if f \mid g and g \mid f, then f = g.” Justify your answer. Does your answer change if F = 
F_2? 3. Let c \in F be non-zero. What are the quotient and the remainder of f on division by the constant polynomial c? 4. Name the method for finding the remainder of f on division by x - c without dividing. 5. Determine whether the following statement is true: “if F is a field and p \in F[x] satisfies p(c) = 0 for every c \in F, then p = 0.” Justify your answer. 1. Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x] with g 
eq 0. Then there are unique q, r \in F[x] with f = qg + r and \deg r < \deg g (@thm-polynomial-division). 2. False in general. In 
Q[x], take f = x and g = 2x. Then g = 2f and f = 	frac12 g, so each divides the other, but f 
eq g. By @prp-divisibility-properties (d), mutual divisibility only gives associates. Over 
F_2, the statement is true: the only non-zero constant in 
F_2 is 1, so associates are equal, and if f \mid g and g \mid f, then either both are 0 or f = 1 \cdot g. 3. The remainder must have degree less than \deg c = 0, so r = 0. Then f = qc, so q = c^{-1} f. In particular every polynomial is divisible by every non-zero constant. 4. The Remainder Theorem (@thm-remainder-theorem): the remainder is the constant f(c). 5. False. Over 
F_2, p = x^2 + x is non-zero but p(0) = p(1) = 0 (@exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2). The statement is true when F is infinite, by @thm-polynomial-function-determines-polynomial (b). B. Practice [B1: Dividing Over Two Fields] 1. In 
Q[x], divide f = x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5 by g = 3x^2 - 1 with remainder. 2. In 
F_5[x], divide f = x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1 by g = 2x^2 + 3 with remainder. Hence decide whether g \mid f in 
F_5[x]. Hint for (b): first find the inverse of 2 in 
F_5. 1. The leading coefficient of g is 3, with inverse 	frac13. First, x^4 / 3x^2 = 	frac13 x^2, and f - 	frac13 x^2 g = -3x^3 + 	frac13 x^2 + 2x - 5. Next, -3x^3 / 3x^2 = -x, and subtracting -xg = -3x^3 + x leaves 	frac13 x^2 + x - 5. Next, 	frac13 x^2 / 3x^2 = 	frac19, and subtracting 	frac19 g = 	frac13 x^2 - 	frac19 leaves x - 	frac{44}{9}, of degree 1 < 2. Hence x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5 =  igl( 	frac13 x^2 - x + 	frac19  igr)(3x^2 - 1) + x - 	frac{44}{9} , with quotient 	frac13 x^2 - x + 	frac19 and remainder x - 	frac{44}{9}, which are the only ones by @thm-polynomial-division. 2. In 
F_5, 2 \cdot 3 = 6 = 1, so 2^{-1} = 3. First, the leading term x^4 divided by 2x^2 is 3x^2, and 3x^2 g = 6x^4 + 9x^2 = x^4 + 4x^2. Subtracting leaves 2x^3 - 4x^2 + 3x + 1 = 2x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 1. Next, 2x^3 / 2x^2 = x, and subtracting xg = 2x^3 + 3x leaves x^2 + 1. Next, x^2 / 2x^2 = 3, and subtracting 3g = 6x^2 + 9 = x^2 + 4 leaves 1 - 4 = -3 = 2. Hence x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1 = (3x^2 + x + 3)(2x^2 + 3) + 2 \quad 	ext{in } 
F_5[x] . The remainder 2 is non-zero, so g 
mid f in 
F_5[x], by @prp-divisibility-properties (e). [B2: A Factor of x^n - c^n] Let F be a field, c \in F and n \ge 1. Prove that x - c \mid x^n - c^n in F[x], and verify that the quotient is x^{n-1} + c\,x^{n-2} + \dots + c^{n-2} x + c^{n-1}. The value of f = x^n - c^n at c is c^n - c^n = 0, so c is a root of f, and @thm-remainder-theorem (b) gives x - c \mid f. For the quotient, let s = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^{j} x^{n-1-j}. Then (x - c)s = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^{j} x^{n-j} - \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^{j+1} x^{n-1-j} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^{j} x^{n-j} - \sum_{j=1}^{n} c^{j} x^{n-j} = x^n - c^n , since the two sums share the terms with 1 \le j \le n - 1, leaving c^0 x^n from the first and c^n x^0 from the second. This shows x^n - c^n = (x - c)s. [B3: A Remainder Without Long Division] 1. In 
Q[x], find the remainder of x^{100} on division by x^2 - 1 without long division. 2. Show that the answer to (a) is the remainder of x^{100} on division by x^2 - 1 over every field F, including 
F_2. Explain why the method of (a) alone does not settle the case F = 
F_2. Hint for (a): part (c) of @exm-remainder-theorem. Hint for (b): imitate the identity of B2. 1. By @thm-polynomial-division, x^{100} = q(x^2 - 1) + r with \deg r \le 1, say r = ax + b. Evaluating at 1 and -1, where x^2 - 1 vanishes (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), gives 1 = a + b and 1 = (-1)^{100} = -a + b. Adding and subtracting, 2b = 2 and 2a = 0, so b = 1 and a = 0. The remainder is 1. 2. Over any field, let s = \sum_{j=0}^{49} x^{2j}. Then (x^2 - 1)s = \sum_{j=0}^{49} x^{2j+2} - \sum_{j=0}^{49} x^{2j} = x^{100} - 1 , because the terms x^2, x^4, \dots, x^{98} occur in both sums. Hence x^{100} = s \cdot (x^2 - 1) + 1, and \deg 1 = 0 < 2, so by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division the remainder is 1 over every field. The method of (a) divides by 2, and over 
F_2 we have 2 = 0; also 1 = -1 there, so evaluating at \pm 1 gives only the single equation a + b = 1, which does not determine a and b. C. Going deeper [C1: Division by a Monic Polynomial Over 
Z] As in the warning after @thm-polynomial-division, 
Z[x] denotes the set of polynomials in 
Q[x] all of whose coefficients are integers. It is closed under addition and multiplication. 1. Let f, g \in 
Z[x] with g monic. Prove that there exist q, r \in 
Z[x] with f = qg + r and \deg r < \deg g. 2. Prove that q and r in (a) are unique, even among q, r \in 
Q[x]. 3. Does (a) remain true if the leading coefficient of g is -1 instead of 1? Justify your answer. Hint for (a): find the one step in the proof of @thm-polynomial-division that leaves 
Z[x]. 1. We repeat the existence proof of @thm-polynomial-division, checking that every polynomial stays in 
Z[x]. Let m = \deg g. The only step that could leave 
Z[x] is forming a b^{-1} x^{n-m} g, where b is the leading coefficient of g. Here b = 1, so a b^{-1} = a \in 
Z and f_1 = f - a x^{n-m} g \in 
Z[x]. The strong induction on \deg f (@thm-strong-induction) then runs word for word inside 
Z[x]: in Case 1, q = 0 and r = f are in 
Z[x]; in Case 2, q = a x^{n-m} + q_1 and r = r_1 are in 
Z[x] because q_1, r_1 are, by the induction hypothesis applied to f_1 \in 
Z[x]. This proves existence in 
Z[x]. 2. Suppose f = qg + r = q'g + r' with q, q', r, r' \in 
Q[x] and \deg r, \deg r' < \deg g. Since 
Q is a field and g 
eq 0, the uniqueness part of @thm-polynomial-division in 
Q[x] gives q = q' and r = r'. In particular the pair found in (a) is the unique one. 3. Yes. If the leading coefficient is b = -1, then b^{-1} = -1 \in 
Z, so a b^{-1} = -a \in 
Z, and the argument of (a) goes through unchanged. What matters is that the leading coefficient has an inverse in 
Z, which is true exactly for \pm 1. [C2: Remainders on Division by a Quadratic] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] and a, b \in F. 1. Suppose a 
eq b. Prove that the remainder of f on division by (x - a)(x - b) is r = f(a)\, rac{x - b}{a - b} + f(b)\, rac{x - a}{b - a} , where  rac{x - b}{a - b} means (a - b)^{-1}(x - b). 2. Now let a = b. Write f = (x - a)h + f(a) by @thm-remainder-theorem. Prove that the remainder of f on division by (x - a)^2 is h(a)(x - a) + f(a). 3. Hence find the remainder of x^{100} on division by x^2 - 3x + 2 in 
Q[x]. 1. Since a 
eq b, a - b is invertible, so r is a well-defined polynomial of degree at most 1. By @thm-polynomial-division, f = q(x - a)(x - b) + s with \deg s \le 1. Evaluating at a and at b (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) gives s(a) = f(a) and s(b) = f(b). Also r(a) = f(a) \cdot 1 + f(b) \cdot 0 = f(a) and r(b) = f(b). So s and r have degree at most 1 and agree at the 2 distinct points a, b. By @thm-polynomial-function-determines-polynomial (a) with n = 1, s = r. This proves the formula. 2. By @thm-remainder-theorem (a) applied to h, h = (x - a)k + h(a) for some k \in F[x]. Substituting, f = (x - a) igl( (x - a)k + h(a)  igr) + f(a) = k\,(x - a)^2 +  igl( h(a)(x - a) + f(a)  igr) . The last bracket has degree at most 1 < 2 = \deg (x - a)^2, so by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division it is the remainder. 3. Here x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2), with a = 1 
eq b = 2, f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 2^{100}. By (a), r = 1 \cdot  rac{x - 2}{1 - 2} + 2^{100} \cdot  rac{x - 1}{2 - 1} = (2^{100} - 1)x + (2 - 2^{100}) . As a check, r(1) = 1 and r(2) = 2^{101} - 2 + 2 - 2^{100} = 2^{100}. [C3: Equal Functions Over 
F_p] Let p be a prime and f, g \in 
F_p[x]. 1. Prove that f(c) = g(c) for every c \in 
F_p if and only if x^p - x \mid f - g in 
F_p[x]. 2. Deduce that f and its remainder on division by x^p - x define the same function 
F_p 	o 
F_p. Use this to find a polynomial of degree less than 5 that defines the same function on 
F_5 as x^7 + x. Hint for (a): @exr-polynomials-c2 and @cor-root-bound-general. 1. (\Leftarrow) Suppose f - g = (x^p - x)h. By @exr-polynomials-c2, c^p - c = 0 for every c \in 
F_p. By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, f(c) - g(c) = (c^p - c)h(c) = 0 for every c. (\Rightarrow) Suppose f(c) = g(c) for every c \in 
F_p. Then the p distinct elements 0, 1, \dots, p - 1 of 
F_p are roots of f - g. Let P = \prod_{c \in 
F_p} (x - c). By @cor-root-bound-general, P \mid f - g. It remains to show P = x^p - x. By @exr-polynomials-c2, every c \in 
F_p is a root of x^p - x, so @cor-root-bound-general gives x^p - x = Pu for some u. Both P and x^p - x are monic of degree p (@thm-degree-of-product), so \deg u = 0, and comparing leading coefficients gives u = 1. Hence P = x^p - x, and x^p - x \mid f - g. 2. Write f = q(x^p - x) + r by @thm-polynomial-division. Then x^p - x \mid f - r, so f and r define the same function by (a). For f = x^7 + x over 
F_5: x^7 = x^2 \cdot x^5 = x^2(x^5 - x) + x^3, so x^7 + x = x^2(x^5 - x) + (x^3 + x) with \deg(x^3 + x) = 3 < 5. Hence x^3 + x defines the same function as x^7 + x on 
F_5.

title: 5.2 Ideals and Greatest Common Divisors
content:
Ideals and Greatest Common Divisors Division with remainder is now available over every field. This section uses it to answer a question about two polynomials f and g: what do all the combinations af + bg, with polynomial coefficients a and b, look like? The answer is that they are exactly the multiples of one polynomial, and that polynomial is the greatest common divisor of f and g. Along the way we meet ideals, the subsets of F[x] adapted to multiplication, and we prove that each of them is generated by a single polynomial. The Euclidean algorithm then computes the greatest common divisor and the coefficients a, b by repeated division. Throughout, F is a field. All the combinations of two polynomials Take f = x^2 - 1 and g = x^2 + x - 2 in 
Q[x], and look at the set \{ af + bg : a, b \in

Ideals In Chapter 1 we studied F[x] as a vector space and its subspaces: subsets closed under addition and under multiplication by scalars. But F[x] also has a multiplication of its own. The subsets that respect it are closed under multiplication by polynomials. Three recurring examples share this feature: - the multiples of a fixed polynomial p; - the combinations af + bg of two fixed polynomials; - the polynomials that vanish at a fixed point c: if f(c) = 0, then (hf)(c) = h(c) \cdot 0 = 0 for every h. By @prp-coprime-criterion, there are a, b \in F[x] with ap + bq = 1. Multiplying by r, r = (ar)p + b(qr). Here p \mid p and p \mid qr by hypothesis, so p \mid r by @prp-divisibility-properties (b). This proves the theorem. The coprimality hypothesis cannot be dropped. Take p = x^2 and q = r = x. Then p \mid qr = x^2, but p 
mid r, since \deg x^2 > \deg x (@prp-divisibility-properties (c)). Here \gcd(p, q) = x 
eq 1: part of p is absorbed by q and part by r. In the next section, @thm-coprime-divides-product becomes Euclid’s lemma for irreducible polynomials, which is the heart of unique factorization. Least common multiples, briefly. For f, g \in F[x], the intersection \langle f angle \cap \langle g angle is again an ideal: it contains 0, so (I1) holds, and (I2) and (I3) hold in each of \langle f angle and \langle g angle, hence in the intersection. Its members are the common multiples of f and g. [Least Common Multiple] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. The least common multiple \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) is the monic generator of the ideal \langle f angle \cap \langle g angle if this ideal is non-zero, and 0 otherwise. Exactly as for the gcd, \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) is a common multiple of f and g that divides every common multiple, by @thm-ideals-principal. If f = 0 or g = 0, the only common multiple is 0; otherwise fg is a non-zero common multiple. For monic f and g, \gcd(f, g) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = fg; this is proved in Exercise C3. For example, in 
Q[x], \gcd(x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2) = x - 1, so \operatorname{lcm}(x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2) = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x + 2). The gcd does not depend on the field A polynomial with rational coefficients is also a polynomial with real and with complex coefficients. Its gcd with another rational polynomial can be computed in 
Q[x], 
R[x] or 
C[x], and the definition does not obviously give the same answer, because the coefficients a, b in \langle f, g angle range over a larger set. The Euclidean algorithm shows the answers agree. Recall that a subfield K of a field L is a subset closed under the field operations (@def-restriction-of-scalars); then K[x] \subseteq L[x], with the same addition and multiplication. [The gcd Is the Same Over a Larger Field] Let K be a subfield of a field L, and let f, g \in K[x]. Then the greatest common divisor of f and g computed in K[x] equals the one computed in L[x]. In particular, f and g are coprime over K if and only if they are coprime over L. If g = 0, both gcds are the monic associate of f (or 0), by @exm-gcd-first (a), and this does not depend on the field. Let g 
eq 0, and run the Euclidean algorithm in K[x]: r_{k-1} = q_{k+1} r_k + r_{k+1} with \deg r_{k+1} < \deg r_k, all in K[x]. Each of these equations also holds in L[x], with the same degree condition. By the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division over L, they are exactly the divisions that the algorithm performs in L[x]. So both runs produce the same last non-zero remainder r_n, and @thm-euclidean-algorithm gives the same gcd c^{-1} r_n in both. This proves the proposition. The gcd does not see the field, but factorization does. Over 
Q, the polynomial x^2 - 2 has no root, by @thm-sqrt2-irrational, so it has no factor x - c with c \in 
Q (@thm-remainder-theorem). Over 
R it factors as (x - \sqrt2)(x + \sqrt2). Yet \gcd(x^2 - 2, x^2 - 2x), say, is the same over 
Q and over 
R. So “coprime” is a robust notion, while “cannot be factored” depends on the field; the next section makes the second notion precise. A useful consequence: if f, g \in 
Q[x] are coprime over 
Q, then they have no common root in 
C. Indeed, af + bg = 1 with a, b \in 
Q[x] \subseteq 
C[x], and evaluating at a common root z would give 0 = 1 by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. So common complex roots can be detected by a computation that never leaves 
Q. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define an ideal of F[x]. 2. State the theorem describing all ideals of F[x]. 3. Determine whether the following statement is true: “for all f, g \in F[x], \Span(f, g) = \langle f, g angle.” Justify your answer. 4. Is \gcd(2x - 2, 4x^2 - 4) = 2x - 2 in 
Q[x]? Justify your answer. 5. Determine whether the following statement is true: “if af + bg = x - 1 for some a, b \in 
Q[x], then \gcd(f, g) = x - 1.” Justify your answer. 6. Name an algorithm that computes \gcd(f, g) using only division with remainder (@thm-polynomial-division). 1. A subset I \subseteq F[x] is an ideal if it is non-empty, f + g \in I for all f, g \in I, and hf \in I for all f \in I and every h \in F[x] (@def-ideal-polynomials). 2. If I 
eq \{0\} is an ideal of F[x], there is exactly one monic d with I = \langle d angle, namely the monic polynomial of least degree in I (@thm-ideals-principal). 3. False. Take f = g = x. Then \Span(x, x) = \{ cx : c \in F \} does not contain x^2, while x^2 = x \cdot x \in \langle x, x angle. The span allows only scalar coefficients. 4. No. The gcd is monic by definition. Since 4x^2 - 4 = (2x - 2)(2x + 2), we have \langle 2x - 2, 4x^2 - 4 angle = \langle 2x - 2 angle = \langle x - 1 angle, so the gcd is x - 1. 5. False. Take f = x and g = x - 1, with a = 0, b = 1. Then af + bg = x - 1, but \gcd(x, x - 1) = 1, because x - (x - 1) = 1 (@prp-coprime-criterion). What is true is that \gcd(f, g) divides every combination af + bg, by @thm-gcd-properties (a) and @prp-divisibility-properties (b). 6. The Euclidean algorithm (@thm-euclidean-algorithm). B. Practice [B1: gcd and Bézout Coefficients of Two Cubics] In 
Q[x], let f = x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 and g = x^3 + x + 2. Use the Euclidean algorithm to find d = \gcd(f, g) and polynomials a, b \in 
Q[x] with d = af + bg. Hence find all complex numbers that are roots of both f and g. Divide f by g: f = 1 \cdot g + r_1 with r_1 = f - g = x^2 - 1. Divide g by r_1: x \cdot r_1 = x^3 - x, and g - x r_1 = 2x + 2, so g = x\, r_1 + r_2 with r_2 = 2x + 2. Divide r_1 by r_2: x^2 - 1 = 	frac12 (x - 1)(2x + 2) + 0. The last non-zero remainder is r_2 = 2x + 2, with leading coefficient 2, so d = x + 1 by @thm-euclidean-algorithm. Back-substituting, r_2 = g - x r_1 = g - x(f - g) = -x f + (1 + x) g. Dividing by 2, x + 1 = \Bigl( - rac{x}{2} \Bigr) f +  rac{x + 1}{2}\, g . Check: -	frac{x}{2}(x^3 + x^2 + x + 1) + 	frac{x+1}{2}(x^3 + x + 2) = 	frac12 igl( -x^4 - x^3 - x^2 - x + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 2  igr) = x + 1. Hence: let z \in 
C. If f(z) = g(z) = 0, then evaluating the identity above in 
C (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) gives z + 1 = 0. Conversely, x + 1 divides f and g (@thm-gcd-properties (a)), so -1 is a root of both. Therefore -1 is the only common complex root. [B2: Ideal or Not?] Determine which of the following subsets of 
R[x] are ideals. For each ideal, find its monic generator. Justify your answers. 1. S_1 = \{ f \in 
R[x] : f(1) = f(-1) \}. 2. S_2 = \{ f \in 
R[x] : f(0) = 0 	ext{ and } f(1) = 0 \}. 3. S_3 = \{ f \in 
R[x] : \deg f \ge 3 \} \cup \{0\}. 4. S_4 = \{ f \in 
R[x] : f(i) = 0 \}, where f(i) means the value at i \in 
C of f regarded as a complex polynomial. 1. Not an ideal. S_1 is a subspace, and 1 \in S_1. But x \cdot 1 = x has x(1) = 1 
eq -1 = x(-1), so x 
otin S_1, and (I3) fails. 2. An ideal. The argument of @exm-ideals-polynomials (b), applied at both points, gives (I1)–(I3). If f \in S_2, then 0 and 1 are distinct roots of f, so x(x - 1) \mid f by @cor-root-bound-general. Conversely every multiple of x^2 - x vanishes at 0 and 1. Hence S_2 = \langle x^2 - x angle, with monic generator x^2 - x. 3. Not an ideal. x^3 \in S_3 and -x^3 + x \in S_3, but their sum x has degree 1 and is non-zero, so (I2) fails. 4. An ideal: evaluation at i respects sums and products (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations over 
C), so the argument of @exm-ideals-polynomials (b) applies. It contains x^2 + 1. A non-zero element of degree at most 1 would be a + bx with a, b \in 
R not both zero and a + bi = 0, which is impossible since the real and imaginary parts give a = b = 0. So the least degree of a non-zero element is 2. If d is the monic generator (@thm-ideals-principal), then \deg d = 2 and d \mid x^2 + 1, so x^2 + 1 = ud with u constant, and comparing leading coefficients gives u = 1. Hence S_4 = \langle x^2 + 1 angle. [B3: The gcd of x^m - 1 and x^n - 1] Let F be a field. For integers m, n \ge 0, not both zero, let \gcd(m, n) denote the largest positive integer dividing both. 1. For m \ge n \ge 1, verify that x^m - 1 = x^{m-n}(x^n - 1) + (x^{m-n} - 1). 2. Prove that \gcd(x^m - 1, x^n - 1) = x^{\gcd(m, n)} - 1 in F[x] for all m, n \ge 0 not both zero, where x^0 - 1 = 0. 3. Hence compute \gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1). Hint for (b): @thm-euclidean-algorithm, run on the exponents. 1. Expanding, x^{m-n}(x^n - 1) + x^{m-n} - 1 = x^m - x^{m-n} + x^{m-n} - 1 = x^m - 1. 2. We use strong induction on s = m + n \ge 1 (@thm-strong-induction). If n = 0, then m \ge 1, \gcd(m, 0) = m, and \gcd(x^m - 1, 0) is the monic associate of x^m - 1, which is x^m - 1 itself (@exm-gcd-first (a)). The case m = 0 is the same, since both gcds are symmetric. Now let m, n \ge 1; by symmetry we may assume m \ge n. By (a) and @lem-euclid-step, \gcd(x^m - 1, x^n - 1) = \gcd(x^n - 1, x^{m-n} - 1) . The pair (n, m - n) is not both zero and has sum m < m + n, so by the induction hypothesis the right side is x^{\gcd(n, m - n)} - 1. Finally, \gcd(n, m - n) = \gcd(m, n): if k \mid m and k \mid n, then k \mid m - n; and if k \mid n and k \mid m - n, then k \mid (m - n) + n = m. So the two pairs have the same positive common divisors, and the same largest one. This completes the induction. 3. By (b), \gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1) = x^{\gcd(12, 18)} - 1 = x^6 - 1. C. Going deeper [C1: Polynomials Vanishing on a Set] Let F be a field and S \subseteq F non-empty. Put I(S) = \{ f \in F[x] : f(s) = 0 	ext{ for all } s \in S \}. 1. Prove that I(S) is an ideal of F[x]. 2. Suppose S = \{ s_1, \dots, s_k \} is finite, with the s_i distinct. Prove that I(S) = \langle (x - s_1) \cdots (x - s_k) angle. 3. Suppose S is infinite. Prove that I(S) = \{0\}. 4. Deduce from (b) and @exr-division-c3 that I(
F_p) = \langle x^p - x angle for every prime p. 1. The zero polynomial vanishes everywhere, so I(S) 
eq \varnothing. If f, g \in I(S) and h \in F[x], then for every s \in S, @thm-evaluation-respects-operations gives (f + g)(s) = 0 + 0 = 0 and (hf)(s) = h(s) \cdot 0 = 0. So (I2) and (I3) hold. 2. Let P = (x - s_1) \cdots (x - s_k). Every multiple hP vanishes at each s_i, since P(s_i) = 0; so \langle P angle \subseteq I(S). Conversely, if f \in I(S), then s_1, \dots, s_k are distinct roots of f, and @cor-root-bound-general gives P \mid f. Hence I(S) = \langle P angle, and since P is monic, it is the monic generator. 3. Let f \in I(S), and suppose f 
eq 0. Since S is infinite, it contains \deg f + 1 distinct elements, all roots of f. This contradicts @cor-root-bound-general. Hence f = 0. 4. By (b), I(
F_p) = \langle P angle with P = \prod_{c \in 
F_p} (x - c). The solution of @exr-division-c3 (a) showed P = x^p - x. Hence I(
F_p) = \langle x^p - x angle. [C2: A Non-Principal Ideal in Two Variables] A polynomial in two variables over F is a finite sum P = \sum_{i, j} a_{ij} x^i y^j with a_{ij} \in F, only finitely many non-zero; two are equal when all coefficients agree. They are added coefficient by coefficient and multiplied by expanding and collecting, and the set F[x, y] of all of them satisfies the laws of @thm-polynomial-ring-laws, which you may use. Ideals of F[x, y] and \langle P_1, \dots, P_k angle are defined exactly as in @def-ideal-polynomials, and @prp-ideal-generated holds with the same proof. For P 
eq 0, let \deg_y P be the largest j with a_{ij} 
eq 0 for some i, and define \deg_x P similarly. 1. Prove that \deg_y(PQ) = \deg_y P + \deg_y Q for non-zero P, Q \in F[x, y]. By symmetry the same holds for \deg_x. 2. Show that \langle x, y angle consists of the polynomials whose constant coefficient a_{00} is 0. 3. Prove that \langle x, y angle 
eq \langle D angle for every D \in F[x, y]. 4. Explain precisely which step of the proof of @thm-ideals-principal has no analogue in F[x, y]. Hint for (a): write P = \sum_{j} p_j(x) y^j with p_j \in F[x], and use @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors. 1. Group terms by the power of y: P = \sum_{j=0}^{s} p_j y^j and Q = \sum_{j=0}^{t} q_j y^j with p_j, q_j \in F[x], s = \deg_y P, t = \deg_y Q, so p_s 
eq 0 and q_t 
eq 0. Expanding, the terms of PQ with y-power greater than s + t are all zero, and the terms with y^{s+t} come only from p_s y^s \cdot q_t y^t, giving (p_s q_t) y^{s+t}. By @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors, p_s q_t 
eq 0 in F[x], so some coefficient of x^i y^{s+t} in PQ is non-zero. Hence \deg_y(PQ) = s + t. 2. Every Ax + By has constant coefficient 0, since each term of Ax and By involves x or y to a positive power. Conversely, if a_{00} = 0, then every term a_{ij}x^iy^j with i \ge 1 is a multiple of x, and every term with i = 0, j \ge 1 is a multiple of y. Grouping them, P = Ax + By for some A, B \in F[x, y]. 3. Suppose \langle x, y angle = \langle D angle. Since x \in \langle D angle, x = HD for some H, so D 
eq 0 and H 
eq 0. By (a), 0 = \deg_y x = \deg_y H + \deg_y D, so \deg_y D = 0: D involves no y. Similarly y = KD gives \deg_x D = 0. So D is a non-zero constant. But D \in \langle x, y angle, so its constant coefficient is 0 by (b), that is, D = 0. This contradiction shows that \langle x, y angle is not principal. 4. The proof of @thm-ideals-principal picks a non-zero d \in I of least degree, writes each f \in I as f = qd + r with r smaller than d by @thm-polynomial-division, notes r = f - qd \in I, and concludes r = 0 from minimality. Measure size in F[x, y] by the total degree, the largest i + j with a_{ij} 
eq 0. Choosing d still works: by (b), every non-zero element of \langle x, y angle has total degree at least 1, and those of total degree 1 are the ax + by with (a, b) 
eq (0, 0). Let d be any of them. Then \langle d angle \subseteq \langle x, y angle by (I3), and the inclusion is strict by (c), so some f \in \langle x, y angle is not a multiple of d. For this f and every Q \in F[x, y], the element R = f - Qd lies in \langle x, y angle and is non-zero, so its total degree is at least 1, the total degree of d. So no remainder smaller than d exists: the step with no analogue is division with remainder, the appeal to @thm-polynomial-division. Concretely, for d = x and f = y, every term of Qx contains x, so the term y survives in y - Qx. The underlying reason is that, viewed as a polynomial in y with coefficients in F[x], the leading coefficient x of d is not invertible in F[x], which is exactly the obstacle of the warning after @thm-polynomial-division. [C3: gcd Times lcm] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x] monic. Put d = \gcd(f, g) and write f = d f_1, g = d g_1 with f_1, g_1 \in F[x]. 1. Prove that \gcd(f_1, g_1) = 1. 2. Prove that m = d f_1 g_1 is a monic common multiple of f and g that divides every common multiple of f and g. 3. Deduce that \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = d f_1 g_1, and hence \gcd(f, g) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = fg. 4. Show by an example in 
Q[x] that the formula in (c) fails if f and g are not monic. Hint for (b): use @thm-coprime-divides-product. 1. The quotients exist by @thm-gcd-properties (a), and d 
eq 0 since f 
eq 0. By @cor-bezout-polynomials, d = af + bg = d(af_1 + bg_1). Canceling d 
eq 0 (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (2)) gives af_1 + bg_1 = 1, so \gcd(f_1, g_1) = 1 by @prp-coprime-criterion. 2. Comparing leading coefficients in f = d f_1 with f, d monic shows f_1 is monic; likewise g_1. So m is monic, and m = f g_1 = g f_1 is a common multiple. Let M be any common multiple, say M = fu. Since g \mid M, write M = gv. Then d f_1 u = d g_1 v, and canceling d gives f_1 u = g_1 v, so g_1 \mid f_1 u. By (a) and @thm-coprime-divides-product, g_1 \mid u, say u = g_1 w. Hence M = f g_1 w = m w, and m \mid M. 3. By (b), m \in \langle f angle \cap \langle g angle, and every element of this ideal is a multiple of m. So \langle f angle \cap \langle g angle = \langle m angle, and m is monic, hence \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = m by @def-lcm-polynomials and @thm-ideals-principal. Then \gcd(f, g) \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = d \cdot d f_1 g_1 = (d f_1)(d g_1) = fg. 4. Take f = g = 2x. Then \gcd(f, g) = x and \operatorname{lcm}(f, g) = x, both monic, so their product is x^2, while fg = 4x^2. In general the two sides differ by the product of the leading coefficients.

title: 5.3 Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization
content:
Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization Every integer n \ge 2 is a product of primes, and Chapter 0 remarked that the convention “1 is not prime” is what makes such factorizations unique. Polynomials over a field behave the same way, with irreducible polynomials in the role of primes and non-zero constants in the role of \pm 1. This section defines irreducible polynomials, proves Euclid’s lemma from the gcd machinery of the previous section, and proves that every non-constant polynomial factors into irreducibles in exactly one way. The catch is that “irreducible” depends on the field: the same polynomial may factor over 
R but not over 
Q, or over 
F_5 but not over 
F_3. So we also collect tools for deciding irreducibility over specific fields: roots in low degree, the Rational Root Theorem, and Eisenstein’s criterion. Throughout, F is a field. Irreducible polynomials For integers, the building blocks are the primes: integers p \ge 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p (@def-divisibility-prime). To transplant this to F[x], recall from the first section that every non-zero constant divides every polynomial, and that multiplying by a non-zero constant changes nothing for divisibility. So the trivial divisors of p are the non-zero constants and the associates cp. A building block should have no others. An irreducible polynomial is a non-constant polynomial that cannot be split into two factors of smaller degree. [Irreducible Polynomial] Let F be a field. A polynomial p \in F[x] is irreducible over F if 1. p is non-constant, that is, \deg p \ge 1; and 2. whenever p = gh with g, h \in F[x], one of g, h is a constant. A non-constant polynomial that is not irreducible is reducible over F. In words: condition (1) excludes 0 and the non-zero constants. Condition (2) says every factorization of p is trivial: one factor is a constant, which is non-zero because p 
eq 0, and the other is then an associate of p. The phrase over F is part of the notion, since g and h must lie in F[x]. Since degrees add (@thm-degree-of-product), a factorization p = gh with p 
eq 0 has \deg g + \deg h = \deg p. So g is constant exactly when \deg h = \deg p. This gives a working form of the definition: a non-constant p is reducible if and only if p = gh with 1 \le \deg g < \deg p and 1 \le \deg h < \deg p. [First Irreducible and Reducible Polynomials] 1. Show that every polynomial of degree 1 is irreducible over every field. 2. Show that the constants 0 and 2 are not irreducible over 
Q. 3. Show that x^2 + x is reducible over every field, and that x^3 is reducible over every field. (a) If \deg p = 1 and p = gh, then \deg g + \deg h = 1 with both degrees in 
N, so one of them is 0: one factor is a constant. Condition (1) holds since \deg p = 1. Hence p is irreducible, whatever the field. For example x, 2x + 4 and x - \sqrt2 (over 
R) are irreducible. (b) Both are constants, so condition (1) fails. They are the degenerate cases, and they matter: 2 divides everything in 
Q[x], like 1 among the integers, and it is not a building block. (c) x^2 + x = x(x + 1) with both factors of degree 1, and x^3 = x \cdot x^2 with factors of degrees 1 and 2. In each case both factors are non-constant, so condition (2) fails. Why insist on “non-constant”? For the same reason 1 is not a prime. If non-zero constants were allowed as building blocks, factorizations could never be unique: x = 2 \cdot 	frac12 x = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 	frac16 x = \cdots over 
Q, with any number of constant factors. The factorization theorem below pulls out one constant in front and uses only non-constant, monic irreducibles. For polynomials of degree 2 and 3, irreducibility is decided by roots alone. [Irreducibility in Degree 2 and 3] Let F be a field and p \in F[x]. 1. p has a factor of degree 1 in F[x] if and only if p has a root in F. In particular, if \deg p \ge 2 and p has a root in F, then p is reducible over F. 2. If \deg p \in \{2, 3\}, then p is irreducible over F if and only if p has no root in F. (a) (\Leftarrow) If c \in F is a root, then p = (x - c)q by @thm-remainder-theorem (b). (\Rightarrow) If p = (ax + b)q with a 
eq 0, then c = -a^{-1} b satisfies ac + b = 0, so p(c) = 0 \cdot q(c) = 0 by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. For the last sentence, if \deg p \ge 2 and p = (x - c)q, then \deg q = \deg p - 1 \ge 1, so both factors are non-constant of degree less than \deg p, and p is reducible. (b) We prove both directions by contraposition. (\Rightarrow) If p has a root, it is reducible by (a), since \deg p \ge 2. (\Leftarrow) Suppose p is reducible. By the working form of the definition, p = gh with \deg g, \deg h \ge 1 and \deg g + \deg h = \deg p \in \{2, 3\}. Two integers that are at least 1 and sum to 2 or 3 cannot both be at least 2, so one of g, h has degree 1. By (a), p has a root in F. This proves the theorem. Now the standard examples, each checked with the theorem. - x^2 + 1 over 
R and over 
C. For real c, c^2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0, so there is no real root, and x^2 + 1 is irreducible over 
R (and over 
Q). Over 
C, x^2 + 1 = (x - i)(x + i) is reducible. - x^2 - 2 over 
Q and over 
R. A rational root would be a rational number with square 2, which does not exist (@thm-sqrt2-irrational). So x^2 - 2 is irreducible over 
Q. Over 
R, x^2 - 2 = (x - \sqrt2)(x + \sqrt2). - x^2 + x + 1 over 
F_2. The values at 0 and 1 are 1 and 1 + 1 + 1 = 1. No root, so it is irreducible over 
F_2. It is the only irreducible polynomial of degree 2 over 
F_2 (Exercise B3). The non-example by minimal change is x^2 + x over 
F_2: change the constant term of x^2 + x + 1 from 1 to 0, and 0 becomes a root, so x^2 + x = x(x + 1) is reducible. What fails is condition (2). “No roots” implies “irreducible” only in degrees 2 and 3. The polynomial (x^2 + 1)^2 = x^4 + 2x^2 + 1 has no real root, since its values are at least 1, but it is reducible over 
R: it is a product of two factors of degree 2. In degree 4 and higher, a polynomial can split into non-linear factors without having any root. Over which of the fields 
Q, 
Q(\sqrt2) (@exm-q-sqrt2-field), 
R is x^2 - 2 irreducible? Is x^2 + 1 irreducible over 
F_5? Over 
Q only. The field 
Q(\sqrt2) contains \sqrt2, a root of x^2 - 2, so x^2 - 2 = (x - \sqrt2)(x + \sqrt2) is reducible there, and likewise over 
R; over 
Q it is irreducible, as shown above. Over
