(c) \A_3 = \R \oplus \R with \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, and p_{\R} = x^2+1, m_{\R} = x^2+1, so p_{\A_3} = (x^2+1)^2 (@thm-det-block-triangular applied to x\I - \A_3, which is block diagonal over 
Q[x]) and m_{\A_3} = \operatorname{lcm}(x^2+1, x^2+1) = x^2+1 (@prp-minimal-polynomial-block-diagonal). Since x^2+1 is irreducible over 
Q, the elementary divisors are x^2+1 and x^2+1; r = 2 and d_1 = d_2 = x^2+1. Both forms are \C(x^2+1) \oplus \C(x^2+1) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \oplus  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \A_3 . Compare @exm-rational-form-4x4: that matrix has the same characteristic polynomial but a different minimal polynomial, so the two are not similar. [B3: Counting similarity classes over a finite field] Work over F = 
F_2. For each polynomial p, find the number of similarity classes of matrices \A \in M_3(
F_2) with p_{\A} = p, and list the invariant factors of each class. 1. p = (x+1)^3. 2. p = x(x+1)^2. 3. p = x^3 + x + 1. Hint: by @cor-similar-iff-same-invariant-factors, a class is a way of writing p = d_1\cdots d_r with d_1 \mid \dots \mid d_r. (a) The only prime involved is x+1, so the elementary divisors are powers (x+1)^{a} with exponents forming a partition of 3. The three partitions (3), (2,1), (1,1,1) give  ig((x+1)^3 ig), \qquad  ig(x+1,\ (x+1)^2 ig), \qquad  ig(x+1,\ x+1,\ x+1 ig) as lists of invariant factors. So there are 3 classes, with representatives \C ig((x+1)^3 ig), (1) \oplus \C ig((x+1)^2 ig) and \I_3 (note -1 = 1 in 
F_2). (b) Now two primes, x with total exponent 1 and x+1 with total exponent 2. For x the only option is the single elementary divisor x; for x+1 the options are (x+1)^2 or x+1, x+1. So there are 2 classes, with invariant factors  ig(x(x+1)^2 ig) \qquad	ext{and}\qquad  ig(x+1,\ x(x+1) ig) . In the first case r = 1 and the matrix is cyclic; in the second r = 2. (c) x^3 + x + 1 has no root in 
F_2 (its values at 0 and 1 are 1 and 1), so it is irreducible (@thm-irreducible-deg-2-3 (b)). A prime of degree 3 in a characteristic polynomial of degree 3 can occur only with exponent 1, so the only possible list of elementary divisors is (x^3+x+1) itself: 1 class, represented by \C(x^3+x+1). C. Going deeper [C1: Which matrices are companion matrices] Let \A \in M_n(F) with n \ge 1. 1. Prove that \A is similar to a companion matrix if and only if m_{\A} = p_{\A}, and that the companion matrix is then \C(p_{\A}). 2. Deduce that \A is similar to a companion matrix if and only if its rational canonical form has exactly one block. 3. Give an example of a matrix in M_2(F) that is not similar to any companion matrix. (a) (\Leftarrow) If m_{\A} = p_{\A}, then \A is cyclic (@thm-cyclic-iff-min-equals-char) and, in the basis generated by a cyclic vector, its matrix is \C(m_{\A}) = \C(p_{\A}); so \A \sim \C(p_{\A}) (@thm-similar-iff-same-operator). (\Rightarrow) Suppose \A \sim \C(q) for some monic q. By @thm-companion-char-min, m_{\C(q)} = p_{\C(q)} = q. Similar matrices share both polynomials (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant, @thm-minimal-polynomial-similarity), so m_{\A} = p_{\A} = q, and the companion matrix is \C(p_{\A}). (b) By @thm-rational-canonical-form the form has one block exactly when r = 1, that is, when d_1 = m_{\A} = p_{\A} (@thm-cyclic-decomposition (b), (c)). Now apply (a). (c) \I_2: here m = x - 1 
e (x-1)^2 = p. Concretely, \I_2 is similar only to itself, and no companion matrix of a monic quadratic is \I_2, since the (2,1) entry of \C(q) is 1 
e 0. [C2: All similarity classes of two by two matrices over the smallest field] Work over F = 
F_2, so that M_2(
F_2) has 16 elements. 1. List the four monic polynomials of degree 2 over 
F_2 and factor each into irreducibles. 2. For each, list the possible lists of invariant factors of a matrix \A \in M_2(
F_2) with that characteristic polynomial. 3. Conclude the total number of similarity classes in M_2(
F_2), and give a representative of each. 4. Check your count against the orbit sizes: \lvert \GL_2(
F_2)vert = 6, and the class of \A has 6/\lvert\{\P : \P^{-1}\A \P = \A\}vert elements. (a) x^2; x^2 + 1 = (x+1)^2; x^2 + x = x(x+1); and x^2+x+1, which has no root in 
F_2 and is therefore irreducible (@thm-irreducible-deg-2-3 (b)). (b) For p = x^2: elementary divisors x^2 (invariant factors (x^2)) or x, x (invariant factors (x, x)) — two options. For p = (x+1)^2: likewise two,  ig((x+1)^2 ig) and (x+1, x+1). For p = x(x+1): each prime occurs once, so the elementary divisors are x, x+1 and there is a single list of invariant factors,  ig(x(x+1) ig). For the irreducible p = x^2+x+1: one option, (x^2+x+1). (c) Total 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 classes, with representatives [ ] using -1 = 1 in 
F_2. (For (x+1)^2 = x^2+1 the coefficients are a_0 = 1, a_1 = 0, so \C =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, the coordinate swap.) (d) The two scalar matrices 0 and \I_2 commute with everything, so their classes have 6/6 = 1 element each. For \diag(0,1), a matrix commutes with it exactly when it is diagonal (compare entries), and the invertible diagonal matrices over 
F_2 are only \I_2, so the class has 6 elements. For \C(x^2) and \C(x^2+1) the commutant inside \GL_2 has 2 elements — by @exr-cyclic-subspaces-and-companion-matrices-c1 the commutant of a cyclic matrix is \{a\I + b\A\}, which here has 4 elements, of which 2 are invertible — so each class has 3 elements. For \C(x^2+x+1), whose order is 3 in \GL_2(
F_2), the commutant is \{a\I + b\A\} again, with 3 invertible elements, so the class has 2 elements. Total: 1 + 1 + 6 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 16 = \lvert M_2(
F_2)vert . \checkmark [C3: A matrix over the rationals is similar to its transpose] 1. Let \A, \B \in M_n(
Q) have the same Jordan form over 
C. Prove that \A and \B are similar over 
Q. 2. Deduce that \A \sim \A	p over 
Q for every \A \in M_n(
Q). 3. Which step of (b) would fail for a general field K in place of 
Q? Hint for (b): @exr-jordan-canonical-form-c1. (a) A matrix in M_n(
Q) is also a matrix in M_n(
C), and p_{\A} splits over 
C (@cor-complex-polynomial-splits), so both have Jordan forms there. Having the same Jordan form, they are similar over 
C (@cor-similar-iff-same-jordan-form). By @cor-similarity-field-independent with K = 
Q and L = 
C, they are similar over 
Q. (b) Let \A \in M_n(
Q). Over 
C, p_{\A} splits, so @exr-jordan-canonical-form-c1 (c) gives \A \sim \A	p over 
C. Both matrices lie in M_n(
Q), so @cor-similarity-field-independent gives \A \sim \A	p over 
Q. (c) The step that fails is the splitting: over a general field K there is no reason for p_{\A} to split, and we have not constructed a larger field where it does. (The conclusion is nevertheless true over every field; Section 7 proves it without any splitting, using the Smith normal form of x\I - \A.) Note that @cor-similarity-field-independent itself needs no hypothesis on K — only the existence of a suitable L does.

title: 9.7 Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form
content:
Polynomial Matrices and the Smith Normal Form The rational canonical form of the previous section is a complete answer to the similarity problem, but the proof did not tell us how to find the invariant factors of a given matrix. This section supplies the missing algorithm, and it comes from an unexpected place: instead of working with \A, we work with the single polynomial matrix x\I - \A, and we reduce it by row and column operations whose scalars are allowed to be polynomials. The reduced form is diagonal, its non-constant diagonal entries are the invariant factors, and two matrices are similar exactly when their reduced forms agree. On the way we finally pay off a promise from Chapter 3: every square matrix is similar to its transpose, over every field. The space as a module over the polynomials Everything in this chapter is built by applying polynomials in T to vectors: the T-annihilator of a vector, the cyclic subspace Z(\v; T), the kernels \ker p(T). Name that structure once. For V a vector space over F and T \in \cL(V), the product F[x] 	imes V 	o V, \qquad p \cdot \v \coloneqq p(T)\,\v satisfies, by @thm-evaluation-homomorphism, exactly the vector space axioms with F replaced by F[x]: it is additive in each factor, (pq)\cdot\v = p\cdot(q\cdot\v), and 1\cdot\v = \v. A set with an addition and a product by the elements of a commutative ring R obeying these rules is an R-module, so the pair (V, T) is the same thing as an F[x]-module that is finite-dimensional over the constants F. We develop no general theory of modules; the point is the dictionary: -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- F[x]-module language operator language ------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------- submodule of V T-invariant subspace (@def-invariant-subspace) submodule generated by \v, that is F[x]\cdot\v cyclic subspace Z(\v; T) (@def-cyclic-subspace) the annihilator of \v in F[x] the T-annihilator of \v V is generated by one element T has a cyclic vector -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A subspace closed under multiplication by x is closed under multiplication by every polynomial, which is why the first two lines match. Where does x\I - \A come from here? Fix \sB = ( _1, \dots,  _n) with \A = [T]_{\sB}. As an F[x]-module, V is generated by  _1, \dots,  _n, subject to the n relations x\cdot _j = \sum_i a_{ij} _i, whose coefficient vectors are the columns of x\I - \A. So x\I - \A is the matrix of relations, and changing generators or replacing one relation by a combination of relations should not change V. That is the intuition behind the operations we now allow; the proofs below are matrix proofs and do not rely on it. Row and column operations with polynomial multipliers A matrix in M_n(F[x]) will be called a polynomial matrix. Over a field we reduced a matrix by three kinds of row operation (@def-elementary-row-operations). Over F[x] we must be careful with one of them: multiplying a row by x cannot be undone, because x has no inverse in F[x]. So the scaling operation keeps its scalar in F, while the operation that adds a multiple of one row to another may use any polynomial multiplier. [Elementary Operations over F\lbrack xbrack] Let \M \in M_n(F[x]). An elementary row operation over F[x] on \M is one of: 1. interchanging two rows; 2. multiplying one row by a non-zero scalar c \in F; 3. adding h times one row to a different row, where h \in F[x] is any polynomial. Elementary column operations over F[x] are defined the same way with “column” in place of “row”. In words: (E1) and (E3) are as over a field, except that (E3) now permits a polynomial multiplier; (E2) is restricted, because only the non-zero constants have inverses in F[x]. Each of the three is reversible by an operation of the same kind: swap back, scale by c^{-1}, add -h times the row back. Two polynomial matrices reachable from one another by such operations should count as the same. As over a field (@def-equivalent-matrices), the clean way to say this is with invertible matrices on both sides — but “invertible” must now mean invertible inside M_n(F[x]). [Invertible Polynomial Matrices] Let \U \in M_n(F[x]). Then \U has an inverse in M_n(F[x]) if and only if \det \U is a non-zero constant. (\Rightarrow) Suppose \U \W = \I with \W \in M_n(F[x]). Taking determinants and using multiplicativity over the commutative ring F[x] (@thm-det-multiplicative and the remark on commutative rings after it), \det \U \cdot \det \W = 1. By @thm-degree-of-product, \deg(\det \U) + \deg(\det \W) = \deg 1 = 0, and degrees of non-zero polynomials are \ge 0, so \deg(\det \U) = 0; that is, \det \U \in F \setminus\{0\}. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \det \U = c \in F \setminus\{0\}. The adjugate identity \U \adj \U = \adj \U\; \U = (\det \U)\,\I holds over any commutative ring (@thm-adjugate-identity and the remark on commutative rings following it), and \adj \U \in M_n(F[x]), since its entries are minors of \U. So \W = c^{-1}\adj \U \in M_n(F[x]) satisfies \U \W = \W \U = \I. [Equivalence over F\lbrack xbrack] Let \M, \M' \in M_n(F[x]). We say \M and \M' are equivalent over F[x], written \M \approx \M', if there are \U, \V \in M_n(F[x]), each invertible in M_n(F[x]), with \M' = \U \M \V . [Operations and Equivalence] Let \M, \M' \in M_n(F[x]). 1. \approx is an equivalence relation on M_n(F[x]). 2. If \M' is obtained from \M by a finite sequence of elementary row and column operations over F[x], then \M \approx \M'. (a) Take \U = \V = \I for reflexivity. If \M' = \U \M \V, then \M = \U^{-1}\M'\V^{-1}, and \U^{-1}, \V^{-1} are invertible in M_n(F[x]); this gives symmetry. If \M' = \U \M \V and \M'' = \U'\M'\V', then \M'' = (\U'\U)\M(\V \V'), and a product of invertible matrices is invertible, which gives transitivity. (b) Each elementary row operation over F[x] is left multiplication by the matrix obtained by performing that operation on \I_n, exactly as over a field (@thm-row-op-is-left-multiplication, whose proof uses only the ring operations). Those three matrices are \P_{ij}, \D_i(c) and \I + h\E_{ij} with i 
e j, of determinants -1, c 
e 0 and 1 respectively (@thm-det-triangular and @thm-det-row-operations, valid over a commutative ring), hence invertible in M_n(F[x]) by @prp-polynomial-matrix-invertible. Column operations are right multiplication by the same matrices. Now use (a). Multiplying a row by a non-constant polynomial is not an allowed operation. It changes the answer. The matrix \M =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} becomes  egin{pmatrix} x & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} after “multiplying row 1 by x”, and the two are not equivalent: their determinants are 1 and x, and by @prp-polynomial-matrix-invertible the first is invertible over F[x] while the second is not. The rule to remember is that only the units of F[x] — the non-zero constants — may be used as scaling factors. The Smith normal form Every polynomial matrix can be brought to a diagonal form whose diagonal entries divide one another in turn, and that form is unique. The existence proof is Euclidean division, run on whichever non-zero entry has the smallest degree: if that entry fails to divide one of its neighbors in the same row or column, the remainder gives a non-zero entry of strictly smaller degree, and degrees cannot decrease forever. [Smith Normal Form] Let F be a field, n \ge 1 and \M \in M_n(F[x]). Then: 1. (Existence) \M is equivalent over F[x], by a finite sequence of elementary row and column operations, to a diagonal matrix \D = \diag(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n) in which every d_i is monic or zero and d_i \mid d_{i+1} for i = 1, \dots, n-1. 2. (Uniqueness) The list (d_1, \dots, d_n) is determined by \M: if \M \approx \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) \approx \diag(e_1, \dots, e_n) with both lists as in (a), then d_i = e_i for every i. The matrix \D is called the Smith normal form of \M, and d_1, \dots, d_n its invariant divisors. Since 0 \mid f holds only for f = 0, the divisibility chain forces the zero entries, if any, to be the last ones. Step roadmap for existence. ① Among all matrices reachable from \M by operations, pick one whose smallest non-zero entry degree is least, and move that entry to the corner. ② That corner entry f must divide every other entry of its row and column: otherwise divide with remainder and produce an entry of smaller degree, contradicting the choice in ①. ③ Clear the first row and column with f; the same remainder trick, after adding a row to the first one, shows f divides every entry of what is left. ④ Induct on the size. The divisibility d_1 \mid d_2 survives the induction because operations replace entries by F[x]-combinations of entries. For uniqueness, find a quantity that can be read off both \M and \D. The greatest common divisor of all k 	imes k minors is such a quantity: minors of a product are F[x]-combinations of minors of the factors (Cauchy–Binet), so the gcd cannot change under equivalence, and for a diagonal matrix with a divisibility chain it is simply d_1d_2\cdots d_k. (a) If \M = 0, it is already of the stated form. So assume \M 
e 0. For a non-zero \N \in M_n(F[x]) put \delta(\N) \coloneqq \min\{\, \deg n_{ij} : n_{ij} 
e 0 \,\} \in 
N , the least degree of a non-zero entry. Let \cS be the set of all non-zero matrices obtainable from \M by finite sequences of elementary row and column operations over F[x]; it contains \M. The set \{\delta(\N) : \N \in \cS\} is a non-empty subset of 
N, so it has a least element; fix \N \in \cS with \delta(\N) least. Step 1. Put a least-degree entry in the corner, monic. Choose (i, j) with n_{ij} 
e 0 and \deg n_{ij} = \delta(\N). Swapping row i with row 1 and column j with column 1 (operations (E1)), and then scaling the new first row by the inverse of the leading coefficient of the corner entry (operation (E2)), we obtain a matrix in \cS whose (1,1)-entry f is monic of degree \delta(\N). These operations permute the entries and rescale some of them, so the new matrix still has least non-zero entry degree \delta(\N). Rename it \N. Step 2. f divides every entry of the first row and the first column. Suppose f 
mid n_{1j} for some j \ge 2. By @thm-polynomial-division, n_{1j} = qf + r with r 
e 0 and \deg r < \deg f. Adding -q times column 1 to column j (operation (E3)) produces a matrix \N' \in \cS whose (1, j)-entry is r 
e 0 with \deg r < \deg f = \delta(\N). Then \delta(\N') < \delta(\N), contradicting the minimality of \delta(\N). Hence f \mid n_{1j} for every j, and the same argument with rows in place of columns gives f \mid n_{i1} for every i. Step 3. Clear the first row and column. For j \ge 2 add -(n_{1j}/f) times column 1 to column j; the multipliers are polynomials by Step 2, and after these operations the first row is (f, 0, \dots, 0) while the first column is unchanged. Then for i \ge 2 add -(n_{i1}/f) times row 1 to row i; since the first row is now (f, 0, \dots, 0), this clears the first column and changes nothing else. The result is  egin{pmatrix} f & 0 \ 0 & \M' \end{pmatrix} \in \cS, \qquad \M' \in M_{n-1}(F[x]), and its least non-zero entry degree is still \delta(\N): it is \ge \delta(\N) by minimality, and f is an entry of degree \delta(\N). Step 4. f divides every entry of \M'. Suppose f 
mid (\M')_{kl} for some k, l. Add row k+1 to row 1. The new first row is  igl(f, (\M')_{k1}, \dots, (\M')_{k,n-1} igr), so the (1, l+1)-entry of the resulting matrix \N'' \in \cS is (\M')_{kl}, which is not divisible by f, while the (1,1)-entry is still f, monic of degree \delta(\N). By minimality \delta(\N'') = \delta(\N), so Step 2 applies to \N'' and says that f divides every entry of the first row of \N'' — a contradiction. Step 5. Induct on n. We prove (a) by induction on n. For n = 1, scale the single entry to be monic (or leave it 0). For n \ge 2, Steps 1–4 give a sequence of operations taking \M to f \oplus \M' with f monic and f dividing every entry of \M'. By the induction hypothesis there are operations taking \M' to \D' = \diag(d_2, \dots, d_n) with every d_i monic or zero and d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_n; performing the corresponding operations on rows and columns 2, \dots, n of f \oplus \M' takes it to f \oplus \D' = \diag(f, d_2, \dots, d_n). It remains to see that f \mid d_2. By @prp-operations-are-equivalence, \D' = \U'\M'\V' for some \U', \V' \in M_{n-1}(F[x]), so every entry of \D' is a sum of products u'_{ik}(\M')_{kl}v'_{lj} (@def-matrix-multiplication) and is therefore divisible by f, since every (\M')_{kl} is. In particular f \mid d_2. Setting d_1 = f finishes the induction. (b) Call a set I \subseteq [n] with |I| = k a k-set. For \M \in M_n(F[x]) and 1 \le k \le n define the k-th determinantal divisor \Delta_k(\M) \coloneqq 	ext{the monic generator of the ideal }  ig\langle\, \det \M_{I,J} : I, J \ k	ext{-sets} \, igangle \subseteq F[x], and \Delta_k(\M) \coloneqq 0 if all the k 	imes k minors of \M vanish. This is well defined by @prp-ideal-generated and @thm-ideals-principal: the ideal generated by the finitely many k 	imes k minors is \langle \Delta_k(\M)angle for exactly one monic \Delta_k(\M) unless the ideal is \{0\}. Equivalently, \Delta_k(\M) is the monic greatest common divisor of the k 	imes k minors: it divides each of them, and every common divisor of them divides it (@thm-gcd-properties, extended from two polynomials to finitely many by the same ideal argument). Claim 1. \M \approx \M' implies \Delta_k(\M) = \Delta_k(\M') for every k. Let \M' = \U \M \V with \U, \V invertible over F[x], and let I, J be k-sets. The submatrix of a product on rows I and columns J is the product of the submatrix of the left factor on rows I and all columns with the submatrix of the right factor on all rows and columns J (@def-matrix-multiplication, read off entry by entry). Applying this twice and then @thm-cauchy-binet over the commutative ring F[x] — legitimate by the remark after that theorem — to the k 	imes n times n 	imes k products involved, \det \M'_{I,J} = \sum_{S} \det \U_{I,S} \, \det (\M \V)_{S,J} = \sum_{S} \sum_{R} \det \U_{I,S}\, \det \M_{S,R}\, \det \V_{R,J}, with S and R running over the k-sets. So every k 	imes k minor of \M' is an F[x]-combination of k 	imes k minors of \M, hence lies in \langle \det \M_{S,R} angle. Therefore \Delta_k(\M) divides every k 	imes k minor of \M', and so \Delta_k(\M) \mid \Delta_k(\M'). Exchanging the roles of \M and \M' using \M = \U^{-1}\M'\V^{-1} gives \Delta_k(\M') \mid \Delta_k(\M). Two monic polynomials dividing each other are equal (@prp-divisibility-properties), and if one is 0 so is the other. Claim 2. If \D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) with d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_n, then \Delta_k(\D) = d_1d_2\cdots d_k. Let I, J be k-sets. If I 
e J, pick i \in I \setminus J; row i of \D has its only possibly non-zero entry in column i 
otin J, so the submatrix \D_{I,J} has a zero row and \det \D_{I,J} = 0. If I = J = \{i_1 < \dots < i_k\}, then \D_{I,I} = \diag(d_{i_1}, \dots, d_{i_k}) and \det \D_{I,I} = d_{i_1}\cdots d_{i_k} (@thm-det-triangular, valid over the commutative ring F[x] by the remark after it). Since i_j \ge j, the chain gives d_j \mid d_{i_j} for each j, hence d_1d_2\cdots d_k \mid d_{i_1}d_{i_2}\cdots d_{i_k} . So d_1 \cdots d_k divides every k 	imes k minor of \D, and it is itself the minor for I = J = \{1, \dots, k\}. Hence the ideal generated by the k 	imes k minors is \langle d_1\cdots d_k angle. If d_1\cdots d_k 
e 0 it is monic, being a product of monic polynomials, and equals \Delta_k(\D). If d_1 \cdots d_k = 0, say d_m = 0 with m \le k, then for every k-set I we have i_k \ge k \ge m, so d_m \mid d_{i_k} forces d_{i_k} = 0 and the minor vanishes; thus \Delta_k(\D) = 0 = d_1\cdots d_k. Now let \M \approx \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) with the d_i as in (a). By Claims 1 and 2, \Delta_k(\M) = d_1d_2\cdots d_k \qquad (k = 1, \dots, n), a quantity depending only on \M. Reading this backwards recovers the d_i: first d_1 = \Delta_1(\M); and for k \ge 2, if \Delta_{k-1}(\M) 
e 0 then d_k = \Delta_k(\M)/\Delta_{k-1}(\M), while if \Delta_{k-1}(\M) = 0 then d_1\cdots d_{k-1} = 0, so some d_m = 0 with m \le k - 1, and the chain forces d_k = 0. Hence any second list (e_1, \dots, e_n) as in (a) satisfies the same recipe and equals (d_1, \dots, d_n). This proves the theorem. The proof is an algorithm, and it is the one to use by hand: hunt for the entry of least degree, divide, and repeat. Smith normal form of \M \in M_n(F[x]). 1. If \M = 0, stop. Otherwise find a non-zero entry of least degree and move it to position (1,1) by a row and a column swap; scale row 1 so that the entry is monic. Call it f. 2. For each other entry g in row 1 or column 1 with f 
mid g, replace g by its remainder on division by f (subtract a multiple of column 1, resp. row 1), move the remainder to the corner, and go back to step 1. 3. When f divides all of row 1 and column 1, clear them. If some entry g of the remaining block is not divisible by f, add its row to row 1 and go back to step 2. 4. Hence \Delta_1 = 1, \qquad \Delta_2 = 1 \ \ (	ext{from } (-1)(-1) = 1), \qquad \Delta_3 = x^{2}, \qquad \Delta_4 = x^{4}, so the Smith normal form is \diag(1, 1, x^2, x^2), the invariant factors are x^2 \mid x^2, m_{\A} = x^2 is the last of them, and the Jordan form is \J_2(0) \oplus \J_2(0). (b) Now x\I - \A = \N_3 \oplus (x) with \N_3 =  egin{pmatrix} x & -1 & 0 \ 0 & x & -1 \ 0 & 0 & x\end{pmatrix}. The minors of \N_3 are \{x, -1, 0\} for k = 1; \{x^2, -x, 1, 0\} for k = 2, the value 1 coming from rows \{1,2\} and columns \{2,3\}; and x^3 for k = 3. By the remark, the k 	imes k minors of x\I - \A are those of \N_3 together with x times its (k-1) 	imes (k-1) minors, so [ ] The Smith normal form is \diag(1, 1, x, x^3): the invariant factors are x \mid x^3, m_{\A} = x^3 is the last of them, and the Jordan form is \J_3(0) \oplus \J_1(0). Compared with (a) the determinants agree but \Delta_3 does not, which is exactly why the two matrices are not similar. (c) x\I - \A =  egin{pmatrix} x - 3 & -1 \ 0 & x-3\end{pmatrix}. Then \Delta_1 = 1 and \Delta_2 = (x-3)^2, so the Smith normal form is \diag(1, (x-3)^2), the only invariant factor is (x-3)^2 = m_{\A} = p_{\A}, and the Jordan form is \J_2(3). Consistently, \A is a companion matrix up to similarity, since m_{\A} = p_{\A} (@thm-cyclic-iff-min-equals-char). [B3: Deciding similarity] Determine whether each pair is similar over the stated field. Justify your answer using @thm-similar-iff-xi-minus-a-equivalent. 1. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix} over 
Q. 2. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -2 \ 1 & 2 & -2 \ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} and \B = \J_2(1) \oplus \J_1(1) over 
Q. 3. \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} and \B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 2 & 0\end{pmatrix} over 
Q. (a) Similar. Here \B = \A	p, so @cor-a-similar-to-transpose applies. (Explicitly, \Delta_1 = 1 and \Delta_2 = x^2 + 1 for both, so both Smith normal forms are \diag(1, x^2+1).) (b) Similar. By @exm-smith-form-3x3 the Smith normal form of x\I - \A is \diag(1, x-1, (x-1)^2). For \B, x\I - \B =  egin{pmatrix} x-1 & -1 \ 0 & x-1\end{pmatrix} \oplus (x-1). Its entry -1 gives \Delta_1 = 1. By the block-minor rule in the solution to @exr-smith-normal-form-b2, the 2 	imes 2 minors are (x-1)^2, from the 2 	imes 2 block, together with the products of a 1 	imes 1 minor of each block, that is (x-1)^2, -(x-1) and 0; so \Delta_2 = x - 1. Finally \Delta_3 = \det(x\I - \B) = (x-1)^3. The Smith normal forms agree, so x\I - \A \approx x\I - \B and \A \sim \B. (c) Similar. Here x\I - \A =  egin{pmatrix} x & 2 \ -1 & x\end{pmatrix}, \qquad x\I - \B =  egin{pmatrix} x & 1 \ -2 & x\end{pmatrix}, and each has an entry that is a non-zero constant, so \Delta_1 = 1 in both cases; and \Delta_2 = \det(x\I - \A) = x^2 + 2 = \det(x\I - \B). So both Smith normal forms are \diag(1, x^2+2), hence x\I - \A \approx x\I - \B and \A \sim \B by @thm-similar-iff-xi-minus-a-equivalent. Note that x^2 + 2 is irreducible over 
Q, so no Jordan form exists over 
Q and @exr-jordan-canonical-form-c1 would not have decided this pair. (Here \B 
e \A	p, so @cor-a-similar-to-transpose does not apply directly; the Smith forms settle it anyway.) C. Going deeper [C1: The same algorithm over the integers] The proof of @thm-smith-normal-form used only one property of F[x]: division with remainder, where the “size” of a non-zero element is its degree. The integers 
Z have the same property, with |a| in place of \deg. 1. State the version of @thm-smith-normal-form for \M \in M_n(
Z) that the same proof gives, saying what replaces “monic”. 2. Compute the Smith normal form over 
Z of \M =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \ 6 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, naming the operations. 3. Every finite abelian group G with n generators is 
Z^n modulo the column span of some \M \in M_n(
Z), the matrix of relations, exactly as V was F[x]^n modulo the columns of x\I - \A. Using (b), identify the group with relation matrix \M as a product of cyclic groups. Hint: for (c), a diagonal relation matrix \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) presents the product of the cyclic groups 
Z/d_i
Z. (a) Every \M \in M_n(
Z) can be brought by integer elementary operations — swap two rows or columns, multiply a row or column by \pm 1 (the units of 
Z), add an integer multiple of one row or column to another — to a diagonal matrix \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) with every d_i \ge 0 and d_i \mid d_{i+1}, and this diagonal is unique. “Monic” is replaced by “non-negative”, which is the normalization available because the units of 
Z are \pm 1. Uniqueness again follows from the determinantal divisors \Delta_k, now non-negative integer gcds of the k 	imes k minors, using the Cauchy–Binet formula over the commutative ring 
Z. (b) The least absolute value among the entries is 2, already in the corner. It divides 4 and 6. Subtract 2 times column 1 from column 2, and 3 times row 1 from row 2:  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \ 6 & 4\end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 6 & -8 \end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & -8\end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix}, the last step multiplying row 2 by -1. Since 2 \mid 8, the Smith normal form is \diag(2, 8). Check: \Delta_1 = \gcd(2,4,6,4) = 2 and \Delta_2 = |\det \M| = |8 - 24| = 16 = 2 \cdot 8. (c) By (b) and the hint, the group is 
Z/2
Z 	imes 
Z/8
Z, of order 16 = |\det \M|. This is the structure theorem for finite abelian groups in miniature: the invariant divisors d_1 \mid \dots \mid d_n of the relation matrix are the orders of the cyclic factors. [C2: Uniqueness by hand in the smallest case] Let \M \in M_2(F[x]) be non-zero. 1. Prove directly, without using determinantal divisors, that \Delta_1(\M) — the monic gcd of the four entries of \M — is unchanged by each of the six elementary operations of @def-polynomial-elementary-operations. 2. Prove that \det(\U \M \V) = c\det \M for a non-zero constant c whenever \U, \V are invertible over F[x]. 3. Deduce that if \diag(d_1, d_2) \approx \diag(e_1, e_2) with all four entries monic or zero, d_1 \mid d_2 and e_1 \mid e_2, then d_1 = e_1 and d_2 = e_2. (a) Write d = \Delta_1(\M), the monic gcd of the entries, that is, the monic generator of the ideal \langle m_{11}, m_{12}, m_{21}, m_{22}angle (@thm-ideals-principal). A swap permutes the entries, so the ideal is unchanged. Scaling a row by c \in F\setminus\{0\} replaces two generators g by cg, and \langle cg angle = \langle g angle since c is a unit, so the ideal is unchanged. Adding h times row 1 to row 2 replaces m_{2j} by m_{2j} + hm_{1j}, which lies in the old ideal; so the new ideal is contained in the old one, and the operation is reversed by adding -h times row 1 to row 2, which gives the reverse containment. The same three arguments apply to columns. Hence d is unchanged. (b) By multiplicativity of the determinant over the commutative ring F[x] (@thm-det-multiplicative and the remark on commutative rings), \det(\U \M \V) = \det \U \cdot \det \M \cdot \det \V, and \det \U, \det \V are non-zero constants by @prp-polynomial-matrix-invertible. Take c = \det \U \det \V. (c) By @prp-operations-are-equivalence and (a), \Delta_1 is an invariant of equivalence as far as elementary operations go; and for a general equivalence \M' = \U \M \V the argument of (a) applies verbatim with the generators of the ideal replaced using m'_{ij} = \sum_{k,l} u_{ik}m_{kl}v_{lj} \in \langle m_{kl}angle, and symmetrically. For the two diagonal matrices, \Delta_1(\diag(d_1,d_2)) = \gcd(d_1, d_2) = d_1 since d_1 \mid d_2 and d_1 is monic (or d_1 = d_2 = 0); likewise \Delta_1(\diag(e_1,e_2)) = e_1. Hence d_1 = e_1. By (b), d_1d_2 = c\,e_1e_2 for some non-zero constant c; if d_1 = e_1 
e 0 then d_2 = c\,e_2, and two monic polynomials (or two zeros) differing by a constant factor are equal, so d_2 = e_2. If d_1 = e_1 = 0, then d_2 = e_2 = 0 by the divisibility chain.

title: 9.8 Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition
content:
Semisimple Operators and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition The Jordan canonical form says that an operator whose characteristic polynomial splits is “a diagonal matrix plus a nilpotent one” — but only after a basis has been chosen. This section turns that sentence into a statement about the operator itself: T = S + N with S diagonalizable, N nilpotent and, crucially, SN = NS; and there is exactly one such pair. Before that we need a name for the operators that deserve to be called diagonalizable even when the field is too small to see it. Diagonalizable once the field is big enough Two operators fail to be diagonalizable for completely different reasons. The rotation \R =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R) has p_{\R} = m_{\R} = x^2 + 1, with no real root, so it has no eigenvectors at all (@exm-complex-eigenvalues-real-matrix). Yet over 
C it becomes \diag(i, -i): the operator was fine, the field was too small. The shear \J_2(0) has m = x^2 and is not diagonalizable over any field, however large: its single eigenvalue 0 has a = 2 and g = 1, and enlarging the field changes neither. What separates the two cases is visible in the minimal polynomial. For \R it is x^2 + 1, irreducible over 
R and appearing to the first power. For \J_2(0) it is x^2, the square of the irreducible x. Chapter 8 proved that T is diagonalizable exactly when m_T is a product of distinct linear factors (@thm-diagonalizable-iff-minimal-distinct-linear). Deleting the word “linear” from that criterion gives the notion we want. A semisimple operator is one whose minimal polynomial is squarefree: no irreducible factor is repeated. [Semisimple Operator] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with \dim V \ge 1, and let T \in \cL(V). We say T is semisimple if m_T = p_1p_2\cdots p_k for distinct monic irreducible p_1, \dots, p_k \in F[x]; equivalently, if no irreducible polynomial p \in F[x] satisfies p^2 \mid m_T. A matrix \A \in M_n(F) is semisimple over F if T_{\A} is. In words: factor m_T into irreducibles over F (@thm-unique-factorization-polynomials). Semisimplicity says every exponent in that factorization is 1. The two descriptions agree: the exponents are all 1 exactly when no p^2 divides m_T, by uniqueness of factorization. Note the dependence on the field, which is built into the word “irreducible over F”. Examples. - Diagonalizable operators. If T is diagonalizable, m_T is a product of distinct linear factors (@thm-diagonalizable-iff-minimal-distinct-linear), and linear polynomials are irreducible (@def-irreducible-polynomial). So T is semisimple. - The rotation. \R \in M_2(
R) above has m_{\R} = x^2 + 1, irreducible over 
R since it has no real root (@thm-irreducible-deg-2-3). One factor, exponent 1: semisimple over 
R, though not diagonalizable over 
R. - Any operator with irreducible minimal polynomial, for the same reason. In particular the companion matrix \C(p) of an irreducible p is semisimple, since m_{\C(p)} = p (@thm-companion-char-min). - The degenerate case. On a space of dimension 1, T = \lambda\,\id_V has m_T = x - \lambda: semisimple. So is \id_V on any V, with m = x - 1. Non-example by minimal change. Over 
R, replace m = x^2 + 1 by m = (x^2+1)^2: the companion matrix \C igl((x^2+1)^2 igr) \in M_4(
R) has m = (x^2+1)^2 (@thm-companion-char-min), so the irreducible x^2 + 1 is repeated and the matrix is not semisimple. The clause that fails is “distinct”: there is one irreducible factor, but it occurs twice. Why this definition. The word simple names the case in which V has no T-invariant subspace except \{\0\} and V. That happens exactly when m_T is irreducible and \dim V = \deg m_T, for then every non-zero \v has T-annihilator m_T and so Z(\v; T) = V (@thm-cyclic-subspace-basis). Semisimple then means “a direct sum of simple pieces”, which is what @thm-primary-decomposition followed by a cyclic decomposition (@thm-cyclic-decomposition) delivers. The definition is the right one because it is exactly diagonalizability after the field has been enlarged enough to split m_T — provided the field is not pathological. Making that precise needs one small fact: the minimal polynomial does not change when the field grows. [The Minimal Polynomial Does Not Notice a Larger Field] Let K \subseteq L be fields and \A \in M_n(K), n \ge 1. Then the minimal polynomial of \A computed in K[x] equals the minimal polynomial of \A computed in L[x]. The degree of m_{\A} is the position of the first linear dependence in the list \I, \A, \A^2, \dots (@prp-minimal-polynomial-first-dependence). Whether a list of matrices with entries in K is dependent is decided by row reducing one matrix with entries in K, and row reduction does not care that a bigger field is available. Write m^K and m^L for the two minimal polynomials, and d = \deg m^K, e = \deg m^L. Since m^K \in K[x] \subseteq L[x] annihilates \A, @thm-minimal-polynomial-divides gives m^L \mid m^K, so e \le d. For the reverse inequality, list the entries of \I, \A, \dots, \A^{e} as the columns of a matrix \B \in M_{n^2 	imes (e+1)}(K), one column per power. A linear combination \sum_{i=0}^{e} c_i\A^i is the zero matrix exactly when \B\c = \0 for \c = (c_0, \dots, c_e). By @prp-minimal-polynomial-first-dependence applied over L, the list (\I, \A, \dots, \A^{e}) is dependent over L, so \B\c = \0 has a non-trivial solution in L^{e+1}, and hence ank_L \B < e + 1 (@thm-rank-nullity-matrix). Now reduce \B to reduced row echelon form by row operations performed inside K (@thm-rref-exists); the resulting matrix \R has entries in K, and the definition of reduced row echelon form (@def-reduced-row-echelon-form) makes no reference to the field, so \R is also the reduced row echelon form of \B over L, by the uniqueness in @thm-rref-unique. The rank is the number of pivots of \R (@cor-rank-from-any-echelon-form), a number read off \R alone. Hence ank_K \B = ank_L \B < e + 1 , so \B\c = \0 has a non-trivial solution in K^{e+1} as well. That solution gives a non-zero f \in K[x] of degree at most e with f(\A) = 0, whence d = \deg m^K \le e by @thm-minimal-polynomial-divides and @prp-divisibility-properties. So d = e, and m^L \mid m^K with both monic of the same degree forces m^L = m^K. [Semisimple Means Diagonalizable After Enlarging the Field] Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let \A \in M_n(K) with n \ge 1, and let L \supseteq K be a field over which m_{\A} splits. Then \A 	ext{ is semisimple over } K \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \A 	ext{ is diagonalizable over } L . By @lem-minimal-polynomial-field-extension the minimal polynomial is the same polynomial m = m_{\A} whether computed over K or over L. By @thm-diagonalizable-iff-minimal-distinct-linear, \A is diagonalizable over L if and only if m is a product of distinct linear factors in L[x], that is, if and only if m splits over L — which it does by hypothesis — with no repeated root. (\Leftarrow) Suppose m has no repeated root in L. If some irreducible p \in K[x] satisfied m = p^2h, then p \mid m and m splits over L, so p has a root \lambda \in L; by @thm-multiplicity-of-product, \operatorname{mult}_\lambda(m) \ge 2\operatorname{mult}_\lambda(p) \ge 2, and \lambda would be a repeated root of m. So no such p exists and \A is semisimple over K. (\Rightarrow) Suppose m = p_1\cdots p_k with p_1, \dots, p_k \in K[x] distinct monic irreducibles. The formal derivative is computed from the coefficients (@def-formal-derivative), so each p_i' is the same polynomial whether read in K[x] or in L[x]. No p_i has a repeated root in L. Since K has characteristic 0 and \deg p_i \ge 1, the derivative p_i' is non-zero of degree \deg p_i - 1, so p_i 
mid p_i'; as p_i is irreducible, @lem-irreducible-gcd gives \gcd(p_i, p_i') = 1, and by @cor-bezout-polynomials there are a, b \in K[x] with ap_i + bp_i' = 1. If \lambda \in L were a repeated root of p_i, then p_i(\lambda) = p_i'(\lambda) = 0 by @thm-repeated-root-derivative (a), applied in L[x]; evaluating the identity at \lambda would give 1 = 0. No two p_i share a root in L. For i 
e j, a monic divisor of the irreducible p_j is 1 or p_j, so p_i 
mid p_j, and @lem-irreducible-gcd gives \gcd(p_i, p_j) = 1. Again by @cor-bezout-polynomials, ap_i + bp_j = 1 for some a, b \in K[x], and a common root in L would give 1 = 0. Therefore, by @thm-multiplicity-of-product, every root of m in L has multiplicity 1: it is a root of exactly one p_i, and a simple one. So m is a product of distinct linear factors over L, and \A is diagonalizable over L. A field over which every irreducible polynomial has distinct roots in a splitting field is called perfect. The proof above shows that every field of characteristic 0 is perfect, and every finite field is perfect as well, although that needs an argument we do not give here. Over a non-perfect field @prp-semisimple-iff-diagonalizable-over-extension can fail: in characteristic p there are irreducible polynomials of the form q(x^p), whose derivative vanishes identically and which acquire repeated roots in a splitting field. Everything in the rest of this section takes place over a field where p_T splits, so this subtlety will not arise again. Over 
Q, which of \A = \C(x^2+1) \oplus \C(x^2+1) \in M_4(
Q) and \B = \C igl((x^2+1)^2 igr) \in M_4(
Q) is semisimple? Is either diagonalizable over 
Q? \A is semisimple. Each block has minimal polynomial x^2 + 1 (@thm-companion-char-min), so m_{\A} = \operatorname{lcm}(x^2+1, x^2+1) = x^2+1 (@prp-minimal-polynomial-block-diagonal), an irreducible polynomial to the first power. \B is not: m_{\B} = (x^2+1)^2 repeats the irreducible x^2+1. Neither is diagonalizable over 
Q, since x^2+1 has no rational root, so neither minimal polynomial is a product of linear factors. Over 
C, however, \A becomes \diag(i, -i, i, -i), while \B becomes \J_2(i) \oplus \J_2(-i), which is not diagonal. Splitting an operator in two Here is the goal. When p_T splits, T is the sum of a diagonalizable operator and a nilpotent operator that commute, in exactly one way, and both summands are polynomials in T. The Jordan form already shows a splitting: in a Jordan basis, \J = \D + \M where \D is the diagonal of \J and \M carries the superdiagonal ones, and these commute because \D is constant on each block. What the theorem adds is that the two pieces do not depend on which Jordan basis was used, and that they can be written down without finding one. [Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition] Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F with \dim V = n \ge 1, and let T \in \cL(V) with p_T split over F. Then: 1. (Existence) There are S, N \in \cL(V) with T = S + N, \qquad S 	ext{ diagonalizable}, \qquad N 	ext{ nilpotent}, \qquad SN = NS ; moreover S = g(T) and N = h(T) for some g, h \in F[x]. 2. (Uniqueness) If T = S' + N' with S' diagonalizable, N' nilpotent and S'N' = N'S', then S' = S and N' = N. We call S the semisimple part and N the nilpotent part of T. Existence. The generalized eigenspace decomposition already puts the answer in front of us: on G_\lambda the operator is \lambda\,\id + 	ext{nilpotent}. Declare S to be \lambda\,\id on G_\lambda for each \lambda and let N be the rest. Then S is diagonalizable because a basis assembled from bases of the G_\lambda consists of eigenvectors of S, and N is nilpotent because it is nilpotent on each piece. That S and N are polynomials in T is the extra information carried by the primary decomposition: its projections are h_i(T). Uniqueness. A second decomposition S' + N' has S' commuting with T, hence with every polynomial in T, hence with S and with N; the same for N'. Then S - S' = N' - N is simultaneously diagonalizable and nilpotent, and the only such operator is 0. (a) Let \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k be the distinct eigenvalues of T and write m_T = (x - \lambda_1)^{s_1}\cdots(x - \lambda_k)^{s_k}, \qquad G_i = G_{\lambda_i}(T), as in @thm-generalized-eigenspace-decomposition, so that V = G_1 \oplus \dots \oplus G_k with G_i = \ker(T - \lambda_i\,\id_V)^{s_i}. The factors (x - \lambda_i)^{s_i} are exactly the primary factors of m_T, since x - \lambda_i is irreducible, so G_i is the i-th primary component of @thm-primary-decomposition. By part (d) of that theorem there are h_1, \dots, h_k \in F[x] such that \pi_i \coloneqq h_i(T) \in \cL(V) is the projection onto G_i along  igoplus_{j 
e i}G_j. Put  egin{aligned} g &\coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_ih_i \in F[x], \ S &\coloneqq g(T) = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i\pi_i, \ N &\coloneqq T - S = h(T) 	ext{ with } h = x - g . \end{aligned} S is diagonalizable. Fix i and \v \in G_i. Then \pi_i\v = \v and \pi_j\v = \0 for j 
e i (@thm-projection-direct-sum), so S\v = \lambda_i\v. Choose a basis of each G_i and let \sB be the concatenation, a basis of V because V =  igoplus_iG_i. Every vector of \sB is an eigenvector of S, so [S]_{\sB} is diagonal and S is diagonalizable (@thm-diagonalization). N is nilpotent. Fix i and \v \in G_i. Then N\v = T\v - \lambda_i\v = (T - \lambda_i\,\id_V)\v, which lies in G_i because G_i is T-invariant, so by induction N^j\v = (T - \lambda_i\,\id_V)^j\v for every j \ge 0. With s = \max_i s_i we get N^{s}\v = (T - \lambda_i\,\id_V)^{s}\v = \0, since (T - \lambda_i\,\id_V)^{s_i}\v = \0 and s \ge s_i. As every \v \in V is a sum of such vectors, N^{s} = 0 and N is nilpotent (@def-nilpotent). They commute. Both S = g(T) and N = h(T) are polynomials in T, and any two polynomials in T commute (@thm-evaluation-homomorphism (c)). This proves (a). (b) Suppose T = S' + N' as stated. First, S' commutes with T: S'T = S'(S' + N') = S'S' + S'N' = S'S' + N'S' = (S' + N')S' = TS' , where the middle equality is the hypothesis S'N' = N'S'. Hence S' commutes with every power of T and so with every polynomial in T, in particular with S = g(T) and N = h(T). The same computation gives N'T = TN', so N' too commutes with S and N. Now set X \coloneqq S - S'. From S + N = T = S' + N' we get X = S - S' = N' - N . The operators S and S' are diagonalizable and commute, so they are simultaneously diagonalizable (@thm-simultaneous-diagonalization): there is a basis \sC in which [S]_{\sC} and [S']_{\sC} are both diagonal. Then [X]_{\sC} = [S]_{\sC} - [S']_{\sC} is diagonal, so X is diagonalizable. On the other hand N and N' are nilpotent and commute, hence so do N' and -N, and X = N' + (-N) is nilpotent by @exr-commuting-operators-c2 (b), whose binomial argument uses only that the two summands commute and so applies verbatim to operators. So X is diagonalizable and nilpotent. Being nilpotent, \spec(X) = \{0\} (@prp-nilpotent-basic (c)); being diagonalizable, [X]_{\sD} is diagonal with the eigenvalues of X on the diagonal for some basis \sD (@thm-diagonalization), so [X]_{\sD} = 0 and X = 0. Hence S' = S and, subtracting from T, N' = N. This proves the theorem. Splitting a matrix into its diagonal part and its off-diagonal part is not the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}, the “obvious” split is \D = \diag(1, 2) plus \E =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. Here \D is diagonal and \E is nilpotent, but \D \E =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} 
e  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \E \D , so the commuting requirement fails, and the split is not the one the theorem produces. Indeed \A has distinct eigenvalues, so it is diagonalizable (@cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable) and its actual decomposition is \S = \A, \N = 0. The off-diagonal part of a matrix is a feature of the basis; the nilpotent part is a feature of the operator. The formulas in the proof are also the recipe: build the projections \pi_i onto the generalized eigenspaces — by Bézout, as in @exm-primary-decomposition — and set S = \sum_i\lambda_i\pi_i. [The Semisimple and Nilpotent Parts of a 3 	imes 3 Matrix] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 & -1 \ -1 & 3 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
Q), \qquad p_{\A} = (x - 2)^2(x - 3). Find the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition \A = \S + \N, and exhibit \S and \N as polynomials in \A. The minimal polynomial. Put \B = \A - 2\I =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & -1 \ -1 & 1 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}. Then \B(\A - 3\I) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & -1 \ -1 & 1 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & 0\end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & -1 \ -1 & -1 & -1\end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 & -1 \ 1 & -1 & 1 \ 2 & -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} 
e 0, so m_{\A} 
e (x-2)(x-3); since m_{\A} \mid p_{\A} and m_{\A} has both 2 and 3 as roots (@thm-minimal-polynomial-roots), m_{\A} = (x-2)^2(x-3). The primary factors are (x-2)^2 and x - 3. Bézout. Dividing, (x-2)^2 = x^2 - 4x + 4 = (x-3)(x-1) + 1, so 1 \cdot (x-2)^2 - (x-1)(x-3) = 1 . Following @thm-kernel-splitting with p = (x-2)^2 and q = x-3: the projection onto \ker q(\A) = G_3(\A) along \ker p(\A) = G_2(\A) is \pi_3 = (\A - 2\I)^2 = \B^2, and \pi_2 = \I - \B^2. Compute. Squaring, \B^2 =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 3 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 1 & -3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 	ext{and } \B^3 = \B^2 	ext{ (as } \B^2(\B - \I) = 0). Hence  egin{aligned} \S = 2\pi_2 + 3\pi_3 &= 2\I + \B^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 \ 0 & 2 & 0 \ 1 & -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}, \ \N = \A - \S &= \B - \B^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \ -1 & 1 & -1 \ -2 & 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} The checks. First \S + \N = \A by construction. Next \N^2 = 0: reading the rows of \N as multiples of (1, -1, 1) shows that \N = \u\w	p with \u = (1, -1, -2) and \w = (1, -1, 1), and \w	p\u = 1 + 1 - 2 = 0, so \N^2 = \u(\w	p\u)\w	p = 0. Next \S is diagonalizable: (\S - 2\I)(\S - 3\I) = \B^2(\B^2 - \I) = \B^4 - \B^2 = 0, because \B^3 = \B^2 gives \B^4 = \B^2; so m_{\S} divides a product of distinct linear factors and \S is diagonalizable (@thm-diagonalizable-iff-minimal-distinct-linear). Finally \S \N = \N \S, since both are polynomials in \A: explicitly \S = 2\I + (\A-2\I)^2 and \N = (\A - 2\I) - (\A-2\I)^2, that is, [ ] As a cross-check, g + h = x, so g(\A) + h(\A) = \A; and 	r \S = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 = 2 + 2 + 3 is the sum of the eigenvalues of \A, while 	r \N = 1 + 1 - 2 = 0, as it must be for a nilpotent matrix (@prp-nilpotent-basic (c) and @thm-trace-det-eigenvalues). Two consequences are worth naming now. Because S and N are polynomials in T, every operator commuting with T automatically commutes with S and with N. And the decomposition is exactly what makes functions of matrices computable in the next section: any reasonable function f will satisfy f(T) = f(S + N) with the two parts handled separately, S by its eigenvalues and N by finitely many terms, since its powers stop. The splitting exists in greater generality. Over a perfect field, every T can be written uniquely as T = S + N with S semisimple in the sense of @def-semisimple-operator, N nilpotent and SN = NS; the proof runs through the primary decomposition of m_T into powers of general irreducibles instead of linear ones. We prove only the split case, which is all we use. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define a semisimple operator, and say how the definition specializes to Chapter 8’s criterion for diagonalizability. 2. State the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition Theorem, including all three conditions on S and N and the uniqueness clause. 3. True or false:  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R) is semisimple. Justify your answer. 4. True or false: if \A = \D + \E with \D the diagonal part of \A and \E the off-diagonal part, then \D is the semisimple part of \A. Justify your answer. 5. Which hypothesis of the uniqueness clause does the pair (\D, \E) of part (d) typically violate? 6. Why does every operator commuting with T commute with the semisimple part of T? (a) T is semisimple if m_T is a product of distinct monic irreducible polynomials over F (@def-semisimple-operator). Requiring those irreducibles to be linear gives @thm-diagonalizable-iff-minimal-distinct-linear, the criterion for diagonalizability. So diagonalizable \Rightarrow semisimple, and the converse holds when m_T splits. (b) If p_T splits, then T = S + N with S diagonalizable, N nilpotent and SN = NS; such S and N are unique, and both are polynomials in T (@thm-jordan-chevalley). (c) True. Its minimal polynomial is x^2 + 1, which has no real root and so is irreducible over 
R (@thm-irreducible-deg-2-3); one irreducible factor, exponent 1. (d) False. For \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} the semisimple part is \A itself, since \A is diagonalizable, whereas \D = \diag(1,2) 
e \A. (e) The commuting condition \D \E = \E \D; see the warning after @thm-jordan-chevalley. (f) Because S = g(T) for some polynomial g (@thm-jordan-chevalley (a)), and an operator commuting with T commutes with every power of T, hence with every polynomial in T. B. Practice [B1: Semisimple and nilpotent parts] For each matrix over 
Q, find the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition \A = \S + \N and express \S as a polynomial in \A. 1. \A_1 =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}. 2. \A_2 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}. 3. \A_3 =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. (a) m_{\A_1} = (x-3)^2, so there is one eigenvalue and G_3 = 
Q^2; the projection onto it is \I. Hence \S = 3\I and \N = \A_1 - 3\I =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, with \N^2 = 0. As a polynomial, \S = 3\I = g(\A_1) with g = 3 the constant polynomial. (Every scalar multiple of \I is diagonalizable, and \S commutes with everything.) (b) \A_2 has the distinct eigenvalues 1 and 3, so it is diagonalizable (@cor-distinct-eigenvalues-diagonalizable). By uniqueness, \S = \A_2 and \N = 0; here g = x. The naive split into \diag(1,3) and  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} is not the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition. (c) p_{\A_3} = (x-2)^2(x-5). Put \M = \A_3 - 2\I =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}. Then \M(\A_3 - 5\I) has (1,2)-entry -3 
e 0, so m_{\A_3} = (x-2)^2(x-5). Bézout: (x-2)^2 = (x-5)(x+1) + 9, so 	frac19(x-2)^2 - 	frac19(x+1)(x-5) = 1, and by @thm-kernel-splitting the projection onto G_5 along G_2 is \pi_5 = 	frac19 \M^2. Computing \M^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 9 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 9\end{pmatrix}, \S = 2\I + 3\pi_5 = 2\I + 	frac13\M^2 =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 3 \ 0 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 5\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \N = \A_3 - \S =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. Checks: \N^2 = 0; \S - 2\I has rank 1, so g_{\S}(2) = 2 = a_{\S}(2) and \S is diagonalizable (@thm-diagonalization); and \S \N =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & 0 \ 0&0&0\0&0&0\end{pmatrix} = \N \S. As a polynomial, \S = 2\I + 	frac13(\A_3 - 2\I)^2 = g(\A_3) with g = 	frac13x^2 - 	frac43x + 	frac{10}{3}. Note that \S keeps the entry 3 in position (1,3): the diagonal part of \A_3 is the wrong answer, and it does not commute with the rest, since \diag(2,2,5)(\A_3 - \diag(2,2,5)) and the reverse product differ in position (1,3) by -9. [B2: When is the nilpotent part zero?] Let V be finite-dimensional with \dim V \ge 1 and let T \in \cL(V) with p_T split, with Jordan–Chevalley decomposition T = S + N. Prove that N = 0 if and only if T is diagonalizable, and that S = 0 if and only if T is nilpotent. If N = 0, then T = S is diagonalizable. Conversely, if T is diagonalizable, then T = T + 0 is a decomposition into a diagonalizable and a nilpotent part that commute (T \cdot 0 = 0 = 0 \cdot T), so by the uniqueness in @thm-jordan-chevalley, S = T and N = 0. If S = 0, then T = N is nilpotent. Conversely, if T is nilpotent, then T = 0 + T is such a decomposition, since the zero operator is diagonalizable and commutes with T; uniqueness gives S = 0 and N = T. [B3: Block diagonal matrices] Let \A_1 \in M_p(F) and \A_2 \in M_q(F) have split characteristic polynomials, with Jordan–Chevalley decompositions \A_i = \S_i + \N_i. Prove that the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition of \A_1 \oplus \A_2 is \A_1 \oplus \A_2 = (\S_1 \oplus \S_2) + (\N_1 \oplus \N_2). Write \S = \S_1 \oplus \S_2 and \N = \N_1 \oplus \N_2. By @thm-block-diagonal-arithmetic (a), \S + \N = (\S_1 + \N_1) \oplus (\S_2 + \N_2) = \A_1 \oplus \A_2. Also p_{\A_1 \oplus \A_2} = p_{\A_1}p_{\A_2} splits (@thm-det-block-triangular, applied over F[x] as the remark after it allows), so @thm-jordan-chevalley applies to \A_1 \oplus \A_2 and it suffices, by uniqueness, to check the three conditions. \S is diagonalizable. Pick invertible \P_i with \P_i^{-1}\S_i\P_i diagonal. Then \P = \P_1 \oplus \P_2 is invertible with \P^{-1} = \P_1^{-1} \oplus \P_2^{-1}, and \P^{-1}\S\P = (\P_1^{-1}\S_1\P_1) \oplus (\P_2^{-1}\S_2\P_2) is diagonal (@thm-block-diagonal-arithmetic (a), (c)). \N is nilpotent. If \N_1^{a} = 0 and \N_2^{b} = 0, then \N^{\max(a,b)} = \N_1^{\max(a,b)} \oplus \N_2^{\max(a,b)} = 0 by @thm-block-diagonal-arithmetic (b). They commute. \S \N = (\S_1\N_1) \oplus (\S_2\N_2) = (\N_1\S_1) \oplus (\N_2\S_2) = \N \S, again by @thm-block-diagonal-arithmetic (a). By the uniqueness in @thm-jordan-chevalley, \S and \N are the semisimple and nilpotent parts of \A_1 \oplus \A_2. C. Going deeper [C1: The multiplicative version] Call U \in \cL(V) unipotent if U - \id_V is nilpotent. Let T \in \cL(V) be invertible with p_T split, and let T = S + N be its Jordan–Chevalley decomposition. 1. Prove that S is invertible. 2. Prove that S^{-1} commutes with N, and that S^{-1}N is nilpotent. 3. Deduce that T = SU with S diagonalizable, U unipotent and SU = US. 4. Prove that this multiplicative decomposition is unique: if T = S'U' with S' diagonalizable, U' unipotent and S'U' = U'S', then S' = S and U' = U. Hint: for (d), turn the multiplicative statement into an additive one by writing T = S' + S'(U' - \id_V). (a) By the proof of @thm-jordan-chevalley, S\v = \lambda_i\v for every \v \in G_{\lambda_i}(T), so \spec(S) = \spec(T) — a basis of eigenvectors of S with these eigenvalues was exhibited there. Since T is invertible, 0 
otin \spec(T) (@thm-invertible-tfae-eigen), so 0 
otin \spec(S) and S is invertible. (b) From SN = NS, multiply on both sides by S^{-1}: S^{-1}(SN)S^{-1} = S^{-1}(NS)S^{-1} gives NS^{-1} = S^{-1}N. Hence (S^{-1}N)^{j} = S^{-j}N^{j} for every j \ge 1, by induction using NS^{-1} = S^{-1}N. With N^{s} = 0 we get (S^{-1}N)^{s} = 0. (c) Put U = \id_V + S^{-1}N. Then SU = S + N = T, and U - \id_V = S^{-1}N is nilpotent by (b), so U is unipotent. They commute: SU = S + N = US, since S(S^{-1}N) = N = (S^{-1}N)S by (b). (d) Suppose T = S'U' with S' diagonalizable, U' unipotent and S'U' = U'S'. Put N' = S'(U' - \id_V), so that T = S' + N'. Then N' is nilpotent: S' commutes with U', hence with U' - \id_V, so (N')^{j} = (S')^{j}(U' - \id_V)^{j} = 0 once j is large. And S'N' = S'S'(U'-\id_V) = S'(U'-\id_V)S' = N'S'. So T = S' + N' satisfies the hypotheses of @thm-jordan-chevalley (b), giving S' = S and N' = N. Then U' - \id_V = (S')^{-1}N' = S^{-1}N = U - \id_V, so U' = U. [C2: The parts inherit every symmetry] Let V be finite-dimensional with \dim V \ge 1, let T \in \cL(V) with p_T split, and let T = S + N be its Jordan–Chevalley decomposition. 1. Prove that if X \in \cL(V) satisfies XT = TX, then XS = SX and XN = NX. 2. Deduce that every T-invariant subspace is S-invariant and N-invariant, and that S and N map each G_\lambda(T) into itself. 3. Give an example of a diagonalizable S and a nilpotent N with SN 
e NS for which S + N is not the operator whose semisimple part is S. (So the commuting hypothesis cannot be dropped from the uniqueness statement.) (a) By @thm-jordan-chevalley (a), S = g(T) and N = h(T) for some g, h \in F[x]. From XT = TX we get XT^{j} = T^{j}X for all j \ge 0 by induction, hence Xf(T) = f(T)X for every f \in F[x] by taking linear combinations. Applying this to f = g and f = h gives XS = SX and XN = NX. (b) Let U \subseteq V be T-invariant. Then U is T^{j}-invariant for every j, hence f(T)-invariant for every f \in F[x] (a sum of vectors of U lies in U); taking f = g, h gives that U is S- and N-invariant. In particular G_\lambda(T) = \ker(T - \lambda\,\id_V)^{n} is T-invariant (@cor-generalized-eigenspace-is-kernel (b)), so S and N map it into itself. (c) Take \S = \diag(1, 2) and \N =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} in M_2(
Q). Then \S is diagonal, \N^2 = 0, and \S \N =  egin{pmatrix} 0&1\0&0\end{pmatrix} 
e  egin{pmatrix} 0&2\0&0\end{pmatrix} = \N \S. Their sum \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} has distinct eigenvalues, so it is diagonalizable, and its semisimple part is \A itself, not \S, with nilpotent part 0, not \N (@exr-jordan-chevalley-b2). Without the commuting hypothesis, an operator can be written as “diagonalizable plus nilpotent” in many ways: for any c \in 
Q, \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & c \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} +  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 - c \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} is such a splitting, the first summand being diagonalizable because its eigenvalues 1, 2 are distinct.

title: 9.9 Functions of Matrices, the Exponential and Linear Differential Equations
content:
Functions of Matrices, the Exponential and Linear Differential Equations We have known since Chapter 3 what p(\A) means for a polynomial p. This section gives a meaning to f(\A) for a much larger class of functions — square roots, logarithms, sines, and above all e^{\A} — and the Jordan form is what makes it possible. The definition needs a well-definedness proof, which turns out to be Hermite interpolation from Chapter 5: whatever f is, f(\A) is really p(\A) for a polynomial p that agrees with f to the right order at each eigenvalue. With e^{t\A} in hand, every linear system of differential equations with constant coefficients is solved in one formula. Throughout this section F = 
C (or 
R, when we say so), so that every characteristic polynomial splits (@cor-complex-polynomial-splits) and Jordan forms exist. What a polynomial does to a Jordan block Start with what we already have. A Jordan block is a scalar plus a nilpotent matrix whose powers stop, and a polynomial applied to it can be read off from a Taylor expansion. [A Polynomial of a Jordan Block] Let F have characteristic 0, let k \ge 1, \lambda \in F and p \in F[x]. Then p(\J_k(\lambda)) is the upper triangular matrix whose (r, r+j)-entry is  igl(p(\J_k(\lambda)) igr)_{r, r+j} =  rac{p^{(j)}(\lambda)}{j!} \qquad (0 \le j \le k - 1, \ 1 \le r \le k - j), with all entries below the diagonal equal to 0. In particular the value p(\lambda) fills the diagonal, p'(\lambda) the superdiagonal, and only the first k derivatives of p at \lambda are involved. Write \J = \J_k(\lambda) = \lambda \I_k + \M with \M = \J_k(0) (@def-jordan-block). Reading off the columns of \M, we have \M\e_1 = \0 and \M\e_r = \e_{r-1} for r \ge 2, so by induction \M^{j}\e_r = \e_{r-j} when r > j and \M^{j}\e_r = \0 when r \le j. Hence, for 0 \le j \le k-1, the matrix \M^{j} has 1 in each position (r, r+j) and 0 elsewhere, and \M^{k} = 0. Let d = \deg p. By @thm-polynomial-taylor (b), applied with c = \lambda and n = d, p(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{d}  rac{p^{(j)}(\lambda)}{j!}\,(x - \lambda)^{j} . Substituting \J for x — legitimate because evaluation at \J is a ring homomorphism (@thm-evaluation-homomorphism) — and using \J - \lambda \I_k = \M, p(\J) = \sum_{j=0}^{d}  rac{p^{(j)}(\lambda)}{j!}\,\M^{j} = \sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,\,k-1)}  rac{p^{(j)}(\lambda)}{j!}\,\M^{j}, since \M^{j} = 0 for j \ge k. Each \M^{j} contributes its coefficient to every position (r, r+j) and to no other position, which is the claim. For p = x^{m} this reads p^{(j)}(\lambda)/j! =  inom{m}{j}\lambda^{m-j}, so  igl(\J_k(\lambda)^{m} igr)_{r,\,r+j} =  inom{m}{j}\lambda^{\,m-j} , which is the formula behind everything that follows, here and in the next section. Functions of a matrix Reading @lem-polynomial-of-jordan-block backwards suggests the definition. The formula for p(\J_k(\lambda)) uses nothing about p except the numbers p(\lambda), p'(\lambda), \dots, p^{(k-1)}(\lambda). Any function that has those derivatives can be inserted instead. To apply f to a matrix, apply it to each Jordan block, putting f^{(j)}(\lambda)/j! on the j-th superdiagonal. [Function of a Matrix] Let \A \in M_n(
C) with Jordan form \J = \J_{k_1}(\lambda_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \J_{k_m}(\lambda_m) and \A = \P \J \P^{-1}. Let f be a complex-valued function that is defined and at least k_i - 1 times differentiable at \lambda_i for every i — for instance, a function given by a convergent power series on a disc around each eigenvalue. Define f igl(\J_k(\lambda) igr) \coloneqq  egin{pmatrix} f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & 	frac{f''(\lambda)}{2!} & \cdots & 	frac{f^{(k-1)}(\lambda)}{(k-1)!} \ & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \ddots & \vdots \ & & \ddots & \ddots & 	frac{f''(\lambda)}{2!} \ & & & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \ & & & & f(\lambda) \end{pmatrix} \in M_k(
C), the upper triangular matrix with f^{(j)}(\lambda)/j! in every position (r, r+j), and f(\A) \coloneqq \P\,\Bigl( f igl(\J_{k_1}(\lambda_1) igr) \oplus \dots \oplus f igl(\J_{k_m}(\lambda_m) igr) \Bigr)\,\P^{-1} . In words: the diagonal of f(\J) records the values f(\lambda_i), and each further superdiagonal records the next derivative, divided by a factorial. For a diagonalizable \A every block has size 1, no derivatives are needed, and the definition says the familiar thing: f(\A) = \P\diag(f(\lambda_1), \dots, f(\lambda_n))\P^{-1}. Well-definedness. Two choices were made: the invertible \P and the order of the blocks. The Jordan form itself is unique only up to the order of the blocks (@thm-jordan-canonical-form), and even for a fixed \J there are many \P with \A = \P \J \P^{-1}. The next theorem removes both worries at once, by identifying f(\A) with p(\A) for a suitable polynomial p, an expression in which no choice appears. [Functions of a Matrix Are Polynomials in It] Let \A \in M_n(
C) with distinct eigenvalues \mu_1, \dots, \mu_d, and write m_{\A} = (x - \mu_1)^{s_1}\cdots(x - \mu_d)^{s_d}, so that s_l is the largest size of a \mu_l-block of the Jordan form of \A (@cor-jordan-invariants (c)). Let f be as in @def-matrix-function-jordan. Then: 1. there is a polynomial p \in 
C[x] with \deg p < \deg m_{\A} and p^{(j)}(\mu_l) = f^{(j)}(\mu_l) \qquad 	ext{for all } l = 1, \dots, d 	ext{ and } j = 0, \dots, s_l - 1 , and p is the only such polynomial of degree less than \deg m_{\A}; 2. for every polynomial q \in 
C[x] satisfying those \deg m_{\A} equations, q(\A) = p(\A); 3. f(\A) = p(\A). In particular f(\A) does not depend on the choice of \P or on the order of the blocks, and f(\A) is determined by the finitely many numbers f^{(j)}(\mu_l). The polynomial p of (a) is the Hermite interpolating polynomial of f on the spectrum of \A. The list of conditions “match f and its first s_l - 1 derivatives at \mu_l” is exactly a congruence modulo (x - \mu_l)^{s_l}, by the Taylor expansion; and the moduli (x-\mu_l)^{s_l} are pairwise coprime. So the Chinese Remainder Theorem produces p and shows it is unique below the degree of the product m_{\A} — this is @exm-hermite-via-crt with more nodes and higher orders. Once p exists, @lem-polynomial-of-jordan-block says that p and f do the same thing to every Jordan block of \A, because a \mu_l-block has size at most s_l and only derivatives up to order s_l - 1 are consulted. (a) For each l let r_l \coloneqq \sum_{j=0}^{s_l-1} rac{f^{(j)}(\mu_l)}{j!}(x - \mu_l)^{j} \in 
C[x]. For g \in 
C[x], the Taylor expansion of @thm-polynomial-taylor (b) at \mu_l, together with the uniqueness of the remainder on division by (x - \mu_l)^{s_l} (@thm-polynomial-division), gives g \equiv r_l \pmod{(x - \mu_l)^{s_l}} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad g^{(j)}(\mu_l) = f^{(j)}(\mu_l) 	ext{ for } j = 0, \dots, s_l - 1 , exactly as in @exm-hermite-via-crt (a) for s_l = 2: the remainder of g on division by (x-\mu_l)^{s_l} is \sum_{j<s_l} rac{g^{(j)}(\mu_l)}{j!}(x-\mu_l)^{j}, and two polynomials of degree less than s_l are equal precisely when their coefficients in the basis  igl(1, x - \mu_l, \dots, (x-\mu_l)^{s_l-1} igr) agree (@thm-polynomial-taylor (a)). The moduli (x - \mu_1)^{s_1}, \dots, (x-\mu_d)^{s_d} are pairwise coprime: for l 
e l', any common divisor divides both, and a monic common divisor would be a power of x - \mu_l and a power of x - \mu_{l'} with \mu_l 
e \mu_{l'}, hence 1 (@lem-monic-divisors, @thm-unique-factorization-polynomials). Their product is m_{\A}. So @thm-crt-polynomials (c) provides exactly one p with \deg p < \deg m_{\A} and p \equiv r_l \pmod{(x-\mu_l)^{s_l}} for every l, which by the displayed equivalence is (a). (b) Let q satisfy the same equations. By the equivalence again, q \equiv r_l \equiv p \pmod{(x-\mu_l)^{s_l}} for every l, so @thm-crt-polynomials (b) gives m_{\A} \mid q - p. Writing q - p = m_{\A}h and evaluating at \A, q(\A) - p(\A) = m_{\A}(\A)h(\A) = 0 since m_{\A}(\A) = 0 (@def-minimal-polynomial). Hence q(\A) = p(\A). (c) Let \J = \J_{k_1}(\lambda_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \J_{k_m}(\lambda_m) be any Jordan form of \A and \A = \P \J \P^{-1}. Fix i and let l be the index with \lambda_i = \mu_l. By @cor-jordan-invariants (c), k_i \le s_l, so @lem-polynomial-of-jordan-block and the equations in (a) give  igl(p(\J_{k_i}(\lambda_i)) igr)_{r, r+j} =  rac{p^{(j)}(\lambda_i)}{j!} =  rac{f^{(j)}(\lambda_i)}{j!} =  igl(f(\J_{k_i}(\lambda_i)) igr)_{r,r+j} \qquad (0 \le j \le k_i - 1), the derivatives involved having order at most k_i - 1 \le s_l - 1. So p(\J_{k_i}(\lambda_i)) = f(\J_{k_i}(\lambda_i)) for every i.
