A Toeplitz matrix — one with constant diagonals, (\A)_{jk} = a_{k-j} with the subscript not reduced modulo n — is not a circulant, and \F does not diagonalize it. Take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} . Every diagonal of \A is constant, so \A is Toeplitz, but the circulant with first row (0, 1, 0) is \S, whose second row is (0, 0, 1), not (1, 0, 1). And \F fails at the very first column:  _0 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1,1,1) and \A _0 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1, 2, 1), which is not a multiple of  _0, so  _0 is not an eigenvector and \F^{*}\A\F is not diagonal. Normality is not the issue: \A is symmetric, hence normal, and @thm-spectral-real does hand it an orthonormal eigenbasis. It is simply a different basis, with the irrational eigenvalues 0, \pm\sqrt2 in place of evaluations of a polynomial at roots of unity. What the wrap-around buys is not diagonalizability; it is the same diagonalizing basis for everybody. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the circulant with first row \c = (c_0, \dots, c_{n-1}), and write down its symbol. 2. State the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the cyclic shift \S on 
C^n. 3. Give the eigenvalues of the circulant with first row \c, and say how many multiplications are needed to compute all of them from \c by direct evaluation. 4. Determine whether the following are true, with a reason. (i) Every Toeplitz matrix is a circulant. (ii) Every circulant is normal. (iii) The Fourier matrix \F is Hermitian. 5. Explain in one sentence why two circulants of the same size commute, without computing any entries. (a) The matrix \C \in M_n(
C) with (\C)_{jk} = c_{k-j}, subscripts modulo n and indices running from 0 to n-1 (@def-circulant). Its symbol is p_{\c}(x) = c_0 + c_1x + \dots + c_{n-1}x^{n-1}. (b) With \omega = e^{2\pi i/n}: the eigenvalues are 1, \omega, \dots, \omega^{n-1}, all distinct, and \omega^{j} has the one-dimensional eigenspace spanned by  _j = n^{-1/2}(1, \omega^{j}, \dots, \omega^{(n-1)j}) (@thm-shift-eigenvectors). (c) The eigenvalues are p_{\c}(\omega^{j}) for j = 0, \dots, n-1 (@thm-circulant-diagonalization). Each evaluation is a sum of n products, so all n of them cost about n^2 multiplications done directly. (d) (i) False: the 3 	imes 3 matrix in the warning above has constant diagonals but is not a circulant. (ii) True, by @thm-circulant-is-polynomial-in-shift (c); equivalently by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, since \C = \F\D\F^{*}. (iii) False. \F is symmetric, but \F^{*} = \conj{\F}, and for n = 4 the entry (\F)_{12} = i/2 is not real (@exm-fourier-matrix-4). \F is Hermitian only for n = 1, 2, where all its entries are real. (e) Both are polynomials in the single matrix \S (@thm-circulant-is-polynomial-in-shift (a)), and two polynomials in one matrix always commute (@thm-polynomial-of-matrix-properties). B. Practice [B1: Eigenvalues of small circulants] For each vector \c, write down the symbol, compute all eigenvalues of the circulant with first row \c, and give its determinant. 1. \c = (1, 1, 1), n = 3. 2. \c = (0, 1, 0, 0), n = 4. 3. \c = (2, -1, 0, -1), n = 4. (a) p_{\c}(x) = 1 + x + x^2. With \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}, the eigenvalues are p_{\c}(1) = 3 and p_{\c}(\omega^{j}) = 1 + \omega^{j} + \omega^{2j} for j = 1, 2. For j 
eq 0, z = \omega^{j} satisfies z 
eq 1 and z^3 = 1, so 1 + z + z^2 = (z^3-1)/(z-1) = 0 — the geometric-series computation of @thm-fourier-matrix-unitary again. The eigenvalues are 3, 0, 0 and \det\C = 0. (This matrix is the all-ones matrix, of rank 1.) (b) p_{\c}(x) = x, so \C = \S. The eigenvalues are \omega^{j} = i^{j}, namely 1, i, -1, -i, and \det\S = 1 \cdot i \cdot (-1) \cdot (-i) =  igl(i \cdot (-i) igr) igl(1 \cdot (-1) igr) = -1 . This agrees with the sign of the permutation: \S permutes the coordinates in one 4-cycle, which is odd. (c) p_{\c}(x) = 2 - x - x^3. Then p_{\c}(1) = 0; p_{\c}(i) = 2 - i - i^3 = 2 - i + i = 2; p_{\c}(-1) = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4; p_{\c}(-i) = 2 + i - i = 2. The eigenvalues are 0, 2, 4, 2, and \det\C = 0. The kernel contains  _0, that is the all-ones vector, as one sees directly: every row of \C sums to 0. [B2: Solve a circulant system by transforming] Let \C be the 4 	imes 4 circulant with first row (3, 1, 0, 1) and let   = (1, 0, 0, 0). Compute the eigenvalues of \C, and solve \C\x =   by transforming, dividing and transforming back. Check your answer against the first two rows of \C. The symbol is p_{\c}(x) = 3 + x + x^3, and with \omega = i, p_{\c}(1) = 5, \quad p_{\c}(i) = 3 + i - i = 3, \quad p_{\c}(-1) = 1, \quad p_{\c}(-i) = 3 . All four are non-zero, so \C is invertible (@cor-circulants-algebra (d)), with \det\C = 5\cdot3\cdot1\cdot3 = 45. Transform: (\F^{*} )_j = 	frac12\sum_m \conj{\omega^{jm}}b_m = 	frac12 for every j, since   = \e_0. Divide: y_j = 	frac12\lambda_j^{-1}, giving \y = 	frac12(	frac15, 	frac13, 1, 	frac13). Transform back: the m-th entry of \x = \F\y is x_m = 	frac12\sum_{j=0}^{3} i^{mj}y_j = 	frac14\Bigl(	frac15 + 	frac{i^{m}}{3} + (-1)^{m} + 	frac{i^{3m}}{3}\Bigr). For m = 1 and m = 3 the two middle terms cancel, since i^{m} + i^{3m} = i^m + \conj{i^m} is 0 when i^m = \pm i; the bracket is 	frac15 - 1, so x_1 = x_3 = -	frac15. For m = 0 the bracket is 	frac15 + 	frac13 + 1 + 	frac13 = 	frac{28}{15}, so x_0 = 	frac{7}{15}. For m = 2 it is 	frac15 - 	frac13 + 1 - 	frac13 = 	frac{8}{15}, so x_2 = 	frac{2}{15}. Hence \x = \Bigl(	frac{7}{15},\ -	frac15,\ 	frac{2}{15},\ -	frac15\Bigr). Check: row 0 of \C is (3,1,0,1) and 3\cdot	frac7{15} - 	frac15 - 	frac15 = 	frac{21-3-3}{15} = 1; row 1 is (1,3,1,0) and 	frac7{15} - 	frac35 + 	frac2{15} = 	frac{7-9+2}{15} = 0. [B3: The convolution theorem in an example] Let \c = (1, 0, 2, 0) and \d = (0, 1, 0, 3) in 
C^4. 1. Compute \c \ast \d. 2. Verify p_{\c\ast\d}(\omega^{j}) = p_{\c}(\omega^{j})p_{\d}(\omega^{j}) for j = 0, 1, 2, 3. 3. Hence write down the first row of the product of the two circulants, without multiplying any matrices. (a) Only c_0 = 1 and c_2 = 2 are non-zero, so (\c\ast\d)_r = d_r + 2d_{r-2}, subscripts modulo 4. With \d = (0,1,0,3): \c \ast \d = (0 + 0,\ 1 + 6,\ 0 + 0,\ 3 + 2) = (0, 7, 0, 5). (b) The symbols are p_{\c}(x) = 1 + 2x^2, p_{\d}(x) = x + 3x^3 and p_{\c\ast\d}(x) = 7x + 5x^3. With \omega = i:  egin{aligned} j = 0: &\quad 3 \cdot 4 = 12, &&\quad 7 + 5 = 12; \ j = 1: &\quad (-1)(-2i) = 2i, &&\quad 7i - 5i = 2i; \ j = 2: &\quad 3 \cdot (-4) = -12, &&\quad -7 - 5 = -12; \ j = 3: &\quad (-1)(2i) = -2i, &&\quad -7i + 5i = -2i . \end{aligned} Here p_{\c}(i) = 1 + 2i^2 = -1 and p_{\d}(i) = i + 3i^3 = i - 3i = -2i, and similarly at the other roots. All four rows agree. (c) By @thm-convolution-theorem (a), the product is the circulant with first row \c\ast\d = (0, 7, 0, 5). C. Going deeper [C1: What commutes with the shift] Let \A \in M_n(
C) satisfy \A\S = \S\A. Prove that \A is a circulant. Hint: consider the eigenspaces of \S. By @thm-shift-eigenvectors, \S has the n distinct eigenvalues \omega^{j}, and E_{\omega^j}(\S) = \Span( _j) is one-dimensional. Since \A commutes with \S, each eigenspace of \S is invariant under \A (@thm-commuting-preserves-eigenspaces). So \A _j \in \Span( _j), that is \A _j = d_j _j for some d_j \in 
C. Therefore the j-th column of \A\F is d_j _j, which is the j-th column of \F\D for \D = \diag(d_0, \dots, d_{n-1}). Hence \A\F = \F\D and \F^{*}\A\F = \D is diagonal, so \A is a circulant by @cor-circulants-algebra (c). This proves the converse of @thm-circulant-is-polynomial-in-shift (c) for the single matrix \S: the commutant of the cyclic shift is exactly the algebra of circulants. [C2: Determinant and invertibility] Let \C be the circulant with first row \c \in 
C^n and symbol p_{\c}. 1. Prove that \det\C = \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} p_{\c}(\omega^{j}), and use it to compute the determinant of the n 	imes n all-ones matrix for every n \ge 2. 2. Prove that \C is invertible if and only if p_{\c} and x^n - 1 are coprime in 
C[x]. 3. Give an example of a 4 	imes 4 circulant with integer entries, none of them 0, whose determinant is 0. (a) This is the last claim of @thm-circulant-diagonalization: from \C = \F\D\F^{*} and \det(\F^{*})\det(\F) = \det(\F^{*}\F) = 1, multiplicativity of the determinant (@thm-det-multiplicative) gives \det\C = \det\D, which is the product of the diagonal entries p_{\c}(\omega^{j}). For the all-ones matrix, \c = (1, 1, \dots, 1) and p_{\c}(x) = 1 + x + \dots + x^{n-1}. Then p_{\c}(1) = n, while for 1 \le j \le n-1 the number z = \omega^{j} satisfies z^n = 1 and z 
eq 1, so p_{\c}(z) = (z^n - 1)/(z - 1) = 0. Hence \det\C = n \cdot 0 \cdots 0 = 0 for every n \ge 2, as it must be, since all the rows are equal. (b) By (a), \det\C 
eq 0 if and only if p_{\c}(\omega^{j}) 
eq 0 for every j, that is, if and only if p_{\c} and x^n - 1 have no common root, the roots of x^n - 1 being exactly 1, \omega, \dots, \omega^{n-1} (@exm-roots-of-unity). Over 
C, having no common root is the same as having no common non-constant factor: such a factor would have a root by @thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra, and that root would be common to both; conversely a common root \alpha makes x - \alpha a common factor. So invertibility of \C is equivalent to p_{\c} and x^n - 1 being coprime (@def-coprime). Combined with @thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible, this is the statement asked for. (c) Take \c = (1, 2, 1, 2), so \C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad p_{\c}(x) = 1 + 2x + x^2 + 2x^3 . Here p_{\c}(i) = 1 + 2i - 1 - 2i = 0, so \det\C = 0 by (a). The reason is visible without any of the theory — rows 0 and 2 are equal — and the Fourier picture names a kernel vector: \C _1 = \0, and since \C is real, the real and imaginary parts of  _1 are in the kernel too, giving \C(1, 0, -1, 0) = \0. [C3: The real orthogonal form of a real circulant] Let \C \in M_4(
R) be the circulant with first row (1, 2, 3, 4), with eigenvalues 10, -2-2i, -2, -2+2i as in @exm-circulant-4x4-eigenvalues. Put \g \coloneqq \sqrt2\,\operatorname{Re} _1, \qquad \h \coloneqq \sqrt2\,\operatorname{Im} _1, the real and imaginary parts taken entrywise. 1. Write \g and \h out, and show that ( _0,  _2, \g, \h) is an orthonormal basis of 
R^4. 2. Writing a + bi \coloneqq -2 + 2i, prove that \C\g = a\g + b\h and \C\h = -b\g + a\h. 3. Hence write down the matrix of \C in the ordered basis of (a), and identify it as an instance of @thm-real-normal-form. Hint for (b): apply \C to  _3 = (\g - i\h)/\sqrt2 and compare real and imaginary parts. (a) With \omega = i,  _1 = 	frac12(1, i, -1, -i), so \g = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 0, -1, 0), \qquad \h = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(0, 1, 0, -1). Also  _0 = 	frac12(1,1,1,1) and  _2 = 	frac12(1,-1,1,-1) are real, so all four vectors lie in 
R^4. Each has norm 1: for instance 
orm{\g}^2 = 	frac12(1 + 1) = 1 and 
orm{ _0}^2 = 	frac14 \cdot 4 = 1. They are pairwise orthogonal for the real dot product. First \g\cdot\h = 0, because the non-zero entries sit in different slots, and  _0\cdot _2 = 	frac14(1 - 1 + 1 - 1) = 0. The four remaining pairings are  egin{aligned}  _0 \cdot \g &= 	frac{1}{2\sqrt2}(1 - 1) = 0, &  _2 \cdot \g &= 	frac{1}{2\sqrt2}(1 - 1) = 0, \  _0 \cdot \h &= 	frac{1}{2\sqrt2}(1 - 1) = 0, &  _2 \cdot \h &= 	frac{1}{2\sqrt2}(-1 + 1) = 0 . \end{aligned} Four orthonormal vectors are independent (@thm-orthogonal-independent) and there are \dim
R^4 = 4 of them, so they form a basis (@thm-right-size-basis). (b) From  _1 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\g + i\h) and  _3 = \conj{ _1} we get  _3 = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\g - i\h). Its eigenvalue is p_{\c}(\omega^{3}) = p_{\c}(-i) = -2 + 2i = a + bi, so a = -2 and b = 2, and \C _3 = (a+bi) _3 reads 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} igl(\C\g - i\,\C\h igr) = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2}(a + bi)(\g - i\h) = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} igl((a\g + b\h) + i(b\g - a\h) igr). Both \C\g and \C\h are real vectors, because \C, \g and \h are real. Comparing real parts gives \C\g = a\g + b\h, and comparing imaginary parts gives -\C\h = b\g - a\h, that is \C\h = -b\g + a\h. With a = -2 and b = 2, \C\g = -2\g + 2\h, \qquad \C\h = -2\g - 2\h . A direct check: \sqrt2\,\C\g = \C(1,0,-1,0) = (1 - 3,\ 4 - 2,\ 3 - 1,\ 2 - 4) = (-2, 2, 2, -2), while \sqrt2\,(-2\g + 2\h) = (-2, 2, 2, -2). (c) Reading the coordinates of the images off (b), the matrix in the ordered basis ( _0,  _2, \g, \h) is  egin{pmatrix} 10 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & -2 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix} = (10) \oplus (-2) \oplus \vLambda(-2 + 2i), since \vLambda(a + bi) has rows (a, -b) and (b, a). This is exactly the shape promised by @thm-real-normal-form for a real normal operator: two 1 	imes 1 blocks for the real eigenvalues, and one rotation-scaling block for the conjugate pair, with b = 2 > 0. The change of basis is orthogonal, because the basis is orthonormal.

title: 11.10 The Sylvester Equation
content:
The Sylvester Equation Chapter 7 wrote an operator with an invariant subspace as a block triangular matrix, with a corner block \C recording how the subspace fails to have an invariant complement (@thm-invariant-subspace-block-triangular). Chapter 9 spent its length on what to do when that corner cannot be cleared. The question of when it can be cleared has an exact answer, and the answer is a linear equation in the unknown matrix \X: \A\X - \X\B = \C . Chapter 7 already turned this equation into an ordinary linear system with the Kronecker product, and stopped one step short of the criterion because that step needs eigenvalues. We have eigenvalues now, and Schur’s factorization of Section 1 to organize them. This section proves the criterion, uses it to clear corners, and reads off what it says about the matrices that commute with a given one. Throughout, the field is 
C unless stated otherwise, and \A \in M_m(
C), \B \in M_n(
C), while the unknown \X and the data \C live in M_{m 	imes n}(
C). The Sylvester operator The left-hand side of the equation is linear in \X: replacing \X by \X + \X' or by c\X does the same to \A\X - \X\B, because matrix multiplication is bilinear (@thm-matrix-multiplication-properties). So the whole question is about one linear map, and it deserves a name. Solving \A\X - \X\B = \C means inverting a single linear operator on the space of m 	imes n matrices. [Sylvester operator] Let \A \in M_m(F) and \B \in M_n(F). The Sylvester operator of the pair (\A, \B) is \cS_{\A,\B} \colon M_{m 	imes n}(F) 	o M_{m 	imes n}(F), \qquad \cS_{\A,\B}(\X) = \A\X - \X\B . The equation \A\X - \X\B = \C, for a given \C \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), is the Sylvester equation. In words: \cS_{\A,\B} multiplies by \A on the left, multiplies by \B on the right, and subtracts. It is an operator on a space of dimension mn, not on F^m or F^n, and that is the only thing that makes the equation look harder than \A\x =  . Three special cases are worth keeping in view. 1. \B = \0. Then \cS_{\A,\0}(\X) = \A\X, and the equation is n copies of \A\x =  , one for each column of \X (@exr-kronecker-product-b2). It is uniquely solvable for every \C exactly when \A is invertible, that is, when 0 
otin \spec(\A). Since \spec(\0) = \{0\}, this already matches the criterion we are heading for. 2. \B = \A and \C = \0. Then \ker \cS_{\A,\A} is the commutant of \A, the set of matrices commuting with \A. This is the question Chapter 7 opened with, and Chapter 9 §04 studied it for a single Jordan or Weyr block. 3. m = n = 1. Then \cS_{a,b}(x) = (a - b)x, which is invertible exactly when a 
eq b. The general criterion will be this one, run over all pairs of eigenvalues. Non-example by minimal change. The map \X \mapsto \A\X - \X\B - \X	p is still linear on M_n(F), but it is not a Sylvester operator: the transpose is not of the form “multiply on one side”. Everything below uses the two-sided product shape and nothing else. Chapter 7 already wrote the matrix of \cS_{\A,\B}. Stacking the columns of \X with the vectorization \vecop of @def-vec-operator and applying the vec identity @thm-vec-identity twice, once with \B = \I_n and once with \A = \I_m,  egin{aligned} \vecop ig(\cS_{\A,\B}(\X) ig) &= \K\,\vecop \X, \ \K &\coloneqq \I_n \otimes \A - \B	p \otimes \I_m . \end{aligned} {#eq-sylvester-kronecker} Here \K \in M_{mn}(F), and \vecop \colon M_{m 	imes n}(F) 	o F^{mn} is an isomorphism. So @eq-sylvester-kronecker says that \K is the matrix of \cS_{\A,\B} with respect to the basis of matrix units ordered column by column. In particular \cS_{\A,\B} is invertible if and only if \K is. That is exactly where Chapter 7 left the problem. What it could not do was compute the eigenvalues of \K. The spectrum of a Kronecker sum Chapter 7 proved how the Kronecker product treats rank, trace and determinant (@thm-kronecker-rank-trace-det) and how it treats products, transposes and inverses (@thm-kronecker-properties). It proved nothing about eigenvalues, and @exr-kronecker-product-c2 got only as far as the case where both factors are already triangular. Schur closes the gap, because over 
C every matrix can be made triangular unitarily, and the mixed product rule carries a pair of unitary conjugations through the Kronecker product in one step. [The Eigenvalues of a Kronecker Sum] Let \A \in M_m(
C) with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m and let \B \in M_n(
C) with eigenvalues \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n, each list repeated according to algebraic multiplicity. Then the mn eigenvalues of \K = \I_n \otimes \A - \B	p \otimes \I_m \in M_{mn}(
C), listed with algebraic multiplicity, are the mn differences \lambda_i - \mu_j (1 \le i \le m,\ 1 \le j \le n). Triangularize both ingredients at once. Schur (@cor-schur-matrix) writes \A = \U\T\U^{*} and \B	p = \V\S\V^{*} with \T, \S upper triangular. The mixed product rule then conjugates both summands of \K by the single unitary matrix \V \otimes \U, because \I_n \otimes \A and \B	p \otimes \I_m each have one trivial factor to absorb the other conjugation. What is left is \I_n \otimes \T - \S \otimes \I_m, and a Kronecker product with one triangular and one identity factor is triangular, so the eigenvalues are visible on the diagonal. By @cor-schur-matrix there are a unitary \U \in M_m(
C) and an upper triangular \T \in M_m(
C) with \A = \U\T\U^{*} and t_{ii} = \lambda_i. By @prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose (b), p_{\B	p} = p_{\B}, so \B	p has eigenvalue list \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n; applying @cor-schur-matrix to \B	p gives a unitary \V \in M_n(
C) and an upper triangular \S \in M_n(
C) with \B	p = \V\S\V^{*} and s_{jj} = \mu_j. Put \W = \V \otimes \U \in M_{mn}(
C). Conjugating every entry of \A \otimes \B conjugates every block a_{ij}\B, so \conj{\A \otimes \B} = \conj{\A} \otimes \conj{\B} (@def-kronecker-product), and combining this with @thm-kronecker-properties (d) gives (\A \otimes \B)^{*} = \A^{*} \otimes \B^{*} whenever the product is defined. Hence \W^{*} = \V^{*} \otimes \U^{*}, and by the mixed product rule @thm-kronecker-properties (c), \W^{*}\W = (\V^{*}\V) \otimes (\U^{*}\U) = \I_n \otimes \I_m = \I_{mn}, so \W is unitary. Using the mixed product rule twice more,  egin{aligned} \W(\I_n \otimes \T)\W^{*} &= (\V\I_n\V^{*}) \otimes (\U\T\U^{*}) = \I_n \otimes \A, \ \W(\S \otimes \I_m)\W^{*} &= (\V\S\V^{*}) \otimes (\U\I_m\U^{*}) = \B	p \otimes \I_m . \end{aligned} Subtracting, \W(\I_n \otimes \T - \S \otimes \I_m)\W^{*} = \K, so \K is similar to \R \coloneqq \I_n \otimes \T - \S \otimes \I_m . \R is upper triangular. Label the rows and columns of an mn 	imes mn matrix by pairs as in @def-kronecker-product: row (j-1)m + i with 1 \le j \le n, 1 \le i \le m, and likewise column (l-1)m + k. In those labels the entries of the two summands are  egin{aligned} (\I_n \otimes \T)_{(j-1)m+i,\,(l-1)m+k} &= \delta_{jl}\,t_{ik}, \ (\S \otimes \I_m)_{(j-1)m+i,\,(l-1)m+k} &= s_{jl}\,\delta_{ik} . \end{aligned} The first is non-zero only when j = l and i \le k, since \T is upper triangular; then (j-1)m + i \le (l-1)m + k. The second is non-zero only when j \le l and i = k; if j = l the two labels are equal, and if j < l then (j-1)m + i \le (j-1)m + m = jm \le (l-1)m < (l-1)m + k , using i \le m, j \le l - 1 and k \ge 1. So each summand vanishes below the diagonal, and so does \R. The diagonal. Taking j = l and i = k above, the diagonal entry of \R in position (j-1)m + i is t_{ii} - s_{jj} = \lambda_i - \mu_j. As (i, j) runs over all mn pairs, so does the position (j-1)m + i, by division with remainder. By @thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form (a), applied to the operator T_{\R} on 
C^{mn} and the standard basis, p_{\R} = \prod_{i,j} ig(x - (\lambda_i - \mu_j) ig). Since \K \sim \R, @thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant gives p_{\K} = p_{\R}. This proves the lemma. Two remarks on what the proof used. The hypothesis F = 
C entered once, in Schur, and through Schur it is the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra again. And the unitarity of \W was a convenience, not a necessity: any similarity triangularizing \A and \B	p would do, but Schur hands us one for free and the Kronecker product of two unitary matrices is unitary, which is worth recording on its own. When the equation is uniquely solvable The criterion now costs one line. [Sylvester’s Theorem] Let \A \in M_m(
C) and \B \in M_n(
C). The following are equivalent. 1. \spec(\A) \cap \spec(\B) = \varnothing: the two matrices have no common eigenvalue. 2. The Sylvester operator \cS_{\A,\B} \colon \X \mapsto \A\X - \X\B is invertible on M_{m 	imes n}(
C). 3. For every \C \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C), the equation \A\X - \X\B = \C has exactly one solution \X. 4. The only \X \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C) with \A\X = \X\B is \X = \0. By @eq-sylvester-kronecker the isomorphism \vecop turns \cS_{\A,\B} into the matrix \K = \I_n \otimes \A - \B	p \otimes \I_m: a matrix \X solves \A\X - \X\B = \C if and only if the vector \vecop\X solves \K\y = \vecop\C, and every \y \in 
C^{mn} and every \z \in 
C^{mn} arise this way. (b) Let \lambda \in \spec(\A) and \mu \in \spec(\B). A right eigenvector \x for \lambda exists by @def-eigenvalue, and a left eigenvector \y for \mu exists by @prp-left-eigenvectors-transpose (b). By (a), \x\y	p is a non-zero matrix with \cS(\x\y	p) = (\lambda - \mu)\x\y	p, so \lambda - \mu is an eigenvalue of \cS with eigenvector \x\y	p. (c) If \lambda \in \spec(\A) \cap \spec(\B), apply (b) with \mu = \lambda: then 0 is an eigenvalue of \cS, so \ker \cS 
eq \{\0\} and \cS is not invertible. This shows one implication of @thm-sylvester-equation directly. (It does not give the converse: knowing every \lambda - \mu is an eigenvalue does not by itself show there are no others.) [C2: The kernel when the spectra meet] Let \A \in M_m(
C) and \B \in M_n(
C) have eigenvalue lists \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m and \mu_1, \dots, \mu_n with algebraic multiplicity, and let d = \#\{(i, j) : \lambda_i = \mu_j\}. 1. Prove that \dim\ker\cS_{\A,\B} \ge 1 if and only if d \ge 1. 2. Prove that \dim\ker\cS_{\A,\B} \le d. 3. Show that the inequality in (b) can be strict, by computing \ker\cS_{\A,\B} for \A = \B = \J_2(0). (a) d \ge 1 says exactly that \A and \B have a common eigenvalue, and by @thm-sylvester-equation ((a) \Leftrightarrow (d)) that is exactly the failure of \ker\cS_{\A,\B} = \{\0\}. (b) The operator \cS_{\A,\B} has matrix \K (@eq-sylvester-kronecker), so \dim\ker\cS_{\A,\B} = g_{\K}(0), the geometric multiplicity of 0 as an eigenvalue of \K (when 0 
otin \spec(\K) both sides are 0 and there is nothing to prove). By @lem-kronecker-sum-spectrum the eigenvalue list of \K consists of the mn differences \lambda_i - \mu_j, so the algebraic multiplicity is a_{\K}(0) = d. By @thm-geometric-le-algebraic, g_{\K}(0) \le a_{\K}(0) = d. (c) Here m = n = 2 and \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \mu_1 = \mu_2 = 0, so d = 4. The kernel is the commutant of \J = \J_2(0): writing \X =  egin{pmatrix} p & q \ r & s \end{pmatrix}, \J\X =  egin{pmatrix} r & s \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \X\J =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & p \ 0 & r \end{pmatrix}, so \J\X = \X\J forces r = 0 and s = p, and leaves q free. Hence \ker\cS_{\J,\J} = \Span(\I_2, \J), of dimension 2 < 4 = d. [C3: Only the scalars commute with everything] Let F be a field, n \ge 2, and let \E_{ij} \in M_n(F) be the matrix unit with 1 in position (i, j) and 0 elsewhere. 1. Suppose \A \in M_n(F) satisfies \A\E_{ij} = \E_{ij}\A for all i 
eq j. Prove that \A = c\I_n for some c \in F. 2. Deduce that the only matrices commuting with every \X \in M_n(F) are the scalar matrices, that is, \ker\cS_{\A,\A} = M_n(F) forces \A scalar. 3. Deduce that the only matrices commuting with every invertible matrix are again the scalar matrices. Hint for (c): \I_n + \E_{ij} is invertible when i 
eq j. (a) Fix i 
eq j. By @thm-three-views-of-product, \A\E_{ij} has column j equal to \A\e_i, that is column i of \A, and all other columns zero; while \E_{ij}\A has row i equal to row j of \A, and all other rows zero. Compare entries. Take k 
eq i. The (k, j) entry of \A\E_{ij} is a_{ki}, and the (k, j) entry of \E_{ij}\A is 0, because row k 
eq i of \E_{ij}\A is zero. Hence a_{ki} = 0 whenever k 
eq i. Since n \ge 2, every index i has some j 
eq i available, so this holds for every i, and \A is diagonal. Now the (i, j) entry: on the left it is a_{ii} (the i-th entry of column i of \A), and on the right it is a_{jj} (the j-th entry of row j of \A). So a_{ii} = a_{jj} for all i 
eq j. Writing c for this common value, \A = c\I_n. (b) If \A\X = \X\A for every \X \in M_n(F), then in particular for \X = \E_{ij} with i 
eq j, so (a) gives \A = c\I_n. Conversely every scalar matrix commutes with everything. Hence \ker\cS_{\A,\A} = M_n(F) if and only if \A is scalar. (c) For i 
eq j we have \E_{ij}^2 = \0, so (\I_n + \E_{ij})(\I_n - \E_{ij}) = \I_n and \I_n + \E_{ij} is invertible. If \A commutes with every invertible matrix, it commutes with \I_n + \E_{ij}, hence with \E_{ij} (subtract \A\I_n = \I_n\A), for all i 
eq j. By (a), \A = c\I_n.

title: 11.11 How Far from Normal
content:
How Far from Normal Every theorem so far in this chapter has been a yes-or-no statement. An operator either commutes with its adjoint or it does not; there either is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors or there is not. That is unsatisfying, because the two matrices  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 10^{-6} \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} and  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 10^{6} \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} are both non-normal, and no one would want to treat them alike. This section replaces the yes-or-no answer with a number. The number comes out of Schur’s theorem almost for free, once we know that the Frobenius norm cannot tell one orthonormal basis from another, and it turns out to measure exactly the mass that a Schur factorization is forced to leave above the diagonal. Throughout, \A \in M_n(
C) and 
C^n carries the standard inner product. Eigenvalues are always counted in 
C and with algebraic multiplicity, so that an n 	imes n matrix always has a list of exactly n of them (@cor-complex-polynomial-splits). The Frobenius norm, officially Chapter 10 made M_{m 	imes n}(F) into an inner product space in its first section, by declaring \inner{\A}{\B} = 	r(\B^{*}\A) , the Frobenius inner product, and observing that it is nothing but the standard inner product of F^{mn} after the entries are listed in a single column. Its induced norm (@def-induced-norm) was named there too, but never given a symbol, and we have already borrowed one on the quiet in @exr-schur-triangularization-c2. It is time to make it official, because the whole of this section is written in it. For \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C), the Frobenius norm of \A is 
orm{\A}_F \coloneqq \sqrt{\inner{\A}{\A}} = \Bigl( \sum_{i,j} \lvert a_{ij} vert^2 \Bigr)^{1/2} . The subscript F is there because 
orm{\cdot} with no subscript already means the norm of a vector, and a matrix will shortly be asked to be both. Two remarks on the formula. First, it treats \A as a list of mn numbers and forgets that they are arranged in a rectangle: it is blind to the difference between  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} and  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. Second, it is computable with no eigenvalues, no row reduction and no choices: add up mn squared moduli. The trace form of the same quantity is the one that does the work. Why is 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 	r(\A^{*}\A)? The (j, j) entry of \A^{*}\A is \sum_i \conj{a_{ij}}a_{ij} = \sum_i \lvert a_{ij}vert^2, the squared length of the j-th column. Summing over j sweeps every entry of \A exactly once, so 	r(\A^{*}\A) = \sum_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert^2. Equivalently, it is \inner{\A}{\A} read off the definition of the Frobenius inner product. Now the property that makes the Frobenius norm the right yardstick in a chapter about orthonormal bases: unitary factors are invisible to it. [Unitary Invariance of the Frobenius Norm] Let \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C), let \U \in \Unit(m) and let \V \in \Unit(n). Then 
orm{\U\A}_F = 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\A\V}_F . In particular, if \A is square and \U is unitary then 
orm{\U^{*}\A\U}_F = 
orm{\A}_F. Using 
orm{\B}_F^2 = 	r(\B^{*}\B), then (\U\A)^{*} = \A^{*}\U^{*} and \U^{*}\U = \I_m, 
orm{\U\A}_F^2 = 	r(\A^{*}\U^{*}\U\A) = 	r(\A^{*}\A) = 
orm{\A}_F^2 . For the right-hand factor, @thm-trace-properties (3) lets the \V travel around the trace, and \V\V^{*} = \I_n: 
orm{\A\V}_F^2 = 	r(\V^{*}\A^{*}\A\V) = 	r(\A^{*}\A\V\V^{*}) = 
orm{\A}_F^2 . Both norms are non-negative reals, so equality of the squares gives equality of the norms. For the last statement, \U^{*} is unitary too, since (\U^{*})^{*}\U^{*} = \U\U^{*} = \I; apply the first equality to the left factor \U^{*} and the second to the right factor \U. The consequence to keep in mind is this. If T \in \cL(V) is an operator on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and we compute 
orm{\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}}_F in an orthonormal basis \sB, the answer does not depend on which orthonormal basis we chose, because two such matrices differ by a unitary similarity (@thm-change-of-basis-maps). So the Frobenius norm is a property of T, not of our coordinates — exactly like the trace and the determinant, and unlike, say, the largest entry. Schur’s inequality Here is the observation the section is built on. Write a matrix in a Schur form \A = \U\T\U^{*}. The diagonal of \T holds the eigenvalues, so \sum_i \lvert\lambda_ivert^2 is the Frobenius mass sitting on the diagonal of \T. The rest of \T sits strictly above it. And by @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant the total mass of \T is the total mass of \A. Rearranged, that is a theorem. Schur’s Inequality Let \A \in M_n(
C) have eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert \lambda_i vert^2 \;\le\; 
orm{\A}_F^2 , with equality if and only if \A is normal. Schur-triangularize, then count. ① \A = \U\T\U^{*} with \T upper triangular and the \lambda_i on its diagonal (@cor-schur-matrix). ② The Frobenius norm does not notice the \U’s, so 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\T}_F. ③ Splitting 
orm{\T}_F^2 into its diagonal part and its strictly upper part gives the inequality on the nose, with the strictly upper part as the exact surplus. ④ For the equality case, that surplus vanishes exactly when \T is diagonal, and “triangular and normal” and “diagonal” were shown to be the same thing in @lem-triangular-normal-diagonal. By @cor-schur-matrix there are a unitary \U and an upper triangular \T = (t_{ij}) with \A = \U\T\U^{*} and t_{ii} = \lambda_i for every i. Since t_{ij} = 0 whenever i > j, the entries of \T fall into the diagonal ones and the strictly upper ones, so by @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant  egin{aligned} 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 
orm{\T}_F^2 &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert t_{ii}vert^2 + \sum_{i < j} \lvert t_{ij}vert^2 \ &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert \lambda_ivert^2 + \sum_{i < j} \lvert t_{ij}vert^2 . \end{aligned} {#eq-schur-split} The second sum is a sum of non-negative reals, so it is \ge 0, and the inequality follows. Moreover equality holds if and only if that sum is 0, which happens if and only if t_{ij} = 0 for all i < j, that is, if and only if this \T is diagonal. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \A is normal. Then so is \T = \U^{*}\A\U: using \U\U^{*} = \I in the middle of each product, \T^{*}\T = \U^{*}\A^{*}\A\U = \U^{*}\A\A^{*}\U = \T\T^{*} . A normal upper triangular matrix is diagonal (@lem-triangular-normal-diagonal), so \T is diagonal and @eq-schur-split gives equality. (\Rightarrow) Suppose equality holds. Then, as noted, \T is diagonal, so \A = \U\T\U^{*} exhibits \A as unitarily diagonalizable, and @cor-spectral-complex-matrix makes \A normal. This proves the inequality and both halves of the equality case. Notice that the proof never had to worry about which Schur factorization was used. The two sides of the inequality — the eigenvalue list and 
orm{\A}_F — are determined by \A alone, so the surplus \sum_{i<j}\lvert t_{ij}vert^2 in @eq-schur-split comes out the same for every triangularization of \A, even though the individual entries t_{ij} certainly do not. That is worth a second look, and we will look at it in a moment. [Both sides of Schur’s inequality] Verify @thm-schur-inequality for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , and locate the surplus inside an explicit Schur factorization (@cor-schur-matrix). Here 	r\A = 0 and \det\A = -2, so p_{\A} = x^2 - 2 and the eigenvalues are \pm\sqrt2. Thus \sum_i \lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 2 + 2 = 4, \qquad 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 0 + 1 + 4 + 0 = 5 , and indeed 4 < 5. The inequality is strict, so @thm-schur-inequality already says that \A is not normal — no product of matrices needed. For the factorization, solve (\A - \sqrt2\I)\x = \0: the first row reads -\sqrt2 x_1 + x_2 = 0, giving the eigenvector (1, \sqrt2) of norm \sqrt3. Take \q_1 = 	frac1{\sqrt3}(1, \sqrt2), \qquad \q_2 = 	frac1{\sqrt3}(-\sqrt2, 1), a pair of orthonormal vectors, and let \U have them as columns. Then \U^{*}\A\U =  egin{pmatrix} \sqrt2 & -1 \ 0 & -\sqrt2 \end{pmatrix} = \T . Its Frobenius mass is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 = 
orm{\A}_F^2, as @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant promises, and the split of @eq-schur-split reads 5 = 4 + 1: the whole surplus is the single entry -1 above the diagonal. The real matrix \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} has 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 2 and no real eigenvalue at all. Does @thm-schur-inequality fail for it? No, because the eigenvalues are counted in 
C. They are i and -i, so \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 1 + 1 = 2 = 
orm{\A}_F^2: equality, which is exactly right, since \A	p\A = \A\A	p = \I makes \A normal. Restricting the eigenvalue list to 
R would leave the left-hand side empty and the statement meaningless; this is one more place where the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra) is doing silent work. The departure from normality Schur’s inequality has a slack term, and the slack term is the interesting object. It is non-negative for every matrix; it vanishes exactly on the normal ones; and, both of its ingredients being unitary-similarity invariants, it survives a change of orthonormal basis. Those are precisely the properties one wants of a measurement, so we name it. The departure from normality is the Frobenius mass that no Schur factorization can push onto the diagonal. [Departure from Normality] Let \A \in M_n(
C) have eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, listed with algebraic multiplicity. The departure from normality of \A is the non-negative real number \Delta(\A) defined by \Delta(\A)^2 \coloneqq 
orm{\A}_F^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert\lambda_ivert^2 . Clause by clause: the quantity on the right is a real number because 
orm{\A}_F^2 and each \lvert\lambda_ivert^2 are real; it is non-negative by @thm-schur-inequality, which is what allows us to take its non-negative square root and call the result \Delta(\A); and the eigenvalue list, though it comes with no preferred order, contributes a sum that does not care about the order. So \Delta(\A) is well defined, with no choices made anywhere. Two facts come straight from @thm-schur-inequality and its proof. - \Delta(\A) = 0 if and only if \A is normal. This is the equality case, restated. - \Delta(\A) =  igl(\sum_{i<j}\lvert t_{ij}vert^2 igr)^{1/2} for every Schur factorization \A = \U\T\U^{*}, by @eq-schur-split. So \Delta(\A) is the length of the strictly upper triangular part of \T, and the remark after @thm-schur-inequality says that this length is the same for all of them, even though the entries are not. And one more, which is the reason the number deserves to be called a measurement rather than a coincidence: \Delta(\U^{*}\A\U) = \Delta(\A) for every unitary \U. Both ingredients are unitary-similarity invariants — the Frobenius norm by @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant, the eigenvalue list because similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant). @exr-defect-from-normality-c1 asks for the details, and for an example showing that ordinary similarity wrecks the number completely. [The defect of a Jordan block] Compute \Delta(\J_k(\lambda)) for the k 	imes k Jordan block with eigenvalue \lambda. The matrix \J_k(\lambda) has \lambda in each of its k diagonal positions and 1 in each of the k - 1 superdiagonal positions, and zeros elsewhere, so 
orm{\J_k(\lambda)}_F^2 = k\lvert\lambdavert^2 + (k - 1) . It is upper triangular, so its eigenvalue list is \lambda repeated k times (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form), giving \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = k\lvert\lambdavert^2. Subtracting, \Delta(\J_k(\lambda))^2 = k - 1, \qquad \Delta(\J_k(\lambda)) = \sqrt{k - 1} . Three things are worth reading off. The answer does not depend on \lambda: sliding a Jordan block up and down the complex plane does not make it more or less normal. It is 0 exactly when k = 1, agreeing with the fact that a 1 	imes 1 matrix is normal. And it grows with the block, which matches what @thm-normal-powers gave us in Section 3: a normal operator has no Jordan block of size larger than 1 (@thm-jordan-canonical-form). Here the defect is counting exactly the superdiagonal ones that normality forbids. A minimal-change non-example makes the same point on a smaller scale. The matrix \diag(1, 3) is normal, so its defect is 0. Change the single entry in position (1, 2) from 0 to 2: \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 14, \qquad \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 1 + 9 = 10 , so \Delta(\A) = 2. The eigenvalues did not move — a triangular matrix wears them on its diagonal — and the entire change went into the defect. That is the general picture for triangular matrices: for them, \Delta is just the length of everything above the diagonal. The defect also bounds something one might actually want to know. Fix a Schur factorization \A = \U\T\U^{*} (@cor-schur-matrix), write \D for the diagonal part of \T, and put \N = \U\D\U^{*}, which is normal by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix. Then 
orm{\A - \N}_F = 
orm{\T - \D}_F = \Delta(\A) , the first step by @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant. So \Delta(\A) is an upper bound for the Frobenius distance from \A to the set of normal matrices. It is not that distance. \Delta is a defect, not a distance. It is tempting to read \Delta(\A) as “how far \A is from the nearest normal matrix”, and the displayed bound above makes the temptation worse. But the bound can be strict. Take \A = \J_2(0) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, so that \Delta(\A) = 1 by @exm-defect-jordan-block. The symmetric — hence normal — matrix \N = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix} satisfies 
orm{\A - \N}_F = \Bigl\lVert 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \BigrVert_F = 	frac1{\sqrt2} < 1 . So some normal matrix is strictly nearer to \A than \Delta(\A). What \Delta(\A) measures is the mass that survives triangularization, which is a genuine and useful quantity, but it is an upper bound for the distance and not the distance itself. Eigenvalues that will not sit still Here is why anyone outside this chapter cares. Eigenvalues are computed, in practice, from data that is only approximately right, so the question “if I move the matrix a little, how far do the eigenvalues move?” is not academic. For a normal matrix the answer is “just as little”. For a matrix with a large defect it can be “enormously further”. The following pair of 2 	imes 2 matrices shows the whole phenomenon with nothing but the quadratic formula. [A perturbation that moves the eigenvalues a thousand times as far] Fix a real number M > 0 and a real \varepsilon with 0 < \varepsilon < M. Compare the effect of adding \varepsilon to the lower-left entry of each of \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & M \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \qquad	ext{and}\qquad \N =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & M \ -M & 1 \end{pmatrix} . Compute the defects of \A and \N, the eigenvalues of both perturbed matrices exactly, and the distance each eigenvalue travels. The two defects. The matrix \A is upper triangular with both diagonal entries 1, so its eigenvalue list is 1, 1 and \Delta(\A)^2 = (1 + M^2 + 1) - (1 + 1) = M^2, \qquad \Delta(\A) = M . The matrix \N is normal: \N	p\N = \N\N	p = (1 + M^2)\I, a direct multiplication. So \Delta(\N) = 0. Its eigenvalues are 1 \pm Mi, since p_{\N} = (x-1)^2 + M^2. The two matrices have the same diagonal and the same entry M in the corner we are leaving alone; where they differ is that one has defect M and the other defect 0. The non-normal one. Perturbing the corner gives \A_{\varepsilon} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & M \ \varepsilon & 1\end{pmatrix}, with p_{\A_{\varepsilon}} = (x - 1)^2 - M\varepsilon, \qquad \lambda_{\pm} = 1 \pm \sqrt{M\varepsilon} . The perturbation has size 
orm{\A_{\varepsilon} - \A}_F = \varepsilon, and each eigenvalue has moved a distance \sqrt{M\varepsilon}, which is \sqrt{M/\varepsilon} times the size of the perturbation. With M = 100 and \varepsilon = 10^{-4}, the perturbation is one ten-thousandth and the eigenvalues move by \sqrt{100 \cdot 10^{-4}} = 1/10: a thousandfold amplification. The normal one. Perturbing the same corner gives \N_{\varepsilon} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & M \ -M + \varepsilon & 1\end{pmatrix}, with p_{\N_{\varepsilon}} = (x - 1)^2 + M(M - \varepsilon), \qquad \mu_{\pm} = 1 \pm i\sqrt{M^2 - M\varepsilon} , the square root being a real number because \varepsilon < M. The eigenvalue 1 + Mi has moved to 1 + i\sqrt{M^2 - M\varepsilon}, a distance of M - \sqrt{M^2 - M\varepsilon} =  rac{M\varepsilon}{M + \sqrt{M^2 - M\varepsilon}} \le  rac{M\varepsilon}{M} = \varepsilon , where the middle equality multiplies top and bottom by M + \sqrt{M^2 - M\varepsilon} and the last step uses \sqrt{M^2 - M\varepsilon} \ge 0. So here the eigenvalues move by at most the size of the perturbation. The same denominator is at most 2M, so the movement is also at least \varepsilon/2: with M = 100 and \varepsilon = 10^{-4} it is a shade over \varepsilon/2. The contrast is not an accident of these two matrices, and it is not a theorem we can prove here either. The general statement — that for a diagonalizable \A every eigenvalue of a perturbed \A + \E lies within \kappa
orm{\E} of some eigenvalue of \A, where \kappa measures how far from unitary the diagonalizing matrix is, and that \kappa = 1 exactly in the normal case — is the Bauer–Fike theorem. It needs matrix norms and a little analysis, and Chapter 19 develops both and proves it. What the example above establishes on its own is modest and exact: of two 2 	imes 2 matrices with the same diagonal and the same large off-diagonal entry, the one with defect 0 amplifies a corner perturbation by a factor of at most 1, and the one with defect M amplifies it by \sqrt{M/\varepsilon}. The defect is not bookkeeping. The amplification \sqrt{M\varepsilon} in @exm-eigenvalue-sensitivity has a square root in it, and that square root is the signature of a repeated eigenvalue. The unperturbed \A has the single eigenvalue 1 twice over with only one eigenvector, so it is a Jordan block in disguise; splitting a double root is what costs the square root. A matrix with well-separated eigenvalues and a large defect behaves less dramatically. The characterizations collected Schur’s inequality gives a normality test of a new kind. Every earlier test compared two matrix products or ranged over all vectors; this one compares two numbers, and one of them is a trace. [Normality as a Trace Identity] Let \A \in M_n(
C) have eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then \A is normal if and only if 	r(\A^{*}\A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert\lambda_ivert^2 . We showed above that 	r(\A^{*}\A) = 
orm{\A}_F^2. So the displayed equation is the equality case of @thm-schur-inequality, which holds exactly when \A is normal. Small as it is, this is the first criterion in the chapter that never asks for \A\A^{*}. If the spectrum is already known — from the characteristic polynomial, or because the matrix arrived in triangular form — normality costs one sum of n^2 squared moduli and one sum of n more. We can now put every description of normality in one place. Sections 3 and 4 proved most of them; this section adds the last one; and one equivalence, the converse of @cor-normal-commuting-poly, has not been proved anywhere and is proved here. [Normality: The Complete List] Let \A \in M_n(
C) have eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, listed with algebraic multiplicity, and put \H = 	frac12(\A + \A^{*}), \qquad \K = 	frac1{2i}(\A - \A^{*}) , both of which are Hermitian, with \A = \H + i\K. The following are equivalent. 1. \A^{*}\A = \A\A^{*}, that is, \A is normal. 2. 
orm{\A\x} = 
orm{\A^{*}\x} for every \x \in 
C^n. 3. \inner{\A\x}{\A\y} = \inner{\A^{*}\x}{\A^{*}\y} for all \x, \y \in 
C^n. 4. \H\K = \K\H. 5. 
C^n has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \A. 6. \A = \U\D\U^{*} for some unitary \U and some diagonal \D. 7. \A^{*} = p(\A) for some polynomial p \in 
C[x]. 8. \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 
orm{\A}_F^2. Let T = T_{\A} on 
C^n with its standard inner product, for which the standard basis is orthonormal; then T^{*} = T_{\A^{*}} by @thm-matrix-of-adjoint, and T is normal exactly when \A is. (a), (b), (c) and (d) are equivalent by @thm-normal-characterizations applied to T, whose four conditions are these four read for T instead of \A. (a) \Leftrightarrow (e) is @thm-spectral-complex, again for T. (a) \Leftrightarrow (f) is @cor-spectral-complex-matrix. (a) \Leftrightarrow (h) is @thm-normal-trace-criterion, since 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 	r(\A^{*}\A). (a) \Rightarrow (g) is @cor-normal-commuting-poly, applied to T and read back as matrices. It remains to prove (g) \Rightarrow (a). Suppose \A^{*} = p(\A) with p = c_0 + c_1x + \dots + c_dx^d. Every power of \A commutes with \A, hence so does any linear combination of powers: p(\A)\A = \sum_{k=0}^{d} c_k\A^{k+1} = \A\,p(\A) . Substituting \A^{*} for p(\A) on both sides gives \A^{*}\A = \A\A^{*}, which is (a). This closes the loop and proves the theorem. This list is the summary result of the chapter, and it is worth reading as a whole rather than as eight separate facts. Conditions (a) and (d) are algebraic: one equation between products. Conditions (b) and (c) are metric: \A and \A^{*} distort lengths and angles identically. Conditions (e) and (f) are geometric: the eigenvectors can be chosen perpendicular. Condition (g) is a surprise, and says that for a normal matrix the adjoint carries no information beyond \A itself. And condition (h) is quantitative: it is the only one on the list that comes with a number attached, so that when it fails one can ask by how much. That number is \Delta(\A), and it is the reason this section exists. The operator versions of (a)–(g) hold verbatim on any finite-dimensional complex inner product space, by passing to the matrix in an orthonormal basis. So does (h), once 
orm{\cdot}_F is read as the Frobenius norm of that matrix, which @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant showed does not depend on which orthonormal basis is used. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define the Frobenius norm of a matrix, and give the expression for 
orm{\A}_F^2 as a trace. 2. State @thm-schur-inequality, including the equality case and how the eigenvalues are counted. 3. Define \Delta(\A), and say why the definition needs @thm-schur-inequality before it can be made. 4. True or false: \Delta(\A) equals the Frobenius distance from \A to the nearest normal matrix. Justify your answer. 5. True or false: if \A and \B are similar then \Delta(\A) = \Delta(\B). Justify your answer. 6. Name the two facts about the Frobenius norm and about triangular matrices that the proof of @thm-schur-inequality rests on. (a) 
orm{\A}_F =  igl(\sum_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert^2 igr)^{1/2}, the norm induced by the Frobenius inner product \inner{\A}{\B} = 	r(\B^{*}\A) of Chapter 10. As a trace, 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 	r(\A^{*}\A). (b) For \A \in M_n(
C) with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n listed in 
C and with algebraic multiplicity, \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 \le 
orm{\A}_F^2, with equality if and only if \A is normal. (c) \Delta(\A)^2 = 
orm{\A}_F^2 - \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2, and \Delta(\A) is its non-negative square root. Without @thm-schur-inequality the right-hand side might be negative, and there would be no real square root to take. (d) False. It is an upper bound for that distance, as the paragraph before the warning shows, but the warning gives \A = \J_2(0) with \Delta(\A) = 1 and a normal matrix at distance 1/\sqrt2. (e) False. The matrices  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} and \diag(1, 2) are similar, since the first is diagonalizable with eigenvalues 1 and 2, yet their defects are 1 and 0. What is true is that \Delta is unchanged by unitary similarity; see @exr-defect-from-normality-c1. (f) That the Frobenius norm is unchanged by unitary factors (@lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant), so that 
orm{\A}_F = 
orm{\T}_F; and that a normal upper triangular matrix is diagonal (@lem-triangular-normal-diagonal), which is what makes the equality case work in the direction (\Leftarrow). B. Practice [B1: Computing the defect] For each matrix below, compute 
orm{\A}_F^2, the eigenvalue list, and \Delta(\A). State in each case whether the matrix is normal, and say how you know without multiplying \A by \A^{*}. 1.  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix} 2.  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} 3. \J_3(2) 4.  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} (a) 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 9 + 16 + 25 = 50. The matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are 3 and 5 (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form) and \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 34. Hence \Delta(\A)^2 = 16 and \Delta(\A) = 4. Since \Delta(\A) 
eq 0, the matrix is not normal (@thm-schur-inequality). (b) 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4. Here 	r\A = 2 and \det\A = 1 + 1 = 2, so p_{\A} = x^2 - 2x + 2 and the eigenvalues are 1 \pm i, each of modulus \sqrt2. Then \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 2 + 2 = 4, so \Delta(\A) = 0 and the matrix is normal. (c) 
orm{\J_3(2)}_F^2 = 3 \cdot 4 + 2 = 14, the eigenvalue is 2 three times, and \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 12. So \Delta^2 = 2 and \Delta = \sqrt2, which is \sqrt{k-1} with k = 3, as @exm-defect-jordan-block says. Not normal. (d) 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 3. The matrix is the cyclic shift, with p_{\A} = x^3 - 1 (expand along the first row, or note \A^3 = \I and \A 
eq \I with \A having no repeated eigenvalue). Its eigenvalues are the three cube roots of unity, each of modulus 1, so \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 3 and \Delta(\A) = 0: normal. [B2: Verifying Schur’s inequality] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} . 1. Compute both sides of @thm-schur-inequality for \A and verify the inequality. 2. Hence determine whether \A is normal, without computing \A^{*}\A or \A\A^{*}. 3. Write down a normal matrix \N with 
orm{\A - \N}_F = \Delta(\A), and verify the equality. (a) 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 1 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 9 = 17. The matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are 1, 2, 3 (@thm-diagonal-of-triangular-form) and \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. Indeed 14 \le 17. (b) The inequality is strict, so by the equality case of @thm-schur-inequality the matrix is not normal. Equivalently \Delta(\A) = \sqrt{17 - 14} = \sqrt3 
eq 0. (c) Since \A is already upper triangular, \A = \I\A\I^{*} is a Schur factorization (@cor-schur-matrix) with \U = \I and \T = \A. The construction before the warning takes \N to be the diagonal part, \N = \diag(1, 2, 3), which is normal. Then \A - \N has the three entries 1 above the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so 
orm{\A - \N}_F = \sqrt3 = \Delta(\A). [B3: The nearest symmetric matrix] Let \A \in M_n(
R) and write \S = 	frac12(\A + \A	p) and \W = 	frac12(\A - \A	p), so that \A = \S + \W with \S	p = \S and \W	p = -\W. 1. Prove that \inner{\B}{\C} = 0 in the Frobenius inner product whenever \B \in M_n(
R) is symmetric and \C \in M_n(
R) is skew-symmetric. 2. Deduce that 
orm{\A - \B}_F \ge 
orm{\W}_F for every symmetric \B \in M_n(
R), with equality only for \B = \S. Hence \S is the nearest symmetric matrix to \A. 3. Carry this out for \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}, and compare the resulting distance with \Delta(\A). (a) For real matrices \inner{\B}{\C} = 	r(\C	p\B). Since \C	p = -\C, this is -	r(\C\B). On the other hand 	r(\C\B) = 	r igl((\C\B)	p igr) by @thm-trace-properties (2), and (\C\B)	p = \B	p\C	p = -\B\C, so 	r(\C\B) = -	r(\B\C) = -	r(\C\B), the last step by @thm-trace-properties (3). A number equal to its own negative is 0, so 	r(\C\B) = 0 and \inner{\B}{\C} = 0. (b) Let \B be symmetric. Then \A - \B = (\S - \B) + \W, where \S - \B is symmetric and \W is skew-symmetric, so the two are orthogonal by (a) and Pythagoras (@thm-pythagoras) gives 
orm{\A - \B}_F^2 = 
orm{\S - \B}_F^2 + 
orm{\W}_F^2 \ge 
orm{\W}_F^2 . Equality forces 
orm{\S - \B}_F = 0, that is \B = \S (@thm-norm-properties (a)). So \S is the unique nearest symmetric matrix, at distance 
orm{\W}_F. (c) Here \S =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & -2\end{pmatrix} and \W =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \ -2 & 0\end{pmatrix}, so the distance from \A to the symmetric matrices is 
orm{\W}_F = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt2. For the defect, 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 4 + 16 + 4 = 24, and \A is triangular with eigenvalues 2 and -2, so \sum_i\lvert\lambda_ivert^2 = 8 and \Delta(\A) = 4. A symmetric matrix is normal, so this again exhibits a normal matrix strictly closer than \Delta(\A): 2\sqrt2 \approx 2.83 < 4. C. Going deeper [C1: Unitary similarity preserves the defect, ordinary similarity does not] 1. Prove that \Delta(\U^{*}\A\U) = \Delta(\A) for every \A \in M_n(
C) and every unitary \U. 2. Give \A, \B \in M_2(
C) that are similar with \Delta(\A) 
eq \Delta(\B), exhibiting an explicit \P with \P^{-1}\A\P = \B. 3. Deduce that two similar matrices with different defects cannot be unitarily similar, and use this to show that  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} and \diag(1, 2) are not unitarily similar. (a) Put \B = \U^{*}\A\U. By @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant, 
orm{\B}_F = 
orm{\A}_F. Also \B is similar to \A, so p_{\B} = p_{\A} (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant) and the two matrices have the same eigenvalue list with multiplicities. Both terms in @def-departure-from-normality therefore agree, so \Delta(\B)^2 = \Delta(\A)^2, and the defects are equal since both are non-negative. (b) Take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} and \B = \diag(1, 2). Then 
orm{\A}_F^2 = 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 with eigenvalues 1, 2, so \Delta(\A)^2 = 6 - 5 = 1 and \Delta(\A) = 1, while \Delta(\B) = 0 because \B is diagonal, hence normal. They are similar: eigenvectors of \A are (1, 0) for \lambda = 1 and (1, 1) for \lambda = 2, so with \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}, whose inverse is  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}, we get \P^{-1}\A\P = \B by direct multiplication. (c) By (a), unitarily similar matrices have equal defects. So if \Delta(\A) 
eq \Delta(\B) then no unitary \U can satisfy \U^{*}\A\U = \B. The pair in (b) has defects 1 and 0, so it is similar but not unitarily similar. (This is the failure of “diagonalizable” to imply “unitarily diagonalizable”, seen through a number instead of through @exm-diagonalizable-not-normal.) [C2: Equality plus a single eigenvalue forces a scalar] Let \A \in M_n(
C) satisfy 
orm{\A}_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lvert\lambda_ivert^2, and suppose \A has only one distinct eigenvalue \lambda, so that p_{\A} = (x - \lambda)^n. 1. Prove that \A = \lambda\I. 2. Deduce that a normal matrix whose characteristic polynomial is x^n is the zero matrix. 3. Show that the hypothesis of equality cannot be dropped, by computing \Delta for a matrix with p_{\A} = (x - \lambda)^n that is not \lambda\I. (a) By the equality case of @thm-schur-inequality, \A is normal. So by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix there are a unitary \U and a diagonal \D with \A = \U\D\U^{*}, the diagonal of \D being the eigenvalue list of \A. That list is \lambda repeated n times, so \D = \lambda\I and \A = \U(\lambda\I)\U^{*} = \lambda\U\U^{*} = \lambda\I . (b) A normal matrix satisfies the equality hypothesis (@thm-schur-inequality again), and p_{\A} = x^n says its only eigenvalue is 0. By (a), \A = 0\cdot\I = 0. In words: a normal nilpotent matrix is zero, which is @thm-normal-powers seen from the quantitative side. (c) Take \A = \J_n(\lambda) with n \ge 2. Its characteristic polynomial is (x - \lambda)^n and it is not \lambda\I, and \Delta(\A) = \sqrt{n-1} 
eq 0 by @exm-defect-jordan-block. So equality in @thm-schur-inequality fails, exactly as it must. [C3: The commutator is at least as big as the defect squared] For \A \in M_n(
C) write [\A, \A^{*}] = \A\A^{*} - \A^{*}\A. 1. Prove that 
orm{[\A, \A^{*}]}_F is unchanged when \A is replaced by \U^{*}\A\U with \U unitary. 2. Let \T =  egin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & b \ 0 & \lambda_2 \end{pmatrix}. Compute [\T, \T^{*}] and show that 
orm{[\T, \T^{*}]}_F^2 = 2\lvert bvert^4 + 2\lvert bvert^2\lvert\lambda_1 - \lambda_2vert^2 . 3. Deduce that every \A \in M_2(
C) satisfies 
orm{[\A, \A^{*}]}_F \ge \sqrt2\,\Delta(\A)^2, and determine exactly when equality holds. Hint for (c): Schur-triangularize, and use (a) to move the computation to the triangular factor. (a) Put \B = \U^{*}\A\U, so \B^{*} = \U^{*}\A^{*}\U. Inserting \U\U^{*} = \I between the factors, [\B, \B^{*}] = \U^{*}(\A\A^{*} - \A^{*}\A)\U = \U^{*}[\A, \A^{*}]\U , and @lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant gives 
orm{[\B, \B^{*}]}_F = 
orm{[\A, \A^{*}]}_F. (b) Multiplying out,  egin{aligned} \T\T^{*} &=  egin{pmatrix} \lvert\lambda_1vert^2 + \lvert bvert^2 & b\conj{\lambda_2} \ \lambda_2\conj{b} & \lvert\lambda_2vert^2 \end{pmatrix}, \[2pt] \T^{*}\T &=  egin{pmatrix} \lvert\lambda_1vert^2 & \conj{\lambda_1}b \ \lambda_1\conj{b} & \lvert bvert^2 + \lvert\lambda_2vert^2 \end{pmatrix} . \end{aligned} Subtracting, [\T, \T^{*}] =  egin{pmatrix} \lvert bvert^2 & b\,\conj{(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1)} \ \conj{b}\,(\lambda_2 - \lambda_1) & -\lvert bvert^2 \end{pmatrix} . Its four squared moduli are \lvert bvert^4, \lvert bvert^2\lvert\lambda_1 - \lambda_2vert^2, \lvert bvert^2\lvert\lambda_1 - \lambda_2vert^2 and \lvert bvert^4. Adding them gives the stated formula. (c) Let \A \in M_2(
C) and write \A = \U\T\U^{*} as in @cor-schur-matrix, with \T upper triangular of the shape in (b) and \lambda_1, \lambda_2 the eigenvalues of \A. By @eq-schur-split, \Delta(\A)^2 = \lvert bvert^2. By (a) and (b), 
orm{[\A, \A^{*}]}_F^2 = 2\lvert bvert^4 + 2\lvert bvert^2\lvert\lambda_1 - \lambda_2vert^2 \ge 2\lvert bvert^4 = 2\,\Delta(\A)^4 , and taking non-negative square roots gives 
orm{[\A, \A^{*}]}_F \ge \sqrt2\,\Delta(\A)^2. Equality holds exactly when \lvert bvert^2\lvert\lambda_1 - \lambda_2vert^2 = 0, that is, when b = 0 or \lambda_1 = \lambda_2. The first case says \Delta(\A) = 0, that is, \A is normal, and then both sides are 0. So equality holds if and only if \A is normal or its two eigenvalues coincide.

title: Positive Matrices and the Singular Value Decomposition
content:
Positive Matrices and the Singular Value Decomposition A matrix that is not square has no eigenvalues. There is no equation \A\v = \lambda\v to write down, because \A\v and \v live in different spaces, and everything Chapters 8 to 11 built on that equation is unavailable. Yet the geometric picture that opened Chapter 11 survives untouched: push the unit sphere of F^n through any \A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F), square or not, and what comes out is an ellipsoid. It has semi-axes, they are perpendicular, and the directions they came from were perpendicular too. Reading that picture as a factorization gives \A = \U\vSigma\V^{*}, the singular value decomposition: every matrix whatsoever maps some orthonormal basis to an orthogonal set. It is the most used factorization in applied linear algebra, and this chapter’s business is to earn it and then spend it. The road runs through positivity. A non-square \A has no eigenvalues, but \A^{*}\A does, and \A^{*}\A is self-adjoint with a non-negative quadratic form — it is a positive semidefinite matrix, the analogue of a non-negative number. Chapter 11 left that class unexamined; here it comes first, with its many equivalent tests, its square root, and the triangular factorization that elimination finds. From the square root comes the absolute value \lvert\Avert, from \lvert\Avert the polar decomposition \A = \W\lvert\Avert, and from the spectral theorem applied to \A^{*}\A the singular value decomposition itself. Once it is in hand, a series of questions that look unrelated turn out to have one answer: what are orthonormal bases of the four fundamental subspaces, what is the best rank-k approximation of a matrix, what should \A^{-1} mean when \A is not invertible, and when is a projection orthogonal. The field is 
R or 
C throughout, as in Chapters 10 and 11, and every statement says which one it needs. What you need. From Chapter 11, the two spectral theorems and their matrix forms (@thm-spectral-complex, @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, @thm-spectral-real, @cor-spectral-real-matrix, @cor-symmetric-rank-one-sum, @thm-principal-axes), the elementary theory of self-adjoint operators (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues, @thm-self-adjoint-orthogonal-eigenspaces, @thm-complex-zero-test, @exr-self-adjoint-operators-c1), commuting families (@cor-simultaneous-unitary-matrix, @cor-simultaneous-orthogonal-real), and the functional calculus with its square root (@def-spectral-resolution, @thm-spectral-resolution, @thm-functional-calculus-properties, @thm-normal-square-root), together with the Frobenius norm and its unitary invariance (@lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant). From Chapter 10, the adjoint and what it does to the four subspaces (@def-adjoint, @thm-adjoint-properties, @thm-matrix-of-adjoint, @thm-four-subspaces-orthogonal, @cor-rank-adjoint), orthogonal decompositions and projections (@thm-orthogonal-decomposition, @def-orthogonal-projection, @thm-projection-formula, @thm-best-approximation), least squares (@thm-least-squares, @cor-least-squares-unique, @thm-minimum-norm-solution, @lem-kernel-normal-equations), Gram matrices (@def-gram-matrix, @thm-gram-matrix-properties), isometries (@def-isometry, @thm-isometry-characterizations, @def-unitary-orthogonal) and the QR factorization (@thm-qr-factorization). From Chapter 7, block multiplication and Schur complements (@thm-block-multiplication, @def-schur-complement, @thm-block-ldu, @thm-schur-determinant, @thm-schur-rank, @thm-block-inverse-formula). From Chapter 6, multiplicativity of the determinant, triangular determinants and the non-negativity of Gram determinants (@thm-det-multiplicative, @thm-det-triangular, @cor-gram-determinant-nonnegative). From Chapter 5, Lagrange interpolation (@thm-lagrange-interpolation). From Chapter 3, projections along a complement (@def-projection-operator, @thm-projection-direct-sum). From Chapter 2, the \L\D\L	p factorization and the invertible matrix theorem it started (@thm-ldlt, @thm-invertible-tfae). Roadmap - Positive semidefinite and positive definite matrices. The definition, the real-versus-complex asymmetry that trips everyone, and the full list of equivalent tests, ending in Sylvester’s criterion and the trap that comes with it. - The square root and Cholesky. The unique positive square root, why it is a polynomial in the matrix, the absolute value \lvert\Avert, and the factorization \A = \L\L^{*} whose algorithm is itself the test for definiteness. - Gram matrices. A matrix is a Gram matrix exactly when it is positive semidefinite; the Gram determinant as a squared volume, and distance to a subspace computed two ways. - Two forms at once. A positive definite form and a self-adjoint one can be diagonalized simultaneously — by congruence, not by similarity — and the generalized eigenvalue problem \B\x = \lambda\A\x follows. - The Loewner order. What \A \succeq \B means, what monotonicity survives it (traces, determinants, inverses), and the chapter’s negative result: squaring does not. - Blocks and Schur complements. Testing a block matrix for positive definiteness one block at a time, and the Fischer and Hadamard determinant inequalities that fall out. - Products entry by entry. The Schur product theorem — the Hadamard product of positive matrices is positive — and Oppenheim’s inequality. - The singular value decomposition. Every matrix is \U\vSigma\V^{*}; the singular values are determined, the unitaries are not, and the compact form reads off orthonormal bases of all four fundamental subspaces. - Polar decomposition and Takagi. \A = \W\lvert\Avert is z = e^{i	heta}r for matrices; \W is the nearest unitary matrix to \A; and a complex symmetric matrix factors as \U\vSigma\U	p. - Low-rank approximation. Truncating the singular value sum gives the best approximation of each rank, in the Frobenius norm, with an error one can write down. - The pseudoinverse. Inverting the non-zero singular values defines \A^{+}; it is pinned down by four conditions, and \A^{+}  is the minimum-norm least-squares solution promised in Chapter 10. - Projections revisited. An idempotent is an orthogonal projection exactly when it is self-adjoint; everything else is oblique, and the obliqueness is a measurable angle. Named moves - Test with \inner{\A\x}{\x}. Positivity is a statement about one scalar function of one vector. Most proofs in the first half of the chapter consist of evaluating that function at a cleverly chosen \x — a standard basis vector, a vector supported on a few coordinates, an eigenvector, or \S\y for a substitution \S. - Factor as \B^{*}\B. Every positive semidefinite matrix is one, and that form turns a statement about the matrix into a statement about lengths: \inner{\B^{*}\B\x}{\x} = 
orm{\B\x}^2. It is also what makes every positive semidefinite matrix a Gram matrix. - Diagonalize, do it to the eigenvalues, come back. The square root, the pseudoinverse and the whole functional calculus are this one move. The work is always in checking that the result does not depend on the diagonalization chosen. - Apply the spectral theorem to \A^{*}\A. When the matrix in front of you is not square, not normal, or not even an operator, this is the way in. The singular value decomposition is nothing but the spectral theorem for \A^{*}\A, read back through \A. - Truncate the sum. Writing \A = \sum_i\sigma_i\u_i\v_i^{*} turns a matrix into a sum of rank-one pieces ordered by importance. Cutting the sum short gives the compact form, the best low-rank approximation and the pseudoinverse, three times from one idea.

title: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content:
Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices Chapter 11 sorted the operators that have an orthonormal eigenbasis. Among them the self-adjoint ones are the matrix analogue of the real numbers, since they are exactly the operators fixed by starring. Inside the real numbers sits a smaller and even more useful set, the non-negative ones, and this section finds its matrix analogue. The answer turns out to have three faces — a sign condition on the spectrum, a sign condition on a scalar function, and a factorization — and the whole of the rest of the chapter is built on the fact that the three agree. Throughout, F = 
R or F = 
C, and F^n carries the standard inner product \inner{\x}{\y} = \y^{*}\x. Which self-adjoint matrices deserve to be called non-negative? A real number t is non-negative in three equivalent ways: t \ge 0; tx^2 \ge 0 for every real x; and t = s^2 for some real s. Each of the three has a matrix reading. “Every eigenvalue is \ge 0” copies the first. “\inner{\A\x}{\x} \ge 0 for every \x” copies the second, because \inner{\A\x}{\x} is the one scalar a matrix attaches to a single vector. “\A = \B^{*}\B” copies the third, with the star doing what nothing does for numbers but everything does for matrices. It is not obvious that the three agree, and for a general matrix they do not: they all fail for  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} in different ways. What makes them agree is self-adjointness, and the middle condition is the one to take as the definition, because it is the one that says something about every vector at once. A matrix is positive semidefinite when its quadratic form never goes negative. [Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite] Let \A \in M_n(F). Then \A is positive semidefinite, written \A \succeq 0, if 1. \A is Hermitian, that is \A^{*} = \A (over 
R: symmetric, \A	p = \A); and 2. \inner{\A\x}{\x} \ge 0 for every \x \in F^n. It is positive definite, written \A \succ 0, if (P1) holds and \inner{\A\x}{\x} > 0 for every non-zero \x \in F^n. The same words apply to an operator T \in \cL(V) on a finite-dimensional inner product space: T is positive semidefinite if T^{*} = T and \inner{T\v}{\v} \ge 0 for every \v \in V, and positive definite if the inequality is strict for \v 
e \0. In words: (P1) puts \A in the class where the analogy with real numbers is available at all, and (P2) says that the number \inner{\A\x}{\x} = \x^{*}\A\x is never negative. The word every in (P2) is the whole content; a single vector proves nothing. In the definite case the vector \x = \0 has to be excluded, since \inner{\A\0}{\0} = 0 for every \A whatsoever. Clause (P1) is also what makes clause (P2) meaningful. For a Hermitian \A, the number \inner{\A\x}{\x} is real for every \x, over 
C as well as over 
R (@prp-self-adjoint-immediate), so comparing it with 0 is legitimate. Without (P1) the number can be a genuine complex number, and “\ge 0” would be meaningless. Positive definite implies positive semidefinite, since a condition that holds strictly for \x 
e \0 holds weakly for \x = \0 too. The reverse fails, and the smallest witness is \diag(1, 0). Before any examples, the trap. Over 
R, clause (P1) has to be assumed; over 
C it comes free. Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}, the quarter turn of 
R^2. Then \inner{\A\x}{\x} = -x_2x_1 + x_1x_2 = 0 for every \x \in 
R^2, so (P2) holds in the strongest possible way, and yet \A	p = -\A 
e \A. A real matrix can pass the quadratic-form test and be nowhere near symmetric, because over 
R the quadratic form cannot see the skew part of a matrix at all (@exr-self-adjoint-operators-c3). So a real definition that dropped (P1) would call the quarter turn positive semidefinite, and none of the theorems below would survive. Over 
C the situation is the opposite, and it is worth recording once. [Over 
C, positivity implies Hermitian] Let \A \in M_n(
C) satisfy \inner{\A\x}{\x} \in 
R for every \x \in 
C^n — in particular, let \inner{\A\x}{\x} \ge 0 for every \x. Then \A^{*} = \A. Put \S = \A - \A^{*}. For every \x, moving the star across (@lem-conjugate-transpose-pairing) and using conjugate symmetry, \inner{\A^{*}\x}{\x} = \inner{\x}{\A\x} = \conj{\inner{\A\x}{\x}} = \inner{\A\x}{\x} , the last equality because the number is real. Hence \inner{\S\x}{\x} = 0 for every \x \in 
C^n, and @thm-complex-zero-test gives \S = 0. So over 
C one may state the definition with (P2) alone; over 
R one may not. We keep (P1) in the definition for both fields, so that a single sentence covers them and so that no reader has to remember which field licenses which shortcut. Now the examples, all checked against (P1) and (P2) in turn. [Five Positive Matrices] Decide which of the following are positive semidefinite, and which are positive definite. 1. \I_n, and more generally \D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n) with every d_i real. 2. \x\x^{*} for a fixed \x \in F^n. 3. Its quadratic form is identically 0, which shows how little the form sees over 
R. (f) Positive semidefinite, not positive definite. Hermitian, with a = 2 \ge 0, d = 1 \ge 0 and ad - \lvert bvert^2 = 2 - 2 = 0. The determinant is 0, so definiteness fails; indeed \A(1+i, -2) = \0. [B2: A parameter] For which t \in 
R is \A(t) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & t & 0 \ t & 2 & t \ 0 & t & 3 \end{pmatrix} positive definite? Justify your answer. \A(t) is symmetric for every real t, so Sylvester’s criterion applies (@thm-pd-characterizations (d)). The leading principal minors are \det \A_1 = 1, \qquad \det \A_2 = 2 - t^2, \qquad \det \A_3 = 6 - 4t^2 , the last by expansion along the first row: 1\cdot(6 - t^2) - t\cdot(3t - 0) = 6 - 4t^2. All three are positive exactly when t^2 < 2 and t^2 < 3/2, that is when t^2 < 3/2. Hence \A(t) \succ 0 if and only if \lvert tvert < \sqrt{6}/2. At t = \sqrt{6}/2 the matrix is positive semidefinite but singular, and for \lvert tvert > \sqrt{6}/2 the determinant is negative, so \A(t) has an odd number of negative eigenvalues and is not even semidefinite. [B3: The inverse of a positive definite matrix] Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succ 0. Prove that \A is invertible and that \A^{-1} \succ 0. By @thm-pd-characterizations (b), every eigenvalue of \A is positive, so 0 
otin \spec(\A) and \A is invertible (@thm-invertible-tfae-eigen). Then (\A^{-1})^{*} = (\A^{*})^{-1} = \A^{-1}, so \A^{-1} is Hermitian. Apply @prp-congruence-positivity (b) with \S = \A^{-1}, which is invertible: \S^{*}\A\S = \A^{-1}\A\A^{-1} = \A^{-1} \succ 0 . (Alternatively: the eigenvalues of \A^{-1} are the reciprocals 1/\lambda_i of those of \A, hence positive, and @thm-pd-characterizations (b) applies again.) C. Going deeper [C1: Zero trace forces zero] Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq 0. 1. Prove that a_{ii} \ge 0 for every i, and that 	r \A \ge 0. 2. Prove that if 	r \A = 0 then \A = 0. 3. Deduce that if \A \succeq 0 and -\A \succeq 0, then \A = 0. (a) a_{ii} = \e_i^{*}\A\e_i = \inner{\A\e_i}{\e_i} \ge 0 by (P2). Summing, 	r \A = \sum_i a_{ii} \ge 0. (b) Write \A = \U\D\U^{*} with \U unitary and \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n) the eigenvalues (@cor-spectral-complex-matrix, @cor-spectral-real-matrix). Then 	r \A = 	r(\D\U^{*}\U) = 	r \D = \sum_i\lambda_i by @thm-trace-properties, and each \lambda_i \ge 0 by @thm-psd-characterizations (b). A sum of non-negative reals is 0 only if every term is 0, so \D = 0 and hence \A = 0. Alternatively, without eigenvalues: by (a) each a_{ii} \ge 0, so 	r \A = 0 forces every a_{ii} = 0. Writing \A = \B^{*}\B (@thm-psd-characterizations (c)), the i-th diagonal entry is 
orm{ _i}^2 for the i-th column  _i of \B; so every column of \B is \0, that is \B = 0 and \A = 0. (c) If both \A \succeq 0 and -\A \succeq 0, then by (a) 	r \A \ge 0 and 	r(-\A) = -	r \A \ge 0, so 	r \A = 0 and (b) gives \A = 0. [C2: The cone of positive matrices] Let \cP_n \subseteq M_n(F) be the set of positive semidefinite matrices. 1. Prove that if \A, \B \in \cP_n and c \ge 0 is real, then \A + \B \in \cP_n and c\A \in \cP_n. (A set with these two properties is a convex cone: it contains (1-t)\A + t\B for 0 \le t \le 1 as well.) 2. Prove that \cP_n contains no line through 0: if \A \in \cP_n and -\A \in \cP_n then \A = 0. 3. Prove that \cP_n is closed under congruence: if \A \in \cP_n and \S \in M_n(F), then \S^{*}\A\S \in \cP_n. Give an example showing that \cP_n is not closed under multiplication. Hint for (c): for the example, two positive semidefinite matrices whose product is not even Hermitian will do. (a) Sums and real multiples of Hermitian matrices are Hermitian. For every \x, \inner{(\A + \B)\x}{\x} = \inner{\A\x}{\x} + \inner{\B\x}{\x} \ge 0 , and \inner{c\A\x}{\x} = c\inner{\A\x}{\x} \ge 0 since c \ge 0. Convexity follows by taking c = 1 - t and c = t and adding. (b) This is @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1 (c). (c) Immediate from @prp-congruence-positivity (a). For the failure of multiplicativity, take \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} , both positive semidefinite (\A = \e_1\e_1	p and \B = \1\1	p). Then \A\B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} , which is not symmetric, so it is not positive semidefinite — it fails (P1), never mind (P2). Section 2 shows what does survive: 	r(\A\B) \ge 0, and \A\B \succeq 0 whenever \A and \B commute. [C3: The largest entry sits on the diagonal] Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq 0. 1. Prove that \lvert a_{ij}vert^2 \le a_{ii}a_{jj} for all i, j. 2. Deduce that if a_{ii} = 0 for some i, then the whole i-th row and i-th column of \A are zero. 3. Deduce that \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert = \max_i a_{ii}. Hint for (a): look at a 2 	imes 2 principal submatrix. (a) For i = j the claim is a_{ii}^2 \le a_{ii}^2. For i 
e j, take I = \{i, j\}. By the proof of @thm-psd-characterizations ((a) \Rightarrow (e)), \A_{I,I} \succeq 0, and @exm-two-by-two-criterion gives a_{ii}a_{jj} - \lvert a_{ij}vert^2 = \det \A_{I,I} \ge 0. (b) If a_{ii} = 0, then (a) gives \lvert a_{ij}vert^2 \le 0 \cdot a_{jj} = 0 for every j, so a_{ij} = 0; and a_{ji} = \conj{a_{ij}} = 0 since \A is Hermitian. (c) Let M = \max_i a_{ii}, a maximum of non-negative reals by @exr-positive-definite-matrices-c1 (a). By (a), \lvert a_{ij}vert \le \sqrt{a_{ii}a_{jj}} \le M for all i, j, so \max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}vert \le M. The reverse inequality holds because the diagonal entries are among the entries. Hence the two maxima are equal.

title: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content:
Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization A non-negative real number has exactly one non-negative square root, and it is the reason “non-negative” is a useful class of numbers at all: it lets us take lengths, define standard deviations, and undo a squaring. Section 1 produced the matrix analogue as one clause of a theorem. This section makes it an object with a name, adds the one property the clause did not mention — that the square root is a polynomial in the matrix — and then turns the same idea into the triangular factorization that elimination discovers, the one Chapter 2 promised and could not yet explain. Throughout, F = 
R or F = 
C, and all matrices are over F. The positive square root @thm-psd-characterizations (d) already says that a positive semidefinite \A has exactly one positive semidefinite square root. That is an existence-and-uniqueness statement, so by the usual convention it deserves a notation. The square root of a positive matrix is what you get by taking square roots of its eigenvalues and leaving the eigenvectors alone. The Positive Square Root Let \A \in M_n(F) with \A \succeq 0. Then there is exactly one \C \in M_n(F) with \C \succeq 0 and \C^2 = \A. We write \C = \A^{1/2}, also \sqrt{\A}. Moreover: 1. \A^{1/2} = p(\A) for some polynomial p with real coefficients (the nodes \lambda_i and the values \sqrt{\lambda_i} are real, so the interpolation of @thm-lagrange-interpolation may be run over 
R, and 
R[x] \subseteq 
C[x]); 2. \A^{1/2}\B = \B\A^{1/2} for every \B \in M_n(F) with \A\B = \B\A; 3. 
ul(\A^{1/2}) = 
ul(\A) and ank \A^{1/2} = ank \A; in particular \A^{1/2} is invertible if and only if \A is. The eigenvalues of \A^{1/2} are the non-negative square roots of those of \A, with the same eigenvectors. Existence and uniqueness are Section 1. What is new is (a), and it is the reason (b) is free.
