title: Bilinear and Quadratic Forms
content:
Bilinear and Quadratic Forms An inner product does two jobs at once. It pairs two vectors and returns a scalar, linearly in each of them; and it measures, because \inner{\v}{\v} is a positive number whenever \v 
e \0. Chapters 10 to 12 leaned on the second job constantly: lengths, angles, orthonormal bases, least squares, positive definiteness and the singular value decomposition are all consequences of positivity. This chapter keeps the pairing and throws the measuring away. What is left is a bilinear form, a function  eta \colon V 	imes V 	o F linear in each slot, with no sign condition, no symmetry required, and no field restriction. The question of the chapter is what survives. A surprising amount does. Forms still have matrices, and the matrices still change by a rule when the basis changes — but the rule is \A \mapsto \P	p\A\P, not \A \mapsto \P^{-1}\A\P. The organizing relation is therefore congruence, not similarity, and the two are genuinely different: congruent matrices need not share a single eigenvalue. What they do share is a rank, a symmetry type, and — over 
R — a triple of signs, which is Sylvester’s law of inertia and the central classification theorem of the chapter. Beyond 
R the classification depends on the arithmetic of the field, and beyond symmetry there is a second world, the alternating forms, where every non-degenerate example looks like every other of the same size. Along the way we meet vectors on which a form vanishes without being zero, the groups that preserve a form, the geometry that physics runs on, and one algebra built to make a quadratic form into a square. The field is a general F here. Since Chapter 9 the book has worked over 
R or 
C, because inner products need them; this chapter opens the field back up, and that is the point rather than an afterthought. Chapters 10 to 12 turn out to have been the positive definite special case of one line of this theory. Two consequences of the general setting are worth flagging in advance. First, “positive” has no meaning over a field with no order, so the definiteness arguments of Chapter 12 simply cannot be run; what replaces them is either a square-class computation or nothing at all. Second, when 1 + 1 = 0 — characteristic 2, @def-characteristic — the identity  eta(\u,\v) = 	frac12 igl(q(\u+\v) - q(\u) - q(\v) igr) is unavailable, and symmetric and alternating forms stop being complementary. Every statement below that needs a characteristic hypothesis carries one, and every statement without one holds over every field. What you need. From Chapter 6, multilinearity and alternation, which this chapter reuses rather than redefines (@def-multilinear-form, @def-alternating-form, @def-skew-symmetric-form, @thm-alternating-properties, @thm-skew-symmetric-alternating), together with the determinant and its multiplicativity (@def-determinant, @thm-det-multiplicative, @thm-det-transpose). From Chapter 3, the matrix of a map, change of coordinates and similarity (@def-matrix-of-linear-map, @thm-matrix-of-map-coordinates, @def-change-of-coordinates-matrix, @thm-change-of-coordinates, @thm-change-of-basis-maps, @def-similar-matrices), together with rank, equivalence of matrices and the rank normal form (@def-rank, @def-equivalent-matrices, @thm-rank-normal-form). From Chapter 4, the dual space and its bases (@def-linear-functional, @def-dual-space, @thm-dual-basis, @cor-dimension-dual-space, @thm-dual-of-subspace, @thm-double-dual-isomorphism). From Chapter 0, fields and characteristic (@def-field, @def-characteristic, @thm-characteristic-prime), the transpose and symmetry (@def-transpose, @def-symmetric-matrix, @thm-transpose-properties), and groups (@def-group, @def-subgroup). From Chapter 2, the \L\D\L	p factorization (@thm-ldlt). From Chapters 10 to 12, everything used for the real and complex specializations: the orthogonal and unitary groups (@def-unitary-orthogonal, @def-unitary-orthogonal-groups), the real spectral theorem and principal axes (@thm-spectral-real, @cor-spectral-real-matrix, @thm-principal-axes), the orthogonal group in low dimension (@prp-orthogonal-group-properties, @thm-orthogonal-canonical-form), and positivity (@def-positive-semidefinite, @thm-psd-characterizations, @thm-pd-characterizations, @prp-congruence-positivity, @thm-simultaneous-congruence). Those last results are used only where the field is 
R or 
C; they are never hypotheses of the general theory. Roadmap - Bilinear forms and their matrices. What a form is, the Gram matrix that records it, the bijection between forms and matrices, and the form’s companion map V 	o V^{*}, whose kernel is the radical and whose invertibility is non-degeneracy. - Congruence. Changing the basis replaces \A by \P	p\A\P. What that relation preserves — rank, symmetry type, non-degeneracy, the square class of the determinant — and what it destroys, starting with the eigenvalues. - Three kinds of form. Symmetric, alternating, skew-symmetric and Hermitian; why the middle two coincide exactly when the characteristic is not 2; polarization, and the quadratic form. - Completing the square. Over any field of characteristic 
e 2, every symmetric form has an orthogonal basis. The proof is an induction, and the algorithm is symmetric row-and-column elimination. - Inertia. Over 
R the number of positive, negative and zero diagonal entries does not depend on the diagonalization. This classifies real symmetric matrices up to congruence and reconciles congruence with the spectral theorem. - Definiteness revisited. Chapter 12’s tests, restated as statements about signatures, and the second-derivative test they decide. - Where the form vanishes. Isotropic vectors, totally isotropic subspaces, hyperbolic planes, and the Witt decomposition of a non-degenerate space. - Witt’s theorems. An isometry between subspaces extends to the whole space; one summand of an orthogonal sum may be canceled from both sides. - Symplectic forms. A non-degenerate alternating form lives only in even dimension and has exactly one shape, over every field, with no characteristic hypothesis anywhere. - The classical groups. \Orth(n), \Orth(p,q), \Unit(n) and the symplectic group, all read off one equation \P	p\A\P = \A. - Minkowski space. The signature (1,3) form, the light cone, hyperbolic rotations, and the triangle inequality running backwards. - A first look at Clifford algebras. Making a quadratic form into a square, and how 
C and the quaternions come out of it. Named moves - Polarize. A symmetric form and its quadratic function q(\v) =  eta(\v,\v) carry the same information, because  eta can be recovered from q by expanding q(\u + \v) and dividing by 2. That division is the whole reason characteristic 2 is excluded whenever it is excluded. - Complete the square. Every diagonalization theorem for symmetric forms in this chapter is this one manipulation, applied by induction on the dimension: isolate a variable that actually appears, absorb its cross terms into a perfect square, and recurse on what is left. - Split off a hyperbolic plane. For indefinite forms this replaces “peel off an eigenvector”. A single non-zero isotropic vector forces a two-dimensional piece of standard shape to split off orthogonally, and the induction runs on the rest. - Count signs, not values. The numbers on a diagonalized form are not invariants; their signs are. Whenever a quantity refuses to be an invariant, ask whether some coarser feature of it is. - Congruence, not similarity. At every theorem, ask which relation is in play. If the matrix is eaten twice by the same vector, the relation is congruence and eigenvalues are not available; if it is eaten once and returns a vector, the relation is similarity and they are.

title: 13.1 Bilinear Forms and Their Matrices
content:
Bilinear Forms and Their Matrices Chapter 6 needed a function of several vectors that was linear in each of them separately, and called it a multilinear form (@def-multilinear-form). Chapter 10 needed a function of two vectors that was linear in the first, conjugate-linear in the second, and positive on the diagonal, and called it an inner product. This section takes the common skeleton of the two — two slots, linear in each, nothing else assumed — and studies it on its own. The payoff is immediate: such a function is recorded by a square matrix, exactly as a linear map is, and the whole rest of the chapter is about how that matrix behaves. Throughout, V is a vector space over a field F. From the second subsection on, V is finite-dimensional with \dim V = n \ge 1, and \sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n) is an ordered basis of V. No hypothesis on the characteristic of F is used anywhere in this section, and none is used in the next one either. Pairing without measuring The dot product on F^n is a machine with two inputs and one scalar output. Over 
R it does two different jobs. It pairs: it takes \x and \y and returns \sum_i x_iy_i, linearly in each of them. And it measures: \x \cdot \x is a sum of squares, so it is positive unless \x = \0, and from that one fact Chapter 10 extracted lengths, angles, orthonormal bases and everything built on them. Measuring is the fragile half. It needs an order on F, so it is meaningless over 
C without a conjugation and meaningless over 
F_5 altogether. Pairing needs nothing: \sum_i x_iy_i makes sense over every field, and so do plenty of other two-slot expressions, such as x_1y_2 - x_2y_1 or x_1y_1 - x_2y_2. Chapter 6 already met the first of these as the signed area, and met the general notion as the case k = 2 of a multilinear form. We give that case its own name, because from here on it is the object of study rather than a step toward the determinant. A bilinear form pairs two vectors of the same space into a scalar, linearly in each slot separately. [Bilinear Form] Let V be a vector space over a field F. A bilinear form on V is a function  eta \colon V 	imes V 	o F that is linear in each argument when the other is held fixed: for all \u, \u', \v, \v' \in V and all c \in F, 1.  eta(\u + \u', \v) =  eta(\u, \v) +  eta(\u', \v) and  eta(c\u, \v) = c\, eta(\u, \v); 2.  eta(\u, \v + \v') =  eta(\u, \v) +  eta(\u, \v') and  eta(\u, c\v) = c\, eta(\u, \v). Equivalently,  eta is a 2-linear form on V in the sense of @def-multilinear-form. In words: (B1) says that for each fixed \v, the function \u \mapsto  eta(\u, \v) is a linear functional on V (@def-linear-functional), and (B2) says the same for \v \mapsto  eta(\u, \v) with \u fixed. The word fixed is the whole content. Nothing is assumed about how the two slots compare:  eta(\u, \v) and  eta(\v, \u) may be unrelated, and  eta(\v, \v) may be any scalar at all, including 0 for a non-zero \v. Two consequences come free from linearity in one slot. Taking c = 0 in (B1) gives  eta(\0, \v) = 0 for every \v, and likewise  eta(\u, \0) = 0. And by induction on the number of terms,  eta\Bigl(\sum_i a_i\u_i,\ \sum_j b_j\v_j\Bigr) = \sum_{i,j} a_ib_j\, eta(\u_i, \v_j), which is the identity everything in this section rests on: a bilinear form is determined by its values on pairs drawn from a spanning set. [Six two-slot functions] Decide which of the following are bilinear forms on the given space over the given field. 1. The dot product on F^n:  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n. 2. On F^n, for a fixed \A \in M_n(F):  eta_{\A}(\x, \y) = \x	p\A\y. 3. On F^2:  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_2 - x_2y_1. 4. On 
R[x]_{\le 2}:  eta(f, g) = \int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,\dd t. 5. On any V: the zero function  eta(\u, \v) = 0. 6. On 
R^n:  eta(\x, \y) = 
orm{\x}\,
orm{\y}, the product of the Euclidean lengths. (a) Fix \y. Then \x \mapsto \sum_i x_iy_i is a linear functional on F^n, since it is a fixed linear combination of the coordinate functionals (@thm-functionals-on-fn). Fixing \x gives the same statement in \y. So (B1) and (B2) hold and the dot product is bilinear. (b) With \A = \I_n this is (a). In general, write out the entries: \x	p\A\y = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}x_iy_j. For fixed \y this is \sum_i  igl(\sum_j a_{ij}y_j igr)x_i, a fixed linear combination of the coordinates of \x, hence a linear functional; symmetrically in \y. So  eta_{\A} is bilinear for every \A, symmetric or not. Part (c) below is the case \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}. (c) This is the signed area of Chapter 6, and it is bilinear by @exm-alternating-forms (a). It is worth noticing what it does on the diagonal:  eta(\x, \x) = x_1x_2 - x_2x_1 = 0 for every \x. A bilinear form may vanish identically on the diagonal without being the zero form. (d) For fixed g, the map f \mapsto \int_0^1 fg is linear, because the integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals and constants come out. Symmetrically in g. So  eta is bilinear. Here  eta(f, f) = \int_0^1 f^2 \ge 0, so over 
R this form does measure: it is the inner product of Chapter 10. (e) Both clauses read 0 = 0 + 0 and 0 = c \cdot 0. The zero form is bilinear on every space over every field. It is the degenerate case, and it matters: it shows that a bilinear form can carry no information whatsoever, and it is the form whose matrix below is the zero matrix. (f) Not bilinear. Fix \y = \e_1. Then  eta(\e_1, \e_1) +  eta(-\e_1, \e_1) = 1 + 1 = 2, while  eta(\e_1 + (-\e_1), \e_1) =  eta(\0, \e_1) = 0. Additivity in the first slot fails, so (B1) fails. The homogeneity half of (B1) also fails, since  eta(-\e_1, \e_1) = 1 
e - eta(\e_1, \e_1). Item (f) is the non-example by minimal change worth remembering: the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality says that \lvert\x \cdot \yvert \le 
orm{\x}
orm{\y}, so 
orm{\x}
orm{\y} sits right next to the dot product numerically, and yet it is not a form at all, because the absolute value hidden in the norm destroys additivity. A second minimal change makes the same point more cheaply:  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_1 + 1 fails (B1) because  eta(\0, \0) = 1 
e 0. Bilinear is not linear. A bilinear form is not a linear function of the pair (\u, \v), and the two properties are not even compatible in general. For the dot product on 
R^2, doubling both arguments multiplies the value by 4:  eta(2\e_1, 2\e_1) = 4, not 2 eta(\e_1, \e_1) = 2. Sums may only be split one slot at a time, with the other slot held frozen. Chapter 6 gave this warning for multilinear forms in general; it is repeated here because it is the mistake readers make most often when a form is written with the familiar-looking symbol \x	p\A\y. The same definition with two different spaces,  eta \colon V 	imes W 	o F linear in each slot, is called a bilinear pairing of V and W. The basic example is the evaluation pairing V^{*} 	imes V 	o F, (\varphi, \v) \mapsto \varphi(\v), which is linear in \varphi by the definition of the operations on V^{*} (@def-dual-space) and linear in \v because \varphi is. We insist on V = W in @def-bilinear-form because the questions of this chapter — is  eta(\u,\v) equal to  eta(\v,\u), what is  eta(\v,\v), which vectors are orthogonal to which — only make sense when both slots hold vectors of the same space. The matrix of a form The displayed expansion above says that a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional space is determined by finitely many numbers: the values  eta(\v_i, \v_j) on pairs of basis vectors. There are n^2 of them, they are indexed by a row and a column, and that is a matrix. Chapter 3 recorded a linear map by a matrix in exactly the same spirit (@def-matrix-of-linear-map); here the recipe is even simpler, because there is no basis of an output space to choose. The matrix of a form is its table of values on pairs of basis vectors. [Matrix of a Bilinear Form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V with ordered basis \sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n). The matrix of  eta with respect to \sB, also called its Gram matrix, is the matrix \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{} \in M_n(F) with entries  igl(\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{} igr)_{ij} \coloneqq  eta(\v_i, \v_j) . In words: the entry in row i and column j is the value of  eta with the i-th basis vector in the left slot and the j-th in the right slot. The order matters, because  eta(\v_i, \v_j) and  eta(\v_j, \v_i) need not agree; the convention chosen here is the one that makes the recovery formula below carry no transpose on the matrix. Chapter 10 also called a matrix of pairings a Gram matrix, and the two conventions differ, so it is worth saying how. @def-gram-matrix set (\G)_{ij} = \inner{\v_j}{\v_i}, with the indices crossed, because an inner product is conjugate-linear in its second slot and the crossing is what makes \G Hermitian and \x^{*}\G\x come out as a squared norm. A bilinear form has no conjugation to accommodate, so here the natural order is the uncrossed one, which is what makes the recovery formula below free of transposes. For a real symmetric form the two agree; in general each is the transpose of the other. Nothing needs checking for well-definedness: once \sB is fixed, each entry is a single value of a function. What does need saying is that no information is lost. [Forms and Matrices Correspond] Let V be an n-dimensional vector space over F with ordered basis \sB, and let  eta be a bilinear form on V with \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{}. 1. For all \u, \v \in V,  eta(\u, \v) = \coord{\u}{\sB}	p\,\A\,\coord{\v}{\sB} . 2. \A is the only matrix in M_n(F) with this property. 3. So clause (B1) holds. Clause (B2) follows by the same argument with the roles of the two arguments exchanged, since the defining expression is symmetric in them. (b) Suppose (\psi, \w) \in \operatorname{rad}( eta), so \psi(\v) + \varphi(\w) = 0 for all \varphi \in V^{*} and all \v \in V. Taking \varphi = 0 gives \psi(\v) = 0 for every \v, so \psi = 0. Taking \v = \0 then gives \varphi(\w) = 0 for every \varphi \in V^{*}, so \ev_{\w} = 0 in V^{**}, and \w = \0 because \ev_V is injective (@thm-evaluation-map-linear-injective). Hence the radical is \{\0\}. (c) The second half of (b) is exactly that statement: \varphi(\v) = 0 for all \varphi \in V^{*} forces \v = \0. It recovers the injectivity of the evaluation map \ev_V \colon V 	o V^{**} of @thm-evaluation-map-linear-injective, which is the first half of @thm-double-dual-isomorphism. So the non-degeneracy of this form is the statement that functionals separate points (@thm-functionals-separate-points).

title: 13.2 Congruence
content:
Congruence The matrix of a form in @def-form-matrix depends on a basis, and a basis is a choice. As with linear maps in Chapter 3, the useful question is therefore not “what is the matrix?” but “which matrices arise from the same form?”. The answer here is \P	p\A\P rather than \P^{-1}\A\P, and one symbol’s difference changes the whole theory: the new relation keeps the rank and the symmetry type of a matrix and throws its eigenvalues away. This section proves the change-of-basis rule, names the relation, sorts the invariants from the casualties, and settles the debt Chapters 11 and 12 ran up when they kept postponing all of this. Throughout, V is a vector space over an arbitrary field F with \dim V = n \ge 1, and  eta is a bilinear form on V. No hypothesis on the characteristic of F is needed in this section. The change-of-basis rule for a form Two bases \sB and \sB' of V give two matrices for one form. The link between them is the change-of-coordinates matrix of @def-change-of-coordinates-matrix, and the computation is three lines, because @thm-form-matrix-determines (a) already expresses the form through coordinates. [Change of Basis for a Form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional V, let \sB and \sB' be ordered bases of V, and let \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB'}{\sB} be the change-of-coordinates matrix from \sB' to \sB. Then \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{} = \P	p\,\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{}\,\P . There is nothing to discover: write the form in \sB-coordinates, substitute \coord{\v}{\sB} = \P\coord{\v}{\sB'} in both slots, and read off the matrix that appears between the two coordinate vectors. The uniqueness clause of @thm-form-matrix-determines then says that matrix is the one we want, with no further checking. Write \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{}. By @thm-change-of-coordinates (a), \coord{\v}{\sB} = \P\coord{\v}{\sB'} for every \v \in V. So for all \u, \v \in V, using @thm-form-matrix-determines (a) and then @thm-transpose-properties (d),  egin{aligned}  eta(\u, \v) &= \coord{\u}{\sB}	p\,\A\,\coord{\v}{\sB} \ &=  igl(\P\coord{\u}{\sB'} igr)	p\A\, igl(\P\coord{\v}{\sB'} igr) \ &= \coord{\u}{\sB'}	p\, igl(\P	p\A\P igr)\,\coord{\v}{\sB'} . \end{aligned} Thus \P	p\A\P is a matrix with the property that characterizes \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{}, and by the uniqueness in @thm-form-matrix-determines (b) it is \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{}. This proves the theorem. Notice that \P is the same matrix as in @thm-change-of-basis-maps: the change-of-coordinates matrix from the new basis to the old one, whose columns are the new basis vectors written in old coordinates. Only the way it acts has changed, from \P^{-1}\A\P to \P	p\A\P. [Killing the cross term] On 
R^2, let  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_1 + 2x_1y_2 + 2x_2y_1 + x_2y_2, so that \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Compute \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{} for \sB' =  igl((1, 0),\ (-2, 1) igr), both by @thm-change-of-basis-form and directly from @def-form-matrix. The columns of \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB'}{\sE} are the vectors of \sB' in standard coordinates, so \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix}, and therefore \P	p\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix} =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}. Directly: with \v'_1 = (1,0) and \v'_2 = (-2,1), the four values are  eta(\v'_1, \v'_1) = 1,  eta(\v'_1, \v'_2) =  eta(\v'_2, \v'_1) = 0 and  eta(\v'_2, \v'_2) = -3. The two computations agree. The new basis was not guessed. In coordinates the form reads q(\x) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + x_2^2 = (x_1 + 2x_2)^2 - 3x_2^2, a perfect square plus a leftover, and the substitution y_1 = x_1 + 2x_2, y_2 = x_2 — that is, \x = \P\y — is what completing the square asks for. A later section turns this into a theorem and an algorithm. Congruent matrices Every invertible \P is a change-of-coordinates matrix between some pair of bases (@prp-invertible-matrix-change-of-basis), so @thm-change-of-basis-form says exactly this: the matrices of one form, over all bases, are the matrices \P	p\A\P with \P invertible. That set deserves a name, and the name is the organizing idea of the chapter. Two matrices are congruent when they record the same form in two bases. Congruent Matrices Let \A, \B \in M_n(F). We say \A is congruent to \B, written \A \simeq \B, if there exists an invertible \P \in M_n(F) such that \B = \P	p\A\P . In words: congruence allows one matrix to be sandwiched by an invertible matrix and its transpose. The word invertible is essential; without it, \A \mapsto \P	p\A\P with \P = 0 would relate everything to 0. The transpose, not the inverse, is what distinguishes the relation from similarity (@def-similar-matrices), and the symbol \simeq is chosen to sit near \sim without being it. Three immediate readings. First, by @thm-change-of-basis-form, \A \simeq \B if and only if \A and \B are the matrices of a single bilinear form in two bases. Second, in the language of quadratic expressions on F^n, \A \simeq \B says that the substitution \x = \P\y turns \x	p\A\x into \y	p\B\y: congruence is invertible change of variables in a quadratic expression. Third, over 
R it is the relation \A \mapsto \S^{*}\A\S of Chapter 12, because there the star is the transpose. [Congruences and a non-congruence] 1. \I_2 \simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} over any field. 2. \I_2 \simeq \diag(4, 1) over 
Q. 3. \A \simeq \A for every \A. 4. \I_2 
ot\simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} over any field. (a) Take \P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix}, which is invertible with determinant 1. Then \P	p\I_2\P = \P	p\P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}. (b) Take \P = \diag(2, 1), invertible over 
Q. Then \P	p\I_2\P = \diag(4, 1). Scaling a basis vector by c scales the corresponding diagonal entry by c^2, which is the single most useful congruence to have in mind. (c) Take \P = \I_n. (d) Suppose  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} = \P	p\I_2\P = \P	p\P for some \P. Then, by @thm-transpose-properties, (\P	p\P)	p = \P	p\P, so the matrix would be symmetric; it is not. This is the non-example by minimal change: one entry of  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} in (a) is altered, and congruence to \I_2 is lost — not for a subtle reason, but because the altered matrix is not the matrix of a symmetric form in any basis. The general statement is @prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry below. Before using the word “congruent” in both directions, we owe the usual check. [Congruence is an equivalence relation] Congruence is an equivalence relation on M_n(F) (@def-equivalence-relation). Reflexive: \A = \I_n	p\A\I_n. Symmetric: suppose \B = \P	p\A\P with \P invertible, and put \Q = \P^{-1}, which is invertible. By @thm-transpose-properties (d), \Q	p\P	p = (\P\Q)	p = \I_n	p = \I_n, so \Q	p\B\Q =  igl(\Q	p\P	p igr)\A igl(\P\Q igr) = \I_n\A\I_n = \A . Transitive: if \B = \P	p\A\P and \C = \Q	p\B\Q with \P, \Q invertible, then \P\Q is invertible and \C = \Q	p\P	p\A\P\Q = (\P\Q)	p\A(\P\Q). This proves the proposition. So the matrices in M_n(F) fall into congruence classes, and the classification problem of this chapter is to describe them. The rest of the section collects the tools for telling classes apart. What congruence preserves Three invariants come out of the definition with almost no work. The first is the rank, which we already know is the co-dimension of the radical (@prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible). [Congruence preserves rank] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \A \simeq \B. Then ank\A = ank\B. Consequently, whether the associated form is non-degenerate is a property of the congruence class, and it is legitimate to speak of the rank of a bilinear form, meaning the rank of its matrix in any basis. Write \B = \P	p\A\P with \P invertible. Then \P	p is invertible, with inverse (\P^{-1})	p (@thm-transpose-properties). Multiplying by invertible matrices on either side does not change the rank (@thm-rank-product-inequality), so ank\B = ank(\A\P) = ank\A. Non-degeneracy is the condition ank\A = n by @prp-nondegenerate-iff-invertible (c), so it too depends only on the class. The last sentence follows because, by @thm-change-of-basis-form, any two matrices of one form are congruent. The second invariant is the symmetry type. Here “alternating” is used in the matrix sense that @def-alternating-form suggests: a zero diagonal on top of skew-symmetry. The next section separates the three conditions carefully; for now we only need that congruence respects each of them. [Congruence preserves the symmetry type] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \B = \P	p\A\P for an invertible \P. 1. If \A	p = \A, then \B	p = \B. 2. If \A	p = -\A, then \B	p = -\B. 3. If \A	p = -\A and every diagonal entry of \A is 0, the same holds for \B. Each implication is an equivalence, since congruence is symmetric (@prp-congruence-equivalence). By @thm-transpose-properties, \B	p = (\P	p\A\P)	p = \P	p\A	p\P. (a) If \A	p = \A, this is \P	p\A\P = \B. (b) If \A	p = -\A, it is \P	p(-\A)\P = -\B. (c) Assume the hypothesis of (c). Then \B is skew-symmetric by (b), so only the diagonal is left to check. For any \x \in F^n, grouping the terms of the double sum in pairs, \x	p\A\x = \sum_{i<j}(a_{ij} + a_{ji})x_ix_j + \sum_i a_{ii}x_i^2 = 0 , since a_{ij} + a_{ji} = 0 by skew-symmetry and a_{ii} = 0 by hypothesis. Writing \p_1, \dots, \p_n for the columns of \P, the i-th diagonal entry of \B = \P	p\A\P is b_{ii} = \e_i	p\P	p\A\P\e_i = \p_i	p\A\p_i, which is 0 by the display. This proves the proposition. The third invariant is the determinant, but only in a weakened sense: congruence multiplies it by a square. [Congruence changes the determinant by a square] Let \A, \B \in M_n(F) with \B = \P	p\A\P for an invertible \P. Then \det\B = (\det\P)^2\,\det\A , with \det\P 
e 0. In particular \det\A = 0 if and only if \det\B = 0, and when they are non-zero, \det\B = c^2\det\A for some c \in F \setminus\{0\}. By @thm-det-multiplicative and @thm-det-transpose, \det\B = \det(\P	p)\det\A\det\P = (\det\P)^2\det\A . Since \P is invertible, \det\P 
e 0 (@thm-det-nonzero-iff-invertible), so (\det\P)^2 
e 0 and the two determinants vanish together. Taking c = \det\P gives the last claim. The determinant itself is therefore not a congruence invariant — @exm-congruence-first (b) moved it from 1 to 4. What is invariant is the determinant read modulo squares. Write F^{	imes} = F \setminus\{0\}, and for a, b \in F^{	imes} declare a and b equivalent when a = c^2b for some c \in F^{	imes}. This is an equivalence relation on F^{	imes} (@def-equivalence-relation): it is reflexive with c = 1, symmetric with c^{-1}, and transitive by multiplying the two scalars. Its classes are called square classes, and the set of them is commonly written F^{	imes}/(F^{	imes})^2. [Discriminant] Let  eta be a non-degenerate bilinear form on an n-dimensional V. The discriminant of  eta is the square class of \det\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{} in F^{	imes}, for any ordered basis \sB of V. This is well defined by @thm-congruence-determinant-class and @thm-change-of-basis-form: another basis changes the determinant by the square (\det\P)^2, hence not its class. The discriminant is coarse but genuinely useful, and how much it sees depends entirely on the field. Over 
C every non-zero number is a square, so there is only one class and the discriminant says nothing. Over 
R there are two, \{t > 0\} and \{t < 0\}, so the discriminant records one bit: the sign of the determinant. Over 
Q there are infinitely many, and the discriminant is a strong invariant. Over 
R, are \diag(1, 1) and \diag(-1, -1) distinguished by their discriminants? No. Both determinants equal 1, so the discriminants agree. And yet the two matrices are not congruent over 
R. Suppose \diag(-1,-1) = \P	p\I_2\P = \P	p\P for an invertible \P. Evaluating both sides on \x = \e_1 gives -1 = \e_1	p\diag(-1,-1)\e_1 = \e_1	p\P	p\P\e_1 = 
orm{\P\e_1}^2 \ge 0 , a contradiction. So the discriminant is not a complete invariant, even over 
R and even for 2 	imes 2 matrices. Proving that the full “sign pattern” is an invariant, and that it is the complete one over 
R, is the law of inertia, proved later in this chapter. What congruence destroys Now the negative result of the section, and the reason the previous three chapters could not have been this one. [Congruent, with no eigenvalue in common] 1. \I_2 \simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} by @exm-congruence-first (a). Compare their eigenvalues. 2.  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} \simeq \diag(1, -3) by @exm-form-in-a-new-basis. Compare their eigenvalues. (a) \I_2 has the single eigenvalue 1, twice. The characteristic polynomial of  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} is x^2 - 3x + 1, whose roots are (3 \pm \sqrt5)/2, that is, approximately 2.618 and 0.382. The two matrices share no eigenvalue. They do share a rank, 2; a symmetry type, symmetric; and a discriminant, since \det = 1 for both. (b) The characteristic polynomial of  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} is x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x-3)(x+1), so its eigenvalues are 3 and -1. Those of \diag(1,-3) are 1 and -3. Again no eigenvalue in common — but this time one positive and one negative on each side, and the determinants are -3 both times. The signs survived; the numbers did not. That is the pattern the law of inertia will explain. Chapter 12 introduced this operation twice and both times deferred it to here. Section 1 of that chapter wrote that “the operation \A \mapsto \S^{*}\A\S is called congruence, and Chapter 13 studies it for its own sake”, keeping only that it preserves the sign of a positive form (@prp-congruence-positivity). Section 4 repeated the promise in fuller form: “Chapter 13 studies congruence in its own right, including what it does preserve; for now, note that it certainly does not preserve eigenvalues, since \S^{*}\I\S = \S^{*}\S can be any positive definite matrix at all.” Both debts are now paid, and it is worth saying the answer in one place. What congruence preserves: the rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank), and with it non-degeneracy and the dimension of the radical; the symmetry type (@prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry); and the square class of the determinant when that is non-zero (@thm-congruence-determinant-class), the discriminant. Over 
R it preserves one thing more, the triple of signs, and that is the deepest of the four; it is proved in the section on inertia. What congruence destroys: the eigenvalues, and therefore the characteristic polynomial, the trace and the determinant itself. Not every similarity invariant is lost — rank and invertibility, parts (a) and (b) of @prp-similarity-invariants, survive both relations — but every invariant that reads the eigenvalues is. Chapter 12’s parenthetical remark is exactly right and can be made sharper: taking \A = \I_n in @def-congruent, the congruence class of \I_n over 
R is the set of all matrices \P	p\P with \P invertible, which by @thm-pd-characterizations (c) is the set of all positive definite matrices. One class, every spectrum with all eigenvalues positive. Congruent and similar are different relations, and neither implies the other. By @exm-congruent-different-eigenvalues (a), \I_2 \simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, while the only matrix similar to \I_2 is \I_2 itself, since \P^{-1}\I_2\P = \I_2 for every invertible \P. In the other direction, \diag(1,2) is similar to  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 0 & 2\end{psmallmatrix} — conjugate by  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1\end{psmallmatrix} — but not congruent to it, because \diag(1,2) is symmetric and the other matrix is not (@prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry). So do not carry any habit across. In particular, “diagonalizable” means two different things in this chapter, and a matrix that is diagonalizable by congruence need not be diagonalizable by similarity, nor conversely. Where the two relations meet There is exactly one situation in which the confusion is harmless: when the change-of-basis matrix satisfies \P	p = \P^{-1}, that is, when \P is orthogonal (@def-unitary-orthogonal-groups). [An orthogonal change of basis is both] Let \A \in M_n(
R) and \Q \in \Orth(n). Then \Q	p\A\Q = \Q^{-1}\A\Q, so this matrix is at once congruent and similar to \A. Consequently, if \A is symmetric, then \A is congruent to the diagonal matrix \D of its eigenvalues, listed with multiplicity in any prescribed order. The first statement is the definition of an orthogonal matrix, \Q	p\Q = \I_n, which gives \Q	p = \Q^{-1}; the matrix \Q	p\A\Q is then congruent to \A by @def-congruent, since \Q is invertible, and similar to \A by @def-similar-matrices. For the second statement, let \A be symmetric. By @cor-spectral-real-matrix there are \Q \in \Orth(n) and a real diagonal \D, carrying the eigenvalues of \A in any prescribed order, with \A = \Q\D\Q	p. Multiplying on the left by \Q	p and on the right by \Q gives \D = \Q	p\A\Q, which is a congruence. This proves the proposition. This is why the real spectral theorem is so strong, and it is what Chapter 11 meant when it said, of the principal axis theorem, that “an orthogonal change of variables is a similarity and a congruence, so it keeps the eigenvalues and the geometry at once”. The general theory of this chapter has no orthogonal matrices to call on — a general field has no inner product, hence no orthogonal group in that sense — so the two relations part company and only congruence remains. What @prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity gives over 
R is a bridge: it says that every real symmetric matrix is congruent to a diagonal matrix, and it identifies the diagonal entries as eigenvalues. The section on inertia will show that the entries are free to move but their signs are not, which is how the two pictures are finally reconciled. Over 
R, which matrices are congruent to \I_n? Exactly the positive definite symmetric matrices. If \B = \P	p\I_n\P = \P	p\P with \P invertible, then \B is symmetric and \x	p\B\x = 
orm{\P\x}^2 > 0 for \x 
e \0, since \P\x 
e \0. Conversely every positive definite \B is \P	p\P for an invertible \P by @thm-pd-characterizations. Compare the similarity class of \I_n, which contains \I_n alone: one relation collapses this class to a point, the other spreads it over every positive definite matrix there is. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the change-of-basis rule for the matrix of a bilinear form, saying which matrix \P appears. 2. Define what it means for \A, \B \in M_n(F) to be congruent. 3. For each of rank, symmetry, determinant, eigenvalues and the square class of a non-zero determinant, say whether it is a congruence invariant. 4. Determine whether the following is correct, with a reason: congruent matrices are similar. 5. State the one circumstance in which a change of basis is simultaneously a similarity and a congruence. (a) @thm-change-of-basis-form: \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{} = \P	p\mtx{ eta}{\sB}{}\P, where \P = \mtx{\id}{\sB'}{\sB} is the change-of-coordinates matrix from the new basis to the old one. (b) @def-congruent: \B = \P	p\A\P for some invertible \P \in M_n(F). (c) Invariant: rank (@thm-congruence-preserves-rank); symmetry (@prp-congruence-preserves-symmetry); the square class of a non-zero determinant (@thm-congruence-determinant-class). Not invariant: the determinant itself, and the eigenvalues (@exm-congruent-different-eigenvalues). (d) Incorrect. \I_2 \simeq  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, but the only matrix similar to \I_2 is \I_2. (e) When the change-of-coordinates matrix \P satisfies \P	p = \P^{-1}, that is, when \P is orthogonal (@prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity). B. Practice [B1: A congruence in 
Q] Let \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} and \P =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}, both over 
Q. 1. Compute \P	p\A\P, and hence write down a matrix congruent to \A that is diagonal. 2. Find the eigenvalues of both matrices and compare them. 3. Compute the discriminant of the form \x	p\A\y and check that it agrees for the two matrices. (a) \P is invertible, with \det\P = -2 
e 0. Then \A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P	p\A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}. So \A \simeq \diag(2, -2) over 
Q. (b) The characteristic polynomial of \A is x^2 - 1, so its eigenvalues are 1 and -1; those of \diag(2,-2) are 2 and -2. No eigenvalue is shared, and each matrix has one positive and one negative eigenvalue. (c) \det\A = -1 and \det\diag(2,-2) = -4 = (-2)^2 \cdot (-1), which is the relation \det\B = (\det\P)^2\det\A of @thm-congruence-determinant-class. The two determinants differ by the square 4, so they lie in the same square class of 
Q^{	imes} and the discriminants agree, as @def-discriminant requires. [B2: A non-congruence over 
Q] 1. Prove that \diag(1,1) and \diag(1,2) are not congruent over 
Q. 2. Prove that they are congruent over 
R, by exhibiting \P. 3. Explain in one sentence why (a) and (b) are consistent. (a) Suppose \diag(1,2) = \P	p\diag(1,1)\P with \P \in M_2(
Q) invertible. By @thm-congruence-determinant-class, 2 = (\det\P)^2 \cdot 1, so \det\P \in 
Q would satisfy (\det\P)^2 = 2. No rational number squares to 2 (@thm-sqrt2-irrational), a contradiction. Hence the two are not congruent over 
Q. (b) Take \P = \diag(1, 1/\sqrt2), which is invertible over 
R. Then \P	p\diag(1,2)\P = \diag(1, 1), and congruence is symmetric (@prp-congruence-equivalence). (c) Congruence is a relation over a specified field: the matrix \P is required to have entries in that field, and 1/\sqrt2 is available in 
R but not in 
Q. Equivalently, 2 is a square in 
R^{	imes} and not in 
Q^{	imes}, so the discriminant separates the two matrices over 
Q and not over 
R. [B3: Completing the square, again] On 
R^2, let  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_1 - x_1y_2 - x_2y_1 + 2x_2y_2. 1. Write down \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sE}{} and expand q(\x) =  eta(\x, \x) as a polynomial in x_1, x_2. 2. Complete the square to find a basis \sB' with \mtx{ eta}{\sB'}{} = \I_2. Verify by computing \P	p\A\P. 3. Hence find the eigenvalues of \A and compare them with those of \I_2. (a) \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 2\end{psmallmatrix}, and q(\x) = x_1^2 - 2x_1x_2 + 2x_2^2. (b) q(\x) = (x_1 - x_2)^2 + x_2^2. So the substitution y_1 = x_1 - x_2, y_2 = x_2, that is x_1 = y_1 + y_2 and x_2 = y_2, makes q = y_1^2 + y_2^2. This is \x = \P\y with \P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \A\P =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \P	p\A\P = \I_2 . By @thm-change-of-basis-form the basis is \sB' =  igl((1,0),\ (1,1) igr), the columns of \P. (c) The characteristic polynomial of \A is x^2 - 3x + 1, with roots (3 \pm \sqrt5)/2; \I_2 has the eigenvalue 1 twice. The two matrices are congruent with no eigenvalue in common. What they share is that all eigenvalues are positive on both sides, which by the check above is no accident: the congruence class of \I_2 over 
R consists of exactly the positive definite matrices. C. Going deeper [C1: Congruence versus equivalence] 1. Prove that if \A \simeq \B then \A and \B are equivalent in the sense of @def-equivalent-matrices. 2. Give two matrices in M_2(
Q) that are equivalent but not congruent, and justify your example. 3. Hence explain what “the congruence classes refine the equivalence classes” means, and say what extra information a congruence class carries that a rank does not. (a) If \B = \P	p\A\P with \P invertible, then \P	p is invertible (@thm-transpose-properties), so \B = \Q\A\P with \Q = \P	p and \P both invertible, which is @def-equivalent-matrices. (b) Take \diag(1,1) and \diag(1,2). Both have rank 2, so they are equivalent by @thm-rank-normal-form (c). They are not congruent over 
Q by @exr-congruence-b2 (a). (c) By (a), each congruence class lies inside a single equivalence class, and by (b) an equivalence class may split into more than one congruence class; that is what “refine” means. An equivalence class is named by the rank alone (@thm-rank-normal-form (c)). A congruence class remembers the rank, and in addition the symmetry type and the discriminant — and over 
R, the signs. Equivalence allows two independent changes of basis, one in each slot; congruence allows only one, used twice, and the extra invariants are the price of that constraint. [C2: Orthogonal congruence] Let \A \in M_n(
R) be symmetric with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n, listed with multiplicity. 1. Prove that \A \simeq \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n). 2. Deduce that if every \lambda_i is non-zero, then \A is congruent to a diagonal matrix all of whose entries are \pm1. 3. Give two real symmetric 2 	imes 2 matrices that are congruent and have no eigenvalue in common. Hint for (b): recall from @exm-congruence-first (b) what scaling a basis vector does to a diagonal entry. (a) This is @prp-orthogonal-congruence-similarity: by @cor-spectral-real-matrix there is \Q \in \Orth(n) with \Q	p\A\Q = \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n), and \Q is invertible, so \A \simeq \D. (b) Let \S = \diag(c_1, \dots, c_n) with c_i = 1/\sqrt{\lvert\lambda_ivert}, which is defined and non-zero because \lambda_i 
e 0. Then \S is invertible and \S	p\D\S = \diag(c_1^2\lambda_1, \dots, c_n^2\lambda_n), whose i-th entry is \lambda_i/\lvert\lambda_ivert = \pm1 according to the sign of \lambda_i. By (a) and transitivity (@prp-congruence-equivalence), \A is congruent to that matrix. (c) By (b), \diag(1, -3) and \diag(2, -1) are both congruent to \diag(1,-1), hence to each other by @prp-congruence-equivalence; explicitly, \P = \diag(\sqrt2, 1/\sqrt3) gives \P	p\diag(1,-3)\P = \diag(2,-1). Their eigenvalues are \{1, -3\} and \{2, -1\}, which are disjoint. Note that the signs match, one positive and one negative on each side; part (b) is the reason, and the law of inertia will say it is forced. [C3: How much the discriminant sees] 1. Show that 
C^{	imes} has exactly one square class, and that 
R^{	imes} has exactly two. 2. List the squares in 
F_5^{	imes} and show that 
F_5^{	imes} has exactly two square classes. 3. Hence determine, for each of 
C, 
R and 
F_5, the largest number of pairwise non-congruent invertible matrices in M_n that the discriminant alone can distinguish. (a) Over 
C, every a 
e 0 has a square root (@exm-complex-square-root), so a = c^2 \cdot 1 and every element is equivalent to 1: one class. Over 
R, squares of non-zero reals are exactly the positive reals, so a and b are equivalent precisely when a/b > 0, which happens exactly when they have the same sign. The classes are the positive reals and the negative reals: two classes, and they are distinct since 1 and -1 are not related. (b) The squares are 1^2 = 1, 2^2 = 4, 3^2 = 4, 4^2 = 1, so the set of non-zero squares is \{1, 4\}. Multiplying \{1,4\} by 2 gives \{2, 3\}, so the classes are \{1, 4\} and \{2, 3\}: two classes, each of size 2, covering all four elements of 
F_5^{	imes}. (c) The discriminant takes one value per square class, so it can separate at most as many classes as there are square classes: one over 
C, two over 
R and two over 
F_5. Over 
C it is therefore useless, and over 
R and 
F_5 it sorts invertible matrices into at most two piles. By @exr-congruence-c2 (b), over 
R every invertible symmetric matrix is congruent to one of the n + 1 matrices \I_p \oplus -\I_{n-p}, whose determinant is (-1)^{n-p}; so the discriminant sees only the parity of n - p, and for n \ge 2 it cannot separate, say, \I_2 from -\I_2. That the n+1 matrices really are pairwise non-congruent is the law of inertia, not anything the discriminant can deliver.

title: 13.3 Three Kinds of Form
content:
Three Kinds of Form A bilinear form has two slots, and so far nothing has related them. Almost every form that occurs in practice does relate them: the dot product does not care which vector goes first, while the determinant of a 2 	imes 2 matrix changes sign when its columns are swapped. This section names the three symmetry conditions the rest of the chapter runs on, shows that two of them are the same condition exactly when 1 + 1 
e 0 in the field, and extracts from a symmetric form the single-variable function q(\v) =  eta(\v, \v) that carries all of its information. Throughout, V is a finite-dimensional vector space over a field F, and  eta is a bilinear form on V (@def-bilinear-form). The characteristic hypothesis is stated wherever it is needed and nowhere else. Symmetric forms The dot product on F^n satisfies \x \cdot \y = \y \cdot \x, and so does every integral pairing \int_0^1 fg, and so does \x	p\A\y whenever \A happens to satisfy \A	p = \A. The condition recurs, so it gets a name. A symmetric form cannot tell its two arguments apart. [Symmetric Bilinear Form] A bilinear form  eta \colon V 	imes V 	o F is symmetric if  eta(\u, \v) =  eta(\v, \u) for all \u, \v \in V. In words: the value is unchanged by swapping the two inputs. The condition is imposed for every pair, not just for pairs of basis vectors — although, as the next result shows, checking it on basis vectors is enough. Three examples and one non-example. - The dot product on F^n,  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n. Each product x_iy_i is unchanged by the swap because multiplication in F is commutative. - A symmetric matrix,  eta(\x, \y) = \x	p\A\y with \A	p = \A (@def-symmetric-matrix). Here \x	p\A\y is a 1 	imes 1 matrix, so it equals its own transpose \y	p\A	p\x = \y	p\A\x by @thm-transpose-properties. - Evaluation pairings. On F[x]_{\le n}, fix scalars t_1, \dots, t_k \in F and set  eta(p, q) = \sum_i p(t_i)q(t_i). Symmetry is again commutativity of F. - A non-example by minimal change. On F^2 put  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_2. It is bilinear, by the one-slot check of @def-multilinear-form. But  eta(\e_1, \e_2) = 1 and  eta(\e_2, \e_1) = 0, so the symmetry clause fails at that one pair. Exactly one clause has been broken: bilinearity survives untouched. The matrix of a form (@def-form-matrix) turns the condition into a matrix condition, and turns “for all \u, \v” into a finite check. [Symmetry Is Visible in the Matrix] Let \sB be a basis of V and \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{}. Then  eta is symmetric if and only if \A	p = \A. (\Rightarrow) Suppose  eta is symmetric. Writing \sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n), the entries of \A are a_{ij} =  eta(\v_i, \v_j), so a_{ij} =  eta(\v_j, \v_i) = a_{ji}, which is @def-symmetric-matrix. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \A	p = \A, and let \u, \v \in V. By @thm-form-matrix-determines,  eta(\u, \v) = \coord{\u}{\sB}	p \A \coord{\v}{\sB} . The right-hand side is a 1 	imes 1 matrix, hence equal to its transpose, which by @thm-transpose-properties is \coord{\v}{\sB}	p \A	p \coord{\u}{\sB} = \coord{\v}{\sB}	p \A \coord{\u}{\sB} =  eta(\v, \u). This proves the equivalence. Because congruence sends \A to \P	p\A\P and (\P	p\A\P)	p = \P	p\A	p\P by @thm-transpose-properties, a congruent copy of a symmetric matrix is symmetric. So the condition \A	p = \A does not depend on which basis was used to build \A — as it must not, since by @prp-form-symmetry-matrix it says something about  eta alone. Alternating and skew-symmetric forms Chapter 6 needed two ways of saying “the value collapses when two arguments coincide”, and found that they are not the same condition. Both were defined there for k-linear forms, and a bilinear form is the case k = 2, so nothing needs redefining. Read at k = 2: -  eta is alternating (@def-alternating-form) if  eta(\v, \v) = 0 for every \v \in V; -  eta is skew-symmetric (@def-skew-symmetric-form) if  eta(\u, \v) = - eta(\v, \u) for all \u, \v \in V. The standard example of both is the signed area  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_2 - x_2y_1 on F^2, which is the determinant of the matrix with columns \x and \y. A second family, the one Section 9 will be about, is the standard alternating form on F^{2m},  eta(\x, \y) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} igl(x_iy_{m+i} - x_{m+i}y_i igr), which pairs the first block of coordinates against the second. Each condition reads off the matrix, and the two readings differ by the diagonal. [Alternation and Skewness in the Matrix] Let \sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n) be a basis of V and \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{}. Then: 1.  eta is skew-symmetric if and only if \A	p = -\A; 2.  eta is alternating if and only if \A	p = -\A and a_{ii} = 0 for every i. (a) repeats the proof of @prp-form-symmetry-matrix with a minus sign throughout. (b) (\Rightarrow) If  eta is alternating then a_{ii} =  eta(\v_i, \v_i) = 0, and  eta is skew-symmetric by @thm-alternating-properties (a), so \A	p = -\A by (a). (\Leftarrow) Suppose \A	p = -\A with zero diagonal, and let \v \in V have coordinates \coord{\v}{\sB} = (c_1, \dots, c_n). By @thm-form-matrix-determines and bilinearity,  eta(\v, \v) = \sum_{i, j} c_ic_j a_{ij} = \sum_{i} c_i^2 a_{ii} + \sum_{i < j} c_ic_j igl(a_{ij} + a_{ji} igr), where the second sum collects the terms (i, j) and (j, i) together. Every a_{ii} is 0, and every a_{ij} + a_{ji} is 0 because \A	p = -\A. So  eta(\v, \v) = 0. This proves the equivalence. Part (b) is the whole difficulty in one line: a skew-symmetric matrix has a_{ii} = -a_{ii}, and usually that forces a_{ii} = 0. Usually, but not always. Where characteristic 2 earns its keep Chapter 0 warned that in a field of characteristic 2 the argument “x = -x, so 2x = 0, so x = 0” divides by 2 = 1 + 1, which is 0 there, and it promised that this is why later results on symmetric bilinear forms would carry the hypothesis “characteristic 
e 2” (@def-characteristic). This is the theorem the promise was about. [Alternating Versus Skew-Symmetric] Let F be a field and let V be a vector space over F. 1. Every alternating bilinear form on V is skew-symmetric. No hypothesis on F or on V is needed. 2. If \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, every skew-symmetric bilinear form on V is alternating. Again V is arbitrary. 3. If \operatorname{char} F = 2 and V 
e \{\0\}, there is a skew-symmetric bilinear form on V that is not alternating. So the converse of (a) holds if and only if \operatorname{char} F 
e 2. For (a), feed \u + \v into both slots and expand: the two diagonal terms vanish by hypothesis, and what is left is exactly the skew identity. For (b), feed \v into both slots of the skew identity, which gives  eta(\v,\v) = - eta(\v,\v); canceling needs 1 + 1 to be invertible, and that is precisely what characteristic 
e 2 supplies. For (c), notice that in characteristic 2 the words “skew-symmetric” and “symmetric” mean the same thing, so any symmetric form that is non-zero on some vector paired with itself is a witness — and the dot product is one. (a) Let  eta be alternating and let \u, \v \in V. Expanding by bilinearity, 0 =  eta(\u + \v, \u + \v) =  eta(\u,\u) +  eta(\u,\v) +  eta(\v,\u) +  eta(\v,\v), and the first and last terms are 0 because  eta is alternating. Hence  eta(\u,\v) = - eta(\v,\u). (This is @thm-alternating-properties (a) at k = 2.) (b) Let  eta be skew-symmetric and \v \in V. Taking \u = \v in the defining identity gives  eta(\v,\v) = - eta(\v,\v), that is, (1 + 1) eta(\v,\v) = 0. Since \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, we have 1 + 1 
e 0 in F: otherwise the smallest positive n with n \cdot 1 = 0 would be 2, which is @def-characteristic. A non-zero element of a field is invertible, so multiplying by (1+1)^{-1} gives  eta(\v,\v) = 0. (This is @thm-skew-symmetric-alternating at k = 2.) (c) Suppose \operatorname{char} F = 2, so that -1 = 1 in F. Since V 
e \{\0\} is finite-dimensional, it has a basis with at least one vector, and we may take \varphi \in V^{*} to be the coordinate functional of its first vector \v_1, so that \varphi(\v_1) = 1. Define  eta(\u, \v) = \varphi(\u)\,\varphi(\v) . This is bilinear, being a product of two linear functionals, and it is symmetric. Because -1 = 1, symmetric and skew-symmetric say the same thing, so  eta is skew-symmetric. But  eta(\v_1, \v_1) = 1 
e 0, so  eta is not alternating. Finally, (b) and (c) together say that the converse of (a) holds exactly when \operatorname{char} F 
e 2. This proves the theorem. The concrete witness is worth writing down. [The dot product over the field with two elements] Let F = 
F_2 and V = 
F_2^2, and let  eta be the dot product,  eta(\x, \y) = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2. Decide whether  eta is symmetric, skew-symmetric and alternating, and compute the function \v \mapsto  eta(\v,\v) on all four vectors of V. The matrix of  eta in the standard basis is \I_2. It is symmetric, so  eta is symmetric by @prp-form-symmetry-matrix. Over 
F_2 we have -\I_2 = \I_2, so the matrix also satisfies \I_2	p = -\I_2, and  eta is skew-symmetric by @prp-alternating-form-matrix (a). It is not alternating: the diagonal entries of \I_2 are 1 
e 0, and indeed  eta(\e_1, \e_1) = 1. On the four vectors,  eta(\v,\v) = v_1^2 + v_2^2. In 
F_2 both elements satisfy c^2 = c, so this equals v_1 + v_2:  eta(\0,\0) = 0, \quad  eta(\e_1,\e_1) = 1, \quad  eta(\e_2,\e_2) = 1, \quad  eta(\1,\1) = 0 . Notice what that list is: the function \v \mapsto  eta(\v,\v) is the linear functional v_1 + v_2. In characteristic 2 a “quadratic” function coming from a bilinear form can be linear, which is the first sign that the notions below will not behave. In characteristic 2, “skew-symmetric” carries no information beyond “symmetric”. Since -1 = 1, the two conditions are literally the same condition, and the useful notion is the strictly stronger one, alternating. This is why Chapter 6 built the determinant on alternation rather than skewness, and why every statement below that pairs symmetric against alternating needs \operatorname{char} F 
e 2. Splitting a form into two halves In characteristic 
e 2 the two conditions are complementary in the strongest possible sense: every bilinear form is a symmetric one plus an alternating one, in exactly one way. The recipe is the one that splits a function on 
R into its even and odd parts. [Symmetric Plus Alternating] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 and let  eta be a bilinear form on V. Then there are a unique symmetric form  eta_{s} and a unique alternating form  eta_{a} on V with  eta =  eta_{s} +  eta_{a}, namely  egin{aligned}  eta_{s}(\u,\v) &= 	frac12 igl( eta(\u,\v) +  eta(\v,\u) igr), \  eta_{a}(\u,\v) &= 	frac12 igl( eta(\u,\v) -  eta(\v,\u) igr). \end{aligned} In matrices: \A = 	frac12(\A + \A	p) + 	frac12(\A - \A	p). Since \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, the element 1 + 1 is non-zero, hence invertible, and 	frac12 denotes (1+1)^{-1}. Both displayed formulas are bilinear, being combinations of the bilinear maps (\u,\v) \mapsto  eta(\u,\v) and (\u,\v) \mapsto  eta(\v,\u), and their sum is  eta. Swapping \u and \v leaves  eta_{s} unchanged, so  eta_{s} is symmetric; and  eta_{a}(\v,\v) = 	frac12( eta(\v,\v) -  eta(\v,\v)) = 0, so  eta_{a} is alternating. For uniqueness, suppose  eta_s +  eta_a =  eta_s' +  eta_a' with  eta_s,  eta_s' symmetric and  eta_a,  eta_a' alternating, and put \delta =  eta_s -  eta_s' =  eta_a' -  eta_a. Then \delta is symmetric, being a difference of symmetric forms, and alternating, being a difference of alternating forms. By @thm-alternating-vs-skew (a) it is also skew-symmetric, so for all \u, \v, \delta(\u,\v) = \delta(\v,\u) = -\delta(\u,\v), giving (1+1)\delta(\u,\v) = 0 and hence \delta(\u,\v) = 0. Therefore  eta_s =  eta_s' and  eta_a =  eta_a', as claimed. Both halves of the argument divided by 1 + 1, and both failures are real. In characteristic 2 the formulas are meaningless, and more than that, the statement itself is false: alternating forms are then a subset of the symmetric ones, not a complement to them. In characteristic 2, symmetric and alternating forms are not complementary. Over 
F_2 take  eta(\x,\y) = x_1y_2 on 
F_2^2. An alternating form is skew-symmetric (@thm-alternating-vs-skew (a)), and skew-symmetric means symmetric here, so every sum of a symmetric form and an alternating form is symmetric. But  eta(\e_1,\e_2) = 1 while  eta(\e_2,\e_1) = 0, so  eta is not symmetric and therefore cannot be written as such a sum at all. The decomposition does not merely lose uniqueness; existence fails. The quadratic form A bilinear form is a function of two vectors, which makes it awkward to plot, to differentiate, or to write on a page. Feeding the same vector into both slots turns it into a function of one vector. Chapter 11 met this function on 
R^n under the name quadratic form and used it to identify conics; here is the general definition, and the surprising fact that nothing is lost. A quadratic form is what a bilinear form sees when both of its arguments are the same vector. [Quadratic Form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on V. The quadratic form associated with  eta is the function q \colon V 	o F, \qquad q(\v) =  eta(\v, \v) . A function q \colon V 	o F is called a quadratic form on V if q(\v) =  eta(\v,\v) for some symmetric bilinear form  eta on V. Two clauses deserve separate readings. The first says how to build q from a given  eta, for any  eta over any field. The second says which functions V 	o F are entitled to the name, and it insists on a symmetric  eta; the polarization theorem below will show that over a field of characteristic 
e 2 this symmetric  eta is then unique, so that “the” bilinear form of a quadratic form is well defined. Insisting on symmetry costs nothing in characteristic 
e 2. If q(\v) =  eta(\v,\v) for some bilinear  eta, then by @thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition we may split  eta =  eta_s +  eta_a, and  eta_a(\v,\v) = 0, so q(\v) =  eta_s(\v,\v) with  eta_s symmetric. The alternating part is invisible to q. In coordinates, with \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{} symmetric and \x = \coord{\v}{\sB}, q(\v) = \x	p\A\x = \sum_{i} a_{ii}x_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j} a_{ij}x_ix_j , {#eq-quadratic-in-coordinates} which is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 2 in the coordinates: hence the name. Reading @eq-quadratic-in-coordinates backwards recovers \A from the polynomial: a_{ii} is the coefficient of x_i^2, and a_{ij} for i 
e j is half the coefficient of x_ix_j. That is word for word the recipe Chapter 11 gave for the symmetric matrix of a real quadratic form, and the halving is the same division by 1 + 1 as everywhere else in this section. [From a polynomial to its matrix and back] Over 
Q, let q(x_1, x_2, x_3) = 2x_1^2 - x_2^2 + 6x_1x_2 - 4x_2x_3. Find the symmetric matrix \A with q(\x) = \x	p\A\x, and evaluate q(1, 1, 1) both from the polynomial and from \A. The squared terms give a_{11} = 2, a_{22} = -1 and a_{33} = 0. The cross terms give a_{12} = a_{21} = 3 (half of 6), a_{23} = a_{32} = -2 (half of -4), and a_{13} = a_{31} = 0 since x_1x_3 does not appear. So \A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 & 0 \ 3 & -1 & -2 \ 0 & -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. From the polynomial, q(1,1,1) = 2 - 1 + 6 - 4 = 3. From the matrix, \A(1,1,1) = (5, 0, -2) and (1,1,1) \cdot (5,0,-2) = 3. The two agree. Now the theorem that makes q as good as  eta. [Polarization] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2. The map  eta \mapsto q, q(\v) =  eta(\v,\v), is a bijection from the set of symmetric bilinear forms on V onto the set of quadratic forms on V. Its inverse is given by either of  egin{aligned}  eta(\u,\v) &= 	frac12 igl(q(\u+\v) - q(\u) - q(\v) igr) \ &= 	frac14 igl(q(\u+\v) - q(\u-\v) igr). \end{aligned} In particular a symmetric form is determined by its quadratic form: if  eta(\v,\v) =  eta'(\v,\v) for all \v, then  eta =  eta'. Only one computation is needed, and it is the expansion of q(\u \pm \v) by bilinearity. Symmetry merges the two cross terms into one, so the cross term appears with a factor 1 + 1, and dividing by it is the whole trick. Surjectivity is the definition of “quadratic form”; injectivity is the displayed formula. Let  eta be symmetric with quadratic form q, and let \u, \v \in V. By bilinearity and then symmetry, q(\u \pm \v) =  eta(\u,\u) \pm  eta(\u,\v) \pm  eta(\v,\u) +  eta(\v,\v), so q(\u \pm \v) = q(\u) + q(\v) \pm (1+1) eta(\u,\v). Since \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, the element 1 + 1 is invertible, and taking the upper sign gives the first formula. Subtracting the two versions gives q(\u+\v) - q(\u-\v) = (1+1)^2 eta(\u,\v), which is the second. The map  eta \mapsto q is onto the set of quadratic forms by @def-quadratic-form, which defines that set as the image. It is injective because the first displayed formula recovers  eta(\u,\v) from q alone; so if two symmetric forms have the same q, the formula returns the same value for each, and they are equal. Hence the map is a bijection with the stated inverse. This proves the theorem. Which bilinear forms are both symmetric and alternating, over a field of characteristic 
e 2? Only the zero form. If  eta is alternating then q = 0, and if  eta is also symmetric then @thm-polarization-forms recovers  eta(\u,\v) = 	frac12(0 - 0 - 0) = 0. (Over 
F_2 the answer is different: every alternating form is symmetric there, as @thm-alternating-vs-skew shows, and there are plenty of non-zero ones.) The second formula of @thm-polarization-forms should look familiar. Over 
R, an inner product is a symmetric bilinear form whose quadratic form is q(\v) = 
orm{\v}^2, and the formula reads \inner{\u}{\v} = 	frac14 igl(
orm{\u+\v}^2 - 
orm{\u-\v}^2 igr), which is exactly @lem-polarization-identities (a). Chapter 10 proved it to show that an isometry automatically preserves angles; the content here is the same, stripped of positivity and of 
R. What Chapter 10 needed positivity for was the norm, not the identity. Hermitian forms Over 
C the pattern changes, because \inner{\v}{\v} is required to be a positive real number and no bilinear form can deliver that: bilinearity gives  eta(i\v, i\v) = i^2 eta(\v,\v) = - eta(\v,\v), so the values at \v and i\v have opposite signs. Chapter 10 solved this by making the second slot conjugate-linear. That fix has nothing to do with positivity, so it can be made here too. [Hermitian Form] Let V be a vector space over 
C. A function  eta \colon V 	imes V 	o 
C is a Hermitian form if it is linear in the first argument, and  eta(\v, \u) = \conj{ eta(\u, \v)} \qquad 	ext{for all } \u, \v \in V . Two remarks on the clauses. First, the two conditions together force conjugate-linearity in the second argument:  eta(\u, c\v) = \conj{ eta(c\v,\u)} = \conj{c\, eta(\v,\u)} = \conj{c}\, eta(\u,\v). So a Hermitian form is not bilinear, and @def-bilinear-form does not cover it. Second, taking \u = \v gives  eta(\v,\v) = \conj{ eta(\v,\v)}, so the associated function q(\v) =  eta(\v,\v) takes real values even though  eta does not. The examples are the ones from Chapter 10 with positivity dropped:  eta(\x,\y) = \y^{*}\A\x on 
C^n for any \A with \A^{*} = \A, including indefinite choices such as \A = \diag(1,-1). The matrix criterion is the same proof as @prp-form-symmetry-matrix with stars in place of transposes. [Hermitian Forms and Hermitian Matrices] Let  eta be linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, let \sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n) be a basis of V, and let \A be the matrix with entries a_{ij} =  eta(\v_j, \v_i). Then  eta is Hermitian if and only if \A^{*} = \A, and in that case  eta(\u,\v) = \coord{\v}{\sB}^{*}\A\coord{\u}{\sB}. The index order a_{ij} =  eta(\v_j, \v_i) is the one used for Gram matrices in Chapter 10 (\G in @def-gram-matrix), chosen so that the displayed formula comes out with no transposing of the answer. Expanding \u = \sum_j c_j\v_j and \v = \sum_i d_i\v_i by linearity in the first slot and conjugate-linearity in the second,  eta(\u,\v) = \sum_{i,j} c_j\conj{d_i}\, eta(\v_j,\v_i) = \sum_{i,j} \conj{d_i}\,a_{ij}c_j , which is the matrix product \coord{\v}{\sB}^{*}\A\coord{\u}{\sB}. If  eta is Hermitian then in particular a_{ji} =  eta(\v_i,\v_j) = \conj{ eta(\v_j,\v_i)} = \conj{a_{ij}}, which is \A^{*} = \A. Conversely, if a_{ji} = \conj{a_{ij}} then conjugating the display gives \conj{ eta(\u,\v)} = \sum_{i,j} d_i\,\conj{a_{ij}}\,\conj{c_j} = \sum_{i,j} \conj{c_j}\,a_{ji}\,d_i =  eta(\v,\u), so  eta is Hermitian. Polarization works for Hermitian forms too, and it is the four-term identity rather than the two-term one: by @lem-polarization-identities (b) with q(\v) =  eta(\v,\v),  eta(\u,\v) = 	frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3} i^k\, q(\u + i^k\v). The computation in Chapter 10 expanded each term using linearity in the first slot, conjugate-linearity in the second and  eta(\v,\u) = \conj{ eta(\u,\v)}, and used positivity nowhere, so it proves this identity too. Note the contrast with the real case: over 
C there is no characteristic to worry about, since \operatorname{char}
C = 0, and the reason a Hermitian form is recoverable from q is the extra room provided by i. A quadratic form over a field of characteristic 2 is a different object, and this book does not define it. Two things go wrong there, and @thm-polarization-forms repairs neither. The form is not determined by q. Over 
F_2, the symmetric form  eta(\x,\y) = x_1y_2 + x_2y_1 has q(\x) = 2x_1x_2 = 0, the same q as the zero form, so  eta \mapsto q is not injective on symmetric forms. And @def-quadratic-form names too few functions. The function q(\x) = x_1x_2 on 
F_2^2 is  eta(\x,\x) for the bilinear  eta(\x,\y) = x_1y_2, yet it is  eta(\x,\x) for no symmetric  eta: for a symmetric \A, @eq-quadratic-in-coordinates gives a_{11}x_1^2 + a_{22}x_2^2 = a_{11}x_1 + a_{22}x_2 over 
F_2, whose values at (1,1), (1,0) and (0,1) are a_{11} + a_{22}, a_{11} and a_{22}, and no choice makes those 1, 0, 0. The theory of quadratic forms in characteristic 2 therefore defines q first, by the axioms q(c\v) = c^2q(\v) and “q(\u+\v) - q(\u) - q(\v) is bilinear”, and treats  eta as derived data. Everything that follows assumes \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 precisely to stay out of that theory. Three kinds of form, then, and three matrix shapes: symmetric, alternating, Hermitian. The next two sections take the first of them and classify it up to congruence, first over any field of characteristic 
e 2, then over 
R. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define what it means for a bilinear form  eta on V to be symmetric, alternating and skew-symmetric. 2. State the relationship between alternating and skew-symmetric forms, including the exact role of the characteristic. 3. Write down the matrix condition, in a fixed basis, for each of the three notions in (a). 4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: over 
Q, a bilinear form is determined by the function \v \mapsto  eta(\v,\v). 5. Why is a Hermitian form not an example of @def-bilinear-form? (a) Symmetric:  eta(\u,\v) =  eta(\v,\u) for all \u,\v. Alternating:  eta(\v,\v) = 0 for all \v. Skew-symmetric:  eta(\u,\v) = - eta(\v,\u) for all \u,\v. (b) Alternating always implies skew-symmetric (@thm-alternating-vs-skew (a)). The converse holds if and only if \operatorname{char} F 
e 2; in characteristic 2 the dot product on 
F_2^2 is skew-symmetric and not alternating. (c) With \A = \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{}: symmetric means \A	p = \A; skew-symmetric means \A	p = -\A; alternating means \A	p = -\A together with a_{ii} = 0 for all i (@prp-form-symmetry-matrix, @prp-alternating-form-matrix). (d) Incorrect. Since \operatorname{char}
Q = 0 
e 2, only the symmetric part is determined: any alternating form has  eta(\v,\v) = 0 identically, so  eta and  eta +  eta_a have the same quadratic form for every alternating  eta_a. What is true is @thm-polarization-forms, which determines  eta among symmetric forms. (e) It is not linear in the second argument:  eta(\u, c\v) = \conj{c}\, eta(\u,\v), and \conj{c} 
e c for c 
otin 
R. B. Practice [B1: Determine which of the following] Over 
Q, with V = 
Q^2 and \x = (x_1,x_2), \y = (y_1,y_2), determine for each of the following bilinear forms whether it is symmetric, whether it is alternating, and whether it is skew-symmetric. Justify each answer. 1.  eta(\x,\y) = x_1y_1 - x_2y_2. 2.  eta(\x,\y) = 3x_1y_2 - 3x_2y_1. 3.  eta(\x,\y) = x_1y_2 + 2x_2y_1. 4.  eta(\x,\y) = 0. Write down the matrix \A in the standard basis in each case and apply @prp-form-symmetry-matrix and @prp-alternating-form-matrix. (a) \A = \diag(1,-1), which satisfies \A	p = \A: symmetric. Not skew-symmetric, since \A	p = -\A would need 1 = -1 in 
Q. Not alternating, since  eta(\e_1,\e_1) = 1. (b) \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 3 \ -3 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}, with \A	p = -\A and zero diagonal: skew-symmetric and alternating. Not symmetric, since 3 
e -3. (c) \A =  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 2 & 0\end{psmallmatrix}. Symmetry would need 1 = 2 and skewness would need 1 = -2, both false in 
Q; so it is neither, and it is not alternating either, since an alternating form is skew-symmetric. (Its diagonal entries do vanish, so  eta(\e_i,\e_i) = 0 for the two basis vectors — but  eta(\1,\1) = 1 + 2 = 3 
e 0. Checking the basis vectors alone is not enough.) (d) The zero form is symmetric, skew-symmetric and alternating at once; its matrix is \0, which satisfies every condition. By the Quick check above it is the only form that is both symmetric and alternating over 
Q. [B2: Polarizing a quadratic form] Over 
R, let q(x_1,x_2,x_3) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 - 2x_2x_3 + 5x_3^2. 1. Find the symmetric matrix \A with q(\x) = \x	p\A\x. 2. Compute  eta(\e_1 + \e_2, \e_3) directly from \A, and again from the polarization formula 	frac12(q(\u+\v) - q(\u) - q(\v)). (a) The squared terms give a_{11} = 1, a_{22} = 0, a_{33} = 5; the cross terms give a_{12} = a_{21} = 2, a_{23} = a_{32} = -1, a_{13} = a_{31} = 0. So \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 0 & -1 \ 0 & -1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. (b) Put \u = (1,1,0) and \v = (0,0,1). Directly, \A\v = (0,-1,5) and \u	p(\A\v) = 0 - 1 = -1. By polarization, q(\u) = 1 + 4 = 5 and q(\v) = 5, while \u + \v = (1,1,1) gives q(\u+\v) = 1 + 4 - 2 + 5 = 8. Hence 	frac12(8 - 5 - 5) = -1. The two agree, as @thm-polarization-forms says they must. [B3: Splitting a form] Let \A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 5 \ -1 & 4 \end{pmatrix} over 
Q, and let  eta(\x,\y) = \x	p\A\y. Write  eta =  eta_s +  eta_a as in @thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition, giving the matrix of each part, and verify that  eta and  eta_s have the same quadratic form. We have \A	p =  egin{psmallmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 5 & 4\end{psmallmatrix}, so 	frac12(\A + \A	p) =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad 	frac12(\A - \A	p) =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 3 \ -3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. The first is symmetric and the second is alternating, and they sum to \A. For the quadratic forms, \x	p\A\x = x_1^2 + 5x_1x_2 - x_2x_1 + 4x_2^2 = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + 4x_2^2, and the symmetric part gives x_1^2 + 2x_1x_2 + 2x_2x_1 + 4x_2^2, the same polynomial. The alternating part contributes 3x_1x_2 - 3x_2x_1 = 0. C. Going deeper [C1: Is this still true over 
F_2?] Let V be a vector space over 
F_2 with \dim V = n \ge 1. 1. Prove that every alternating bilinear form on V is symmetric. 2. Prove that the alternating forms on V form a subspace of the space of all bilinear forms, and compute its dimension. 3. Deduce that for n = 2 there is exactly one non-zero alternating form on V, and write down its matrix. Hint: for (b), use @prp-alternating-form-matrix. (a) Let  eta be alternating. By @thm-alternating-vs-skew (a),  eta(\u,\v) = - eta(\v,\u). Over 
F_2 we have -1 = 1, so - eta(\v,\u) =  eta(\v,\u) and  eta is symmetric. (b) Fix a basis \sB. The map  eta \mapsto \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{} is a linear bijection from bilinear forms to M_n(
F_2) (@thm-form-matrix-determines). By @prp-alternating-form-matrix (b),  eta is alternating exactly when its matrix satisfies \A	p = -\A with zero diagonal; over 
F_2 the first condition is \A	p = \A, so the image is the set of symmetric matrices with zero diagonal. Such a matrix is determined freely by its entries a_{ij} with i < j, of which there are  inom{n}{2}. These conditions are linear, so the set of alternating forms is a subspace, of dimension n(n-1)/2. (c) For n = 2 the dimension is 1, so the space of alternating forms is \{\0,  eta\} for a single non-zero  eta, whose matrix must be  egin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix} — the only symmetric 
F_2-matrix with zero diagonal other than \0. Concretely  eta(\x,\y) = x_1y_2 + x_2y_1, and indeed  eta(\x,\x) = 2x_1x_2 = 0. [C2: How much of a form does q see?] Let \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 and let  eta be any bilinear form on V, with q(\v) =  eta(\v,\v). 1. Prove that two bilinear forms have the same quadratic form if and only if their difference is alternating. 2. Deduce that the set of bilinear forms with a given quadratic form q contains exactly one symmetric form. 3. For \dim V = n, how many bilinear forms share a given quadratic form when F = 
F_3? (a) (\Rightarrow) Suppose  eta_1(\v,\v) =  eta_2(\v,\v) for all \v. Then \delta =  eta_1 -  eta_2 is bilinear with \delta(\v,\v) = 0 for all \v, which is @def-alternating-form at k = 2. (\Leftarrow) If \delta =  eta_1 -  eta_2 is alternating then  eta_1(\v,\v) -  eta_2(\v,\v) = \delta(\v,\v) = 0 for every \v. (b) Existence: by @thm-symmetric-alternating-decomposition write  eta =  eta_s +  eta_a; then  eta_s is symmetric with the same quadratic form, since  eta_a(\v,\v) = 0. Uniqueness: two symmetric forms with the same q are equal by @thm-polarization-forms. (c) By (a), the forms sharing q are exactly  eta_s +  eta_a with  eta_a alternating, so there are as many as there are alternating forms. Over a field with 3 elements, an alternating form corresponds by @prp-alternating-form-matrix (b) to a matrix with \A	p = -\A and zero diagonal, which is determined freely by the  inom{n}{2} entries above the diagonal. So there are 3^{n(n-1)/2} of them. [C3: A Hermitian form is a real symmetric form in disguise] Let  eta be a Hermitian form on 
C^n with matrix \A = \A^{*} as in @prp-hermitian-form-matrix, and regard 
C^n as a real vector space of dimension 2n by forgetting multiplication by i. 1. Prove that 	au(\u,\v) = \operatorname{Re} eta(\u,\v) is a symmetric 
R-bilinear form on that real space, with 	au(\v,\v) =  eta(\v,\v). 2. Prove that \omega(\u,\v) = \operatorname{Im} eta(\u,\v) is an alternating 
R-bilinear form. 3. For n = 1 and \A = (1), write both 	au and \omega as explicit forms on 
R^2. (a) Taking real parts of an 
R-linear identity is 
R-linear, and  eta is additive in each slot and commutes with real scalars in each slot (conjugation fixes 
R), so 	au is 
R-bilinear. Symmetry:  eta(\v,\u) = \conj{ eta(\u,\v)}, and conjugate numbers have equal real parts, so 	au(\v,\u) = 	au(\u,\v). Finally  eta(\v,\v) is real, as noted after @def-hermitian-form, so 	au(\v,\v) =  eta(\v,\v). (b) 
R-bilinearity is the same argument with imaginary parts. Conjugate numbers have opposite imaginary parts, so \omega(\v,\u) = -\omega(\u,\v): \omega is skew-symmetric, and since \operatorname{char}
R = 0 
e 2, @thm-alternating-vs-skew (b) makes it alternating. (Directly:  eta(\v,\v) is real, so its imaginary part is 0.) (c) Here  eta(u,v) = u\conj{v} for u, v \in 
C. Writing u = x_1 + ix_2 and v = y_1 + iy_2, we get u\conj{v} = (x_1y_1 + x_2y_2) + i(x_2y_1 - x_1y_2). So 	au is the dot product on 
R^2 and \omega(\x,\y) = x_2y_1 - x_1y_2, the negative of the signed area.

title: 13.4 Completing the Square
content:
Completing the Square Every symmetric matrix over 
R can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix, which is Chapter 11’s spectral theorem. That theorem needs 
R, an inner product and the existence of eigenvalues. This section proves a weaker conclusion under far weaker hypotheses: over any field of characteristic 
e 2, with no inner product, no order and no eigenvalues available, every symmetric form still becomes diagonal after a change of basis — provided we ask only for congruence, not for similarity. The proof is one algebraic manipulation, completing the square, run by induction; and the induction has a case that a careless proof loses. Throughout, F is a field with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2 (@def-characteristic), V is a finite-dimensional vector space over F,  eta is a symmetric bilinear form on V (@def-symmetric-form), and q(\v) =  eta(\v,\v) is its quadratic form (@def-quadratic-form). Orthogonality without an inner product Chapter 10 called two vectors orthogonal when their inner product vanished. The word survives the loss of positivity unchanged, because only the vanishing was ever used. [Orthogonal Basis for a Form] Let  eta be a bilinear form on V. Vectors \u, \v \in V are orthogonal with respect to  eta if  eta(\u,\v) = 0. An ordered basis \sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n) of V is an orthogonal basis for  eta if  eta(\v_i, \v_j) = 0 \qquad 	ext{whenever } i 
e j . The definition is engineered to say exactly one thing about matrices: by @def-form-matrix, \sB is an orthogonal basis for  eta precisely when \mtx{ eta}{\sB}{} is a diagonal matrix, with q(\v_1), \dots, q(\v_n) down the diagonal. Two warnings come free. The vectors of such a basis are not required to satisfy q(\v_i) = 1, and over a general field they usually cannot be rescaled to. And a vector may be orthogonal to itself: q(\v_i) = 0 is allowed, and for a degenerate form it is unavoidable. What an orthogonal basis buys is that q becomes a sum of squares with no cross terms. If \v = c_1\v_1 + \dots + c_n\v_n and d_i = q(\v_i), then expanding by bilinearity and deleting the i 
e j terms, q(\v) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i\,c_i^2 . {#eq-diagonal-quadratic-form} That is the “sum of squares” a reader has met when completing the square in two variables, and @eq-diagonal-quadratic-form is the reason the whole section is called what it is. The theorem, and the case that breaks it Here is the naive argument, and it is worth seeing it fail.
