title: Exercise (C1: The Gram matrix determines the list)
content: Let \((\v_1, \dots, \v_k)\) be a list in an inner product space \(V\) and \((\w_1, \dots, \w_k)\) a list in an inner product space \(W\) , both over \(F\) , with the same Gram matrix: \(\inner{\v_j}{\v_i} = \inner{\w_j}{\w_i}\) for all \(i, j\) . Prove that \(\sum_j x_j\v_j = \0\) if and only if \(\sum_j x_j\w_j = \0\) , for every \(\x \in F^k\) . Deduce that there is a well-defined isomorphism \(T \colon \Span(\v_1, \dots, \v_k) \to \Span(\w_1, \dots, \w_k)\) with \(T\v_j = \w_j\) for every \(j\) . Prove that \(T\) is an isometric isomorphism, that is, \(\inner{T\u}{T\u'} = \inner{\u}{\u'}\) for all \(\u, \u'\) in the domain.

title: Exercise (C2: Gram–Schmidt on a dependent list)
content: Let \((\v_1, \dots, \v_m)\) be a list in an inner product space, not assumed independent, and run the recursion of @thm-gram-schmidt . Let \(k\) be the smallest index with \(\v_k \in \Span(\v_1, \dots, \v_{k-1})\) . Prove that the recursion is defined up to \(\e_{k-1}\) and that \(\w_k = \0\) , so the step \(\e_k = \w_k/\norm{\w_k}\) fails. Repair the process: show that if, whenever \(\w_k = \0\) , we discard \(\v_k\) and continue with \(\v_{k+1}\) , the output is an orthonormal basis of \(\Span(\v_1, \dots, \v_m)\) . Run the repaired process on \(((1,1,0), (2,2,0), (1,0,1))\) in \(\nR^3\) .

title: Theorem 10.2.5 (Properties of the Gram Matrix)
content: Let \((\v_1, \dots, \v_k)\) be a list in an inner product space \(V\) over \(F\) , with Gram matrix \(\G\) . Then: \(\G\) is Hermitian , \(\G^{*} = \G\) , and its diagonal entries are the real numbers \(\norm{\v_i}^2 \ge 0\) ; \(\x^{*}\G\x = \big\lVert \textstyle\sum_{j} x_j\v_j \big\rVert^2\) for every \(\x \in F^k\) ; \(\G\) is invertible if and only if \((\v_1, \dots, \v_k)\) is linearly independent; \(\det \G\) is a real number with \(\det \G \ge 0\) , and \(\det \G > 0\) exactly when the list is linearly independent.

title: Theorem 10.2.2 (Gram–Schmidt Process)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space and let \((\v_1, \dots, \v_m)\) be a linearly independent list in \(V\) . Define recursively \[ \w_k = \v_k - \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \inner{\v_k}{\e_i}\,\e_i , \qquad \e_k = \frac{\w_k}{\norm{\w_k}} \qquad (k = 1, \dots, m). \] Then every \(\w_k\) is non-zero, so the recursion is defined, and: \((\e_1, \dots, \e_m)\) is an orthonormal list; \(\Span(\e_1, \dots, \e_k) = \Span(\v_1, \dots, \v_k)\) for every \(k = 1, \dots, m\) ; if \((\v_1, \dots, \v_r)\) is already orthonormal for some \(r \le m\) , then \(\e_i = \v_i\) for \(i \le r\) . In particular, every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis.

title: Theorem 10.2.1 (Coordinates, Inner Products and Norms in an Orthonormal Basis)
content: Let \((\e_1, \dots, \e_n)\) be an orthonormal basis of an inner product space \(V\) , and let \(\u, \v \in V\) . Then: \(\displaystyle \v = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \inner{\v}{\e_i}\,\e_i\) ; \(\displaystyle \inner{\u}{\v} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \inner{\u}{\e_i}\,\conj{\inner{\v}{\e_i}}\) ; \(\displaystyle \norm{\v}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert \inner{\v}{\e_i} \rvert^2\) ( Parseval’s identity for a finite orthonormal basis).

title: Corollary 10.3.4 (Projecting with an orthogonal basis)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) , and let \((\u_1, \dots, \u_k)\) be an orthogonal basis of \(U\) , so that \(\inner{\u_i}{\u_j} = 0\) for \(i \neq j\) and every \(\u_i \neq \0\) . Then \[ P_U\v = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{\inner{\v}{\u_i}}{\inner{\u_i}{\u_i}}\,\u_i \qquad \text{for every } \v \in V . \]

title: Definition 10.3.3 (Distance to a subspace)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) and let \(\v \in V\) . The distance from \(\v\) to \(U\) is \[ d(\v, U) = \min_{\u \in U} \norm{\v - \u} = \norm{\v - P_U\v} . \]

title: Definition 10.3.1 (Orthogonal complement)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) and let \(S \subseteq V\) be any subset. The orthogonal complement of \(S\) is \[ S^{\perp} = \{\, \v \in V : \inner{\v}{\s} = 0 \text{ for every } \s \in S \,\}, \] read “ \(S\) perp”.

title: Definition 10.3.2 (Orthogonal projection)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) . By @thm-orthogonal-decomposition (a), every \(\v \in V\) has a unique splitting \(\v = \u + \w\) with \(\u \in U\) and \(\w \in U^{\perp}\) . The orthogonal projection onto \(U\) is the operator \(P_U \in \cL(V)\) defined by \[ P_U\v = \u . \]

title: Example (The best quadratic approximation to a cubic)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 3}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , let \(U = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) . Find the polynomial of \(U\) closest to \(x^3\) , and the distance.

title: Example (Distance from a point to a plane)
content: In \(\nR^3\) with the dot product, let \(U = \{ (x, y, z) : x + y + z = 0 \}\) and \(\v = (1, 2, 3)\) . Find \(P_U\v\) and \(d(\v, U)\) , twice: once through \(U^{\perp}\) , and once through an orthonormal basis of \(U\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define the orthogonal complement \(S^{\perp}\) of a subset \(S\) of an inner product space. True or false: \(S^{\perp}\) is a subspace only when \(S\) is a subspace. Justify your answer. State the Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem, including every hypothesis. Let \(U\) be a \(3\) -dimensional subspace of \(\nR^7\) . What is \(\dim U^{\perp}\) , and what is \(\dim(U^{\perp})^{\perp}\) ? What quantity does \(P_U\v\) minimize, and over what set? Name two differences between \(U^{\perp}\) and the annihilator \(U^{0}\) .

title: Exercise (B1: A complement and a projection in \nR^4)
content: In \(\nR^4\) with the dot product, let \(U = \Span\bigl((1, 1, 0, 0),\ (0, 0, 1, 1)\bigr)\) . Find a basis of \(U^{\perp}\) and verify the dimension count. Compute \(P_U\v\) and \(d(\v, U)\) for \(\v = (1, 2, 3, 4)\) . Verify directly that \(\v - P_U\v \in U^{\perp}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Distance from a point to a plane)
Exercise (B3: The best quadratic approximation to a quartic)
content: On \(\nR[x]_{\le 4}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1}p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , let \(U = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) . Find \(P_U(x^4)\) and \(d(x^4, U)\) . Hint: the orthogonal basis of @exm-best-quadratic-approximation still works.

title: Exercise (C1: Perp turns sums into intersections)
content: Let \(U\) and \(W\) be subspaces of an inner product space \(V\) . Prove that \((U + W)^{\perp} = U^{\perp} \cap W^{\perp}\) . (No finiteness is needed.) Assume now that \(V\) is finite-dimensional. Deduce that \((U \cap W)^{\perp} = U^{\perp} + W^{\perp}\) .

title: Exercise (C2: A subspace with no orthogonal complement)
content:
Let \(V = 
R[x]\) , with the coefficient inner product \[ \inner{p}{q} = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_kb_k \quad 	ext{for } p = \sum_k a_kx^k,\ q = \sum_k b_kx^k, \] a finite sum, since a polynomial has only finitely many non-zero coefficients. Let \(U = \{\, p \in V : p(1) = 0 \,\}\) . Verify that \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}\) is an inner product on \(V\) and that \(U\) is a subspace with \(U

title: Exercise (C3: Which projections are orthogonal)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let \(P \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \(P^2 = P\) . Prove that the following are equivalent: \(P = P_U\) for some subspace \(U\) ; \(\inner{P\u}{\v} = \inner{\u}{P\v}\) for all \(\u, \v \in V\) ; \(\ker P = (\im P)^{\perp}\) . Hint: for (b) \(\Rightarrow\) (c), pair a vector of \(\ker P\) with \(P\v\) .

title: Proposition 10.3.1 (Perp is always a subspace)
content: For every subset \(S\) of an inner product space \(V\) , the set \(S^{\perp}\) is a subspace of \(V\) . Moreover \(S^{\perp} = \Span(S)^{\perp}\) .

title: Theorem 10.3.5 (Best Approximation Theorem)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) , and let \(\v \in V\) . Then \[ \norm{\v - P_U\v} \le \norm{\v - \u} \qquad \text{for every } \u \in U, \] and equality holds only for \(\u = P_U\v\) .

title: Theorem 10.3.2 (Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) and let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of \(V\) . Then: \(V = U \oplus U^{\perp}\) ; \((U^{\perp})^{\perp} = U\) ; if in addition \(V\) is finite-dimensional, then \(\dim U^{\perp} = \dim V - \dim U\) .

title: Theorem 10.3.3 (Projection formula)
content: Let \(U\) be a finite-dimensional subspace of an inner product space \(V\) , with orthonormal basis \((\e_1, \dots, \e_k)\) . Then for every \(\v \in V\) : \(\displaystyle P_U\v = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \inner{\v}{\e_i}\e_i\) ; \(\inner{P_U\u}{\v} = \inner{\u}{P_U\v}\) for all \(\u, \v \in V\) ; \(\norm{P_U\v} \le \norm{\v}\) , with equality if and only if \(\v \in U\) .

title: Corollary 10.4.4 (Uniqueness of the least-squares solution)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and \(\b \in F^m\) . The following are equivalent: \(\A\x = \b\) has exactly one least-squares solution (for one, equivalently for every, \(\b\) ); the columns of \(\A\) are linearly independent, that is \(\rank \A = n\) ; \(\A^{*}\A\) is invertible. In that case the least-squares solution is \(\x = (\A^{*}\A)^{-1}\A^{*}\b\) .

title: Example (The least-squares line through four points)
content: Find the line \(y = c + dt\) that minimizes the sum of the squared vertical errors at the four data points \[ (1, 3), \quad (2, 1), \quad (3, 5), \quad (4, 5). \] Compute the residual and the minimum value of the sum of squares.

title: Example (The least-squares parabola)
content: Find the quadratic \(y = a + bt + ct^2\) minimizing the sum of squared errors at \[ (-2, 7), \quad (-1, 6), \quad (0, 2), \quad (1, 0), \quad (2, 5). \]

title: Example (A minimum-norm solution)
content: Find the solution of smallest norm of \[ \begin{cases} x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 3, \\ x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 7. \end{cases} \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define a least-squares solution of \(\A\x = \b\) , and write down the normal equations. True or false: if \(\A\x = \b\) is consistent, then its solutions are exactly its least-squares solutions. Justify your answer. Explain in one sentence why the normal equations are always consistent. Give a condition on the columns of \(\A\) equivalent to uniqueness of the least-squares solution. Where does the minimum-norm solution of a consistent system live, and why is it unique there? True or false: \((\A^{*}\A)^{-1} = \A^{-1}(\A^{*})^{-1}\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: A least-squares line)
content: Find the least-squares line \(y = c + dt\) for the data \((0, 3), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 6)\) . Compute the residual, verify that it is orthogonal to both columns of \(\A\) , and give the minimum sum of squares.

title: Exercise (B2: A least-squares parabola)
content: Find the least-squares quadratic \(y = a + bt + ct^2\) for the data \((-1, 2), (0, 8), (1, 6), (2, 16)\) , and the minimum sum of squares. Hint: write down \(\A\tp\A\) from the power sums \(\sum t_i^k\) , \(k = 0, \dots, 4\) .

title: Exercise (C3: A rank-deficient least-squares problem)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \b = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}. \] Show that \(\A\x = \b\) is inconsistent and that \(\rank\A = 2\) . title: Lemma 10.4.1 (Moving a matrix across the inner product)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Then for all \(\x \in F^n\) and \(\y \in F^m\) , \[ \inner{\A\x}{\y} = \inner{\x}{\A^{*}\y}, \qquad \inner{\y}{\A\x} = \inner{\A^{*}\y}{\x} . \]

title: Lemma 10.4.3 (The null space of \A^{*}\A)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Then \(\nul(\A^{*}\A) = \nul(\A)\) .

title: Theorem 10.4.2 (Least Squares Theorem)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and \(\b \in F^m\) , and write \(U = \col(\A)\) . For \(\x \in F^n\) , the following are equivalent: \(\norm{\A\x - \b} \le \norm{\A\z - \b}\) for every \(\z \in F^n\) ; \(\A\x = P_U\b\) ; \(\A^{*}\A\x = \A^{*}\b\) . Moreover such an \(\x\) always exists. A vector satisfying these conditions is called a least-squares solution of \(\A\x = \b\) , and the equations in (c) are the normal equations .

content:
Let \(\A \in M_{m 	imes n}(F)\) and let \(  \in F^m\) be such that \(\A\x =  \) is consistent. Write \(K =

orm{\x_{\min}} < 
orm{\x}\) for every other solution \(\x\) . We call \(\x_{\min}\) the minimum-norm solution .

title: Corollary 10.5.2 (The Riesz map)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) . Define \[ \Phi \colon V \to V^{*}, \qquad \Phi(\w) = \inner{\cdot}{\w} . \] Then \(\Phi\) is a bijection, and for all \(\w, \w' \in V\) and \(c \in F\) , \[ \Phi(\w + \w') = \Phi(\w) + \Phi(\w'), \qquad \Phi(c\w) = \conj{c}\,\Phi(\w). \] In particular \(\Phi\) is an isomorphism of vector spaces when \(F = \nR\) , and is conjugate-linear when \(F = \nC\) .

title: Example (A functional with no Riesz vector)
content: Let \(V = \nR[x]\) with the coefficient inner product \(\inner{p}{q} = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_kb_k\) for \(p = \sum_k a_kx^k\) and \(q = \sum_k b_kx^k\) (a finite sum, and an inner product by @exr-orthogonal-complements-and-projections-c2 (a)). Show that \(\varphi(p) = p(1)\) has no Riesz vector.

title: Example (Two Riesz vectors)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 1}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{0}^{1} p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , find the Riesz vector of \(\varphi(p) = p(0)\) . On \(V = M_n(\nC)\) with the Frobenius inner product \(\inner{\A}{\B} = \tr(\B^{*}\A)\) , find the Riesz vector of \(\varphi(\A) = \tr\A\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the Riesz Representation Theorem, including every hypothesis. Write down the formula for the Riesz vector of \(\varphi\) in terms of an orthonormal basis, and say where the conjugate comes from. True or false: over \(\nC\) , the Riesz map \(\Phi \colon V \to V^{*}\) is a linear isomorphism. Justify your answer. In what sense does an inner product answer the question Chapter 4 left open about \(V \cong V^{*}\) ? Under \(\Phi\) , which subspace of \(V^{*}\) corresponds to \(U^{\perp}\) ? Give an example showing that the theorem fails in infinite dimension.

title: Exercise (B1: Riesz vectors for evaluation)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) use the node inner product \(\inner{p}{q} = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)\) . Find the Riesz vectors of \(\varphi(p) = p(0)\) and of \(\psi(p) = p(1)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Riesz vectors on matrices)
content: On \(M_n(\nC)\) with the Frobenius inner product \(\inner{\A}{\B} = \tr(\B^{*}\A)\) , find the Riesz vector of: \(\varphi(\A) = a_{12}\) (assume \(n \ge 2\) ); \(\varphi_{\C}(\A) = \tr(\C\A)\) , for a fixed \(\C \in M_n(\nC)\) .

title: Exercise (B3: The correspondence in \nR^4)
content: In \(\nR^4\) with the dot product, let \(U = \Span\bigl((1, 0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 0, 1)\bigr)\) . Find a basis of \(U^{\perp}\) and a basis of \(U^{0}\) , and verify that \(\Phi\) carries the first to the second.

title: Exercise (C1: Riesz without an orthonormal basis)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space and let \(\varphi \in V^{*}\) be non-zero. Write \(K = \ker\varphi\) . Prove that \(\dim K^{\perp} = 1\) . Let \(\u\) span \(K^{\perp}\) with \(\norm{\u} = 1\) . Prove that \(\w = \conj{\varphi(\u)}\,\u\) satisfies \(\varphi(\v) = \inner{\v}{\w}\) for all \(\v \in V\) . Deduce @thm-riesz-representation , including the case \(\varphi = 0\) . Hint for (b): split \(\v\) using \(V = K \oplus K^{\perp}\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Evaluation at 0 is not represented)
content: Let \(V = \nR[x]\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{0}^{1}p(t)q(t)\,\dd t\) , and let \(\varphi(p) = p(0)\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(w = \sum_{j=0}^{d} c_jx^j\) satisfied \(\inner{p}{w} = p(0)\) for every \(p \in V\) . Show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{d} \frac{c_j}{k + j + 1} = 0\) for every integer \(k \ge 1\) , and that the same sum equals \(1\) for \(k = 0\) . Let \(N(s) = \sum_{j=0}^{d} c_j \prod_{i \neq j}(s + i + 1)\) , the product running over \(i \in \{0, \dots, d\}\setminus\{j\}\) . Show that \(N(k) = 0\) for every integer \(k \ge 1\) , and deduce that \(N\) is the zero polynomial. Deduce that every \(c_j = 0\) , and hence a contradiction.

title: Theorem 10.5.3 (Perp corresponds to the annihilator)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) , let \(U\) be a subspace and let \(\Phi\) be the Riesz map. Then \[ \Phi(U^{\perp}) = U^{0} . \] Equivalently, a functional \(\varphi \in V^{*}\) annihilates \(U\) if and only if its Riesz vector lies in \(U^{\perp}\) .

title: Theorem 10.5.1 (Riesz Representation Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) and let \(\varphi \in V^{*}\) . Then there is a unique \(\w \in V\) such that \[ \varphi(\v) = \inner{\v}{\w} \qquad \text{for every } \v \in V . \] If \((\e_1, \dots, \e_n)\) is any orthonormal basis of \(V\) , then \(\w = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \conj{\varphi(\e_i)}\,\e_i\) .

title: Corollary 10.6.6 (Rank of the Adjoint)
content: Let \(V, W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) and \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then \(\rank T^{*} = \rank T\) ; \(\ker(T^{*}T) = \ker T\) , and consequently \(\rank(T^{*}T) = \rank T\) .

title: Definition 10.6.1 (Adjoint)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . The adjoint of \(T\) is the unique linear map \(T^{*} \in \cL(W, V)\) satisfying \[ \inner{T\v}{\w} = \inner{\v}{T^{*}\w} \qquad \text{for all } \v \in V \text{ and all } \w \in W . \]

title: Definition 10.6.3 (Normal Operator)
content: An operator \(T \in \cL(V)\) on a finite-dimensional inner product space is normal if it commutes with its adjoint: \[ T^{*}T = TT^{*} . \]

title: Definition 10.6.2 (Self-adjoint Operator)
content: An operator \(T \in \cL(V)\) on a finite-dimensional inner product space is self-adjoint if \(T^{*} = T\) , that is, if \[ \inner{T\u}{\v} = \inner{\u}{T\v} \qquad \text{for all } \u, \v \in V . \] The matrix counterpart is the Hermitian matrix of @def-conjugate-transpose , \(\A^{*} = \A\) ; over \(\nR\) this says \(\A\tp = \A\) , and the matrix is symmetric .

title: Example (Differentiation on a Polynomial Space)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]_{\le 2}\) define \(\inner{p}{q} \coloneqq a_0b_0 + a_1b_1 + a_2b_2\) for \(p = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2\) and \(q = b_0 + b_1x + b_2x^2\) . (This is the standard inner product of \(\nR^3\) transported by the coordinate map, so it is an inner product, and \(\sE = (1, x, x^2)\) is an orthonormal basis.) Find the adjoint of \(D \colon V \to V\) , \(D(p) = p'\) .

title: Example (Four Adjoints)
content: Compute the adjoint in each case. In (a) and (b) the spaces carry the standard inner product; in (c) and (d), \(V\) and \(W\) are arbitrary finite-dimensional inner product spaces. \(T_{\A} \colon \nC^3 \to \nC^2\) for \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + i & 0 & 2 \\ i & 1 & -i \end{pmatrix}\) . The forward shift \(S \colon F^3 \to F^3\) , \(S(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (0, x_1, x_2)\) . \(\id_V\) and the zero map \(V \to W\) . The orthogonal projection \(P_U \colon V \to V\) onto a subspace \(U \subseteq V\) .

title: Example (The Transpose Rule Breaks)
content: Work in \(\nR^2\) with the standard inner product and let \(T(x_1, x_2) = (x_2, 0)\) . Let \(\sB = (\b_1, \b_2)\) with \(\b_1 = (1, 0)\) and \(\b_2 = (1, 1)\) . Compute \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) and \(\mtx{T^{*}}{\sB}{\sB}\) , and compare the second with the transpose of the first.

title: Example (All Four Subspaces of a 3 × 3 Matrix)
content: For \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(\nR\) , find bases of the four subspaces and verify the two orthogonality statements.

title: Example (A Map With No Adjoint)
content: On \(V = \nR[x]\) , all polynomials, define \(\inner{p}{q} \coloneqq \sum_{k \ge 0} a_kb_k\) , a finite sum since the coefficients vanish eventually. Show that \(T \colon V \to V\) , \(T(p) \coloneqq p(1) \cdot 1\) , has no adjoint.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the defining property of the adjoint \(T^{*}\) of \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) , including the domain and codomain of \(T^{*}\) and all quantifiers. Which hypothesis of @thm-adjoint-exists is used to produce \(T^{*}\) , and which theorem supplies it? True or false: \((cT)^{*} = cT^{*}\) for every scalar \(c\) . Justify your answer. Justify your answer. Give an example of a normal operator that is not self-adjoint.

title: Exercise (C3: The adjoint in an arbitrary basis)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space, let \(\sB = (\b_1, \dots, \b_n)\) be any ordered basis of \(V\) , let \(\G\) be its Gram matrix, \(g_{ij} = \inner{\b_j}{\b_i}\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Prove that \(\inner{\u}{\v} = \coord{\v}{\sB}^{*}\,\G\,\coord{\u}{\sB}\) for all \(\u, \v \in V\) . Deduce that \(\mtx{T^{*}}{\sB}{\sB} = \G^{-1}\left(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\right)^{*}\G\) . Check that (b) returns @thm-matrix-of-adjoint when \(\sB\) is orthonormal, and verify it on @exm-adjoint-nonorthonormal-basis . Hint: for (b), write the defining identity of \(T^{*}\) in the coordinates of (a) and use that \(\x^{*}\M\y = \x^{*}\N\y\) for all \(\x, \y\) forces \(\M = \N\) .

title: Proposition 10.6.7 (First Properties of Self-adjoint Operators)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint on a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\) over \(F\) . \(\inner{T\v}{\v} \in \nR\) for every \(\v \in V\) , even when \(F = \nC\) . If \(\sB\) is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) , the diagonal entries of \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) are real. \(T\) is normal.

title: Theorem 10.6.1 (Existence and Uniqueness of the Adjoint)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then there is exactly one map \(T^{*} \colon W \to V\) such that \[ \inner{T\v}{\w}_W = \inner{\v}{T^{*}\w}_V \qquad \text{for all } \v \in V,\ \w \in W, \] and this \(T^{*}\) is linear.

title: Theorem 10.6.2 (Properties of the Adjoint)
content: Let \(U, V, W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) . For \(S, T \in \cL(V, W)\) , \((S + T)^{*} = S^{*} + T^{*}\) . For \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) and \(c \in F\) , \((cT)^{*} = \conj{c}\,T^{*}\) . For \(T \in \cL(U, V)\) and \(S \in \cL(V, W)\) , \((ST)^{*} = T^{*}S^{*}\) . \(T^{**} = T\) for every \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) , and \((\id_V)^{*} = \id_V\) . If \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) is invertible, then \(T^{*}\) is invertible and \((T^{*})^{-1} = (T^{-1})^{*}\) .

title: Theorem 10.6.4 (The Adjoint Is the Dual Map Read Through Riesz)
content: Let \(V, W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) and \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then \[ \Phi_V \circ T^{*} = T' \circ \Phi_W . \]

title: Theorem 10.6.5 (The Four Fundamental Subspaces)
content: Let \(V, W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then \(\ker T^{*} = (\im T)^{\perp}\) ; \(\im T^{*} = (\ker T)^{\perp}\) ; \(V = \ker T \oplus \im T^{*}\) ; \(W = \im T \oplus \ker T^{*}\) .

title: Theorem 10.6.3 (The Matrix of the Adjoint Is the Conjugate Transpose)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) , let \(\sB = (\v_1, \dots, \v_n)\) be an orthonormal basis of \(V\) and \(\sC = (\w_1, \dots, \w_m)\) an orthonormal basis of \(W\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . Then \[ \mtx{T^{*}}{\sC}{\sB} = \left(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC}\right)^{*} . \]

title: Definition 10.7.1 (Isometry)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be inner product spaces over \(F\) . A linear map \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) is an isometry if \[ \norm{T\v} = \norm{\v} \qquad \text{for every } \v \in V . \]

title: Definition 10.7.2 (Unitary and Orthogonal)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) . An operator \(T \in \cL(V)\) is unitary if \[ T^{*}T = TT^{*} = \id_V , \] equivalently if \(T\) is an invertible isometry. When \(F = 
R\) , such a \(T\) is also called orthogonal . A matrix \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) with \(\A^{*}\A = \I_n\) is a unitary matrix ; a matrix \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) with \(\A	p\A = \I_n\) is an orthogonal matrix .

title: Definition 10.7.3 (The Unitary and Orthogonal Groups)
content: For \(n \ge 1\) set \[ \Unit(n) \coloneqq \{ \A \in M_n(\nC) : \A^{*}\A = \I_n \}, \qquad \Orth(n) \coloneqq \{ \A \in M_n(\nR) : \A\tp\A = \I_n \}, \] and \(\SO(n) \coloneqq \{ \A \in \Orth(n) : \det \A = 1 \}\) , the special orthogonal group .

content: Classify each of the following as a rotation or a reflection, and give the angle or the mirror line. \(\A = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\sqrt3 \\ \sqrt3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\B = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 4 & -3 \end{pmatrix}\) .

content: Let \(\sigma \in S_n\) and let \(\P_{\sigma} \in M_n(\nR)\) be its permutation matrix ( @def-permutation-matrix ), whose \(j\) -th column is \(\e_{\sigma(j)}\) . title: Proposition 10.7.1 (Eigenvalues of an Isometry Have Modulus 1)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be an isometry of an inner product space over \(F\) , and let \(\lambda \in F\) be an eigenvalue of \(T\) . Then \(\lvert\lambda\rvert = 1\) . In particular, if \(F = \nR\) then \(\lambda = 1\) or \(\lambda = -1\) .

title: Proposition 10.7.4 (The Groups and Their Determinants)
content: \(\Unit(n)\) and \(\Orth(n)\) are groups under matrix multiplication, and \(\Orth(n) = \Unit(n) \cap M_n(\nR)\) . If \(\A \in \Unit(n)\) then \(\lvert\det \A\rvert = 1\) . If \(\A \in \Orth(n)\) then \(\det \A = 1\) or \(\det \A = -1\) . \(\SO(n)\) is a subgroup of \(\Orth(n)\) .

title: Theorem 10.7.3 (Characterizations of Isometries)
content: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V, W)\) . The following are equivalent. \(T\) is an isometry: \(\norm{T\v} = \norm{\v}\) for every \(\v \in V\) . \(T\) preserves inner products: \(\inner{T\u}{T\v} = \inner{\u}{\v}\) for all \(\u, \v \in V\) . \(T^{*}T = \id_V\) . \(T\) sends every orthonormal list in \(V\) to an orthonormal list in \(W\) . \(T\) sends some orthonormal basis of \(V\) to an orthonormal list in \(W\) . For one (equivalently every) pair of orthonormal bases \(\sB\) of \(V\) and \(\sC\) of \(W\) , the matrix \(\A = \mtx{T}{\sB}{\sC} \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) , where \(n = \dim V\) and \(m = \dim W\) , satisfies \(\A^{*}\A = \I_n\) ; that is, the \(n\) columns of \(\A\) are orthonormal vectors of \(F^m\) . If in addition \(\dim W = \dim V\) , then (a)–(f) are further equivalent to each of \(T\) is invertible with \(T^{-1} = T^{*}\) ; \(TT^{*} = \id_W\) .

title: Theorem 10.7.5 (Classification of the Plane Isometries)
content: Let \(\A \in \Orth(2)\) . If \(\det \A = 1\) , then \(\A = \R_{\theta}\) for a unique \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\) . If \(\det \A = -1\) , then \(\A = \M_{\theta}\) for a unique \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\) . In this case \(\A^2 = \I\) , the eigenvalues of \(\A\) are \(1\) and \(-1\) , and \(\A\) is the reflection in the line \(L = \Span\bigl((\cos\tfrac\theta2, \sin\tfrac\theta2)\bigr)\) : it fixes \(L\) pointwise and negates \(L^{\perp}\) . Consequently \(\Orth(2) = \{\R_{\theta}\} \cup \{\M_{\theta}\}\) , and \(\SO(2) = \{\R_{\theta} : \theta \in [0, 2\pi)\}\) .

content:
Let \(f \colon 
R^n 	o 
R^n\) be any function, not assumed linear, with \[ 
orm{f(\x) - f(\y)} = 
orm{\x - \y} \qquad 	ext{for all } \x, \y \in 
R^n . \] If \(f(\0) = \0\) , then \(f\) is linear and orthogonal. In general, \(f(\x) = \A\x +  \) for a unique \(\A \in \Orth(n)\) and a unique \(  \in 
R^n\) .

title: Theorem 10.7.6 (Every Element of SO(3) Is a Rotation)
content: Let \(\A \in \SO(3)\) . Then there is a unit vector \(\u \in \nR^3\) with \(\A\u = \u\) , and an orthonormal basis \(\sB = (\u, \w_1, \w_2)\) of \(\nR^3\) in which \[ \mtx{T_{\A}}{\sB}{\sB} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ 0 & \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix} \] for some \(\theta\) . That is, \(\A\) fixes the axis \(\Span(\u)\) and rotates the plane \(\Span(\u)^{\perp}\) by \(\theta\) . Moreover \(\tr \A = 1 + 2\cos\theta\) .

title: Definition 10.8.2 (Givens Rotation)
content: Let \(1 \le i < j \le m\) and let \(c, s \in \nR\) with \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\) . The Givens rotation \(\G(i, j; c, s) \in M_m(\nR)\) is the identity matrix with the four entries in rows and columns \(i, j\) replaced by \[ \begin{pmatrix} g_{ii} & g_{ij} \\ g_{ji} & g_{jj} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} c & s \\ -s & c \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Definition 10.8.1 (Householder Reflection)
content: Let \(\w \in F^m\) be non-zero . The Householder reflection determined by \(\w\) is \[ \H_{\w} = \I_m - \frac{2\,\w\w^{*}}{\norm{\w}^2} \in M_m(F) . \]

title: Example (Hessenberg form of a 3 \times 3 matrix)
content: Reduce \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \] to upper Hessenberg form by a unitary similarity.

title: Example (A 3 \times 3 QR by reflections)
content: Triangularize \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \] by Householder reflections, and read off \(\Q\) and \(\R\) .

title: Example (A 3 \times 2 QR, and a least-squares problem)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \b = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} . \] Find the QR factorization of \(\A\) . Find the \(\x \in \nR^2\) minimizing \(\norm{\A\x - \b}\) , using (a).

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State @thm-qr-factorization in full, including the two normalizations that make \(\Q\) and \(\R\) unique. Which hypothesis on \(\A\) does @thm-qr-factorization need, and which does @thm-qr-householder need? Explain the difference in one sentence. Write down the Householder reflection determined by \(\w\) , and list three of its properties. In @thm-householder-maps-vector , which of the two possible targets \(\pm\norm{\x}\e_1\) is chosen, and why? True or false: applying reflections on both sides, as in @thm-hessenberg-form , can be pushed to make every complex matrix unitarily similar to an upper triangular one. Justify your answer. Why must the reflection used at step \(k\) of @thm-hessenberg-form fix \(\e_1, \dots, \e_k\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: QR by Gram–Schmidt)
content: Find the QR factorization of \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \] in the sense of @thm-qr-factorization , and verify that \(\R = \Q\tp\A\) for the top-left \(2 \times 2\) entries.

title: Exercise (B2: The same matrix by reflections)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}\) , the matrix of @exm-qr-3x2 . Find \(\w_1\) and the reflection \(\H_1\) of @thm-householder-maps-vector for the first column of \(\A\) , and compute \(\H_1\A\) . Find the second reflection and hence a factorization \(\A = \Q\R\) with \(\Q \in M_3(\nR)\) orthogonal and \(\R \in M_{3\times2}(\nR)\) upper triangular. Compare the \(\R\) of (b) with the \(\R\) of @exm-qr-3x2 , and say exactly how the two factorizations differ.

title: Exercise (B3: A least-squares fit through QR)
content: Fit a line \(y = c_0 + c_1t\) to the data \((t, y) = (0,1), (1,3), (2,2)\) in the least-squares sense, by finding the QR factorization of the design matrix and solving \(\R\x = \Q\tp\b\) . Compute the residual and check the answer against the normal equations.

title: Exercise (B4: Determine which are QR factorizations)
content: Determine which of the following are QR factorizations of the matrix on the left in the sense of @thm-qr-factorization . Justify your answer; for those that are not, name the clause that fails and repair it if possible. \(\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 7\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac15\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 5 & \tfrac{31}{5} \\ 0 & \tfrac{17}{5}\end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \tfrac12 \\ 0 & \tfrac12\end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: All the QR factorizations of a matrix)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m\times n}(F)\) have independent columns, with QR factorization \(\A = \Q\R\) as in @thm-qr-factorization . Prove that an upper triangular \(\S \in M_n(F)\) with \(\S^{*}\S = \I_n\) is diagonal, with diagonal entries of modulus \(1\) . Deduce that the pairs \((\Q_1, \R_1)\) with \(\Q_1^{*}\Q_1 = \I_n\) , \(\R_1\) upper triangular and invertible, and \(\A = \Q_1\R_1\) , are exactly the pairs \((\Q\D^{-1}, \D\R)\) for \(\D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n)\) with \(\lvert d_k\rvert = 1\) . Hence give a second proof of the uniqueness statement of @thm-qr-factorization .

title: Exercise (C2: Reflections do not mind dependence)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \] whose third column is the sum of the first two. Run the Gram–Schmidt process of @thm-gram-schmidt on the columns of \(\A\) and say precisely which step fails. Carry out the Householder reduction of @thm-qr-householder on \(\A\) and exhibit \(\R\) . Explain, using @thm-qr-factorization , why no factorization \(\A = \Q\R\) with \(\Q^{*}\Q = \I_3\) and \(\R\) upper triangular with positive diagonal can exist.

title: Exercise (C3: Triangularizing with rotations)
content: Let \((a, b) \in \nR^2\) be non-zero and \(r = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) . Verify that the Givens rotation \(\G\) of @def-givens-rotation with \(c = a/r\) and \(s = b/r\) satisfies \(\G(a,b) = (r, 0)\) , and that \(\G \in \SO(2)\) . Use (a) to write \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) as \(\Q\R\) with \(\Q \in \SO(2)\) and \(\R\) upper triangular with positive diagonal. How many Givens rotations does it take to triangularize a general \(3\times3\) real matrix, and which entries does each one kill? Compare with the number of Householder reflections.

title: Proposition 10.8.2 (Properties of a Householder Reflection)
content: Let \(\w \in F^m\) be non-zero and \(\H = \H_{\w}\) . Then \(\H^{*} = \H\) ( \(\H\) is Hermitian); \(\H^2 = \I_m\) , so \(\H^{-1} = \H\) ; \(\H\) is unitary; \(\H\w = -\w\) , and \(\H\v = \v\) for every \(\v \perp \w\) ; \(\det \H = -1\) .

title: Theorem 10.8.5 (Reduction to Hessenberg Form)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) , \(n \ge 1\) . Then there is a unitary \(\Q \in M_n(F)\) such that \(\Z = \Q^{*}\A\Q\) is upper Hessenberg , that is, \[ z_{ij} = 0 \qquad \text{whenever } i > j + 1 . \] The matrix \(\Q\) can be taken to be a product of \(n - 2\) factors, each a Householder reflection or an identity matrix (and \(\Q = \I_n\) when \(n \le 2\) ). For \(n = 4\) the pattern is \[ \Z = \begin{pmatrix} \ast & \ast & \ast & \ast \\ \ast & \ast & \ast & \ast \\ 0 & \ast & \ast & \ast \\ 0 & 0 & \ast & \ast \end{pmatrix}. \]

title: Theorem 10.8.3 (A Reflection Flattening a Vector)
content:
Let \(\x \in F^m\) be non-zero, and let \[ \alpha =  egin{cases} x_1/\lvert x_1vert, & x_1 
eq 0, \ 1, & x_1 = 0, \end{cases} \qquad \w = \x + \alpha
orm{\x}\,\e_1 . \] Then \(\w 
eq \0\) and \[ \H_{\w}\,\x = -\alpha
orm{\x}\,\e_1 . \] In particular \(\H_{\w}\x\) is a multiple of \(\e_1\) of length \(
orm{\x}\) . Over \(
R\) , \(\alpha\) is the sign of \(x_1\) (or \(1\) if \(x_1 = 0\) ), and \(\H_{\w}\x = \mp
orm{\x}\e_1\) according to that sign.

title: Theorem 10.8.1 (QR Factorization)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) have linearly independent columns. Then there are matrices \(\Q \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and \(\R \in M_n(F)\) with the columns of \(\Q\) orthonormal, equivalently \(\Q^{*}\Q = \I_n\) ; \(\R\) upper triangular with positive real diagonal entries; \(\A = \Q\R\) . Moreover \(\Q\) and \(\R\) are unique : any pair satisfying (a), (b), (c) is this one. The pair \((\Q, \R)\) is the QR factorization of \(\A\) .

title: Theorem 10.8.4 (QR by Householder Reflections)
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . Then there are a unitary \(\Q \in M_m(F)\) and an \(\R \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) with \(r_{ij} = 0\) whenever \(i > j\) , such that \[ \A = \Q\R . \] Moreover \(\Q\) can be taken to be a product of at most \(\min(n, m-1)\) Householder reflections. No hypothesis on the columns of \(\A\) is needed.

title: Definition 10.9.1 (Fourier Coefficients With Respect to an Orthonormal List)
content: Let \((\e_1, \dots, \e_k)\) be an orthonormal list in an inner product space \(V\) and let \(\v \in V\) . The scalars \[ \inner{\v}{\e_1},\ \dots,\ \inner{\v}{\e_k} \in F \] are the Fourier coefficients of \(\v\) with respect to the list.

title: Example (The Fourier Coefficients of f(x) = x)
content: In \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) , let \(f(x) = x\) . Find all \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) , write down \(S_nf\) , and say what @thm-fourier-best-approximation (c) gives.

title: Example (The Trigonometric System Is Orthonormal)
content: Fix \(n \ge 1\) . Show that the list of \(2n + 1\) functions \[ \frac{1}{\sqrt2},\ \cos x,\ \sin x,\ \cos 2x,\ \sin 2x,\ \dots,\ \cos nx,\ \sin nx \] is orthonormal in \(V = C[-\pi, \pi]\) with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State Bessel’s inequality, saying exactly what is assumed about the space and what is assumed about the list. State Parseval’s identity, including the condition under which equality holds for a given vector. True or false: Bessel’s inequality requires the ambient space to be finite-dimensional. Justify your answer. Write down the inner product used on \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) in this section, including its normalizing constant, and say what the constant is for. State what @thm-fourier-best-approximation gives about \(S_nf\) , and name one thing it does not give. True or false: if \((\e_1, \dots, \e_k)\) is an orthonormal list and \(\sum_i\lvert\inner{\v}{\e_i}\rvert^2 = \norm{\v}^2\) for one particular \(\v \ne \0\) , then the list is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Fourier coefficients)
content: Work in \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) . Find all Fourier coefficients \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) of each of the following, and in each case write down \(S_2f\) . \(f(x) = \lvert x \rvert\) . \(f(x) = x^2\) . \(f(x) = 3 - 2\sin x + \sin 3x\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Verifying Bessel for a truncation)
content: In \(\nR^4\) with the dot product let \(\e_1 = \tfrac12(1, 1, 1, 1)\) , \(\e_2 = \tfrac12(1, -1, 1, -1)\) and \(\v = (2, 0, 0, 2)\) . Verify @thm-bessel-inequality for \(\v\) and this list, compute the deficit, and check against \((\ast)\) by computing \(\norm{\v - P_U\v}\) directly, where \(U = \Span(\e_1, \e_2)\) . For \(f(x) = \lvert x \rvert\) and \(n = 1\) , write out both sides of @thm-fourier-best-approximation (c) using @exr-bessel-parseval-fourier-b1 (a), and show that the resulting inequality is equivalent to \(96 \le \pi^4\) .

title: Exercise (B3: The best approximation by \Span(1, \cos x))
content: In \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) , let \(U = \Span(1, \cos x)\) and \(f(x) = x^2\) . Find \(P_Uf\) and \(d(f, U)^2\) . Hint: the list \((1, \cos x)\) is orthogonal but not orthonormal.

title: Exercise (C1: Parseval for the full trigonometric system)
content: This exercise uses an input from analysis that this book does not prove : the trigonometric system is complete in \(C[-\pi, \pi]\) , meaning that for every \(f \in C[-\pi, \pi]\) , \[ \frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k^2 + b_k^2\big) = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)^2\,\dd t . \] Apply this to \(f(x) = x\) and deduce that \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1/k^2 = \pi^2/6\) . Hence deduce that \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1/(2k - 1)^2 = \pi^2/8\) . Say precisely which step used the analysis input, and explain why no result of this section can supply it.

title: Exercise (C2: Chebyshev orthogonality by substitution)
content: Let \(\inner{p}{q}_w = \int_{-1}^{1} p(t)q(t)(1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\,\dd t\) on \(\nR[x]\) , the Chebyshev inner product of the text. Prove that for every \(n \ge 0\) there is a polynomial \(T_n\) of degree \(n\) with \(T_n(\cos\theta) = \cos n\theta\) for all \(\theta\) , and find \(T_0, T_1, T_2, T_3\) . Prove that \(\inner{p}{q}_w = \int_0^{\pi} p(\cos\theta)\,q(\cos\theta)\,\dd\theta\) for all polynomials \(p, q\) . Deduce that \(\inner{T_m}{T_n}_w = 0\) for \(m \ne n\) , and compute \(\inner{T_n}{T_n}_w\) . Hint for (a): the identity \(\cos((n+1)\theta) + \cos((n-1)\theta) = 2\cos\theta\cos n\theta\) .

title: Theorem 10.9.1 (Bessel’s Inequality)
content: Let \(V\) be an inner product space over \(F\) , not assumed finite-dimensional , and let \((\e_1, \dots, \e_k)\) be an orthonormal list in \(V\) . Then for every \(\v \in V\) , \[ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\v}{\e_i} \rvert^2 \;\le\; \norm{\v}^2 . \]

title: Theorem 10.9.3 (Fourier Partial Sums Are Best Approximations)
content: Let \(f \in C[-\pi, \pi]\) , let \(n \ge 1\) , and let \(a_k, b_k\) be the Fourier coefficients of \(f\) . Put \[ S_nf = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n}\big(a_k\cos kx + b_k\sin kx\big) . \] Then, with \(\inner{f}{g} = \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} fg\) : \(S_nf = P_{W_n}f\) ; \(\norm{f - S_nf} \le \norm{f - g}\) for every \(g \in W_n\) , with equality only for \(g = S_nf\) ; \(\displaystyle \frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{n}\big(a_k^2 + b_k^2\big) \le \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(t)^2\,\dd t\) .

title: Theorem 10.9.2 (Parseval’s Identity)
content: Let \((\e_1, \dots, \e_k)\) be an orthonormal list in an inner product space \(V\) and let \(\v \in V\) . Then \[ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lvert \inner{\v}{\e_i} \rvert^2 = \norm{\v}^2 \quad\text{if and only if}\quad \v \in \Span(\e_1, \dots, \e_k) . \] In particular, if \((\e_1, \dots, \e_k)\) is an orthonormal basis of \(V\) , the identity holds for every \(\v \in V\) .

title: Definition 10.10.1 (Orthogonal Polynomial Sequence)
content:
Let \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}\) be an inner product on \(
R[x]\) , or on \(
R[x]_{\le n}\) . An orthogonal polynomial sequence for it is a sequence \(p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots\) of polynomials (a finite list \(p_0, \dots, p_n\) in the second case) such that \(\deg p_k = k\) for every index \(k\) ; \(\inner{p_j}{p_k} = 0\) whenever \(j 
e k\) . The sequence is monic if every \(p_k\) has leading coefficient \(1\) .

title: Example (The monic Legendre polynomials, continued)
content: For \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} pq\) , @exm-gram-schmidt-legendre gave \(p_0 = 1\) , \(p_1 = x\) , \(p_2 = x^2 - \tfrac13\) , with \(\inner{p_0}{p_0} = 2\) , \(\inner{p_1}{p_1} = \tfrac23\) and \(\inner{p_2}{p_2} = \tfrac{8}{45}\) . Use @thm-three-term-recurrence to obtain \(p_3\) , and check the recurrence reproduces \(p_2\) .

title: Example (Two-point Gauss–Legendre)
content: Take \(w = 1\) on \((-1, 1)\) and \(k = 2\) . Find the nodes and weights, and test the resulting rule on \(f = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3\) and on \(f = x^4\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define what it means for \(p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots\) to be a monic orthogonal polynomial sequence for an inner product on \(\nR[x]\) . State the three-term recurrence, including the formulas for \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) and the starting values. True or false: \(b_k > 0\) for every \(k \ge 1\) . Justify your answer. For \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_{-1}^{1} pq\) , how many roots does \(p_7\) have, of what kind, and where? True or false: for every inner product on \(\nR[x]\) one has \(\inner{xp}{q} = \inner{p}{xq}\) . Justify your answer. How many nodes does a Gaussian rule need in order to integrate every polynomial of degree at most \(11\) exactly?

title: Exercise (B1: A weighted interval)
content: On \(\nR[x]\) put \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_0^1 p(t)q(t)\,t\,\dd t\) . Compute the monic \(p_0\) , \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) , and verify directly that \(p_2 \perp \nR[x]_{\le 1}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Two rows of the table)
content: Verify the degree- \(1\) and degree- \(2\) entries of the table for two of the classical families. Chebyshev: \(w(t) = (1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\) on \((-1, 1)\) . You may use, without proof, that \(\int_{-1}^{1} (1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\dd t = \pi\) and \(\int_{-1}^{1} t^2(1 - t^2)^{-1/2}\dd t = \pi/2\) . Laguerre: \(w(t) = e^{-t}\) on \((0, \infty)\) . You may use, without proof, that \(\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-t}\,\dd t = k!\) .

title: Exercise (B3: One more Legendre polynomial)
content: Continue @exm-legendre-recurrence : compute \(\inner{p_3}{p_3}\) for \(p_3 = x^3 - \tfrac35 x\) , then use @thm-three-term-recurrence to find \(p_4\) . Verify that \(\inner{p_4}{1} = \inner{p_4}{x^2} = 0\) .

title: Exercise (B4: A two-point rule on the unit interval)
content: Work on \((0, 1)\) with \(w = 1\) . Exercise B2 of Section 2 ( @exr-orthonormal-bases-b2 ) found the monic orthogonal polynomials \(1\) , \(x - \tfrac12\) , \(x^2 - x + \tfrac16\) . Write down the two-point Gaussian rule for \(\int_0^1 f\) . Check it on \(f = x^3\) , and show that it fails on \(f = x^4\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Interlacing roots)
content: Let \(w\) be a weight on \((a, b)\) and let \((p_k)\) be its monic orthogonal polynomial sequence. The roots of \(p_k\) are said to interlace those of \(p_{k+1}\) when exactly one root of \(p_k\) lies strictly between each pair of consecutive roots of \(p_{k+1}\) . This is true for every \(k\) ; prove the first two cases by hand. Let \(r\) be the root of \(p_1\) and \(s_1 < s_2\) the roots of \(p_2\) . Prove that \(s_1 < r < s_2\) . Let \(u_1 < u_2 < u_3\) be the roots of \(p_3\) . Prove that \(u_1 < s_1 < u_2 < s_2 < u_3\) . Hint: evaluate the three-term recurrence at a root.

title: Exercise (C2: The ceiling is 2k − 1)
content:
Let \(w\) be a weight on \((a, b)\) and let \(k \ge 1\) . Let \(t_1, \dots, t_k\) be any \(k\) distinct real numbers and \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k\) any real numbers. Prove that there is an \(f \in 
R[x]_{\le 2k}\) with \(\int_a^b fw 
e \sum_i \alpha_i f(t_i)\) . Hence deduce that the Gaussian rule of @thm-gaussian-quadrature is exact on \(
R[x]_{\le 2k-1}\) and on no larger space \(
R[x]_{\le d}\) .

title: Lemma 10.10.4 (Even multiplicities mean no sign change)
content: Let \(I \subseteq \nR\) be an open interval and let \(f \in \nR[x]\) be non-zero. If \(\operatorname{mult}_r(f)\) is even for every \(r \in I\) , then \(f \ge 0\) throughout \(I\) , or \(f \le 0\) throughout \(I\) .

title: Proposition 10.10.2 (Existence and uniqueness of the monic sequence)
content:
Let \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}\) be an inner product on \(
R[x]\) . For each \(k \in 
N\) there is exactly one monic \(p_k\) of degree \(k\) with \(\inner{p_k}{q} = 0\) for every \(q \in 
R[x]_{\le k-1}\) . These \(p_k\) form the unique monic orthogonal polynomial sequence, and \((p_0, \dots, p_k)\) is an orthogonal basis of \(
R[x]_{\le k}\) for every \(k\) . The same holds on \(
R[x]_{\le n}\) for \(k \le n\) .

title: Proposition 10.10.1 (Multiplication by x is symmetric)
content: Let \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}\) be an inner product on \(\nR[x]\) coming from a weight, or the node inner product on \(\nR[x]_{\le n}\) . Then \[ \inner{xp}{q} = \inner{p}{xq} \] for all polynomials \(p, q\) in the space (in the node case, for all \(p, q\) of degree at most \(n - 1\) , so that \(xp\) and \(xq\) still lie in it).

title: Theorem 10.10.6 (Gaussian Quadrature)
content: Let \(w\) be a weight on \((a, b)\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_a^b pqw\) , let \(k \ge 1\) , and let \(t_1 < \dots < t_k\) be the roots of the monic orthogonal polynomial \(p_k\) , which lie in \((a, b)\) by @thm-orthogonal-polynomial-roots . Let \(\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k \in \nR[x]_{\le k-1}\) be the Lagrange polynomials for these nodes ( @def-lagrange-basis ) and set \[ \alpha_i = \int_a^b \ell_i(t)\,w(t)\,\dd t \qquad (i = 1, \dots, k). \] Then every \(\alpha_i\) is strictly positive , and \[ \int_a^b f(t)\,w(t)\,\dd t = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i\,f(t_i) \] for every \(f \in \nR[x]_{\le 2k-1}\) .

title: Theorem 10.10.5 (Roots of an Orthogonal Polynomial)
content: Let \(w\) be a weight on \((a, b)\) , let \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_a^b pqw\) , and let \((p_k)\) be the monic orthogonal polynomial sequence. For every \(k \ge 1\) , the polynomial \(p_k\) has \(k\) distinct real roots, and every one of them lies in the open interval \((a, b)\) .

title: Theorem 10.10.3 (Three-Term Recurrence)
content: Let \((p_k)\) be the monic orthogonal polynomial sequence of @prp-monic-orthogonal-sequence , for an inner product satisfying @prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric . For a weight on an interval this covers every \(k\) ; for the node inner product on \(n\) nodes, where @prp-multiplication-by-x-symmetric holds only up to degree \(n - 1\) , read the statement for \(k + 1 \le n\) . Put \(p_{-1} = 0\) and, for \(k \ge 0\) , \[ a_k = \frac{\inner{xp_k}{p_k}}{\inner{p_k}{p_k}}, \qquad b_k = \frac{\inner{p_k}{p_k}}{\inner{p_{k-1}}{p_{k-1}}} \ \ (k \ge 1). \] Then \(p_0 = 1\) , \(p_1 = x - a_0\) , and \[ p_{k+1} = (x - a_k)\,p_k - b_k\,p_{k-1} \qquad \text{for every } k \ge 1 . \] Moreover \(b_k > 0\) for every \(k \ge 1\) .

title: Corollary 11.1.5 (Determinant Is the Product of the Eigenvalues)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then \(\det\A = \lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n\) .

title: Corollary 11.1.3 (Schur Factorization)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) with \(n \ge 1\) , and let \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(\A\) , each listed as often as its algebraic multiplicity, in any prescribed order. Then there are a unitary \(\U \in M_n(
C)\) and an upper triangular \(\T \in M_n(
C)\) with \[ \A = \U\T\U^{*}, \qquad t_{ii} = \lambda_i \quad (1 \le i \le n) . \]

title: Corollary 11.1.6 (Diagonalizable Matrices Are Everywhere)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) and let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Then there is a diagonalizable \(\A' \in M_n(\nC)\) with \[ \lvert a_{ij} - a'_{ij} \rvert < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } i, j . \] In this sense every complex square matrix is a limit of diagonalizable ones.

title: Corollary 11.1.4 (Trace Is the Sum of the Eigenvalues)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then \(\tr\A = \lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_n\) .

title: Example (An Eigenline Whose Complement Is Not Invariant)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) act on \(\nC^2\) . Check that \(\e_1\) is an eigenvector and decide whether \((\Span(\e_1))^{\perp}\) is invariant.

title: Example (A Two-by-Two Schur Factorization)
content: Find a unitary \(\U\) and an upper triangular \(\T\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U = \T\) , as in @cor-schur-matrix , for \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Example (A Three-by-Three Schur Factorization)
content: Find a unitary \(\U\) and an upper triangular \(\T\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U = \T\) , as in @cor-schur-matrix , for \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -3 & -2 \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content:
State @thm-schur-triangularization , including the field and every hypothesis. In the proof, an eigenvector of \(T^{*}\) is taken rather than one of \(T\) . Say why, in one sentence, and name the property of \((\Span(\v))^{\perp}\) that is wanted. True or false: if \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) is upper triangular in some orthonormal basis, then its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries of that triangular matrix. Justify your answer. Which step of the proof of @thm-schur-triangularization fails over \(
R\) ? Give a matrix in \(M_2(
C)\) that is upper triangular in an orthonormal basis but is not diagonal in any.

title: Exercise (B1: A Schur form with complex entries)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) , regarded as a complex matrix. Find the eigenvalues of \(\A\) . Find a unitary \(\U \in M_2(\nC)\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U\) upper triangular, and compute that triangular matrix. Explain why no real orthogonal \(\Q\) makes \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) upper triangular.

title: Exercise (B2: A three-by-three Schur form)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) . Verify that \((1, -1, 0)\) is an eigenvector and find the corresponding eigenvalue. Extend it to an orthonormal basis of \(\nR^3\) and compute \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) for the resulting \(\Q\) . Hence write down the eigenvalues of \(\A\) with their algebraic multiplicities.

title: Exercise (C1: Cayley–Hamilton from the triangular factors)
content: Let \(\T \in M_n(\nC)\) be upper triangular with diagonal entries \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , and set \(\N_k = (\T - \lambda_1\I)(\T - \lambda_2\I)\cdots(\T - \lambda_k\I)\) for \(1 \le k \le n\) . Deduce the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem ( @thm-cayley-hamilton ) for every \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) , using @cor-schur-matrix . Hint for (a): the \(j\) -th column of \(\T - \lambda_j\I\) has its only possibly non-zero entries in rows \(1, \dots, j - 1\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Distinct eigenvalues are dense, but not over the reals)
content: Sharpen @cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby : prove that for every \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) and every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(\A'\) with \(n\) distinct eigenvalues and \(\lvert a_{ij} - a'_{ij} \rvert < \varepsilon\) for all \(i, j\) . Show that the analogous statement fails over \(\nR\) : for \(\R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) there is an \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that no real matrix within \(\varepsilon\) of \(\R\) , entry by entry, has a real eigenvalue at all. Hint for (b): a real \(2 \times 2\) matrix with entries \(a, b, c, d\) has real eigenvalues exactly when \((a - d)^2 + 4bc \ge 0\) .

title: Lemma 11.1.1 (Eigenvectors of the Adjoint Cut Out Invariant Subspaces)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) , let \(T \in \cL(V)\) , and let \(W \subseteq V\) be a \(T^{*}\) -invariant subspace. Then \(W^{\perp}\) is \(T\) -invariant.

title: Theorem 11.1.7 (Real Schur Form)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) with \(n \ge 1\) . Then there are an orthogonal \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) and a matrix \(\T \in M_n(\nR)\) with \[ \A = \Q\T\Q\tp, \] where \(\T\) is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks of size \(1 \times 1\) and \(2 \times 2\) , and every \(2 \times 2\) diagonal block has a conjugate pair of non-real eigenvalues.

title: Theorem 11.1.2 (Schur’s Unitary Triangularization)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\nC\) with \(\dim V = n \ge 1\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . There is an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) such that \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) is upper triangular. More precisely, let \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) be the eigenvalues of \(T\) , each listed as often as its algebraic multiplicity, in any order we please. Then \(\sB\) can be chosen so that the \(i\) -th diagonal entry of \(\mtx{T}{\sB}{\sB}\) is \(\lambda_i\) .

title: Example (A Hermitian Two-by-Two)
content: For \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \\ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) on \(\nC^2\) , find the eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify that the two eigenvectors are orthogonal.

title: Example (Four Tests)
content:
Determine which of the following are self-adjoint. Justify your answer; for those that are not, name the failing pair of vectors. \(T_{\A}\) on \(
C^2\) with the standard inner product, \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(T_{\B}\) on \(
C^2\) with the standard inner product, \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & i \ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . Differentiation \(D\) on \(V = 
R[x]_{\le 2}\) with \(\inner{p}{q} = \int_0^1 pq\) . The orthogonal projection \(P_U\) onto a subspace \(U\) of any \(V\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State what it means for \(T \in \cL(V)\) to be self-adjoint, in terms of \(T^{*}\) and in terms of inner products, and say what the matrix condition is and in which bases it may be used. True or false: a symmetric matrix in \(M_2(\nC)\) has real eigenvalues. Justify your answer. Which field does @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue concern, and which earlier theorem supplies the eigenvalue it borrows? True or false: if \(T\) is self-adjoint and \(U\) is any subspace, then \(U^{\perp}\) is \(T\) -invariant. Justify your answer. State the difference between @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test and @thm-complex-zero-test , and give the standard example showing the second has no real analogue. Give a normal operator on \(\nR^2\) that is not self-adjoint.

title: Exercise (B1: Determine which are self-adjoint)
content:
Determine which of the following operators are self-adjoint. Justify your answer; for those that are not, exhibit a pair \(\u, \v\) with \(\inner{T\u}{\v} 
e \inner{\u}{T\v}\) , or compute \(T^{*}\) . \(T_{\A}\) on \(
C^2\) , \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 + i \ 2 - i & -5 \end{pmatrix}\) , standard inner product. \(T_{\B}\) on \(
C^2\) , \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) , standard inner product. \(T_{\C}\) on \(
R^3\) , \(\C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) , standard inner product. \(S^{*}S\) , for an arbitrary \(S \in \cL(V, W)\) between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. \(P_U - P_{U^{\perp}}\) , for a subspace \(U\) of a finite-dimensional \(V\) . \(T(x_1, x_2) = (x_2, x_1)\) on \(

title: Exercise (B2: Eigenvalues and orthogonality)
content:
For \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
C)\) , check that \(\A\) is Hermitian, find its eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify that the eigenvectors are orthogonal. For \(\S =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 3 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
R)\) , find the eigenvalues with their multiplicities and bases of the eigenspaces, and verify that the two eigenspaces are orthogonal. Hence write down an orthonormal basis of \(
R^3\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(\S\) .

title: Exercise (B3: A self-adjoint square root of zero)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint with \(T^2 = 0\) . Prove that \(T = 0\) . Deduce that a self-adjoint \(T\) with \(T^k = 0\) for some \(k \ge 1\) is zero.

title: Exercise (C1: The operator S^{*}S)
content: Let \(S \in \cL(V, W)\) between finite-dimensional inner product spaces over \(F\) , and set \(T = S^{*}S \in \cL(V)\) . Prove that \(T\) is self-adjoint and that \(\inner{T\v}{\v} \ge 0\) for every \(\v \in V\) , with equality if and only if \(S\v = \0\) . Deduce that every eigenvalue of \(T\) is a non-negative real number. Prove that \(T\) is invertible if and only if \(S\) is injective. Hint for (a): the quantity \(\inner{T\v}{\v}\) is a norm squared in disguise.

title: Exercise (C2: Sums and products)
content: Let \(S, T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint. Prove that \(S + T\) and \(cT\) are self-adjoint for every real scalar \(c\) , and show by example that \(cT\) need not be self-adjoint for \(c \in \nC\) . Prove that \(ST\) is self-adjoint if and only if \(ST = TS\) . Give self-adjoint \(S, T \in \cL(\nC^2)\) with \(ST\) not self-adjoint.

title: Exercise (C3: What the real quadratic form does determine)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\nR\) and \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Call \(T\) skew-adjoint if \(T^{*} = -T\) . Prove that \(\inner{T\v}{\v} = 0\) for every \(\v \in V\) if and only if \(T\) is skew-adjoint. Deduce that every \(T \in \cL(V)\) can be written uniquely as \(T = A + B\) with \(A\) self-adjoint and \(B\) skew-adjoint, and that \(\inner{T\v}{\v} = \inner{A\v}{\v}\) for every \(\v\) . Conclude that over \(\nR\) the function \(\v \mapsto \inner{T\v}{\v}\) determines \(A\) and nothing about \(B\) . Contrast this with the complex case.

title: Theorem 11.2.6 (The Zero Test over the Complex Numbers)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be any operator. If \(\inner{T\v}{\v} = 0\) for every \(\v \in V\) , then \(T = 0\) .

title: Theorem 11.2.2 (Real Self-adjoint Operators Have an Eigenvalue)
content:
Let \(V 
e \{\0\}\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(
R\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint. Then: every root of \(p_T\) in \(
C\) is real, so \(p_T\) splits over \(
R\) ; \(T\) has an eigenvalue.

title: Theorem 11.2.4 (Self-adjointness Passes to Orthogonal Complements)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint and let \(U \subseteq V\) be a \(T\) -invariant subspace. Then: \(U^{\perp}\) is \(T\) -invariant; \(T|_U \in \cL(U)\) and \(T|_{U^{\perp}} \in \cL(U^{\perp})\) are self-adjoint, for the inner products inherited from \(V\) .

title: Theorem 11.2.3 (Distinct Eigenvalues Give Orthogonal Eigenvectors)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint, and let \(\u, \v \in V\) satisfy \(T\u = \lambda\u\) and \(T\v = \mu\v\) with \(\lambda \ne \mu\) . Then \(\inner{\u}{\v} = 0\) . Consequently \(E_\lambda(T) \perp E_\mu(T)\) for distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda, \mu\) .

title: Theorem 11.2.1 (Self-adjoint Operators Have Real Eigenvalues)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F = \nR\) or \(F = \nC\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint. Then every eigenvalue of \(T\) is real.

title: Theorem 11.2.5 (The Zero Test for Self-adjoint Operators)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F = \nR\) or \(F = \nC\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be self-adjoint . If \(\inner{T\v}{\v} = 0\) for every \(\v \in V\) , then \(T = 0\) .

title: Corollary 11.3.2 (Kernel, Image and an Orthogonal Splitting)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional inner product space \(V\) . Then: \(\ker T = \ker T^{*}\) ; \(\im T = \im T^{*}\) ; \(V = \ker T \oplus \im T\) , and the two summands are orthogonal to each other.

title: Corollary 11.3.4 (Eigenvectors for Distinct Eigenvalues Are Orthogonal)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal, let \(\lambda \neq \mu\) be eigenvalues of \(T\) , and let \(T\u = \lambda\u\) and \(T\v = \mu\v\) . Then \(\inner{\u}{\v} = 0\) . Hence \(E_{\lambda}(T) \perp E_{\mu}(T)\) whenever \(\lambda \neq \mu\) .

Decide which of the following matrices are normal, with the standard inner product on \(

C\) . \(\M =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . \(\N =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) .

content: State the definition of a normal operator, and state one equivalent condition phrased in terms of norms. True or false: every self-adjoint operator is normal, and every normal operator is self-adjoint. Justify both halves. Let \(T\) be normal with \(T\v = 3\v\) . What is \(T^{*}\v\) ? What if \(T\v = 3i\v\) ? Give a normal operator on \(\nR^2\) that is neither self-adjoint nor unitary. True or false: if \(S\) and \(T\) are normal then \(S + T\) is normal. Justify your answer. Explain in one sentence why a normal operator cannot be nilpotent unless it is zero.

title: Exercise (B2: The splitting of a singular normal operator)
content:
Let \(\C =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & -1 \ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(

R^3 = \ker T \oplus \im T\) with the two summands orthogonal, as @cor-normal-kernel (c) predicts.

title: Exercise (B3: Triangular and normal, by hand)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ 0 & d \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nC)\) . Compute the \((1,1)\) entries of \(\A^{*}\A\) and of \(\A\A^{*}\) . Hence prove that \(\A\) is normal if and only if \(b = 0\) , that is, if and only if \(\A\) is diagonal. Which upper triangular matrices in \(M_2(\nC)\) are unitary? Hint: for (a), you only need one entry of each product.

title: Exercise (C1: A normal operator with no proper invariant subspace)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space with \(V 
eq \{\0\}\) , and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal. Suppose the only \(T\) -invariant subspaces of \(V\) are \(\{\0\}\) and \(V\) . Show that \(\dim V = 1\) . Show that the conclusion fails over \(
R\) , by exhibiting a normal operator on \(
R^2\) whose only invariant subspaces are \(\{\0\}\) and \(
R^2\) . Where exactly does the argument of (a) use that the field is \(
C\) ? Hint: an eigenvector spans an invariant subspace.

title: Exercise (C2: Arithmetic of normal operators)
content: Let \(S, T \in \cL(V)\) be normal. Prove that \(T^{*}\) is normal and that \(cT\) is normal for every \(c \in F\) . Prove that \(p(T)\) is normal for every polynomial \(p \in F[x]\) . Give a concrete \(S\) and \(T\) , both normal, with \(ST\) not normal. (Part (b) shows that this cannot happen when \(S\) is a polynomial in \(T\) .)

title: Exercise (C3: Normality depends on the inner product)
content: Normality is a property of \(T\) together with an inner product, not of \(T\) alone. Work on \(V = \nR^2\) with the operator \(T\) whose standard matrix is \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . Verify that \(T\) is normal for the standard inner product. Now use \(\inner{\x}{\y}_{\G} = \y\tp\G\x\) with \(\G = \diag(1, 2)\) , which is an inner product on \(\nR^2\) . Using the rule \(\mtx{T^{*}}{\sE}{\sE} = \G^{-1}\A\tp\G\) in the standard basis \(\sE\) ( @exr-adjoints-c3 ), compute the matrix of the adjoint of \(T\) for this inner product. Show that \(T\) is not normal for \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\G}\) , and reconcile this with (a).

title: Proposition 11.3.6 (An Invariant Subspace of a Normal Operator Is Reducing)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional inner product space, and let \(U \subseteq V\) be \(T\) -invariant. Then \(U\) is \(T^{*}\) -invariant, \(U^{\perp}\) is \(T\) -invariant, and \(T|_U\) is a normal operator on \(U\) .

title: Theorem 11.3.1 (Characterizations of Normality)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . The following are equivalent. \(T\) is normal. \(
orm{T\v} = 
orm{T^{*}\v}\) for every \(\v \in V\) . \(\inner{T\u}{T\v} = \inner{T^{*}\u}{T^{*}\v}\) for all \(\u, \v \in V\) . Suppose in addition that \(F = 
C\) , and set \[ A = 	frac12(T + T^{*}), \qquad B = 	frac1{2i}(T - T^{*}), \] so that \(A\) and \(B\) are self-adjoint and \(T = A + iB\) . Then (a)–(c) are further equivalent to \(AB = BA\) .

title: Theorem 11.3.3 (An Eigenvector of a Normal Operator Is an Eigenvector of Its Adjoint)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal, let \(\lambda \in F\) and let \(\v \in V\) . Then \[ T\v = \lambda\v \quad \text{if and only if} \quad T^{*}\v = \conj{\lambda}\,\v . \] In particular \(E_{\lambda}(T) = E_{\conj{\lambda}}(T^{*})\) , and \(\lambda \in \spec(T)\) if and only if \(\conj{\lambda} \in \spec(T^{*})\) .

title: Theorem 11.3.5 (A Normal Operator Has No Hidden Kernel)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal. Then \(\ker T^{k} = \ker T\) for every integer \(k \ge 1\) . In particular, a normal nilpotent operator is the zero operator.

title: Corollary 11.4.5 (The Adjoint of a Normal Operator Is a Polynomial in It)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) . Then there is a polynomial \(p \in \nC[x]\) of degree less than \(k\) with \(T^{*} = p(T)\) .

title: Corollary 11.4.4 (The Spectrum Decides)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space. \(T\) is self-adjoint if and only if every eigenvalue of \(T\) is real. \(T\) is unitary if and only if every eigenvalue of \(T\) has modulus \(1\) . \(\inner{T\v}{\v}\) is a non-negative real number for every \(\v \in V\) if and only if every eigenvalue of \(T\) is a non-negative real.

title: Corollary 11.4.3 (Unitary Diagonalization)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) . Then \(\A\) is normal if and only if there exist a unitary \(\U \in \Unit(n)\) and a diagonal \(\D \in M_n(\nC)\) with \[ \A = \U\D\U^{*} . \] A matrix admitting such a factorization is called unitarily diagonalizable . The diagonal of \(\D\) is the list of eigenvalues of \(\A\) with multiplicity, in an order that may be prescribed in advance, and the columns of \(\U\) are a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

title: Example (Diagonalizable, and no orthonormal eigenbasis)
content: For \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) , find an invertible \(\P\) with \(\P^{-1}\A\P\) diagonal, and show that no orthogonal \(\Q\) makes \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) diagonal.

title: Example (Unitarily diagonalizing a Hermitian matrix)
content: Find a unitary \(\U\) and a diagonal \(\D\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U = \D\) , for \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \\ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix} . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content:
State the complex spectral theorem, including every hypothesis, and state its matrix form. What goes wrong with the proof if the field is \(
R\) ? Name the exact step. True or false: a matrix in \(M_n(
C)\) with \(n\) distinct eigenvalues is unitarily diagonalizable. Justify your answer. Let \(\A \in M_3(
C)\) be normal with \(\spec(\A) = \{2, 2, -1\}\) as a list with multiplicity. Is the unitary \(\U\) in \(\A = \U\D\U^{*}\) determined by \(\A\) and the order of \(\D\) ? What is determined? A normal operator \(T\) satisfies \(T^{*} = T^{3}\) . What can you say about its eigenvalues? Explain why @lem-triangular-normal-diagonal cannot be weakened to “a normal matrix with some of its below-diagonal entries zero is diagonal”.

title: Exercise (B1: Unitarily diagonalize)
content: For each matrix, find a unitary \(\U\) and a diagonal \(\D\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U = \D\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -i \\ i & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A = \tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ i & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A circulant, diagonalized)
content: Let \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}\) , so \(\omega^3 = 1\) and \(1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0\) , and let \[ \C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nC) . \] Verify that \(\C\) is normal. Show that \(\f_j = \tfrac1{\sqrt3}(1, \omega^{j}, \omega^{2j})\) is an eigenvector of \(\C\) for \(j = 0, 1, 2\) , and find the eigenvalue. Deduce a unitary \(\F\) with \(\F^{*}\C\F\) diagonal, and write down the diagonal explicitly.

title: Exercise (B3: Decide unitary diagonalizability)
content: Determine which of the following matrices are unitarily diagonalizable over \(\nC\) , and which are merely diagonalizable. Justify your answer. \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Operators of finite order)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, and suppose \(T^{k} = \id_V\) for some integer \(k \ge 1\) . Prove that every eigenvalue of \(T\) is a \(k\) -th root of unity. Deduce that \(T\) is unitary and unitarily diagonalizable. Show that the hypothesis “normal” cannot be dropped from (b) by exhibiting a \(T\) with \(T^{2} = \id_V\) that is not unitary.

title: Exercise (C2: Same spectrum, same multiplicities)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(\nC)\) be normal, and suppose they have the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities, that is, the same characteristic polynomial. Prove that there is a unitary \(\W\) with \(\B = \W\A\W^{*}\) (one says \(\A\) and \(\B\) are unitarily similar ). Give two matrices in \(M_2(\nC)\) with the same characteristic polynomial that are not unitarily similar, and say which hypothesis of (a) they violate. Deduce that two normal matrices are unitarily similar if and only if they are similar.

title: Exercise (C3: Normality cannot be dropped)
content:
@cor-normal-spectral-corollaries reads the class of a normal operator off its spectrum. This exercise shows that each part fails without that hypothesis. Give \(\A \in M_2(
C)\) with both eigenvalues real that is not Hermitian. Give \(\A \in M_2(
C)\) with both eigenvalues of modulus \(1\) that is not unitary. Over \(
R\) , give \(\A \in M_2(
R)\) with \(\inner{\A\x}{\x} \ge 0\) for every \(\x \in 
R^2\) whose eigenvalues are not non-negative reals. Why does no such example exist over \(
C\) ?

title: Lemma 11.4.1 (A Normal Triangular Matrix Is Diagonal)
content: Let \(\T = (t_{ij}) \in M_n(\nC)\) be upper triangular and normal. Then \(\T\) is diagonal.

title: Theorem 11.4.2 (Complex Spectral Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\nC\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . The following are equivalent. \(T\) is normal. \(V\) has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\) .

title: Corollary 11.5.2 (Orthogonal Diagonalization)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) . Then \(\A\) is symmetric if and only if there are an orthogonal \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) and a real diagonal \(\D\) with \[ \A = \Q\D\Q\tp . \] The diagonal of \(\D\) is the eigenvalue list of \(\A\) with multiplicity, in any prescribed order, and the columns of \(\Q\) are a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

title: Corollary 11.5.4 (Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) be symmetric, and let \((\q_1, \dots, \q_n)\) be an orthonormal basis of \(
R^n\) with \(\A\q_i = \lambda_i\q_i\) . Then \[ \A = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i\,\q_i\q_i	p , \] and each \(\q_i\q_i	p\) is the matrix of the orthogonal projection of \(
R^n\) onto the line \(\Span(\q_i)\) .

title: Example (Finding the axes of a conic)
content: Identify the curve \(3x^2 - 2xy + 3y^2 = 1\) in \(\nR^2\) , and find its axes and their half-lengths.

title: Example (A normal real operator with no eigenvector)
content: Let \(T \in \cL(\nR^2)\) be the quarter turn, with matrix \[ \R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \] in the standard basis. Show that \(T\) is normal, and that \(T\) has no eigenvalue and no eigenvector in \(\nR^2\) .

title: Example (Orthogonally diagonalizing a 3 by 3 matrix)
content: Orthogonally diagonalize \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \] and write it as a sum of rank-one orthogonal projections.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the real spectral theorem and its matrix form, with every hypothesis. Which two results from Section 2 does the induction use, and what does each one supply? True or false: a normal operator on a real inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Justify your answer. What are the possible diagonal blocks in the real normal form of a normal operator, and what does the condition \(b > 0\) rule out? Given a symmetric \(\A\) with orthonormal eigenvectors \(\q_1, \q_2\) and eigenvalues \(9\) and \(1\) , describe the curve \(\x\tp\A\x = 1\) . True or false: a real matrix with real eigenvalues is symmetric. Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: Orthogonally diagonalize)
content: For each symmetric matrix, find an orthogonal \(\Q\) and a diagonal \(\D\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q = \D\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Identify the conic)
content: Identify the curve \(5x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2 = 1\) : say what kind of conic it is, find its axes, and find their half-lengths.

title: Exercise (B3: A sum of rank-one projections)
content: Using your answer to @exr-spectral-theorem-real-b1 (b), write \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \] as \(\sum_i \lambda_i\q_i\q_i\tp\) , with the three matrices \(\q_i\q_i\tp\) written out, and verify the identity by adding them.

title: Exercise (C1: One eigenvalue only)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric with every eigenvalue equal to \(\lambda\) . Prove that \(\A = \lambda\I\) . Show that (a) fails without symmetry, by exhibiting a matrix in \(M_2(\nR)\) whose only eigenvalue is \(0\) and which is not \(\0\) . Deduce that a symmetric \(\A\) with \(\A^2 = \A\) is the matrix of an orthogonal projection.

title: Exercise (C2: Diagonalizing two matrices at once)
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric with \(\A\B = \B\A\) . Prove that each eigenspace \(E_{\lambda}(\A)\) is \(\B\) -invariant, and that the restriction of \(T_{\B}\) to it is self-adjoint. Prove that there is a single \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) and \(\Q\tp\B\Q\) both diagonal. Show that the conclusion fails without commutativity, using \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . Hint for (b): apply @thm-spectral-real inside each eigenspace of \(\A\) .

title: Exercise (C3: A rotation-scaling in normal form)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ -4 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) . Verify that \(\A\) is normal and not symmetric, and find its complex eigenvalues. Find an orthogonal \(\Q\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q = \vLambda(\lambda)\) for the eigenvalue \(\lambda\) with positive imaginary part. Explain why no orthogonal \(\Q\) makes \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) diagonal, and why this does not contradict @thm-spectral-complex .

title: Theorem 11.5.5 (Principal Axis Theorem)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nR)\) be symmetric, let \(q(\x) = \x\tp\A\x\) , and let \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q = \D = \diag(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n)\) , the columns \(\q_1, \dots, \q_n\) of \(\Q\) being an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Substituting \(\x = \Q\y\) , that is, taking \(y_i = \inner{\x}{\q_i}\) to be the coordinates of \(\x\) in that basis, \[ q(\x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i y_i^2 . \] In particular, for \(n = 2\) with \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0\) , the level set \(\{q = 1\}\) is an ellipse whose axes lie along \(\q_1\) and \(\q_2\) , with half-lengths \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_1}\) and \(1/\sqrt{\lambda_2}\) .

title: Theorem 11.5.3 (Real Normal Form of a Normal Operator)
content:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(
R\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) be normal. Then \(V\) has an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of \(T\) is block diagonal, \[ (c_1) \oplus \dots \oplus (c_p) \oplus \vLambda(\lambda_1) \oplus \dots \oplus \vLambda(\lambda_q), \] with \(c_1, \dots, c_p \in 
R\) and, for each \(j\) , \(\lambda_j = a_j + b_ji\) with \(b_j > 0\) and \[ \vLambda(\lambda_j) =  egin{pmatrix} a_j & -b_j \ b_j & a_j \end{pmatrix} \] the rotation-scaling block of @def-real-jordan-block . In matrix form: \(\A \in M_n(
R)\) is normal if and only if \(\A = \Q\B\Q	p\) with \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) and \(\B\) of the displayed shape.

title: Theorem 11.5.1 (Real Spectral Theorem)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(\nR\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . The following are equivalent. \(T\) is self-adjoint. \(V\) has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\) .

title: Corollary 11.6.2 (Orthogonal Matrices in Dimension Three)
page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \(\Q \in \Orth(3)\) . Then there are an orthonormal basis \((\u, \w_1, \w_2)\) of \(\nR^3\) and an angle \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) such that, in that basis, the matrix of \(T_{\Q}\) is \[ [1] \oplus \R_{\theta} \quad\text{if } \det\Q = 1, \qquad [-1] \oplus \R_{\theta} \quad\text{if } \det\Q = -1 . \] In particular every \(\Q \in \SO(3)\) fixes the line \(\Span(\u)\) pointwise and rotates the plane \(\Span(\u)^{\perp}\) by \(\theta\) .

page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix

For those in \(\SO(3)\) , find the axis and the angle; for those in \(\Orth(3)\) with determinant \(-1\) , give the canonical form \([-1] \oplus \R_{\theta}\) and say what the map is geometrically. \(\tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -8 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & -8 \\ 7 & 4 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} -7 & 4 & 4 \\ 4 & -1 & 8 \\ 4 & 8 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} 7 & -4 & -4 \\ -4 & 1 & -8 \\ -4 & -8 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\tfrac19\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -8 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & -8 \\ 7 & 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\) .

page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Write the matrix \(\M = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) as a Householder reflection \(\H_{\w}\) , and say which plane is its mirror. Following the proof of @thm-cartan-dieudonne-small , write \(\Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) as a product of Householder reflections, and check the count against \(\det\Q\) .
