Chapter 10 proved more: \(\Q\) equals \(\R_{\theta}\) or \(\M_{\theta}\) ( @thm-orthogonal-2x2 ). Explain exactly what information (a) loses, and why the canonical form must lose it. Deduce that any two reflections of \(\nR^2\) are orthogonally similar, and that \(\R_{\alpha}\) and \(\R_{\beta}\) are orthogonally similar if and only if \(\beta = \pm\alpha\) .

page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix

page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content:
Let \(\x, \y \in 
R^n\) with \(

title: Theorem 11.6.7 (Reflections Generate the Orthogonal Group)
page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) and \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) . Then \(\Q\) is a product of at most \(n\) Householder reflections. (The identity is the empty product, of zero reflections.)

title: Theorem 11.6.1 (Canonical Form of an Orthogonal Matrix)
page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix
content: Let \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) . Then there are integers \(p, q, m \ge 0\) with \(p + q + 2m = n\) , and angles \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_m\) with \(0 < \theta_j < \pi\) , and a matrix \(\P \in \Orth(n)\) , such that \[ \P\tp\Q\P = \I_p \oplus (-\I_q) \oplus \R_{\theta_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus \R_{\theta_m} . \] Moreover \(\det \Q = (-1)^q\) , and \(p\) , \(q\) and the multiset \(\{\theta_1, \dots, \theta_m\}\) are determined by \(\Q\) .

title: Theorem 11.6.4 (Rodrigues’ Rotation Formula)
page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix

title: Theorem 11.6.5 (Axis and Angle from the Matrix)
page: 11.6 The Shape of an Orthogonal Matrix

title: Corollary 11.7.3 (Commuting Symmetric Matrices)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let \(\cF \subseteq \cL(V)\) be a non-empty commuting family of self-adjoint operators. Then \(V\) has an orthonormal basis of common eigenvectors. Equivalently, if \(\A_1, \dots, \A_r \in M_n(\nR)\) are symmetric and pairwise commuting, there is \(\Q \in \Orth(n)\) with every \(\Q\tp\A_i\Q\) diagonal.

title: Corollary 11.7.2 (Commuting Normal Matrices)
content: Let \(\A_1, \dots, \A_r \in M_n(\nC)\) be normal and pairwise commuting. Then there is a unitary \(\U \in \Unit(n)\) such that \(\U^{*}\A_i\U\) is diagonal for every \(i\) . The same holds for an arbitrary commuting family of normal matrices in \(M_n(\nC)\) .

title: Example (Two Commuting Symmetric Matrices, Diagonalized Together)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nR) . \] Check that \(\A\B = \B\A\) and find \(\Q \in \Orth(3)\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) and \(\Q\tp\B\Q\) both diagonal.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State @thm-simultaneous-unitary-diagonalization , naming every hypothesis. Which result of Chapter 8 makes the eigenspaces of one member invariant under the others, and which hypothesis does it use? Why is the restriction of a normal operator to an invariant subspace again normal, and which earlier result says so? Why does the same fail for a subspace that is not invariant? True or false: two commuting diagonalizable matrices are simultaneously unitarily diagonalizable. Justify your answer. True or false: if \(S\) and \(T\) are normal then \(S + T\) is normal. Justify your answer. Which hypothesis of @thm-simultaneous-unitary-diagonalization is dropped in @thm-simultaneous-unitary-triangularization , and what is lost in the conclusion?

title: Exercise (B1: Diagonalize two at once)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nR) . \] Verify that \(\A\B = \B\A\) and that both are symmetric. Find \(\Q \in \Orth(3)\) with \(\Q\tp\A\Q\) and \(\Q\tp\B\Q\) both diagonal, and write down the two diagonal matrices. Explain why \(\A\) on its own does not determine \(\Q\) up to permuting and rescaling columns, but the pair does.

title: Exercise (B2: Check the two warnings)
content: For \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\) , find an invertible \(\P\) with \(\P^{-1}\A\P\) and \(\P^{-1}\B\P\) diagonal, and show that no unitary \(\P\) does this. For \(\X = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\Z = \diag(1,-1)\) , write down an orthogonal \(\Q_1\) diagonalizing \(\X\) and an orthogonal \(\Q_2\) diagonalizing \(\Z\) , and prove that no single invertible matrix diagonalizes both.

title: Exercise (B3: Triangularize two at once)
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) in \(M_2(\nC)\) . Verify that \(\A\B = \B\A\) . Determine whether \(\A\) and \(\B\) are simultaneously diagonalizable, and justify your answer. Exhibit a unitary \(\U\) with \(\U^{*}\A\U\) and \(\U^{*}\B\U\) both upper triangular, as @thm-simultaneous-unitary-triangularization promises.

title: Exercise (C1: A special case of a theorem of Fuglede)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(S, T \in \cL(V)\) be both normal , with \(ST = TS\) . Prove that \(ST^{*} = T^{*}S\) and \(S^{*}T = TS^{*}\) . Deduce that \(S + T^{*}\) and \(ST^{*}\) are normal. Give an example of two commuting operators, not both normal, for which the conclusion of (a) fails as stated for the pair — that is, exhibit commuting \(S, T\) with \(ST^{*} \neq T^{*}S\) . Note on the hypotheses: a theorem of Fuglede says that in (a) the operator \(S\) need not be assumed normal — it is enough that \(T\) be normal and that \(S\) commute with \(T\) . That stronger statement is true and is not proved in this book; (a) is only the case in which both are normal, and its proof uses the normality of \(S\) in an essential way.

title: Exercise (C2: A commuting family of orthogonal projections)
content:
Let \(V 
eq \{\0\}\) be a finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F = 
R\) or \(
C\) , and let \(P_1, \dots, P_r \in \cL(V)\) be the orthogonal projections onto subspaces \(U_1, \dots, U_r\) , pairwise commuting. Prove that there is an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) such that every vector of \(\sB\) lies in \(U_i\) or in \(U_i^{\perp}\) , for every \(i\) . Deduce that \(P_iP_j\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(U_i \cap U_j\) . Prove that \(P_i + P_j\) is an orthogonal projection if and only if \(U_i \perp U_j\) , and identify the subspace in that case. Hint for (a): the eigenvalues of an idempotent operator.

title: Theorem 11.7.4 (Sums and Products of Commuting Normal Operators)
content: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(S, T \in \cL(V)\) be normal with \(ST = TS\) . Then \(S + T\) and \(ST\) are normal.

title: Theorem 11.7.1 (One Orthonormal Eigenbasis for a Commuting Family)
content: Let \(V \neq \{\0\}\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(\cF \subseteq \cL(V)\) be a non-empty commuting family of normal operators. Then \(V\) has an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) each of whose vectors is an eigenvector of every \(T \in \cF\) ; equivalently, \([T]_{\sB}\) is diagonal for every \(T \in \cF\) . Conversely, if some orthonormal basis \(\sB\) makes every \([T]_{\sB}\) diagonal, then \(\cF\) is commuting and every member of \(\cF\) is normal.

title: Theorem 11.7.5 (Simultaneous Unitary Triangularization)
content: Let \(V \neq \{\0\}\) be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let \(\cF \subseteq \cL(V)\) be a non-empty commuting family. Then there is an orthonormal basis \(\sB\) of \(V\) such that \([T]_{\sB}\) is upper triangular for every \(T \in \cF\) . In particular, if \(\A_1, \dots, \A_r \in M_n(\nC)\) commute pairwise, there is \(\U \in \Unit(n)\) with every \(\U^{*}\A_i\U\) upper triangular.

title: Definition 11.8.2 (Function of an Operator)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) and spectral resolution \(T = \sum_i\lambda_iP_i\) . For any function \(f \colon \spec(T) \to F\) , define \[ f(T) \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{k}f(\lambda_i)\,P_i \ \in \cL(V) . \]

title: Definition 11.8.1 (Spectral Resolution)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , let \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) be the distinct eigenvalues of \(T\) , and write \(E_i = E_{\lambda_i}(T)\) for the corresponding eigenspaces. Let \[ P_i \coloneqq P_{E_i} \in \cL(V) \] be the orthogonal projection onto \(E_i\) ( @def-orthogonal-projection ). The identity \[ T = \lambda_1P_1 + \lambda_2P_2 + \dots + \lambda_kP_k \] is the spectral resolution of \(T\) , and the family \((P_1, \dots, P_k)\) is the resolution of the identity attached to \(T\) .

title: Example (A Square Root, and Three Impostors)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) . Find its spectral resolution, compute \(\sqrt{\A}\) and \(\A^{m}\) , and find a symmetric square root of \(\A\) other than \(\sqrt{\A}\) .

title: Example (Two Projections That Are Not Orthogonal)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) , which is diagonalizable with eigenvalues \(1\) and \(2\) . Compute the projections \(\vpi_1, \vpi_2\) of @thm-primary-decomposition for \(\A\) , verify that \(\A = \vpi_1 + 2\vpi_2\) , and decide whether they are orthogonal projections.

title: Example (A Symmetric 3 \times 3 Matrix)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nR)\) . Find the spectral resolution of \(\A\) .

content: Let \(\H = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . Compute \(e^{\,i\theta\H}\) for \(\theta \in \nR\) . Then find a Hermitian \(\K\) with \(e^{i\K} = \Q\) , where \(\Q = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) .

content:
Find the spectral resolution of each of the following matrices, and check in each case that the projections are self-adjoint, idempotent, mutually annihilating and sum to \(\I\) . \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \ 1 + i & 3 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
C)\) . \(\S =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 3 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(
R)\) . \(\U = 	frac{1}{\sqrt2} egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
C)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Computing through the resolution)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(\C = \begin{pmatrix} 13 & 12 \\ 12 & 13 \end{pmatrix} \in M_2(\nR)\) . Find the spectral resolution of \(\C\) . Hence compute \(\sqrt{\C}\) , and verify by squaring. Hence give a closed formula for \(\C^{m}\) and write down \(\C^{100}\) . Hence compute \(e^{\C}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Is it a spectral resolution?)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content:
Determine which of the following displays the spectral resolution of the operator \(T_{\A}\) on the stated space. Justify your answer; for those that do not, name the condition of @thm-spectral-resolution-unique that fails and say what the correct resolution is. On \(
R^2\) : \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\) , with \(\mu_1 = 2\) , \(\Q_1 =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) , \(\mu_2 = -1\) , \(\Q_2 =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) . On \(
R^2\) : \(\A = 3\I\) , with \(\mu_1 = \mu_2 = 3\) , \(\Q_1 = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) , \(\Q_2 = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) . On \(
R^2\) : \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) , with \(\mu_1 = 3\) , \(\Q_1 = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) , \(\mu_2 = 1\) , \(\Q_2 = 	frac12 egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The projections are polynomials in the operator)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k \in F\) and resolution of the identity \((P_1, \dots, P_k)\) . Prove that \(P_i = \ell_i(T)\) , where \(\ell_i \in F[x]\) is the \(i\) -th Lagrange basis polynomial for the nodes \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) . Deduce that for every \(f \colon \spec(T) \to F\) there is a polynomial \(p\) of degree less than \(k\) with \(f(T) = p(T)\) . Deduce that every operator commuting with \(T\) commutes with each \(P_i\) , re-proving @thm-functional-calculus-properties (e) by a different route. Hint for (a): @def-lagrange-basis produces a polynomial taking prescribed values at prescribed nodes.

title: Exercise (C2: When the projections have rank one)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , with \(\dim V = n\) and resolution of the identity \((P_1, \dots, P_k)\) . Prove that \(\rank P_i = \dim E_{\lambda_i}(T)\) and that \(\sum_i\rank P_i = n\) . Deduce that every \(P_i\) has rank \(1\) if and only if \(T\) has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues. Suppose every \(P_i\) has rank \(1\) . Prove that every \(S \in \cL(V)\) commuting with \(T\) is a polynomial in \(T\) .

title: Exercise (C3: What the functional calculus forgets)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) , and let \(f, g \colon \spec(T) \to F\) . Prove that \(f(T) = 0\) if and only if \(f(\lambda_i) = 0\) for every \(i\) . Deduce that \(f(T) = g(T)\) if and only if \(f = g\) . Deduce that \(\{ p(T) : p \in F[x] \} = \Span(P_1, \dots, P_k)\) , a subspace of \(\cL(V)\) of dimension exactly \(k\) . Deduce that \(m_T = (x - \lambda_1)(x - \lambda_2)\cdots(x - \lambda_k)\) , so that the minimal polynomial of an operator satisfying \((\ast)\) has no repeated root.

title: Theorem 11.8.3 (Properties of the Functional Calculus)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) and resolution of the identity \((P_1, \dots, P_k)\) . Let \(f, g \colon \spec(T) \to F\) and \(c \in F\) , with \(f + g\) , \(cf\) and \(fg\) taken pointwise. (Compatibility) For every \(p \in F[x]\) , the operator \(p(T)\) of @def-polynomial-of-operator equals \(\sum_ip(\lambda_i)P_i\) ; that is, it agrees with @def-function-of-normal-operator applied to the restriction of \(p\) to \(\spec(T)\) . (Algebra homomorphism) \((f + g)(T) = f(T) + g(T)\) , \((cf)(T) = c\,f(T)\) , \((fg)(T) = f(T)g(T) = g(T)f(T)\) , and \(1(T) = \id_V\) . (Adjoints) \(f(T)^{*} = \conj{f}(T)\) , where \(\conj{f}(\lambda) = \conj{f(\lambda)}\) . In particular \(f(T)\) is self-adjoint when \(f\) is real-valued, and unitary when \(\lvert f(\lambda_i) \rvert = 1\) for every \(i\) . (Spectral mapping) \(f(T)\) satisfies \((\ast)\) , with the same orthonormal eigenbasis as \(T\) , and \(\spec(f(T)) = f(\spec(T))\) . (Commutation) If \(S \in \cL(V)\) commutes with \(T\) , then \(S\) commutes with every \(P_i\) and hence with \(f(T)\) . In particular \(T\) and \(f(T)\) commute.

title: Theorem 11.8.4 (The Square Root of a Non-negative Normal Operator)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(V\) be a non-zero finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) with \(\spec(T) \subseteq [0, \infty)\) . Then there is exactly one operator \(S \in \cL(V)\) such that \(S\) satisfies \((\ast)\) ; \(\spec(S) \subseteq [0, \infty)\) ; \(S^2 = T\) . It is \(S = \sum_i\sqrt{\lambda_i}\,P_i\) , where \(T = \sum_i\lambda_iP_i\) is the spectral resolution of \(T\) . This \(S\) is self-adjoint, and it commutes with every operator that commutes with \(T\) .

title: Theorem 11.8.1 (The Spectral Resolution and Its Projections)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(T \in \cL(V)\) satisfy \((\ast)\) , with distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k\) , eigenspaces \(E_i = E_{\lambda_i}(T)\) and \(P_i = P_{E_i}\) . Then: \(V = E_1 \oplus \dots \oplus E_k\) , and \(E_i \perp E_j\) whenever \(i \ne j\) ; \(P_i^{*} = P_i\) and \(P_i^2 = P_i\) for every \(i\) , and \(P_iP_j = 0\) whenever \(i \ne j\) ; \(P_1 + \dots + P_k = \id_V\) ; \(T = \lambda_1P_1 + \dots + \lambda_kP_k\) ; \(TP_i = P_iT = \lambda_iP_i\) for every \(i\) .

title: Theorem 11.8.2 (Uniqueness of the Spectral Resolution)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(V\) be a non-zero finite-dimensional inner product space over \(F\) and let \(T \in \cL(V)\) . Suppose \[ T = \mu_1Q_1 + \mu_2Q_2 + \dots + \mu_mQ_m , \] where \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_m \in F\) are distinct and \(Q_1, \dots, Q_m \in \cL(V)\) are non-zero operators satisfying \(Q_i^{*} = Q_i\) and \(Q_i^2 = Q_i\) for every \(i\) ; \(Q_iQ_j = 0\) whenever \(i \ne j\) ; \(Q_1 + \dots + Q_m = \id_V\) . Then \(T\) satisfies \((\ast)\) , \(\spec(T) = \{\mu_1, \dots, \mu_m\}\) , and \(Q_i\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(E_{\mu_i}(T)\) for every \(i\) . In particular \(m\) is the number of distinct eigenvalues of \(T\) , and the given decomposition is the spectral resolution of \(T\) .

title: Theorem 11.8.5 (Unitary Matrices Are Exponentials of Hermitian Matrices)
page: 11.8 Spectral Resolutions and Functions of a Normal Operator
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) . If \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) is normal with spectral resolution \(\A = \sum_{i}\lambda_i\P_i\) , then \(e^{\A} = \sum_{i}e^{\lambda_i}\P_i\) . If \(\H \in M_n(\nC)\) is Hermitian, then \(e^{i\H} \in \Unit(n)\) , and \(\det e^{i\H} = e^{\,i\tr\H}\) . Conversely, every \(\U \in \Unit(n)\) equals \(e^{i\H}\) for some Hermitian \(\H\) , which may be chosen with \(\spec(\H) \subseteq [0, 2\pi)\) .

title: Corollary 11.9.5 (Circulants Form a Commutative Algebra)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content:
Let \(\cC_n \subseteq M_n(
C)\) be the set of circulants of size \(n\) . Then: \(\cC_n\) is a subspace of \(M_n(
C)\) of dimension \(n\) , with basis \(\I, \S, \dots, \S^{n-1}\) ; \(\cC_n\) is closed under products, and any two of its members commute; \(\A \in \cC_n\) if and only if \(\F^{*}\A\F\) is diagonal; a circulant \(\C\) is invertible if and only if \(p_{\c}(\omega^{j}) 
eq 0\) for every \(j\) , and then \(\C^{-1}\) is again a circulant.

title: Definition 11.9.1 (Circulant matrix)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content:
Let \(n \ge 1\) and let \(\c = (c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{n-1}) \in 
C^n\) . The circulant with first row \(\c\) is the matrix \(\C \in M_n(
C)\) whose entries are \[ (\C)_{jk} = c_{k-j} \qquad (0 \le j, k \le n-1), \] where the subscript \(k - j\) is read modulo \(n\) . The polynomial \[ p_{\c}(x) = c_0 + c_1x + c_2x^2 + \dots + c_{n-1}x^{n-1} \in 
C[x] \] is called the symbol of \(\C\) .

title: Example (The running example, diagonalized)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Find the eigenvalues and the determinant of the circulant \(\C\) with first row \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) , and write down \(\F^{*}\C\F\) .

title: Example (A circulant system)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Solve \(\C\x = \b\) for the circulant \(\C\) with first row \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) and \(\b = (1, 1, -1, -1)\) .

title: Example (Convolution in size four)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\c = (1, 2, 3, 4)\) and \(\d = (1, 1, 0, 0)\) . Compute \(\c \ast \d\) , and verify @thm-convolution-theorem (b) at all four roots of unity.

title: Example (The Fourier matrix of size four)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Write out \(\F\) for \(n = 4\) , and check one orthogonality relation by hand.

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Define the circulant with first row \(\c = (c_0, \dots, c_{n-1})\) , and write down its symbol. State the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the cyclic shift \(\S\) on \(\nC^n\) . Give the eigenvalues of the circulant with first row \(\c\) , and say how many multiplications are needed to compute all of them from \(\c\) by direct evaluation. Determine whether the following are true, with a reason. (i) Every Toeplitz matrix is a circulant. (ii) Every circulant is normal. (iii) The Fourier matrix \(\F\) is Hermitian. Explain in one sentence why two circulants of the same size commute, without computing any entries.

title: Exercise (B1: Eigenvalues of small circulants)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: For each vector \(\c\) , write down the symbol, compute all eigenvalues of the circulant with first row \(\c\) , and give its determinant. \(\c = (1, 1, 1)\) , \(n = 3\) . \(\c = (0, 1, 0, 0)\) , \(n = 4\) . \(\c = (2, -1, 0, -1)\) , \(n = 4\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Solve a circulant system by transforming)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\C\) be the \(4 \times 4\) circulant with first row \((3, 1, 0, 1)\) and let \(\b = (1, 0, 0, 0)\) . Compute the eigenvalues of \(\C\) , and solve \(\C\x = \b\) by transforming, dividing and transforming back. Check your answer against the first two rows of \(\C\) .

title: Exercise (B3: The convolution theorem in an example)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\c = (1, 0, 2, 0)\) and \(\d = (0, 1, 0, 3)\) in \(\nC^4\) . Compute \(\c \ast \d\) . Verify \(p_{\c\ast\d}(\omega^{j}) = p_{\c}(\omega^{j})p_{\d}(\omega^{j})\) for \(j = 0, 1, 2, 3\) . Hence write down the first row of the product of the two circulants, without multiplying any matrices.

title: Exercise (C1: What commutes with the shift)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) satisfy \(\A\S = \S\A\) . Prove that \(\A\) is a circulant. Hint: consider the eigenspaces of \(\S\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Determinant and invertibility)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\C\) be the circulant with first row \(\c \in \nC^n\) and symbol \(p_{\c}\) . Prove that \(\det\C = \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} p_{\c}(\omega^{j})\) , and use it to compute the determinant of the \(n \times n\) all-ones matrix for every \(n \ge 2\) . Prove that \(\C\) is invertible if and only if \(p_{\c}\) and \(x^n - 1\) are coprime in \(\nC[x]\) . Give an example of a \(4 \times 4\) circulant with integer entries, none of them \(0\) , whose determinant is \(0\) .

title: Exercise (C3: The real orthogonal form of a real circulant)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\C \in M_4(\nR)\) be the circulant with first row \((1, 2, 3, 4)\) , with eigenvalues \(10, -2-2i, -2, -2+2i\) as in @exm-circulant-4x4-eigenvalues . Put \[ \g \coloneqq \sqrt2\,\operatorname{Re}\f_1, \qquad \h \coloneqq \sqrt2\,\operatorname{Im}\f_1, \] the real and imaginary parts taken entrywise. Write \(\g\) and \(\h\) out, and show that \((\f_0, \f_2, \g, \h)\) is an orthonormal basis of \(\nR^4\) . Writing \(a + bi \coloneqq -2 + 2i\) , prove that \(\C\g = a\g + b\h\) and \(\C\h = -b\g + a\h\) . Hence write down the matrix of \(\C\) in the ordered basis of (a), and identify it as an instance of @thm-real-normal-form . Hint for (b): apply \(\C\) to \(\f_3 = (\g - i\h)/\sqrt2\) and compare real and imaginary parts.

title: Theorem 11.9.4 (Circulant Diagonalization)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\C \in M_n(\nC)\) be the circulant with first row \(\c\) and symbol \(p_{\c}\) . Then every Fourier vector is an eigenvector of \(\C\) , \[ \C\f_j = p_{\c}(\omega^{j})\,\f_j \qquad (j = 0, 1, \dots, n-1), \] and consequently \[ \F^{*}\C\F = \diag\bigl(p_{\c}(1),\ p_{\c}(\omega),\ \dots,\ p_{\c}(\omega^{n-1})\bigr) . \] The same unitary \(\F\) works for every circulant of size \(n\) , and \(\det\C = \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} p_{\c}(\omega^{j})\) .

title: Theorem 11.9.1 (Circulants Are Exactly the Polynomials in the Shift)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\c \in \nC^n\) and let \(\C\) be the circulant with first row \(\c\) , with symbol \(p_{\c}\) . Then: \(\C = p_{\c}(\S)\) ; conversely, \(q(\S)\) is a circulant for every \(q \in \nC[x]\) . \(\C^{*}\) is the circulant with first row \((\conj{c_0}, \conj{c_{n-1}}, \conj{c_{n-2}}, \dots, \conj{c_1})\) . \(\C\) is normal, and any two circulants of the same size commute.

title: Theorem 11.9.6 (Convolution Theorem)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: Let \(\c, \d \in \nC^n\) with circulants \(\C, \C'\) and symbols \(p_{\c}, p_{\d}\) . Then: \(\C\C'\) is the circulant with first row \(\c \ast \d\) ; for every \(j\) , \(\; p_{\c \ast \d}(\omega^{j}) = p_{\c}(\omega^{j})\,p_{\d}(\omega^{j})\) . In words: convolving the first rows corresponds to multiplying the eigenvalue lists entry by entry.

title: Theorem 11.9.3 (The Fourier Matrix Is Unitary)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: The list \((\f_0, \f_1, \dots, \f_{n-1})\) is an orthonormal basis of \(\nC^n\) . Equivalently, the Fourier matrix \[ \F \coloneqq \frac{1}{\sqrt n} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ 1 & \omega & \cdots & \omega^{n-1} \\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 1 & \omega^{n-1} & \cdots & \omega^{(n-1)^2} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad (\F)_{mj} = \frac{\omega^{mj}}{\sqrt n}, \] whose \(j\) -th column is \(\f_j\) , is unitary: \(\F^{*}\F = \F\F^{*} = \I\) .

title: Theorem 11.9.2 (Eigenvectors of the Cyclic Shift)
page: 11.9 Circulants and the Discrete Fourier Transform
content: For \(j = 0, 1, \dots, n-1\) let \[ \f_j \coloneqq \tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\bigl(1,\ \omega^{j},\ \omega^{2j},\ \dots,\ \omega^{(n-1)j}\bigr) \in \nC^n, \] that is, \((\f_j)_m = \omega^{jm}/\sqrt n\) . Then \(\S\f_j = \omega^{j}\f_j\) . Consequently \(\S\) is a unitary matrix with the \(n\) distinct eigenvalues \(1, \omega, \dots, \omega^{n-1}\) , and each eigenspace \(E_{\omega^j}(\S)\) is the line \(\Span(\f_j)\) .

title: Corollary 11.10.3 (Block Diagonalization by a Sylvester Solution)
content: Let \(\A \in M_m(F)\) , \(\B \in M_n(F)\) and \(\C \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) , and put \[ \M = \begin{pmatrix} \A & \C \\ \0 & \B \end{pmatrix} \in M_{m+n}(F). \] If \(\X \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) satisfies \(\A\X - \X\B = -\C\) , then with \(\P = \begin{pmatrix} \I_m & \X \\ \0 & \I_n \end{pmatrix}\) we have \(\P^{-1}\M\P = \A \oplus \B\) . In particular \(\M \sim \A \oplus \B\) . Conversely, if \(\P^{-1}\M\P = \A \oplus \B\) for some \(\X \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and the matrix \(\P\) built from it as in (a), then that \(\X\) satisfies \(\A\X - \X\B = -\C\) . If \(F = \nC\) and \(\spec(\A) \cap \spec(\B) = \varnothing\) , then a solution \(\X\) exists, and it is unique; so \(\M \sim \A \oplus \B\) for every corner \(\C\) .

title: Corollary 11.10.4 (Disjoint Spectra Split the Commutant)
content:
Let \(\A_1 \in M_{n_1}(
C), \dots, \A_r \in M_{n_r}(
C)\) have pairwise disjoint spectra, and put \(\D = \A_1 \oplus \dots \oplus \A_r \in M_N(
C)\) , \(N = n_1 + \dots + n_r\) . Let \(\Z \in M_N(
C)\) satisfy \(\D\Z = \Z\D\) , and partition \(\Z\) into blocks \(\Z_{pq} \in M_{n_p 	imes n_q}(
C)\) for the partition \(N = n_1 + \dots + n_r\) . Then \[ \Z_{pq} = \0 \quad 	ext{for all } p 
eq q, \] so \(\Z = \Z_{11} \oplus \dots \oplus \Z_{rr}\) is block diagonal , and each diagonal block satisfies \(\A_p\Z_{pp} = \Z_{pp}\A_p\) .

title: Definition 11.10.2 (Lyapunov equation)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) and \(\Q \in M_n(
C)\) . The Lyapunov equation for the pair \((\A, \Q)\) is \[ \A\X + \X\A^{*} = -\Q , \] with unknown \(\X \in M_n(
C)\) . Call \(\A\) stable when every \(\lambda \in \spec(\A)\) has \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda < 0\) .

title: Definition 11.10.1 (Sylvester operator)
content: Let \(\A \in M_m(F)\) and \(\B \in M_n(F)\) . The Sylvester operator of the pair \((\A, \B)\) is \[ \cS_{\A,\B} \colon M_{m \times n}(F) \to M_{m \times n}(F), \qquad \cS_{\A,\B}(\X) = \A\X - \X\B . \] The equation \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) , for a given \(\C \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) , is the Sylvester equation .

title: Example (Clearing a Corner)
content: Block-diagonalize \[ \M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_4(\nQ) . \]

title: Example (Solving a Sylvester Equation)
content: Over \(\nC\) , solve \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) for \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \C = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define the Sylvester operator of a pair \((\A, \B)\) with \(\A \in M_m(F)\) , \(\B \in M_n(F)\) , and state the dimension of the space it acts on. Write down the matrix of the Sylvester operator with respect to the vectorization \(\vecop\) , and say which Chapter 7 result produces it. State the criterion for \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) to have exactly one solution for every \(\C\) , over \(\nC\) . True or false: if \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) has at least one solution for every \(\C\) , then that solution is unique. Justify your answer. True or false: if \(\spec(\A) \cap \spec(\B) = \varnothing\) , then \(\A\X + \X\B = \C\) has exactly one solution for every \(\C\) . Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: A Sylvester equation by vectorization)
content: Over \(\nQ\) , let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \B = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \C = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}. \] Compute \(\spec(\A)\) and \(\spec(\B)\) , and decide whether \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) has exactly one solution. Write down \(\K = \I_2 \otimes \A - \B\tp \otimes \I_2\) , and check that its diagonal entries are the four differences \(\lambda_i - \mu_j\) . Solve the equation.

title: Exercise (B2: Block-diagonalizing a 3 × 3 matrix)
content: Let \[ \M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \in M_3(\nQ) . \] Partition \(\M\) as \(3 = 2 + 1\) , name the blocks \(\A\) , \(\B\) , \(\C\) , and explain why @cor-block-diagonalization applies. Solve the corresponding Sylvester equation. Write down \(\P\) and verify that \(\P^{-1}\M\P = \A \oplus \B\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Which equations are uniquely solvable?)
content:
Determine, for each of the following, whether the stated equation has exactly one solution \(\X \in M_2(
C)\) for every right-hand side \(\C \in M_2(
C)\) . Justify your answer. \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) with \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) , \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) with \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) , \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A\X + \X\B = \C\) with \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) , \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} -1 & 5 \ 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) with \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) , \(\B =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) with \(\A \in M_2(
C)\) nilpotent and \(\B \in M_2(
C)\) invertible.

title: Exercise (C1: Eigenvectors of the Sylvester operator)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_m(
C)\) and \(\B \in M_n(
C)\) , and let \(\cS = \cS_{\A,\B}\) . Suppose \(\A\x = \lambda\x\) with \(\x \in 
C^m\) non-zero, and suppose \(\y \in 
C^n\) is a left eigenvector of \(\B\) for \(\mu\) , so that \(\y	p\B = \mu\y	p\) ( @def-left-eigenvector ). Prove that \(\x\y	p 
eq \0\) and that \(\cS(\x\y	p) = (\lambda - \mu)\,\x\y	p\) . Deduce that every difference \(\lambda - \mu\) with \(\lambda \in \spec(\A)\) and \(\mu \in \spec(\B)\) is an eigenvalue of \(\cS\) . Hence give a second proof that \(\cS\) is not invertible when \(\A\) and \(\B\) have a common eigenvalue, one that uses no Kronecker products.

title: Exercise (C2: The kernel when the spectra meet)
content: Let \(\A \in M_m(\nC)\) and \(\B \in M_n(\nC)\) have eigenvalue lists \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m\) and \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n\) with algebraic multiplicity, and let \(d = \#\{(i, j) : \lambda_i = \mu_j\}\) . Prove that \(\dim\ker\cS_{\A,\B} \ge 1\) if and only if \(d \ge 1\) . Prove that \(\dim\ker\cS_{\A,\B} \le d\) . Show that the inequality in (b) can be strict, by computing \(\ker\cS_{\A,\B}\) for \(\A = \B = \J_2(0)\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Only the scalars commute with everything)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(n \ge 2\) , and let \(\E_{ij} \in M_n(F)\) be the matrix unit with \(1\) in position \((i, j)\) and \(0\) elsewhere. Suppose \(\A \in M_n(F)\) satisfies \(\A\E_{ij} = \E_{ij}\A\) for all \(i \neq j\) . Prove that \(\A = c\I_n\) for some \(c \in F\) . Deduce that the only matrices commuting with every \(\X \in M_n(F)\) are the scalar matrices, that is, \(\ker\cS_{\A,\A} = M_n(F)\) forces \(\A\) scalar. Deduce that the only matrices commuting with every invertible matrix are again the scalar matrices. Hint for (c): \(\I_n + \E_{ij}\) is invertible when \(i \neq j\) .

title: Lemma 11.10.1 (The Eigenvalues of a Kronecker Sum)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_m(
C)\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m\) and let \(\B \in M_n(
C)\) with eigenvalues \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n\) , each list repeated according to algebraic multiplicity. Then the \(mn\) eigenvalues of \[ \K = \I_n \otimes \A - \B	p \otimes \I_m \in M_{mn}(
C), \] listed with algebraic multiplicity, are the \(mn\) differences \(\lambda_i - \mu_j\) \((1 \le i \le m,\ 1 \le j \le n)\) .

title: Theorem 11.10.2 (Sylvester’s Theorem)
content:
Let \(\A \in M_m(
C)\) and \(\B \in M_n(
C)\) . The following are equivalent. \(\spec(\A) \cap \spec(\B) = \varnothing\) : the two matrices have no common eigenvalue . The Sylvester operator \(\cS_{\A,\B} \colon \X \mapsto \A\X - \X\B\) is invertible on \(M_{m 	imes n}(
C)\) . For every \(\C \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C)\) , the equation \(\A\X - \X\B = \C\) has exactly one solution \(\X\) . The only \(\X \in M_{m 	imes n}(
C)\) with \(\A\X = \X\B\) is \(\X = \0\) .

title: Definition 11.11.1 (Departure from Normality)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , listed with algebraic multiplicity. The departure from normality of \(\A\) is the non-negative real number \(\Delta(\A)\) defined by \[ \Delta(\A)^2 \coloneqq \norm{\A}_F^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert\lambda_i\rvert^2 . \]

title: Example (The defect of a Jordan block)
content: Compute \(\Delta(\J_k(\lambda))\) for the \(k \times k\) Jordan block with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) .

title: Example (A perturbation that moves the eigenvalues a thousand times as far)
content: Fix a real number \(M > 0\) and a real \(\varepsilon\) with \(0 < \varepsilon < M\) . Compare the effect of adding \(\varepsilon\) to the lower-left entry of each of \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & M \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \N = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & M \\ -M & 1 \end{pmatrix} . \] Compute the defects of \(\A\) and \(\N\) , the eigenvalues of both perturbed matrices exactly, and the distance each eigenvalue travels.

title: Example (Both sides of Schur’s inequality)
content: Verify @thm-schur-inequality for \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \] and locate the surplus inside an explicit Schur factorization ( @cor-schur-matrix ).

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define the Frobenius norm of a matrix, and give the expression for \(\norm{\A}_F^2\) as a trace. State @thm-schur-inequality , including the equality case and how the eigenvalues are counted. Define \(\Delta(\A)\) , and say why the definition needs @thm-schur-inequality before it can be made. True or false: \(\Delta(\A)\) equals the Frobenius distance from \(\A\) to the nearest normal matrix. Justify your answer. True or false: if \(\A\) and \(\B\) are similar then \(\Delta(\A) = \Delta(\B)\) . Justify your answer. Name the two facts about the Frobenius norm and about triangular matrices that the proof of @thm-schur-inequality rests on.

title: Exercise (B1: Computing the defect)
content: For each matrix below, compute \(\norm{\A}_F^2\) , the eigenvalue list, and \(\Delta(\A)\) . State in each case whether the matrix is normal, and say how you know without multiplying \(\A\) by \(\A^{*}\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\) \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) \(\J_3(2)\) \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\)

title: Exercise (B2: Verifying Schur’s inequality)
content: Let \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} . \] Compute both sides of @thm-schur-inequality for \(\A\) and verify the inequality. Hence determine whether \(\A\) is normal, without computing \(\A^{*}\A\) or \(\A\A^{*}\) . Write down a normal matrix \(\N\) with \(\norm{\A - \N}_F = \Delta(\A)\) , and verify the equality.

title: Exercise (C1: Unitary similarity preserves the defect, ordinary similarity does not)
content:
Prove that \(\Delta(\U^{*}\A\U) = \Delta(\A)\) for every \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) and every unitary \(\U\) . Give \(\A, \B \in M_2(
C)\) that are similar with \(\Delta(\A) 
eq \Delta(\B)\) , exhibiting an explicit \(\P\) with \(\P^{-1}\A\P = \B\) . Deduce that two similar matrices with different defects cannot be unitarily similar, and use this to show that \( egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\diag(1, 2)\) are not unitarily similar.

title: Exercise (C2: Equality plus a single eigenvalue forces a scalar)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) satisfy \(\norm{\A}_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lvert\lambda_i\rvert^2\) , and suppose \(\A\) has only one distinct eigenvalue \(\lambda\) , so that \(p_{\A} = (x - \lambda)^n\) . Prove that \(\A = \lambda\I\) . Deduce that a normal matrix whose characteristic polynomial is \(x^n\) is the zero matrix. Show that the hypothesis of equality cannot be dropped, by computing \(\Delta\) for a matrix with \(p_{\A} = (x - \lambda)^n\) that is not \(\lambda\I\) .

content:
For \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) write \([\A, \A^{*}] = \A\A^{*} - \A^{*}\A\) . Prove that \(

orm{[\T, \T^{*}]}_F^2 = 2\lvert bvert^4 + 2\lvert bvert^2\lvert\lambda_1 - \lambda_2vert^2 . \] Deduce that every \(\A \in M_2(
C)\) satisfies \(
orm{[\A, \A^{*}]}_F \ge \sqrt2\,\Delta(\A)^2\) , and determine exactly when equality holds. Hint for (c): Schur-triangularize, and use (a) to move the computation to the triangular factor.

title: Theorem 11.11.3 (Normality as a Trace Identity)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then \(\A\) is normal if and only if \[ \tr(\A^{*}\A) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert\lambda_i\rvert^2 . \]

title: Theorem 11.11.2 (Schur’s Inequality)
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(\nC)\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n\) , listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert \lambda_i \rvert^2 \;\le\; \norm{\A}_F^2 , \] with equality if and only if \(\A\) is normal .

title: Definition 12.1.1 (Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) . Then \(\A\) is positive semidefinite , written \(\A \succeq 0\) , if \(\A\) is Hermitian , that is \(\A^{*} = \A\) (over \(\nR\) : symmetric, \(\A\tp = \A\) ); and \(\inner{\A\x}{\x} \ge 0\) for every \(\x \in F^n\) . It is positive definite , written \(\A \succ 0\) , if (P1) holds and \(\inner{\A\x}{\x} > 0\) for every non-zero \(\x \in F^n\) . The same words apply to an operator \(T \in \cL(V)\) on a finite-dimensional inner product space: \(T\) is positive semidefinite if \(T^{*} = T\) and \(\inner{T\v}{\v} \ge 0\) for every \(\v \in V\) , and positive definite if the inequality is strict for \(\v \ne \0\) .

title: Example (A Covariance-style Matrix)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Three quantities are measured on four occasions, and each column of \[ \X = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \in M_{4\times 3}(\nR) \] has been adjusted to sum to \(0\) . Show that \(\A = \X\tp\X\) is positive definite, and check the verdict against Sylvester’s criterion.

title: Example (Five Positive Matrices)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Decide which of the following are positive semidefinite, and which are positive definite. \(\I_n\) , and more generally \(\D = \diag(d_1, \dots, d_n)\) with every \(d_i\) real. \(\x\x^{*}\) for a fixed \(\x \in F^n\) . The Gram matrix \(\G\) of a list \((\v_1, \dots, \v_k)\) in an inner product space. The zero matrix \(0 \in M_n(F)\) . \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Example (The 2 \times 2 Test)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ \conj{b} & d\end{pmatrix}\) be Hermitian, so \(a, d \in \nR\) and \(b \in F\) . State and justify the tests for \(\A \succ 0\) and for \(\A \succeq 0\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: State the definition of \(\A \succeq 0\) and of \(\A \succ 0\) , including every quantifier and the field. Explain why clause (P1) cannot be dropped from the real definition, with a concrete matrix. True or false: if \(\A\) is Hermitian and every leading principal minor of \(\A\) is \(\ge 0\) , then \(\A \succeq 0\) . Justify your answer. Write down the three conditions of the \(2 \times 2\) test for \(\A \succeq 0\) . Name the item of @thm-psd-characterizations that says every positive semidefinite matrix is a Gram matrix.

title: Exercise (B1: Determine the definiteness)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content:
For each matrix below, determine whether it is positive definite, positive semidefinite but not positive definite, or neither. Justify your answer. \( egin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . \( egin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . \( egin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \ -1 & 2 & -1 \ 0 & -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) over \(
R\) . The all-ones matrix \(\J \in M_3(
R)\) . \( egin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) over \(

C\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A parameter)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: For which \(t \in \nR\) is \[ \A(t) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & t & 0 \\ t & 2 & t \\ 0 & t & 3 \end{pmatrix} \] positive definite? Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B3: The inverse of a positive definite matrix)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with \(\A \succ 0\) . Prove that \(\A\) is invertible and that \(\A^{-1} \succ 0\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Zero trace forces zero)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with \(\A \succeq 0\) . Prove that \(a_{ii} \ge 0\) for every \(i\) , and that \(\tr \A \ge 0\) . Prove that if \(\tr \A = 0\) then \(\A = 0\) . Deduce that if \(\A \succeq 0\) and \(-\A \succeq 0\) , then \(\A = 0\) .

title: Exercise (C2: The cone of positive matrices)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\cP_n \subseteq M_n(F)\) be the set of positive semidefinite matrices. Prove that if \(\A, \B \in \cP_n\) and \(c \ge 0\) is real, then \(\A + \B \in \cP_n\) and \(c\A \in \cP_n\) . (A set with these two properties is a convex cone : it contains \((1-t)\A + t\B\) for \(0 \le t \le 1\) as well.) Prove that \(\cP_n\) contains no line through \(0\) : if \(\A \in \cP_n\) and \(-\A \in \cP_n\) then \(\A = 0\) . Prove that \(\cP_n\) is closed under congruence: if \(\A \in \cP_n\) and \(\S \in M_n(F)\) , then \(\S^{*}\A\S \in \cP_n\) . Give an example showing that \(\cP_n\) is not closed under multiplication. Hint for (c): for the example, two positive semidefinite matrices whose product is not even Hermitian will do.

title: Exercise (C3: The largest entry sits on the diagonal)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with \(\A \succeq 0\) . Prove that \(\lvert a_{ij}\rvert^2 \le a_{ii}a_{jj}\) for all \(i, j\) . Deduce that if \(a_{ii} = 0\) for some \(i\) , then the whole \(i\) -th row and \(i\) -th column of \(\A\) are zero. Deduce that \(\max_{i,j}\lvert a_{ij}\rvert = \max_i a_{ii}\) . Hint for (a): look at a \(2 \times 2\) principal submatrix.

title: Lemma 12.1.3 (Shifting by t\I, minor by minor)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) and \(t \in F\) . Then \[ \det(\A + t\I_n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} E_k(\A)\, t^{\,n-k}, \] where \(E_0(\A) = 1\) and, for \(1 \le k \le n\) , \(E_k(\A) = \sum_{\lvert I\rvert = k} \det \A_{I,I}\) is the sum of all \(k \times k\) principal minors of \(\A\) .

title: Proposition 12.1.1 (Over \nC, positivity implies Hermitian)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content:
Let \(\A \in M_n(
C)\) satisfy \(\inner{\A\x}{\x} \in 
R\) for every \(\x \in 
C^n\) — in particular, let \(\inner{\A\x}{\x} \ge 0\) for every \(\x\) . Then \(\A^{*} = \A\) .

title: Proposition 12.1.2 (Congruence preserves positivity)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) be Hermitian and \(\S \in M_{n \times m}(F)\) . Then \(\S^{*}\A\S \in M_m(F)\) is Hermitian, and: if \(\A \succeq 0\) , then \(\S^{*}\A\S \succeq 0\) ; if \(\A \succ 0\) and \(\nul(\S) = \{\0\}\) , then \(\S^{*}\A\S \succ 0\) . In particular, for \(m = n\) and \(\S\) invertible, \(\A \succ 0\) if and only if \(\S^{*}\A\S \succ 0\) .

title: Theorem 12.1.6 (Invertible Matrix Theorem, with Positive Definiteness)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with \(F = \nR\) or \(F = \nC\) . The following are equivalent, and each is equivalent to each of the conditions of @thm-invertible-tfae , @thm-invertible-tfae-det and @thm-invertible-tfae-eigen . \(\A\) is invertible. \(\A^{*}\A \succ 0\) . \(\A\A^{*} \succ 0\) . For a general \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) , one always has \(\A^{*}\A \succeq 0\) , with \(\A^{*}\A \succ 0\) if and only if the columns of \(\A\) are linearly independent.

title: Theorem 12.1.5 (Characterizations of Positive Definiteness, with Sylvester’s Criterion)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) be Hermitian, and for \(1 \le k \le n\) let \(\A_k\) be its leading principal submatrix, the top-left \(k \times k\) corner. The following are equivalent. \(\A \succ 0\) . Every eigenvalue of \(\A\) is a positive real number. \(\A = \B^{*}\B\) for some invertible \(\B \in M_n(F)\) . (Sylvester’s criterion) \(\det \A_k > 0\) for every \(k = 1, \dots, n\) .

title: Theorem 12.1.4 (Characterizations of Positive Semidefiniteness)
page: 12.1 Positive Semidefinite and Positive Definite Matrices
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) be Hermitian. The following are equivalent. \(\A \succeq 0\) . Every eigenvalue of \(\A\) is a non-negative real number. \(\A = \B^{*}\B\) for some \(\B \in M_n(F)\) . \(\A = \C^2\) for exactly one \(\C \in M_n(F)\) with \(\C \succeq 0\) . Every principal minor of \(\A\) is \(\ge 0\) .

title: Definition 12.2.1 (Absolute Value of a Matrix)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Let \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) . The absolute value of \(\A\) is \[ \lvert\A\rvert \coloneqq (\A^{*}\A)^{1/2} \in M_n(F) , \] the unique positive semidefinite square root of \(\A^{*}\A\) .

title: Example (Two Absolute Values)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Compute \(\lvert\A\rvert\) for \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) and for \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) , both over \(\nR\) .

title: Example (A Cholesky Factorization, and One That Fails)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Factor \[ \A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 & 6 \\ -2 & 5 & -1 \\ 6 & -1 & 26 \end{pmatrix} \] as \(\L\L\tp\) , and run the same algorithm on the matrix \(\A'\) obtained from \(\A\) by changing the \((3,3)\) entry to \(9\) .

title: Example (Two Square Roots)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Compute \(\A^{1/2}\) for \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 13 & 12 \\ 12 & 13\end{pmatrix}\) ; \(\B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) , in each case by the spectral resolution and by a polynomial.

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: State what \(\A^{1/2}\) is, including the two conditions that pin it down. Define \(\lvert\A\rvert\) for \(\A \in M_{m \times n}(F)\) and say what size it is. State the Cholesky factorization theorem. True or false: every Hermitian matrix has exactly one Hermitian square root. Justify your answer. Explain in one sentence why the Cholesky algorithm is a test for positive definiteness.

title: Exercise (B1: Square roots)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Compute \(\A^{1/2}\) for each of the following, and in each case give a polynomial \(p\) with \(p(\A) = \A^{1/2}\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{pmatrix}\) . \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & -6 \\ -6 & 10\end{pmatrix}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Cholesky, and a planted failure)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Find the Cholesky factor of \(\A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 14\end{pmatrix}\) , and hence write down \(\det \A\) . Run the same algorithm on \(\A' = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 9\end{pmatrix}\) and say what the outcome proves.

title: Exercise (B3: An absolute value)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content:
Let \(\A =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix} \in M_2(
R)\) . Compute \(\lvert\Avert\) , verify \(
orm{\lvert\Avert\x} = 
orm{\A\x}\) directly, and determine whether \(\lvert\Avert = \A\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The trace of a product of positive matrices)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Let \(\A, \B \in M_n(F)\) with \(\A \succeq 0\) and \(\B \succeq 0\) . Prove that \(\tr(\A\B) = \tr(\A^{1/2}\B\A^{1/2})\) , and deduce that \(\tr(\A\B) \ge 0\) . Prove that \(\tr(\A\B) = 0\) if and only if \(\A\B = 0\) . Hint for (b): a positive semidefinite matrix of trace \(0\) is \(0\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Commuting positive matrices)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Let \(\A \in M_n(F)\) with \(\A \succeq 0\) . Prove without using @thm-psd-square-root (a) that if \(\B\A = \A\B\) , then \(\B\A^{1/2} = \A^{1/2}\B\) . Hint: show that \(\B\) maps each eigenspace of \(\A\) into itself. Let \(\B \succeq 0\) with \(\A\B = \B\A\) . Prove that \(\A\B \succeq 0\) and that \((\A\B)^{1/2} = \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Why definiteness is needed)
page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content: Give a positive semidefinite \(\A \in M_2(\nR)\) , not positive definite, together with two different lower triangular \(\L\) satisfying \(\A = \L\L\tp\) . Which hypothesis of @thm-cholesky fails? Prove that if \(\A \succeq 0\) then \(\A + t\I \succ 0\) for every real \(t > 0\) , and hence that every positive semidefinite matrix is a limit of positive definite ones in the entrywise sense.

page: 12.2 Square Roots and the Cholesky Factorization
content:
